items.body: A single digit can at once summarise knowledge, pace, behaviour and the local strictness of the school. The same grade can therefore be awarded fairly and still not be compared automatically across classes. An anonymous test measures something other than a report card; an average can hide a specific gap; and the school’s strictness may not be visible from the digit when a pupil applies further. 1. A report card at which three meanings miss one another Imagine a parents’ evening in January. A parent sees a three in mathematics and reads mediocrity from it. The teacher sees the same three and knows that the pupil can handle the algorithm but falls on the word problem. The headteacher defends the comparability of the report card against neighbouring schools, because grades enter admission. The guidance counsellor reads behaviour, homework and whether the child brings a notebook. The pupil reads a label: either I can, or I cannot. The debate about the fairness of grades breaks into several different needs. The parent compares school success, the teacher looks for a gap in skill, the headteacher watches the consequences for the move to secondary school, the counsellor attendance and discipline, and the pupil easily turns the digit into a verdict on the self. The three can be relevant for each of them, but it is not enough by itself for choosing a field of study. Without a description of the task and the criteria it is not clear how much of the result is knowledge, pace, support at home, the strictness of the teaching staff or the composition of the class. A “good grade” is therefore not a stable property of the pupil, but a local sum of several measures. Before we start comparing strictness, we have to decide whether we are reading mastery of the material, work habits, behaviour or standing relative to the class. A test, a notebook and a report card may weight each of these things differently. A grade is not knowledge. Knowledge is not effort. Effort is not readiness for secondary school. And a report card is not an admission procedure. — Jiný Kontext What studies of grades say — and what does not follow from them We know: in the Czech data examined, grades are related to the local strictness of the school, to sex and to educational aspirations even after standardised test results are taken into account. [3] [5] [6] [22] We do not know: observational data alone do not split this relationship into the influence of the pupil’s behaviour, the teacher’s expectations, family support, the composition of the school and other unobserved factors. They cannot determine the cause of a particular child’s grade, nor support the claim that changing one digit will by itself change that child’s future path. 2. What all fits into one grade The digit on the report card is produced by a combination of the pupil’s performance, the tasks chosen, the teacher’s rules and the context of the class. Each component changes the information value of the result. Even two schools with the same framework curriculum may therefore not mark the same work in the same way. Five layers of one classification Knowledge and skill: what an anonymous task could still capture. Performance in time: writing pace, stage fright, homework, a forgotten aid. Socio-emotional layer: conscientiousness, sitting quietly, the impression of the family. Local norm: the strictness of the teaching staff and the composition of the class. Use of the number: an application, a self-image, a reward, a punishment. The Education Act requires that the assessment of a pupil be pedagogically justified and professionally sound. The decree on basic education leaves schools wide autonomy in the choice of numerical classification, verbal assessment and a combination of the two. That is an essential feature of the law. It is not automatic comparability of a one between two buildings. [1] [2] This is where the first error of most readings at home appears. The headline announces that the child “has a three”, but in reality it compares four different profiles. One understands the concept and bungles the arithmetic. The second commands the formula and does not know why it holds. The third writes excellently and loses points for the notebook. The fourth sits in a strict school, where the same work would elsewhere be marked a two. All four can leave with the field “3 — good”. Breaking the grade down shows where to look for a correction. A penalty for forgotten sports kit says nothing about equations; a one that fails at the entrance exam may reflect the local norm; and a difference between identically written tests may come from further assessment criteria. The sentence “has a three”, without these facts, does not say what the pupil should practise next. Illustrative diagram: The same digit can, in another regime of strictness, behaviour and use, produce a different path. 3. Useful assessment must make correction possible Teachers and parents usually look for a grade that ranks the class “fairly”. That is reasonable, but incomplete. Equally important is what the error looks like, whether the pupil recognises it, how much it costs to correct, and whether the verdict is reversible. A slip in a dictation is a cheap error if the comment arrives in time. A three on the report card in May, from which an application is filed in June, sometimes is not. Black and Wiliam, in the review Assessment and Classroom Learning (1998), showed that assessment which tells the pupil during learning where they stand and what to do next is associated with improved results; this is not one test in one school, but a synthesis of the empirical literature on formative use. Hattie and Timperley, in The Power of Feedback (2007), distinguish feedback on the task, on the process and on the person; feedback of the type “you are a pupil who gets ones” is a different object from “this is where the unit is lost”. These are peer-reviewed reviews, not proof that the Czech report card is pointless. They show what a number is enough for, and what it is not. [16] [17] Type of failure What it looks like How to test it What limits the harm Compression Four different gaps receive the same digit Ask which skill the grade is punishing A separate field for knowledge and for behaviour Local norm The same test, a different grade between schools Compare the grade with an anonymous test, not with a feeling A comment on the strictness of the teaching staff Non-cognitive admixture A notebook and silence improve the grade on the same test Anonymous work beside a named report card Assess behaviour separately Wrong use The digit becomes the choice of a field of study Whether the pupil can say what to correct Entrance exams and a second figure beside the grade An average makes sense only when the school can show what behind it can be corrected. When applying for a Maturita programme it is especially dangerous to mistake local strictness for inability. A report card does not predict a future professional error; it can, however, offer the reader a concrete trace for learning — or only a stamp. Beside the pupil’s performance it is necessary to watch whether the gap is visible, whether the assessment can be corrected, and what effect it has on the next path. A school with a smaller share of ones, but a clear description of skills mastered and not mastered, can give a family more useful information than a mild one without support. 4. A grade summarises performance, but does not explain it Grades are needed because they replace part of impression with a brief record. The problem begins when one field starts to stand for the whole of ability. In its publication on grades and educational expectations (Grade Expectations, 2012) the OECD notes that grades serve several functions at once — they inform, rank, motivate, punish — and that reading them as a single yardstick is therefore risky. This is an international synthesis on PISA data, not an audit of one Czech class. [18] Every report card contains hidden decisions. Who chose the tasks? Does homework count? Is late submission punished? Is a one for the few, or for most? Is the exact procedure assessed, or the result? The answer to any of these questions can change the order of pupils who would stand next to one another in an anonymous test. In a study by Münich and Protivínský (2022), the IDEA think-tank at CERGE-EI measured the strictness of grading on the Czech PISA 2018 sample: that is, among fifteen-year-old pupils, in mathematics, reading and science, on a representative school sample. They defined strictness as the relationship between the test score and the grades at a given school. In their model, the classification of pupils with comparable test results differed between schools by about one grade on average. This is one observational study on one PISA cycle, not proof of teacher dishonesty and not an experiment with the same written paper in two schools. It shows that a grade also contains a local marking bar. [5] [6] What must accompany the digit Subject, period (term, year) and whether it is coursework or the report card. What enters the average: papers, homework, activity, behaviour. Frame of reference: this class, this school, or an external test. Population: one pupil, or a comparison between schools. Known limits: anonymity, sex, socioeconomic status. An analysis of specific tasks helps a family more than someone else’s ranking of schools. A list of what the child can and cannot do offers a plan for correction; an average of 2.4 without that information does not. A public test can complete the comparison, but further learning has to start from the gap that was found. 5. Compare schools, not digits The market in grades can be described without a false podium of winners. The map below does not say which school is generally first. It shows the work around which each regime builds assessment, what kind of information it brings, and which failure the reader should look for on purpose. Regime Main working position What to check on the report card Typical reason for the choice Classification 1–5 Quick ranking and an administrative close What exactly entered the average Legibility for parents and secondary schools Verbal assessment A description of progress and the next step Whether the text says what to do, or only praises Diagnosis at a younger age Criteria table Met / partly / not, against a specific aim Whether the pupil sees the criteria in advance Comparability without a single digit Anonymous test A comparison of knowledge without a name and a notebook Whether the test measures the same material as the grade A check on local strictness Entrance examination An external filter for secondary school Whether the grade and the test speak of the same pupil A decision the report card alone cannot carry The table does not judge teachers as a group. Assessment can differ between year-groups and in the course of a year. Its purpose is to expose a digit that does not show a specific gap and, instead of helping with learning, turns into a label on the pupil. How to read the diagram: A one here is not a ranking of quality. The diagram joins performance, the rules of assessment and the purpose for which the grade is used. 6. Behaviour is not knowledge. It still enters the same field In the study What do the grades on the report card hide? (Münich, Protivínský, 2018), IDEA compared report-card grades with anonymously marked tests at the transition to secondary school. In mathematics, girls with comparable test results had, in the model used, a grade better by 0.6 of a classification step on average than boys. In Czech the authors did not find the same difference at comparable results. This is an observational comparison of non-anonymous classification and an anonymous test in one educational transition, not the same paper once with a name and once without, and not proof of a universal mechanism. [3] [4] [22] Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext As a possible explanation the authors discuss socio-emotional skills and other features of performance that an anonymous test does not capture but a teacher can see in class. The study itself does not determine how much of the difference is explained by conscientiousness, behaviour, teacher expectations or another factor. A school may also want to assess work habits; it should then say that it includes them in the grade. Otherwise the parent reads the three only as a message about equations. Federičová (2019), using data on applications to multi-year grammar schools, found that filing an application was strongly related to grades, especially to ones, more than to the expected result on the test, and that differences in applications by boys and girls persisted even at comparable chances of admission. This is an observational study of one type of transition; it does not by itself prove that the grade caused the decision. It does show that the grade enters the setting in which families make the choice. [7] 7. A strict school is not the same as a demanding school In conversation, strictness is confused with quality. It is not automatically the same thing. On PISA 2018, Münich and Protivínský (2022) divided schools by how strictly they grade relative to the test. In strictly grading schools, 7 percent of the fifteen-year-old pupils at those schools received grade 1 in mathematics; in mildly grading schools, 25 percent. The most common grades in strict schools were steps 3 and 4, which together were taken by about two thirds of the pupils. This is the distribution of grades inside these groups of schools, not the claim that 7 and 25 percent are the share of pupils with the same PISA score. A separate conclusion of the study says that at the same academic results the grade differs between schools by a step on average. The two sentences must be kept apart. [6] At comparable test results, pupils from strictly grading schools reported lower study ambitions than pupils from mildly grading schools. Of pupils with a one in mathematics, 87 percent wanted to complete a university degree; of pupils with a three, 39 percent. These are aspirations in the PISA 2018 questionnaire, not later actual diplomas. The result documents a link between grade, local strictness and aspirations; without further research it does not determine how large a part of the difference the grade itself caused. [5] [6] An illustration, not a report. Adam, at a strict village school, understands geometry, brings home a three from written tests, and the family reads an average. Tomáš, at a mild city school, collects ones for notebooks and, at the unified entrance exam, meets a task that the algorithm from the worksheet does not solve. The report card told both of them something. It need not have told either of them the same thing as what they can do. 8. The test and the grade capture different parts of performance In the sample examined, girls in the ninth year had better grades on average, while on anonymously marked entrance tests in mathematics they achieved lower results on average than boys. That is how the 2018 IDEA study opens its problem. It is not, however, the same work marked in two ways. The grade summarises a longer period in class; the entrance test captures performance on a different task and at a different moment. [3] [22] In the 2022 study, 20 percent of girls and 13 percent of boys have a one in mathematics. Again this is a description of classification, not of anonymous literacy. Anyone who turns these shares into the sentence “girls are better at mathematics” joins two layers. Anyone who turns the test into the sentence “grades are useless” erases information about work, attendance and support at home that the teacher sees and the test does not. [6] An honest reading therefore keeps two numbers side by side. It does not pick the one that better fits the wish. A pleasant average can hide the same old problem A good-looking 1.8 acts as a grade of understanding. It is not that automatically. When reading a report card it is necessary to check separately whether the average has not merged two different gaps into a smooth but non-existent picture of “it is going well”. The quality of the digit lowers the cost of talking to a secondary school. At the same time it can raise the cost of finding a substantive gap, because the result does not look suspicious. 9. PISA is not a report card. A report card is not PISA The Czech debate often reads grades as proof that “children cannot do mathematics”. The international survey measures a different object. In PISA 2022, where mathematics was the main domain, Czech fifteen-year-old pupils scored 487 points. The Czech School Inspectorate ranks them among countries with an above-average result; nine countries achieved a statistically significantly better result, twelve had a comparable result. In the country note on Czechia the OECD states that 74 percent of Czech pupils reached at least level 2 in mathematics, more than the OECD average of 69 percent. This is the literacy of fifteen-year-olds in one cycle, not grades on a report card and not the Maturita. The OECD average in PISA 2022 mathematics is 472 points in the summary publication; older cycles had a different average, so 487 should not be read against a number from another wave. [11] [12] [13] TIMSS 2023 measured pupils in year 8. Czech pupils scored 518 points in mathematics, above the average of all participating countries (478) and above the average of the thirteen EU member states in that survey (503). Czechia took part in the eighth-year survey in 1995, 1999, 2007 and 2023; against 1995 this was a fall, against 2007 an improvement. This is a different age, a different framework of tasks and a different year from PISA 2022. Neither survey says what grade a pupil has in geometry in March. [14] [15] The tension between decent literacy on a test and a feeling of failure at school is therefore not necessarily a dispute about “which number is true”. It is a dispute about what each number sees. PISA does not punish forgotten sports kit. A grade need not see a task with a graph from an unfamiliar situation. 10. What has to be checked behind the digit Before the report card the parent guesses. With the report card the parent checks something harder: whether the digit supports the sentence they want to make from it. A one is navigation toward an impression of success. It is not automatic proof that the pupil knows the same material as a pupil who gets ones a district away. Slow writing, an error in units and standing in a weaker class can all contribute to the same three, but they describe different parts of performance. The summary verdict “is average” therefore has no support without an analysis of the specific work. A four-step check of the grade Existence: the number is from this term and this subject. Components: which papers, which weighted average, which behaviour. Support: a specific gap really supports a specific sentence about ability. Scope: school, class and sex fit, and whether an external test exists. The most reliable working procedure therefore separates reading from deciding. First comes a table: what the pupil can do, what not, what is behaviour, what is the school’s norm. Only then the application. If the teacher cannot say which task the child should repeat, the claim is not raised to talent or inability merely because it is on paper. 11. A summative verdict is not a map of learning The difference is not whether the school “assesses”. It is when, and for what. A summative grade closes a period. It says where the pupil ended, at a moment when in that term they can often do nothing more about it. A formative description runs along the way. It says which step holds, which does not, and what to try. In Strategy 2030+ and in the methodological recommendation for years 1 and 2, the Ministry of Education separates the formative approach from mere verbal style: a text without a next step does not fulfil a formative function. [8] [9] From the 2027/2028 school year it will not be possible to assess year 1 on the report card with a grade; verbal assessment, including criterion-referenced assessment, will be allowed. From 2028/2029 the same for year 2. This is a change in the lowest years, not the abolition of classification in the ninth year, and not a promise that a new form will by itself improve learning. Schools may choose among classification, words and a combination earlier; the duty shifts gradually. [9] [10] The aim of the ministry text is not a resignation of standards. It is a reduction of outside pressure where a relationship to learning is only just being formed. That is a policy choice with empirical support in the literature on feedback. It is not proof that from the sixth year the digit is harmless. 12. The price of a one is the price of the raw material, not the price of the path A school uses several languages at once. The teacher pays with time spent writing in the class register. The parent pays with calm, or with anxiety. The system pays with the grade as a filter. The pupil pays with a self-image. A direct comparison “has a one”, without knowing what the one will be used for, therefore misleads. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext A cheap one at a mild school can be economically excellent for peace at home. The same one can be expensive at the entrance exam if it does not cover the material of the test. A strict three can be needlessly expensive if the family turns it into an apprenticeship track, even though an anonymous test says something else. It can, however, be cheaper if the pupil sees the gap from the comment and corrects it before the application is assembled. The real price of an accepted decision Grade + teacher’s time on a comment + practice at home + an external test + the price of a wrong application. A decision is cheap only when it passes a check and can still be changed. 13. What to read from a report card A reasonable reading does not start with the digit, but with the kind of use. The recommendations below are not a ranking of schools. They are a signpost to a first analysis. For each subject it makes sense to ask the same question twice: what the number measures, and what it may be used for. Need First figure Decisive test Unacceptable shortcut Find the gap A comment on one task The pupil can say what to try tomorrow Read only the average Compare with classmates The grade in this class Whether the class is strong or mild Take a three as a national percentile Compare schools PISA/TIMSS, entrance exams, IDEA The same population and the same year Mix 487 PISA points with a grade from a notebook Choice of secondary school Test + grades + aspirations Whether the school’s strictness has lowered the aim File an application on the strength of one three Behaviour A separate verbal field Whether the notebook did not enter mathematics Punish sports kit with an equation Younger years A criterion-referenced description Whether the text passes the formative test Replace the digit with empty praise Neither a foreign review of formative assessment nor the Czech PISA average will show whether a particular teacher counts aids, or what stands behind a three in algebraic fractions. The share of ones at a school also does not describe the cause of one pupil’s grade. [13] [6] The rules of the specific class therefore have to be checked. 14. Fourteen days that say more than a class average A short analysis of the report card can replace both panic and a wave of the hand. It is not meant to confirm the label “a pupil who gets ones”, but to find the specific skill hidden behind the digit and to check whether it can be corrected. Fourteen days from impression to decision Days 1–2: Write down the subjects in which the number surprised you, and the price of a possible wrong choice of field. Days 3–4: Ask for a breakdown: which papers, what weights, whether behaviour entered. Days 5–7: Give the pupil three tasks from the gap and keep a register: can / can with a hint / cannot. Days 8–10: Compare the grade with one external figure, if it exists: entrance exams, a comparative paper, another teacher’s comment. Days 11–12: Separate what is knowledge, what is pace, what is the notebook. Day 13: A stress test: a mid-range task, a task from a graph, a task without a formula. Day 14: Decide what the grade may be used for, and set a date for the next review. What needs to be tested The first test concerns the components of the average. The second concerns the local bar: is a one rare, or common? The third concerns sex and behaviour: would an anonymous hand receive the same digit for the same work? The fourth concerns use: is an application to be made from the number, or only a plan at home? How to test what a grade hides Put several familiar tasks into the week and watch whether the pupil fails where the grade punished, or elsewhere. Ask about the contradiction between notebook and paper. Require one sentence “what tomorrow”. Repeat the task in a different order. And do not assess only the correct result: record whether the pupil admitted not knowing, or masked the gap with an average. The pilot should also have exclusion conditions. For example: the teacher cannot say what the number measures; the grade will be used as the only criterion for an application; behaviour and knowledge cannot be separated. A high average must not override a gap whose impact the family cannot accept. 15. The entrance exam sees something other than the class register The unified entrance examination is another layer, not a correction of the report card. Cermat sets it as a unified test in mathematics and in Czech for applicants to Maturita programmes. Report-card grades may join it as a further criterion, according to the school’s setting. This is a different population from PISA 2018, a different age from TIMSS year 8, and a different purpose from a term average. [19] That is both an advantage and a warning. The family can at last see an anonymous task. At the same time it must not mistake a percentile from the entrance exam for proof that the teacher “measured nothing” all year. The entrance exam does not see homework or pace in the sixth year. The report card does not see a non-standard task that the workbook did not practise. Federičová (2019) found that filing an application to a multi-year grammar school was strongly related to grades, especially to ones, more than to the expected result on the test. The selection of applicants therefore begins before the pupil sits down to the unified paper. The study itself, however, does not allow us to say how many children did not apply because of the grade and how many for other reasons. [7] An honest comparison therefore keeps three objects apart: the school grade, the unified test and international literacy. They can be joined in one sentence about talent. That cannot be passed off as a measurement. The unified exam gives the parent a second point of control beside the teacher’s assessment. It makes it possible to compare whether school preparation worked with similar material and whether the grade agrees with a more anonymous performance. Even a percentile, however, is not a complete measure of talent and cannot be mistaken for a PISA result. 16. A formative stamp is not a formative approach From the 2027/2028 school year the ministry takes the report-card grade away from the first year, and from 2028/2029 from the second year as well. Schools may use verbal and criterion-referenced assessment earlier. The methodology warns expressly that a verbal text without a next step does not fulfil a formative function. A change of stamp is therefore not a change of teaching. [9] [10] That matters more than the dispute “for or against grades”. The family is not buying a form. It is buying whether the child will hear what to try tomorrow. A teacher who writes a paragraph of praise without a gap instead of a three has only translated compression into prose. A teacher who, with a classification, can say “this is where the unit is lost” already has the formative layer — the digit merely accompanies it. Strategy 2030+ emphasises a formative approach and at the same time admits that a summative close of a period will remain part of the system. This is a strategy document, not a promise that from the sixth year the average will disappear. The lowest years are the first test. They are not the whole reform of reading a report card. [8] A parent who in 2026 reads a three in the eighth year is not yet protected by this change. The decree’s autonomy of the school still applies, and it is still true that a one from a strict building and from a mild building are not the same object. The reform of years 1 and 2 is a laboratory field. It is not an automatic transfer into the ninth year, where a digit is turned into an application. 17. The result is decided by the use of the grade The first generation of school assessment needed to rank the class quickly. The next generation added an average and entrance exams. Today’s report card sells something larger: a place from which the family reads the future. Schools therefore do not compete only over who “teaches better”. They compete — often unintentionally — over whose digit will be readable outside the building. The more comfortable a single five-step scale is, the higher the price of leaving an error can be. Aspirations adjust. The application is not filed. The pupil stops distinguishing what they can do from the digit they hold. The brevity of classification is useful when a result is handed on, but it requires conscious reading. The family needs a supplementary figure on skill, behaviour kept separate, information about local strictness, and a later check on whether the original reading still holds. A useful grade is not automatically a one from a mild school or a three from a strict one. It must make it possible to find what the pupil has mastered and what should be corrected; its gaps should be visible, reversible and still usable for learning . The moment the digit only closes a notebook, we choose a shortcut. The moment an application, a self-image and an estimate of talent are made from it, we choose the structure of a path. And then the question is no longer: “What grade does the child have?” Before the next decision it is therefore necessary to find out: What exactly did this digit measure, what did it erase — and which decision may we still make from it? — Jiný Kontext

items.title: Mathematics maturita: What the difference between two years really measures
items.subtitle: When the failure rate on the mathematics maturita moves from 4.9% to 12.4%, the gap alone does not say whether pupils’ knowledge, the difficulty of the test, the mix of those who entered, or several of these at once has changed. In 2025 an expert commission judged the test harder than in the previous three years and widened the original scoring key for one item; the published papers still do not give an exact causal breakdown of the year-on-year jump.

items.body: A year-on-year change in the failure rate can come from the difficulty of the test, the mix of those who entered, the scoring key and the pass mark. A test can be marked correctly and still not be comparable with last year without a further method. A disputed item can move candidates who sit near the threshold, and a low failure rate by itself says nothing about a generation’s intelligence. 1. The May conference at which six readings miss one another Picture a May press conference. The minister reads the net failure rate and looks for whether this was an excess. The director of Cermat defends the catalogue of requirements and the common scheme. A grammar-school mathematics teacher sees items his class knows. A teacher on a vocational extension programme sees the same paper as a filter that cuts his pupils differently. A parent hears that “it was harder this year”. A candidate with 16 points hears that the next sitting is in the autumn. The quarrel about difficulty mixes several questions. The minister watches the public effect of the result, Cermat the tie to the catalogue and the construction of the test, schools the preparation and the composition of their groups, the parent the year-on-year gap, and the candidate a concrete point threshold. One percentage can matter for each of these views and still not prove the cause of the change. From the figure of 12.4 percent one cannot, without further analysis, infer that the year-group is less hard-working. The fairness of the exam depends at once on content, difficulty, key, threshold, the mix of those who entered, and the chance to repair a mistake. Before we look for a culprit, we have to say whether we are comparing cohorts, whole tests, single items, scoring keys or the pass mark. These quantities can move differently from year to year, and they cannot be folded into one verdict on the year-group. The test is not the year-group. The year-group is not the cohort. The cohort is not the scoring key. And the failure rate is not intelligence. — Jiný Kontext What is documented about the difference between the years We know: in 2025 the failure rate was higher than in 2024, the expert commission judged the paper harder, and for item 25 it widened the original key by one further correct variant. [1] [22] We do not know: the published papers do not split the whole year-on-year gap into the effect of item difficulty, the mix of those who entered, pupils’ preparation and other factors. One therefore cannot claim that the jump was caused only by the construction of the test, or only by a weaker cohort. 2. The result is made of six different decisions The published percentage of those who failed is the product of the pupils’ work and of the construction of the exam. The paper, the key, the threshold and the mix of those who entered all shape it. The same catalogue therefore does not, by itself, guarantee that two spring sittings measured the same difficulty. Six layers of one written test Catalogue of requirements: what the items may contain. The paper: the concrete items, their order, constructed-response and multiple-choice parts. Key and revision: which answer counts, which is accepted later. Pass mark: 33 percent, 17 points out of 50. Cohort: who chose mathematics, and from which type of school. Public reading: headlines about a generation, covid, or Cermat. Cermat’s catalogue sets the knowledge and skills that may be examined in the common part. The mathematics written test in the spring 2025 paper states a maximum of 50 points, a pass mark of 33 percent, 25 items and a time limit on the answer sheet. The first part is constructed-response items 1–14, the second multiple-choice items 15–25 with options, for which the instruction says exactly one answer is correct. That is a description of a particular booklet. It is not proof that each item had a single mathematically admissible solution. [3] [4] This is where the first error of most year-on-year comparisons is born. The headline announces a contest of year-groups, but in fact it compares two papers of different difficulty, a different key and a different share of grammar schools. Or, the other way round, it merely sets raw points against the same threshold and sells the result as a verdict on knowledge. An honest comparison has to state not only the percentage, but also the population of first-time candidates, the subject, the sitting, any revision of the key, and whether the same scale was used. A breakdown by test, key and group of those who entered helps the search for an explanation. A jump in the failure rate may go with the difficulty of the test, a change after revision with the scoring of an item, and the gap between grammar schools and vocational extension programmes with the composition of the populations. The summary sentence “the candidates failed” does not tell these possibilities apart. Illustrative scheme: The same catalogue can, in another paper, with another key and another cohort, produce another percentage. 3. An exam error must be detectable and correctable The state usually wants an exam with a clear threshold. That is reasonable, and incomplete. Just as important is what the error looks like, whether it can be seen, what it costs to repair, and whether the verdict can be reversed. A slip in a constructed-response item is expensive if the whole item falls with it. A pretended uniqueness in a multiple-choice item is more expensive if the key is repaired only after the press conference. Sixteen points cannot be given back in that sitting. The autumn resit is another day, not the same measurement. Decree No. 177/2009 Coll. defines the pass mark as the lowest result a pupil must reach in order to pass the written test. The result in the common part is verbal: passed or failed, with a percentage. That is a legal construction of a certificate, not a psychometric guarantee that 17 points this year are the same as 17 points last year. [5] Type of failure What it looks like How to test it What limits the harm Difficulty drift The same threshold, a different bar of items Anchor items, IRT, an independent year-to-year audit Do not change the cut-off and the paper together without saying so A faulty key The item has more solutions, the key has one Review before the results are published A revision that does not change the rules in silence A binary threshold 16 points fall, 17 pass The share of pupils in the band ±2 points A resit, a reasoned change of the threshold A different cohort A different share of grammar schools and vocational extension programmes Compare school types separately Do not read one percentage as one population In the reading it matters whether the system can find its own error and repair it. A subjective sense of difficulty is not the same thing as a change of key on an item that decides the result. And a pool of grammar schools and vocational extension programmes should not be sold as a homogeneous picture of “mathematics in the Czech Republic” without a split by school type. The content of the test is therefore only one axis. The second is the observability of the key, the third the reversibility of the points, and the fourth the effect on further study. A test with a slightly weaker average item, but a published link to last year’s difficulty, can be safer for trust than a showy paper without that support. 4. The failure rate alone does not describe a year-group’s ability The percentage of those who failed is needed, because it replaces part of the impressions. The problem starts when one number begins to stand for a whole generation. For the spring sitting of 2025 the ministry of education said that the net failure rate on the written tests was 12.3 percent, and that this matches the level of 2021 and 2022. In mathematics more than 19 percent of pupils chose the second compulsory exam, 14.9 thousand candidates sat the test, and the net failure rate of first-time candidates was 12.4 percent, which the ministry compared with 2023. In grammar schools 3.7 percent of pupils failed in mathematics, in secondary vocational schools almost a third, in vocational extension programmes 47 percent. That is the spring sitting of 2025 and the net failure rate of first-time candidates in that subject, not the autumn resits and not PISA. [1] A year earlier, in spring 2024, the failure rate of first-time candidates in mathematics was 4.9 percent. The year-on-year jump to 12.4 percent is a jump in the share who failed on the same kind of institutional exam, not a measurement that the “average ability” of the cohort changed by the same multiple. The minister of education said of 2025 that the mathematics written test was harder than last year’s, or rather that last year’s was easier than it should have been. The independent expert commission of the ministry said that, on the analyses supplied, the 2025 test looks harder than in the previous three years, especially against 2024, and at the same time asked for more credible statistical analyses for a year-on-year comparison. That is a judgement on one sitting, not a published linking of five years onto one psychometric scale. [1] [7] [22] What has to stand beside the percentage The sitting: spring, autumn; first-time candidates, or everyone. Subject and choice: mathematics versus English. School type: grammar school, secondary technical school, secondary vocational school, vocational extension. Whether a revision of the key has already taken place. What the number does not measure: an anchored difficulty against last year. The national percentage is the start of a reading, not its proof. Item statistics, a split by school type and a description of how the test was built can explain more than a quarrel over whether 12.4 percent is “within the norm”. 5. Compare the construction, not the generations The market of readings can be mapped without a false podium of winners. The map below does not say which year-group is worse in general. It shows what work each layer builds the result around, what kind of error it brings, and what the reader should look for on purpose. Layer Main working position What to check Typical false conclusion Catalogue The lawful content of the items Whether the item is in the catalogue “This must not be asked” without support Paper The concrete difficulty of the year Item statistics, not an impression “The generation can do less” Key What counts as correct Whether the item has one solution “The pupil cannot do mathematics” Cut-off 17 out of 50 The share in the band around the threshold “He passed, so he can do it” Cohort Who chose the subject School type separately One percentage for the whole country PISA/TIMSS A different population, a different construct Age, year, framework of items “The maturita refutes PISA” The table does not judge Cermat as an institution. Each year uses a different booklet, and the result depends on the concrete construction and on the review. The point is to stop a percentage without a key and without a description of the cohort from locking a whole year-group into a label. How to read the scheme: The height of the failure-rate column is not a measure of intelligence. It has to be read with the test, the key, the threshold and the mix of those who entered. 6. A raw point is not an anchored point In the published marking, the Czech state maturita adds points for items and compares them with a fixed percentage threshold. That is classical test theory in an operational sense: raw score, cut-off, passed/failed. The international PISA survey, by contrast, maps performances onto a scale with item-response models and links cycles with anchor items; the PISA 2022 technical report describes this as a condition of comparison across years and countries. The purpose is different — monitoring of systems, not a certificate for one person — and so is the method. It does not follow that the maturita “has no value”. It follows that 17 points in 2024 and 17 points in 2025 are not, without further work, the same point on the same scale. [10] [11] [6] Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext Embretson and Reise, in their IRT textbook, show why a raw sum is not enough when item difficulty changes: the same number of correct answers can mean a different ability. Brennan’s Educational Measurement places standardisation and linking among the conditions of a fair comparison of forms. These are methodological books, not an audit of Cermat. They explain what a year-on-year comparison would need, and why a mere failure rate will not replace it. [13] [14] The public materials on the mathematics written tests that a reader can ordinarily reach show the booklet, the key and the summary or item results. They do not show the ordinary reader an anchor set that would join the years 2021–2025 on one IRT scale. A missing publication is not proof that no internal calibration exists. It is a reason not to read the jump from 4.9 to 12.4 as a jump in ability. That is a reasonable reading, and incomplete if we stop there. Cermat also publishes aggregated item results, including the share of omitted answers; the expert commission nevertheless asked for more credible statistical analyses for a year-on-year comparison of difficulty. A request for further analysis is not proof that no calibration exists inside the office. It means that the papers laid before the commission were not enough for a convincing year-on-year conclusion. [7] [22] For a certificate of one person, IRT is not the only path. One can keep the same cut-off and change the paper, if it is said openly that the bar sat somewhere else this year. One can keep the paper and move the cut-off, as in 2021. One cannot do both in silence and still claim that the percentage measures the pupil. 7. The threshold of 17 out of 50 is not a small detail The mathematics written test has a maximum of 50 points. The threshold of 33 percent corresponds to 17 points; Cermat states the same construction for the optional extended mathematics paper as well. A candidate with 16 points failed. A candidate with 17 passed. The binary break is a property of the certificate. It is not a property of mathematics as a field. [4] [18] In the band of 15–18 points, what decides is not “a systemic grasp of the secondary-school syllabus” as a whole. What decides is whether one item fell on a numerical slip, whether item 25 carried four points, whether the key accepts two paths. The ministry press release on spring 2025 does not give, as a separate figure, how many first-time candidates sit in this band in a given year. The missing figure is not a trifle. It is precisely the band in which the construction of the exam most changes a life. 8. The key is repaired. The pupil’s ability is not In the spring sitting of 2025 the independent expert commission found that, for both parts of item 25, variant A had to be accepted as well, beyond the original key. The marking was then adjusted so that the original incompleteness of the key would not put pupils at a disadvantage; the ministry and contemporary news sources describe how the points were compensated. [1] [8] [9] [22] That is a later repair of one item in one sitting. It shows that the original key for this item was not complete; it does not show intent, nor a general defect of the whole test. The booklet, for multiple-choice items 15–25, says that exactly one answer is correct. When an item fails that condition, the layer of the key has failed, not necessarily the pupil. Repairing the key can save the pupil. It does not change, after the fact, what he could do on Friday morning. It changes what the state writes down about that ability. This repair is a known procedure in testing: a disputed item is dropped, or more paths are accepted, so that no one is harmed. The problem is not that the procedure exists. It is the time and the place of the check. If the public first hears that 12.4 percent is within the norm, and only then that one item did not have a single solution, it reads the percentage before it knows the key. The order of the layers is turned around. That does not mean every hard item is faulty. A hard item with a unique solution is a legitimate filter. An item that promises one answer in the booklet and has several in the mathematics is a different object. An honest audit will keep them apart. A headline about a generation will not join them. What needs to be tested The first test concerns the uniqueness of the wording before print. The second concerns items with an anomalously low success rate: is that difficulty, or a faulty key? The third concerns whether the revision came before, or after, the public reading of the number. A test that answers a day earlier need not be better if, a week later, no one can say which key was in force. 9. Choosing mathematics is not the same as difficulty Mathematics in the common part is not compulsory for everyone. The pupil chooses between it and a foreign language. In 2025, according to the ministry, more than 19 percent chose it, interest rising for a third year; English was taken by the majority, just under 80 percent of first-time candidates, with a failure rate of 3.5 percent. Czech, compulsory for all, had a failure rate of 9 percent against 2.8 percent a year earlier. That is spring 2025 and first-time candidates. Another subject is another population. [1] [7] So 12.4 percent in mathematics cannot be added to 9 percent in Czech as “the level of the candidates”. Those who choose mathematics are not a random sample of the year-group. A grammar school with 3.7 percent failing and a vocational extension programme with 47 percent on the same test show that the paper cuts different schools differently. That may be the intent of the certificate. It must not be read as a single curve of ability. 10. PISA is not the maturita. The maturita is not PISA PISA 2022 measured the mathematical literacy of fifteen-year-olds: 487 points in the Czech Republic, 74 percent above level 2 against 69 percent in the OECD. TIMSS 2023 measured eighth grades: 518 points against 478 internationally and 503 for the thirteen EU countries in the survey. The 2025 maturita measured a voluntarily chosen written test among 14.9 thousand candidates. These are three populations, three construct frameworks, three purposes. [11] [12] [15] PISA asks whether the pupil can read a situation and use mathematics. The maturita catalogue and the booklets often rest on school procedure: rearranging expressions, equations, trigonometry, a multiple-choice option. A tension between a decent literacy of fifteen-year-olds and a swinging failure rate among maturita candidates therefore need not mean that “the international test is lying”. It can mean that the national certificate measures something else, and on top of that moves the bar between years. Anyone who turns 487 points into the sentence that the maturita is pointless erases the purpose of the certificate. Anyone who turns 12.4 percent into the sentence that Czechs cannot do mathematics erases PISA, TIMSS and the grammar school with 3.7 percent. The difference of constructs can be stated without a ranking. PISA does not punish a pupil for choosing mathematics or English. The maturita does: the subject is a choice, and the cohort is filtered by it. PISA does not promise that 487 points is a ticket to a faculty. The maturita promises passed or failed. When both numbers are stood in one sentence, the impression of a quarrel about the truth appears. In fact it is a quarrel about which instrument may serve which purpose. 11. What must be traceable in the booklet and the key Before the revision the public guesses whether the item was hard. After the revision it checks whether the source — booklet, key, press release — speaks of the same rule. A citation of the catalogue is a navigation to the content. It is not proof that item 25 had one solution. Alignment of the items with the catalogue, a likeness of the failure rate to 2023, and a change of key on one item can all hold at once. That does not mean that “nothing happened”: each claim judges a different property of the exam, and the effect of the revision on pupils at the threshold has to be judged on its own. A four-step check of the maturita number Existence: the figure is from the spring sitting, first-time candidates, the given subject. Key: the original one was in force, or the revised one. Support: the percentage really carries a sentence about knowledge, or about the paper. Scope: grammar school, vocational extension, or the whole. The most reliable procedure keeps the publication of the booklet, the item statistics and the reading about a generation apart. If the key cannot be traced, a claim about the “correct solution” is not promoted into a mathematical constant. 12. The price of a point is the price of the raw material, not the price of the certificate Cermat, the school and the family use several price languages. The point is the raw material. The certificate is the result. The autumn sitting is a repair exchange. A year of waiting for university is something else. A direct comparison of “more failed this year” without the price of that wait misleads. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext A cheap test with a 4.9 percent failure rate can be expensive if the bar fell below the catalogue and the certificate lost its signal. An expensive test with 12.4 percent can be cheaper if it better separates those who know the material — and more expensive if it mainly separates those who had bad luck on an item with a faulty key. The real price of an accepted result Paper + key + cut-off + resit + deferred study + trust in the certificate. A result is cheap only when it can be defended by the same rule as last year, or when it is said openly that the rule is not the same. 13. What to read from the spring results A reasonable reading does not start with the headline, but with the kind of question. The recommendations below are not a ranking of year-groups. They are a signpost to the first analysis. Need First figure The decisive test An unacceptable shortcut Compare the years Failure rate of first-time candidates Whether a linking of difficulty exists “The generation can do half as much” Compare schools Grammar school 3.7%; vocational extension 47% The same test, a different cohort One number for the whole country Judge an item Booklet and key One solution, or more Read a multiple-choice option as the mathematics itself Judge the threshold 17 out of 50 The band around the cut-off 16 points as proof of illiteracy Bring in PISA 487 points, 15-year-olds, 2022 A different population Refute the maturita with PISA, and the reverse Read 2024 4.9% Whether the test was easier than it should have been Take 4.9% as a new standard of ability The Czech booklet has to be judged directly. A general IRT textbook will not score the wording of item 25, a summary of all the written tests will not describe the mathematics, and the result of the grammar schools cannot be sold as the result of the vocational extension programmes. [1] [13] 14. A week that says more than the year-on-year headline The reading can be done without denying the difficulty and without a hunt for the year-group. A short audit is enough. The aim is not to prove that Cermat failed. The aim is to find the layer in which the number was made. Seven days from headline to reading Day 1: Separate the subject, the sitting, the first-time candidates. Day 2: Add the school type and the share who chose mathematics. Day 3: Open the booklet and the key, not only the percentage. Day 4: Find out whether an item was revised. Day 5: Compare with last year only where the definition is the same. Day 6: Set PISA and TIMSS aside as another object, or describe them with age and year. Day 7: Write what the number measures, and what it expressly does not. Three tests of one item The first is the wording: does the text allow more than one path? The second is the key: does it match the sentence “exactly one answer”? The third is the effect: did the revision change only the points, or also the public story about the year-group? Before a conclusion about the generation A petition, teachers’ impressions and a judgement of higher difficulty can all hold at the same time as the fact that 12.4 percent is not outside the range of all previous years. The conclusion “the pupils are worse” does not follow from that concurrence. One can say that the paper was harder against 2024, and that the original key of item 25 did not contain every correct variant. From the revision it does not follow that no key existed before the exam, or that the whole test was prepared carelessly. [22] The check should end with a rule of reading: what the percentage may be used for, which revision of the key will be published, and when the comparison of years will be repeated. Because the booklets change, every year-on-year conclusion has to state the date and the method of comparability. 15. A grammar-school 3.7 percent is not a vocational-extension 47 percent For spring 2025 the ministry split the school types: grammar schools 3.7 percent failing in mathematics, secondary vocational schools almost a third, vocational extension programmes 47 percent. The same paper, the same maximum of 50 points, the same cut-off of 17 points. A different school. That is the net failure rate in one sitting, not proof that the vocational extension programme “cannot teach” and the grammar school “can do everything”. It shows that one national 12.4 percent is a mix of cohorts, not one curve. [1] Anyone who turns the average into a sentence about all the candidates does what grades do: compresses four schools into one digit. The political impression of “excess, or the norm” is then run on a mixture. An audit should start with a table by type. Only then ask about the paper. English with 3.5 percent failing among most of the year-group is another different object. Czech at 9 percent against last year’s 2.8 percent shows that the jump need not sit only in mathematics. That too is not proof about intelligence. It is a reason not to read one subject as the whole maturita. [7] 16. The year 2021 showed that the threshold is a lever In 2021 the ministry lowered the mathematics pass mark after the fact from 33 to 27 percent. The reason given pointed to distance teaching. At the original threshold, according to the official calculation of the time, the failure rate would have reached 24.9 percent. Out of 50 points, 14 were enough. That is one extraordinary intervention, not a new standard of the catalogue. [17] Something more precise is said here than “covid spoiled mathematics”. The cut-off is a political lever and a psychometric one. It can put out the share who fail without a single item being changed. It can also — if it stays still while the paper grows heavier — manufacture a year-on-year jump that looks like a worsening of the pupils. Spring 2025 did not, according to the minister, reach for this lever. The revision went through the key of item 25. Those are two different tools. Both change the record about the pupil. Neither changes, after the fact, what he could do on Friday. The public has a right to know which tool was used. Otherwise it reads 12.4 percent as the character of the year-group. An illustration, not a report. A candidate who in spring 2024 — a year with a failure rate of 4.9 percent — scores 18 points leaves with the certificate. A candidate a year later does comparable work, scores 16 points and waits for the autumn. The difference need not be in intelligence. It can be in the paper, in the key, and on which side of the threshold he landed. This pair must not be sold as two concrete scripts. It can be used as a question about the band that the state does not measure in the same headline as 12.4 percent. 17. Trust rests on a traceable key and on comparability The first generation of the state maturita promised comparability against a school exam. The next generation added a written test and a fixed threshold. Today’s result sells something larger: a place from which the state, universities and families read who “can do mathematics”. So the contest is not only over the items. It is over trust in the key, in the cut-off and in the year-on-year story. The more comfortable a single percentage is, the higher the price can be when it turns out that an item had two solutions, or that last year’s test was easier than it should have been. The common exam supplies a comparison that a school grade alone does not. For that comparison to be readable, the state needs a timely review of items, a published method of comparability, statistics split by school type, and a regular check of what the 17-point threshold means. The quality of the maturita is not set by the lowest failure rate, nor by the highest. What decides is whether a disputed item can be traced, its effect repaired, and a test error stopped from being read as the character of a generation. At the moment when the test only closes secondary school, we are choosing a certificate. At the moment when we build a sentence about intelligence from 4.9 and 12.4 percent, we are choosing a reading of society. And then the question is no longer: “Can this year’s candidates do mathematics?” When the result is read, what therefore decides is: Which part did we measure this year — the paper, the key, the threshold, or the pupil’s performance — and which error can we still repair? — Jiný Kontext

items.title: Enforcement cases are down. Debtors, not as much. What actually changed?
items.subtitle: A drop of hundreds of thousands in enforcement cases looks like improvement. Data from the Chamber of Court Executors show that what is leaving the register are mainly unsuccessful proceedings. The number of people on the books is falling much more slowly.
