items.body: A reimbursed application, an installed device and a saved megawatt-hour are three different results. Exhausted allocation can accompany smaller-than-planned savings, a project energy label need not match how the building is run, and an electric vehicle with no tailpipe emissions still carries emissions from electricity generation and from manufacturing the vehicle. Evaluation must therefore also count additionality, rebound and how impact is verified. 1. An allocation in which the application and the kilowatt-hour miss each other Imagine a meeting on “green” subsidies. The director of the State Environmental Fund holds up a conference figure: by its fifteenth anniversary the New Green Savings programme had approved 412 thousand applications worth more than 91 billion koruna. [1] The environment minister adds the boiler-replacement programmes: 130 thousand households applied, replacement in 115 thousand of them cost more than 13 billion. [2] The industry deputy shows guarantees from the National Recovery Plan: the National Development Bank supported the purchase of 6 325 electric vehicles and 2 759 charging stations, guarantees amounting to 2.5 billion koruna. [3] The auditor from the NKÚ puts conclusion 20/19 on the table: for apartment buildings, by 31 December 2020 IROP had reached savings of 1.3 PJ against a plan of 3.1 PJ (41 per cent), NZÚ 0.4 PJ against a plan of 2.8 PJ (13.5 per cent). [5] The economist asks how much of that would have happened even without the subsidy. The technician asks whether, after insulation, the heating is set to 20 or to 23 degrees. Behind the word “work” in the subsidy debate lie different ledgers. The fund tracks money and units, the ministry the replacement of equipment, the bank contracts, the NKÚ fulfilment of the plan as of the audit date, the economist additionality and the technician the actual operation of the building. Exhausted allocation may be a correct figure for take-up, but it does not answer the question of energy or climate impact. That requires knowing the number and operation of devices, consumption, additionality, the emission factor and the gap between the actual building and the project. The dispute should therefore not begin with whether to insulate, but with the choice of success indicator. An invoice, a project calculation, a meter and a tonne of CO2 describe different phases of a programme and cannot be swapped without a methodological conversion. A reimbursed application is not a saved megawatt-hour. A unit in the register is not a tonne that did not leave through the chimney. — Jiný Kontext What we know about subsidy impact — and what we do not yet We know: Public sources document the volume of support, the number of approved projects and, in audit 20/19, also fulfilment of the then savings plan for a specific segment of apartment buildings. [1] [3] [5] It can be assumed: technically correctly executed insulation or replacement of a heat source can reduce consumption or emissions, but the size of the benefit depends on the starting condition and on operation. From the cited materials we do not know: a uniform, measured net climate effect of all programmes after deducting weather, changes in behaviour and measures that recipients would have carried out even without support. 2. From the koruna to a real saving The figure “91 billion for savings” denotes the scale of support, not automatically the amount of energy saved. Between payment and net climate effect lie the installed device, the projected impact, actual operation and a comparison with the scenario without the subsidy. A programme can therefore look different according to which phase we are measuring. Five layers of one subsidy success Input: allocation and reimbursed koruna. Output: the number of façades, boilers, panels, vehicles. Projected impact: the saving from the PENB and from standard tables. Measured impact: electricity, gas and heat readings before and after, under the same pattern of use. Net climate effect: additionality, rebound, fuel, the grid emission factor, the life cycle. The fund records the flow of money, the energy specialist the project calculation, the occupant influences operation and the power system the emission factor of a kilowatt-hour. The auditor then compares the plan with the result as of a given date. The claim “the subsidy saved energy” therefore needs to state whether it is a model, a meter reading, or a net effect against the scenario without support. The division into layers determines where to turn when there is a discrepancy. If the allocation is exhausted and the reported saving lags the plan, the cause may be the setting of the target, the pace of delivery, the mix of projects, the calculation method or actual operation. The gap between the project label and consumption may arise from weather, the condition of the building, quality of workmanship or user behaviour. Without suitable operational data it is not possible to decide among these explanations. Illustrative scheme: The chain between the climate and a press release runs through the koruna, the unit, the label, the meter reading and the net effect. A break in any link changes the meaning of success without changing the payment. 3. A programme must be able to detect its own error Administrators usually look for the programme with the highest number of applications. That is reasonable, but incomplete. Equally important is what an error looks like, whether it can be recognised, how much overlooking it costs and whether the result is reversible. A badly filled-in form is a cheap error. A badly counted tonne in a national plan is expensive. An unused boiler can be replaced. Ten years of reporting without a meter reading sometimes cannot. In inspection 20/19 the NKÚ did not say that insulation makes no sense. It said that by 31 December 2020 the programmes for apartment buildings had paid out roughly a third of the earmarked money and that reported savings had not reached the original plan. [5] [6] This is an audit of one period, two programmes and the apartment-building segment, not proof that every koruna of NZÚ for family houses is lost. Type of failure What it looks like How to test it What limits the harm Input failure Success = exhausted allocation Separate koruna from GJ Mandatory meter reading Output failure Success = number of units Fuel, mileage, temperature Check of operation Model failure PENB ≠ consumption Before/after on the same building Measured conditional payment Additionality failure Paying for what would have happened even without support Comparison with the unsupported Targeting those who would not build without the subsidy When choosing a programme it is not enough to compare the volume of money distributed. What matters is whether evaluation captures deviation from the plan and the deadweight of support. For a programme worth tens of billions, the number of approved applications must not remain the sole indicator of success. The technical effectiveness of a measure is only part of the assessment. The programme must also make it possible to measure impact or to model it transparently, to estimate additionality and to convert energy into emissions. A smaller programme with a better evaluation may provide a more reliable figure than rapid take-up without these supports. 4. A projected result is not a consumption reading Energy performance certificates are needed because they provide a standardised calculation of the building. In subsidy administration, supported measures work with project documentation, expert assessments and an energy evaluation according to the programme rules; this is not necessarily a reading of actual consumption before and after the intervention. [12] [15] The calculation therefore cannot by itself be passed off as the consumption of a particular household. Actual operation is affected among other things by weather, the set temperature, ventilation and the number of users. Every calculation contains hidden decisions. What temperature? What ventilation? What thermal bridges? What user profiles? The answer to any of these questions can change the promised saving. In 2020 the European Court of Auditors, on the energy efficiency of buildings, warned that a stronger emphasis on cost-effectiveness is still needed — that is, on what a koruna actually buys, not only on what a project promises. [13] This is a Union audit of cost-effectiveness, not of Czech PENB in particular; the direction of the reservation is the same. What must be stated for reported petajoules Whether it is a plan, a calculation, or a meter reading. The population: apartment buildings, family houses, public buildings. The period and the date to which the saving is related. The specific subsidy in Kč/GJ and what is in it. Whether after the intervention the temperature, the heated area, or the number of occupants changed. For the running of a programme a smaller set of houses with readings before and after, weather normalisation and a description of use can be useful. Such a pilot can reveal an error of method, but thirty purposively selected buildings are not a representative estimate of the whole programme. The project calculation and operational measurement should complement each other; each answers a different question. 5. Compare evaluations, not press releases The market in subsidy titles can be described without a false ranking of winners. The following map does not say which programme is generally first. It shows what kind of work the individual layers assess and which failure the reader should look for during the debate. Programme / layer Main working position What to verify Typical reason for choice in the report NZÚ Insulation, PV, heat sources Whether the saving is PENB, or measurement Volume of applications and billions [1] Boiler-replacement programmes Replacement of class 1 and 2 boilers Fuel after the sustainability period Number of units [2] Electromobility Guarantee Company BEVs and charging Mileage and the grid mix Number of vehicles and guarantees [3] IROP apartment buildings Renovation outside Prague Fulfilment of the PJ plan Union allocation [5] NKÚ / ECA / OECD System audit Date, sample, definition of the saving An independent cut through the report The table does not judge technologies as such. The same device can have a different impact according to operation and fuel. Its purpose is to show whether, besides purchasing the device, the programme also tracks its use and can later verify the result. How to read the scheme: Input, output and impact are separate ledgers. The take-up of money cannot by itself be converted into saved energy or emissions. 6. New Green Savings: what the NKÚ actually calculated Audit conclusion 20/19 covers measures to reduce the energy intensity of apartment buildings from IROP and from NZÚ in 2015 to 2020. By 31 December 2020 IROP reported 1.27 PJ, rounded in public communication to 1.3 PJ, that is 41.0 per cent of the original plan of 3.1 PJ. NZÚ in the Apartment Buildings sub-programme 0.4 PJ, 13.5 per cent of the plan of 2.8 PJ. Roughly 3.4 billion was paid out from IROP and 0.5 billion from the NZÚ apartment-building sub-programme, about a third of the then allocation for these calls. [5] [6] Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext That is more important than a dispute over whether 14 per cent is “too little”. The figure measures fulfilment of the original savings plan as of a date, not the physical impossibility of insulation. The NKÚ also states that funds in NZÚ were provided efficiently in terms of the specific subsidy; in its response the Ministry of the Environment pointed to a delayed start, competition with IROP and to the fact that the forecasts were based on the older Green Savings programme. [6] This is a dispute about the ambition of the plan and about take-up, not proof that every house lies on its label. The conference statistic of 412 thousand applications and more than 91 billion describes a different object: the entire history of NZÚ including family houses, as of the fifteenth-anniversary date. [1] Subsequent summaries speak of higher cumulatives. That is not necessarily a contradiction. It is a different date and a different perimeter of the programme. Anyone who adds boilers and vehicle guarantees here gets “over 110 billion” as a sum of families of policies, not as a single audited flow. The original savings plan for apartment buildings is therefore not the same as later overall take-up of NZÚ. Mixing them is the same error as mixing the PENB and the meter. 7. A boiler in the protocol is not fuel in the firebox The programme for replacing old boilers documented replacements of devices whose aim was to reduce emissions from local heating. As of August 2024 the Ministry of the Environment reported 130 thousand applications and more than 13 billion koruna for 115 thousand completed replacements. The estimate of remaining class 1 and 2 boilers was up to 150 thousand; the ministry at the same time said it did not have precise data. [2] The ban on operating these boilers has applied from 1 September 2024. The number of replacements documents the programme’s output, not by itself the size of the change in local emissions. The cited public summaries report the number of replacements, but they do not provide a nationwide long-term series on the fuel and the mode of operation of each supported boiler. From these sources it is therefore not possible to confirm how the devices are used after five years. The ČHMÚ states that households account for more than 95 per cent of nationwide emissions of benzo[a]pyrene; this inventory share, however, does not determine the state of a particular firebox. [18] Replacement of a device and its subsequent operation are two different inspection questions. The unreplaced remainder in the same valley can outweigh the benefit of the neighbours who did replace. That is not an argument against boiler-replacement programmes. It is an argument against a report that ends with the delivery note. The 2021 census gives the structure of household heating; it does not say what is burning in a particular firebox on a Tuesday evening. [7] 8. Electric mobility: a zero tailpipe is not a zero grid The Electromobility Guarantee programme from the NPO supported 6 325 vehicles and 2 759 charging stations. Guarantees reached 2.5 billion koruna. The original target was 4 055 vehicles and 1 500 stations. Intake of applications stopped after the allocation was exhausted. [3] [4] That documents the number of supported outputs and the financial instrument; the climate effect still requires data on the replaced vehicle, mileage and electricity. Life-cycle analysis adds a part that the tailpipe does not show. A ČVUT paper reports for Czech electricity generation in 2024 approximately 340 g CO2eq/kWh against 432 g in 2019. [8] [9] This average is not the same as the residual supply mix reported by OTE, nor the time profile of a particular charging session. [21] In the life cycle of electric vehicles the EEA distinguishes emissions from vehicle operation, electricity generation and battery manufacture; zero tailpipe emissions therefore do not mean zero emissions of the whole cycle. [10] What needs to be tested The first test concerns mileage. A ČVUT scenario analysis compares the Hyundai Kona in several powertrains and shows that the point at which the higher manufacturing emissions of a battery vehicle are offset by the operating saving changes markedly with battery size, the electricity emission factor and the compared powertrain. [9] This is not a universal Czech kilometre figure, nor a result of the Electromobility Guarantee programme; evaluating it would require data on the vehicles actually replaced and on mileage. The second test concerns use. A company car with high mileage and night-time charging is a different object from a household’s second car with fifteen thousand kilometres a year. The third concerns the guarantee: 2.5 billion are guarantees, not the same as a grant paid out on a vehicle. Anyone who adds them to the 91 billion of NZÚ into one “success package” is adding different instruments. If the programme supports a vehicle that hardly drives, its contribution to decarbonisation over its lifetime is questionable. That does not mean that an electric vehicle makes no sense. It means that evaluation must know the mileage and the kilowatt-hour, not only the registration plate. 9. Rebound is not fraud. It is behaviour after heat becomes cheaper Energy economics identifies rebound: when the unit price of a service falls, part of the technical saving may return as higher use. A UKERC review summarises a wide range of estimates for household heating; the size depends on income, price, starting comfort and climate. [11] [22] This is international literature, not a measured average of Czech NZÚ recipients. An illustration, not a report: before renovation the family heated the living room to 19.5 °C and the bedrooms to 17 °C. After insulation and a heat pump the project promised a sharp drop in consumption. After three years the whole house is at 23 °C. The real saving is positive and substantially lower than the label. The report may show the full theoretical saving. In physics what shows is the comfort the house can afford for the first time. That is not necessarily abuse. It is a predictable reaction to cheaper heat. A programme that does not count it is not measuring impact. It is measuring a hypothesis about behaviour that did not occur. Jevons’s paradox in its strong form — that efficiency raises consumption above the original level — is a different, stronger thesis and is not evidenced for Czech insulation from the available audits. Weaker rebound yes: as a mechanism that evaluation should look for, not as an invented Czech percentage. 10. Deadweight: a subsidy may pay for what would have happened anyway The second mechanism is additionality. Boomhower and Davis showed on California data how to measure inframarginal participation: the share of those who would have bought the measure even without support. [19] The OECD in the Environmental Performance Review of the Czech Republic 2023 points to the need for more targeted and evaluated instruments, not to every koruna being wasted. [14] A Czech “40 to 55 per cent of PV recipients would have built anyway” is not in this text as a measured figure. The cited sources contain no econometric estimate of NZÚ additionality for this cut. A foreign percentage therefore cannot be transferred onto Czech recipients. If some households would have carried out the measure even without support, without an estimate of this deadweight it is not possible to determine how large the climate effect really is additional relative to the scenario without the subsidy. NZÚ Light and targeting low-income households can increase the availability of measures for groups with limited capital. [1] [15] The public summaries cited in the article do not themselves, however, give a causal comparison with what the same households would have done without support. The number of applications therefore speaks to use of the programme, not by itself to additionality. 11. An application is the start of the audit trail Before the subsidy portal the office had to trust an invoice. With a digital application it checks something more complicated: whether the document exists, whether it describes the same building, whether the calculation supports the promised saving and whether after three years it still holds. The application is navigation towards evidence. It is not automatic proof of consumption. The figure of 412 thousand applications, 13.5 per cent of the then plan for apartment buildings and 6 325 supported cars comes from different programmes, periods and layers of assessment. They cannot be added into the conclusion “green policy delivered on climate”, because they combine input, fulfilment of a specific plan and output without a figure for mileage. Four-step check of a report Existence: primary document, date, institution. Perimeter: which programme, which population, which period. Support: is it a koruna, a unit, PJ from a PENB, or a meter reading? Scope: does the unit match the unit with which the argument is made. The most reliable procedure separates searching from celebrating. First a table of claims, sources and limitations. Only then the press release. For every petajoule it is recorded whether it was calculated or measured. If the source cannot be opened, the claim is not promoted to a tonne of CO2 merely because the number is round. 12. The energy-performance law does not measure the occupant Act No. 406/2000 Coll. and the related decrees regulate certificates, audits and duties in larger changes to completed buildings. [12] Standardised energy assessment makes it possible to compare buildings, but it does not directly reproduce the actual behaviour of every household. That appears only in operational data, which moreover need to be cleaned at least of weather and changes in use. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext NKÚ inspection 20/19 found, for the measures tracked for apartment buildings, lower fulfilment of the original plan than the programmes had assumed. [5] [6] This single audit cannot be passed off as a summary conclusion about industry, state buildings or all later calls. It does, however, show why every figure must state the perimeter, the date and the method of calculation. In the Union framework there is added EU ETS 2 for buildings and road transport: a carbon price is meant to complement the subsidy. [20] This is not a finished Czech substitution programme. It is a different instrument, which measures fuel by price, not by application. The signpost for the debate is whether a blanket subsidy, a targeted loan, or a carbon price better hits additionality. The answer is not in the number of stamps. 13. What in the programme remains unmeasured The question “how much have we handed out?” is important, but narrow. The administrator also needs to know where meter readings are stored, for how long, who may see them, whether before/after series are kept and whether fuel is checked after the sustainability period. “We have 412 thousand applications” does not mean “we have 412 thousand measured savings”. Differences among programmes are marked in the official materials. NZÚ, boiler schemes, NRB guarantees and IROP have different inputs and different outputs. [1] [2] [3] [5] It does not follow that each is pointless. It follows that success cannot be judged by the logo without the name of the layer. Evaluation should track the flow from the public koruna through the project, construction and operation to energy and emissions. At each step the result can be changed by quality of delivery, behaviour, fuel or the grid; without this trail a net climate effect cannot be derived from an application. The ECA stresses cost-effectiveness and the OECD the need for better targeted and evaluated instruments. [13] [14] The cited materials at the same time do not document a uniform national database from which consumption before and after the intervention could be calculated for all the programmes listed. That is a limit of this article and of public comparison, not proof that no operational data exist. 14. The price of a koruna is not the price of a tonne saved The market uses several price languages at once. Policy pays a billion. The household pays the top-up. The climate pays a tonne that was not deducted. An agent can make dozens of applications even though the saving is one and that one is on paper. Direct comparison of programme price lists without knowing the layer is therefore misleading. A cheap subsidy per unit can be expensive per tonne if deadweight is high. An expensive subsidy for a low-income household can be cheap per tonne if, without it, heating would never be clean. For apartment buildings the NKÚ reported a specific subsidy of 2 681 Kč/GJ for IROP and 1 271 Kč/GJ for NZÚ; the Ministry of the Environment argued that the latter is favourable. [5] [6] The specific subsidy measures the koruna per reported gigajoule. It does not measure whether the gigajoule exists in a meter reading. The real price of an accepted result Subsidy + top-up + administration + inspection + rebound + deadweight + the grid emission factor + the price of a mistaken report. Cost-effectiveness can be judged only when the impact is estimated or measured by a transparent method and its uncertainties are stated. A meter reading is strong support for building operation, but a model calculation can also be valid if it has reasonable inputs, a correction of conditions and verification against data. Allocation alone is not enough for comparison. Fluctuating conditions also belong in the evaluation. Building consumption before and after the intervention needs to be normalised for weather and use. For electric vehicles a hypothetically low mileage would reduce the operating benefit relative to manufacturing emissions; the cited programme statistics, however, do not report the actual mileage of supported vehicles, so this magnitude cannot be quantified here. It is therefore useful to state the cost per verified or transparently modelled GJ or tonne, not only the cost per application. For the result it must be clear whether it comes from measurement, a normalised estimate or a project calculation and how temperature, mileage and other variables are treated. 15. What to choose instead of a blanket stamp The name of the programme is not a suitable first criterion. The following table assigns to each objective a control mechanism and proposes comparing two instruments on the same objects and in the same period; it is not a ranking of technologies. Need First group of instruments Decisive test Unacceptable shortcut Heat saving in the house NZÚ, IROP, loans Reading before/after, same use The label as consumption A cleaner boiler in the valley Boiler schemes, NZÚ Light Fuel after 3–5 years The delivery note as emissions Company kilometres Guarantee, tax, company fleet Mileage and the electricity mix Tailpipe zero = climate zero Low-income households Targeted pre-financing Additionality against a control A blanket bonus for the well-off Systemic decarbonisation ETS 2, a standard, measurement A tonne per koruna Volume of allocation as a verdict Czech evaluation must add to the Union cost-effectiveness audit local operation: winter consumption, fuel in the boiler and the mileage of supported vehicles. If public materials contain only an invoice, the assessment should admit this limit instead of calculating a non-existent meter reading. Different target groups may require targeted pre-financing, a guarantee or a carbon price. Using more than one instrument is defensible if the report keeps their inputs, outputs and impacts separate. 16. A short audit that says more than the number of applications A running audit need not wait ten years, nor anticipate the cancellation of a programme. On a smaller, described sample it can verify the method, find the gap between project and operation and prepare a more representative long-term evaluation. Eight steps from impression to decision — as an operational minimum, not as a substitute for an NKÚ audit Separate input, output and impact into three columns. For a sample of buildings request a reading before and after. Record temperature, floor area and the number of persons. For boilers check the fuel, not only the boiler label. For vehicles check mileage and the source of electricity. Estimate additionality at least by comparison with the unsupported. Calculate Kč per accepted GJ, not per application. Publish what the sample does not measure. Three tests of real impact The first is temporal: when was the intervention and when was it measured? The second is about origin: is it a PENB, an invoice, or a meter? The third is contradictory: is there an independent source that challenges the promised saving? A programme that answers a billion earlier need not be better if after five years nobody can find out how much energy remains. Before launching the next call Write which layer is the success indicator. Condition part of the payment on a meter reading. Separate low-income households from a blanket transfer. For cars require mileage, for boilers fuel. Set a date when the plan will be opened again. The evaluator should if possible not see only the press release. For buildings they track GJ. For boilers dust and BaP. For cars tonnes at a given mix. Each failure is classified: model, behaviour, fuel, additionality, or under-absorption. Comparison of programmes requires the same period, a climate correction and a description of use. A project calculation and direct measurement have different uncertainty; if we put them side by side, the difference of method must be visible. The output of evaluation should be a rule for using the programme: what impact it tracks, which data support it, who checks the method and when revision comes. Tariffs, the energy mix and prices change, so a conclusion without a date quickly goes stale. 17. Trust arises only when impact can be traced The first generation of green programmes sold boilers and façades. The next generation the number of applications. Today’s reports sell something larger: the impression that the climate is being managed because the allocation disappeared from the account. That is why the contest is not only over the best technology. It is over which metric is allowed to speak for physics. The more convenient the report that arises, the higher the cost of leaving it can be. Petajoules are hard to convert back into meter readings. Cars are hard to convert back into tonnes. People stop distinguishing their own consumption from the programme in which they reported it. Insulation, heat pumps and electric vehicles can bring substantial benefit. Public support, however, needs transferable data, a documented conversion from the koruna to energy or emissions, and a procedure for when the project calculation disagrees with operation. The quality of a programme is not determined by the highest number of applications nor the fastest take-up. What decides is whether its declared impact matches actual operation and whether deviations are visible, measurable and fiscally manageable . At the moment when the state pays an invoice, it is choosing a unit. At the moment when it reports the unit as a tonne, it is also choosing a new structure of accountability. And then the question is no longer: “How much have we handed out?” At the next call let us therefore ask: Which impact can we document, what uncertainty remains in it, and who decides when operational data disagree with the project? — Jiný Kontext

items.title: Speed limits and accidents: What the data says versus political rhetoric
items.subtitle: A higher motorway limit and urban 30 zones are often treated as one dispute, even though they involve different roads, users and consequences. Police statistics describe accidents and their classified causes; they do not by themselves prove the effect of a single sign. A decision needs actual speed, traffic volume, geometry, conditions and the long-term accident record.

items.body: The legal limit, actual speed, and speed appropriate to conditions are not the same thing. A driver can adhere to the maximum limit and still be driving inappropriately on a wet single-carriageway road. National accident statistics may fall without any change to the basic 50/90/130 table, and a divided motorway has a different risk profile than a street with pedestrians. Accident fatality figures alone, without data on kilometres driven, do not determine the level of risk. 1. The sign, appropriateness, and impact are not the same Imagine a parliamentary committee meeting on speed. The Minister of Transport holds up the annual report: in 2024, the police investigated 92 217 accidents, with 438 fatalities and 1 609 serious injuries. In 2025 85 518 accidents and 421 fatalities — the lowest number since consistent statistics began in 1961. [1] [2] A Vision Zero advocate wants a blanket thirty in built-up areas. A proponent of traffic flow wants 150 km/h on a selected motorway. A traffic engineer puts the ERSO data on the table: in 2022, 39.8 per cent of passenger cars on motorways drove within the limit, 54.5 per cent outside built-up areas, and 57.3 per cent in built-up areas. [4] A police officer reminds them of Section 18: speed must be adapted to conditions, not just the sign. [5] An emergency doctor speaks about the impact of a collision with a pedestrian at fifty. The "slow down versus speed up" debate mixes several distinct goals. The Ministry monitors the trend in fatalities, advocates of 30 zones focus on vulnerable road users in built-up areas, drivers want motorway flow, ERSO tracks compliance with limits, the law focuses on appropriateness, and medical professionals focus on the consequences of the impact. Each goal may be legitimate, but one cannot derive a solution for all roads from a single one. A proposed limit must combine the sign with geometry, weather, compliance, traffic volume and composition, and the presence of unprotected road users. It is therefore necessary first to determine the type of road and the measured outcome. The D3 pilot, a residential street, a frozen single-carriageway road, and the penalty point system have different users and different indicators; they should not form a single, undifferentiated dispute. The number on the sign determines the legal maximum. Actual speed and the police classification of the cause of an accident are different data points. — Jiný Kontext What we know about the D3 pilot — and what we do not yet What we know: The Ministry of Transport has published the section, the launch date, the rules for variable signage, and the ongoing proportions of the various modes. [23] What we are observing: Under the 150 mode, average speed increased by approximately 10 km/h, and some drivers continued to exceed the limit. What we do not know from the data so far: The long-term causal effect on the accident rate and the severity of consequences; the Ministry has extended the pilot precisely because the period was not sufficiently representative. 2. From the limit to the consequence of the accident The statement "speed is to blame for the death" does not say whether it was a breach of the maximum limit, a failure to adapt to conditions, or the greater severity of the impact. The outcome is influenced by actual speed in conjunction with the road surface, geometry, the vehicle, and the type of road user. Two accidents under the same sign may therefore have different mechanisms. Five layers of a single speed tragedy Formal limit: 50 / 90 / 130, local regulation, 30 zone. Proportionality: § 18 para. 1 — skills, road surface, visibility, line of sight. [5] Actual speed: the speed at which the car was travelling, not the speed indicated on the sign. Geometry and traffic: width, curvature, crash barriers, pedestrians, lorries in 80. Consequence: kinetic energy, mass, angle, protection of the crew and persons outside. The basic statutory table establishes the rules, while geometry influences the intuitive choice of speed, the radar its enforcement, and vehicle assistants the possibility of avoiding a collision. Police speed categories therefore require further breakdown according to the extent of the limit breach, conditions, and the course of the accident. Without this distinction, an accident becomes merely a dispute over a sign. If a driver exits a bend at the limit of 90 on icy roads, the speed may be disproportionate to the conditions even without exceeding the maximum. If a wide municipal through-road leads to frequent speeding, a new sign alone may not change the actual speed without adjustments to geometry or enforcement. On the motorway, it is necessary to monitor both absolute speed and the differences between the flows of cars and HGVs. Illustrative diagram: The chain between the sign and the victim passes through proportionality, actual speed, geometry, and impact energy. A break in any link changes the meaning of the slogan "slow down". From the sign to the crash outcome An illustrative chain between the limit, measured speed and the consequence of impact. From the sign to the crash outcome Sign Conditions Speed Road Outcome JINÝ KONTEXT Illustrative diagram: The chain shows layers, not the effect of one sign and not an annual statistic. 3. The limit must correspond to the risk of the section. The public often compares only the limit numbers. Equally important are the traffic, geometry, and vulnerable road users in the given section. Exceeding the maximum is an offence on every type of road, but the probability and severity of the consequence vary by environment. An incorrectly set sign can be replaced; the consequence of a collision cannot. BESIP and CDV state that inappropriate speed accounts for approximately 40 per cent of fatal accidents, and explicitly add that this is not just about exceeding the maximum, but about failing to adapt to conditions. [3] [8] This is a police classification of causes, not laboratory proof that 40 per cent of victims were speeding in dry conditions. Between 2021 and 2023, CDV counted 492 fatalities and 1 230 serious injuries in this category. [8] Type of failure What it looks like How to test it What limits the harm Sign failure Limit does not match geometry Measurement of actual speeds, not just the regulation Construction, narrowing, threshold Failure of proportionality Below the limit, above the conditions Protocols, weather, visibility § 18, telematics Failure of enforcement The limit exists, the radar does not Proportion within the limit (ERSO, CDV) Average speed measurement Failure of location Motorway debate on the urban body Separate types of roads A different limit for a different world A political decision must determine what risk the limit is intended to reduce in a given section and how the effect is to be measured. Exceeding the maximum speed limit and speed inappropriate to conditions must be reported separately, as their overlap is not complete. The safety of a section is influenced, alongside vehicle capabilities, by actual speed, geometry, separation of opposing traffic, enforcement, and the presence of vulnerable road users. These characteristics form a hypothesis that must be verified by comparable exposure and accident rates; signs and crash barriers alone do not determine the safety ranking. 4. Annual statistics do not prove the effect of a single sign Yearbooks are necessary because they replace a series of impressions with data. The problem arises when a single annual figure is taken to represent the effect of a single sign. Police in 2024: 92 217 accidents, 438 deaths, 1 609 serious injuries, damage of 7 991.7 million CZK. In 2025: 85 518 accidents, 421 deaths, 1 647 serious injuries, damage of 8 346.9 million CZK. [1] [2] The year-on-year decrease of 17 fatalities is a fact. It is not proof that it was caused by a specific amendment to the speed limit. Every report contains methodological decisions. What constitutes an "accident" in the police definition? Which cause is designated as the primary one? How is inappropriate speed coded? In the Czech Republic overview 2024, ERSO states that in 2021, out of 532 deaths, 22 occurred on motorways, 323 on roads outside built-up areas, and 187 in built-up areas. [4] These are absolute numbers and proportions of victims, not the risk per vehicle kilometre travelled; to compare the safety of different road types, corresponding traffic exposure data would be required. What must accompany claims about the effect of a speed limit The year, the definition of fatality (within 24 hours vs. 30 days, if they differ). The type of road, not the republic as a whole. Whether it concerns the limit, proportionality, or actual speed. The proportion of vehicles within the limit on the given section. The convergence of cars, infrastructure, and rescue operations. For the design of a pilot project, a sectional cut including weather, geometry, intensity, and actual speeds is therefore useful. Thirty days may reveal average speed and the level of compliance, but usually not enough to evaluate changes in rare outcomes, such as fatal accidents. Those require a longer period, comparable exposure, and a suitable control section. 5. Let us compare roads, not slogans about speed. The network can be described without a false sense of winners. The following map does not say who is for life and who is for freedom. It shows what kind of risk individual worlds carry and which failures the debate should specifically seek. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext World Main risk What to verify Typical reason for slogan Motorways High absolute speed, differences between lanes, fatigue Intensity, telematics, speeds and accidents Smooth flow, 150 km/h [5] First and second-class roads outside built-up areas Trees, bends, overtaking 61 % of deaths (2021) [4] "District roads kill" Built-up area 50 Pedestrians, cyclists, crossings Actual speed, construction 30 zones Through traffic Width increases to 70 in a fifty zone Geometry vs sign Traffic calming Frozen Third Class Proportionality below the limit Protocols, weather § 18, not a new table The table does not assess drivers as a group. It distinguishes between environments in which the same person faces different obstacles, speeds, and vulnerable road users. Therefore, the argument regarding pedestrians in a built-up area cannot be directly transferred to the D3, and vice versa. How to read the diagram: The physics of the impact is the same, but a built-up area, a single-carriageway road, and a motorway differ in geometry, traffic composition, and the presence of vulnerable road users. Safety indicators must therefore correspond to the specific environment. The same limit, different roads Risk links the sign, measurement, geometry and crash data. The same limit, different roads Limit Measured Geometry Crash Risk JINÝ KONTEXT Interpretive diagram: The examples are illustrative; position and size express neither frequency nor severity. 6. The trend is falling. Table 50/90/130 has barely moved. The long-term series is sober. Deaths have fallen by more than 70 per cent compared to 2000. The basic limits of 50 in built-up areas, 90 outside, and 130 on motorways have remained in place with local adjustments throughout this period. [5] Year Total accidents Fatalities Seriously injured 2000 211 584 1 486 5 500 2010 75 522 753 3 135 2020 94 797 460 1 807 2024 92 217 438 1 609 2025 85 518 421 1 647 Source: Directorate of the Traffic Police; the figure for 2020 is based on police information of 94 797 accidents. [1] [2] [14] This decline cannot be attributed to a general reduction in basic limits. Long-term development is influenced simultaneously by vehicles, infrastructure, behaviour, enforcement, and the emergency response system; however, the contribution of each component cannot be calculated from the time series alone. [6] [7] [20] Evans describes safety as an interplay between the vehicle, the road, and behaviour, rather than a single lever. [6] This does not prove that limits are redundant; it merely limits the causal conclusion drawn from the aggregate trend. The BESIP 2021–2030 strategy set a lower target for fatalities for 2024 than what eventually occurred; the Deputy Police President stated regarding the figure 438 that the target of 408 was not met. [1] The decline is historically low. It is not a fulfilled plan. Both sentences can be true at the same time. Meanwhile, the number of registered vehicles has increased, but the state of the register is not the same as the number of kilometres driven. To determine the level of risk, traffic exposure by road type is necessary. The current decline in the absolute number of victims is a positive trend, but not in itself an evaluation of the 150 km/h limit. 7. Kinetic energy does not increase linearly The laws of physics cannot be overruled. Kinetic energy increases with the square of the velocity: E_k = 1/2 m v^2. An increase from 50 km/h to 60 km/h means an energy increase of 44 per cent. An increase from 130 km/h to 150 km/h is an increase of 33 per cent. This is arithmetic, not accident statistics. It explains why ten kilometres per hour in a built-up area near a pedestrian is a different gamble than twenty on a divided motorway. Braking distance adds reaction time. With a one-second reaction time on dry asphalt, a vehicle at 50 km/h stops within a few dozen metres; a vehicle at 60 km/h is still moving at that same point. The exact metres depend on tyres, gradient, and surface; the order of magnitude is robust, not a centimetre-accurate textbook price list. Elvik's power model relates changes in average speed to changes in accidents of various severities: fatal outcomes react more sharply than minor ones. [11] It is a statistical model derived from numerous studies, not a promise that a blanket −10 km/h on Czech motorways will reduce fatalities by a fixed percentage, regardless of compliance or traffic composition. For pedestrians, individual risk curves vary according to data, age, vehicle type, and the definition of impact speed. WHO, ERSO, and ITF overviews agree on the main point: as impact speed increases, the probability of severe or fatal injury rises sharply. [15] [16] [19] The exact percentage at 30 or 50 km/h should therefore not be transferred between studies as a universal constant. Furthermore, an environment with pedestrians is not a direct analogue to a directionally separated motorway. 8. Inappropriate speed is not the same as exceeding the speed limit. Czech media cite that inappropriate speed is the cause of more than 40 per cent of fatal accidents. [3] It is necessary to keep these two states separate. The first is an offence against the limit: 105 km/h where 90 applies. The second is the obligation under Section 18, Paragraph 1 to adapt speed to abilities, load, road conditions, weather, and visibility; a driver may only drive at a speed that allows them to stop within the distance they can see. [5] If a vehicle emerges from a bend on a frozen rural road in fog at 60 km/h with a limit of 90, the police may, after investigation, deem the speed inappropriate for the conditions. A lower limit may influence behaviour, but it does not in itself guarantee that the chosen speed will be safe on ice. The CDV explicitly distinguishes between exceeding the limit and a speed that does not correspond to the conditions. [8] The categories may overlap, but they are not identical. A lower limit may reduce actual speeds and the severity of consequences; however, the police share of "inappropriate speed" does not in itself indicate what effect a specific change in signage would have. A sign and a crash count are not the same The legal maximum and a classified crash cause answer different questions. A sign and a crash count are not the same Limit Data Sign Maximum Speed Crash Cause JINÝ KONTEXT Interpretive diagram: The sides do not prove causation; they separate the limit from data that one sign cannot replace. 9. Most drivers do not read the sign. They read the road. ERSO Country Overview Czechia 2024 cites Baseline measurements: in 2022, 39.8 per cent of monitored passenger cars on motorways, 54.5 per cent on rural roads, and 57.3 per cent in built-up areas were within the speed limit. [4] Field measurements cited by the CDV report 37.0 per cent on motorways, 48.0 on rural roads, and 64.9 in built-up areas. [9] These are specific selections of locations and time periods, not a census of all Czech journeys. They show the difference between the regulation and the observed speed within the monitored sample. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext In the ESRA3 survey, 24.4 per cent of Czech respondents expressed support for a blanket thirty in built-up areas; more than 68 per cent of drivers surveyed did not expect speed checks, and nearly 60 per cent admitted to exceeding the motorway limit in the last 30 days. [9] [10] These are sample-based and partly self-reported data, not the behaviour of all drivers. BESIP data on regular speeding comes from a different type of communication and cannot be simply merged with field measurements. [3] What needs to be tested The first test concerns geometry: does the width encourage a speed that the sign prohibits? The second concerns enforcement: average speed cameras or a single sign outside a built-up area? The third concerns the expectation of being caught. Simply changing the number without narrowing the road, adding speed bumps, and enforcing the law changes the regulation. It does not automatically change the 85 percentile of speed. A wide, straight road in a built-up area may encourage higher speeds, especially if enforcement and traffic-calming measures are lacking. Nevertheless, the sign remains legally binding and may influence the behaviour of some drivers; geometry determines whether the desired speed is also intuitive. 10. Motorway 150 and urban 30 are two different worlds. The debate in Czechia polarises two proposals that share the word "speed" but not the physics. Section 18, paragraph 7 of the Act allows for a local increase of the motorway speed limit by up to 20 km/h, i.e. to 150, and in municipalities, according to paragraph 6, a reduction below 50. [5] The pilot operation on the D3 was launched on 1 October 2025 on the section between kilometres 84 and 131. Variable signage, adjusted according to traffic and weather, sets the limit at 100, 130 or 150 km/h. In May 2026, the Ministry of Transport extended it until the end of 2026, as winter operation in the higher mode provided only a limited sample; in the first six months, the 150 mode was active 39 per cent of the time, and the average speed of passenger vehicles was approximately 10 km/h higher than in the 130 mode. [23] These are provisional data from a single section, not final proof of safety or a result applicable to all motorways. 30 zones are primarily used where motor vehicles encounter pedestrians and cyclists. Precise risk curves vary between studies, but safety system overviews link lower impact speeds with a significantly lower probability of fatal injury to unprotected road users. [15] [16] [19] This supports targeted traffic calming in areas with pedestrians, rather than a blanket proposal applied automatically without assessing the street network. Mechanically linking both topics into a general opposition to or support of "speed" ignores the fact that pedestrians should not be on motorways and lorries should not drive in residential zones as if they were on the D1. These are two different worlds. A discussion on both without a table of road types is a discussion of slogans. An illustrative comparison might place side by side driving on a dual-carriageway motorway under good conditions and driving on a nighttime third-class road lined with trees. Both situations require adherence to the limit and proportionality, but they differ in geometry, oncoming traffic, obstacles, and the possibility of enforcement. Absolute numbers of fatalities off motorways suggest this difference, but without vehicle-kilometres, they do not quantify the relative risk of either journey. [4] 11. The radar monitors speed, not the entire section. Before the radar, a police officer had to drive behind the car. With section control, something else is monitored: the average between two points on a selected section. It does not see black ice beyond the horizon. It does not see overtaking on a single lane. The sign and the radar are navigation aids for the law. They are not automatic proof that the section is safe. The drop in the number of fatalities from 438 to 421, the proportion of inappropriate speed in fatal accidents, and the 39.8 per cent of vehicles within the limit on monitored motorways have different denominators. It cannot be inferred from them that lowering the motorway limit to 110 will save forty per cent of victims; such a conclusion would confuse a nationwide trend, police classification, and compliance measurements. Four-stage password check Network type: motorway, municipality, district road. Variable: limit, proportionality, actual speed, consequences. Support: primary statistics, not a headline. Scope: the victim population matches the population in question. The most reliable approach separates the search from the password. First, a table of the section, accidents, speeds, and geometry. Only then a proposal for the limit. If the source cannot be opened, the claim is not elevated to a "massacre" simply because the number 150 sounds high. 12. The law measures obligation. It does not measure geometry. Act No. 361/2000 Coll., in Section 18, imposes the duty to adapt speed, sets maximums, and allows for local adjustments upwards or downwards. [5] Technical conditions TP 145 describe the principles of 30 zones. [12] That is a regulation and a design manual. It is not the 85th percentile on a through-road that remained four lanes wide. The ŘSD uses linear control and variable limits; on the pilot section D3, the system evaluates weather, traffic detectors, and operational status. [17] [23] A variable sign can respond to conditions more accurately than a fixed maximum, provided the system is functioning and drivers obey the signage. Effectiveness must be evaluated on a specific section and cannot be automatically extrapolated to all motorways. Active assistants can prevent a collision or reduce the impact speed, while passive elements protect the crew during a crash. [20] The level of protection varies by collision type and participant; therefore, improvements in crew protection cannot be translated into an equivalent benefit for pedestrians or cyclists without further data. 13. Risk is posed by both speed and its variance The question "what maximum?" is important, but narrow. Higher absolute speed reduces reaction time and increases impact energy; meanwhile, speed differentials between vehicles alter the frequency of manoeuvres and conflicts. [16] [19] On a motorway, it is therefore necessary to monitor the average, percentiles, and the speed distribution of passenger cars and HGVs. However, safety of a section cannot be calculated from variance alone without accident and exposure data. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext In a built-up area, a pedestrian may suffer the consequences; on a rural road at night, a tree may be the deciding factor, and on a bridge, the wind. Telematics can capture certain conditions, whereas a fixed sign cannot. The sign, therefore, remains a necessary but crude tool. More than two-thirds of drivers do not expect to be checked. [9] A limit without enforcement is a letter. A letter may civilise some people. It is not measured in 100 per cent. CDV and ERSO demonstrate this through compliance figures, not moral appeals. 14. The cost of a minute is not the cost of a crash The driver counts time, the municipality counts noise, the hospital counts injuries, and the insurer counts damage. The claim "150 saves time, 30 saves lives" is therefore incomplete without knowing the road type, intensity, and actual change in speed. A cheap minute on a motorway can be expensive if it increases the variance relative to a truck. An expensive minute in a 30 zone may be cheap if it reduces impact energy against a body near a school. Elvik shows that fatal outcomes respond more sharply to speed than minor ones. [11] That is why the Safe System focuses more strictly on the upper end, not proof for every campaign slogan. The true cost of an adopted limit Signage + geometry + enforcement + compliance + variance + vehicles + rescue + who is outside the car. The costs and benefits of a limit can only be assessed with actual speed, compliance, intensity, and consequences. A 30 zone without street modifications may have less impact on the 85 percentile than a combination of signage, construction, and enforcement. In a 150 regime, variable signage must respond reliably to weather and traffic; current pilot data do not yet determine the long-term cost of accidents or the final balance of benefits. [23] It is therefore useful to measure the cost per adopted section , rather than the cost per ideology. "Adopted" means that the limit, construction, and enforcement work together, and that accidents on that section are analysed by cause, not by television headlines. 15. What to choose for which road The choice of measure should be based on the type of road and the control mechanism, not on political affiliation. The following table does not assign a winner; it suggests comparable sections and measurements for each objective. Requirement First group of measures The Decisive Test An Unacceptable Shortcut Protection by the School 30 Zone + Construction Actual Speed, Not Just the Sign A Blanket Slogan Without Thresholds Municipal through-road Narrowing, Traffic Islands, Crossings 85th Percentile Before/After New 40 on a Wide Four-Lane Road District Road in Winter § 18, Guardrails, Avenues Proportion of Disproportionality in Reports Nationwide −20 km/h Selected Motorway Telematics, Possible 150s Variance, Weather, Section Accidents “150 = Massacre” Without Section Data Nationwide Trend Cars, Roads, Rescue A Series of 2000–2025 Attributing the Decline to a Single Amendment Foreign experience must be verified on Czech infrastructure. A German motorway is not the D1 and a Dutch 30 zone may not correspond to a Czech municipal through-road. The pilot should include wet conditions, darkness, lorries, and pedestrians, and allow for the conclusion that the sign alone is insufficient without structural modifications. School streets, motorways, and third-class roads may require different regimes, as do tunnels and clear stretches of road. However, the driver must be able to clearly discern from the design and signage which regime is currently in effect. 16. A short section test that says more than a slogan Before the pilot, a brief diagnostic can describe the geometry, traffic, speeds, and evaluation plan. Such a snapshot does not replace long-term accident assessment. Its aim is to determine the baseline, risk situations, and the data that the administrator will collect before and after the change. Fourteen days from the sign to the section Days 1–2: Type of communication, accidents over 3–5 years, proportion of pedestrians and trees. Days 3–4: Measurement of actual speeds, 85 percentile, proportion within the limit. Days 5–7: Geometry: width, visibility, crash barriers, crossings. Days 8–10: Enforcement: radar, average speed cameras, expectation of checks. Days 11–12: Weather and telematics, if it is a motorway. Day 13: Protocols: how many "inappropriate" entries were below the table. Day 14: Pilot protocol: control section, tracking length, and revision date. Fourteen days of preparation may suffice to set up measurements, but not to draw conclusions about fatal or serious accidents. For those, a longer comparable period is necessary, as is traffic intensity and, if possible, a control section; a low number of events means wide statistical uncertainty. Three section tests The first is the consistency between the sign and the road design. The second is the proportion of vehicles within the limit. The third is the composition of causes in the protocol. A product that provides an answer a week earlier is not necessarily better if, a year later, no one can determine whether the 85 percentile has moved. Before changing the limit Distinguish between motorways, built-up areas, and district roads. Do not change the sign without an enforcement plan. For 30, demand road design, not just a sign. Demand telematics and section assessment from 150. Read § 18 as carefully as the table of maxims. If possible, the assessor should not know which camp proposed the section. They monitor speeds, accidents, serious injuries, and pedestrians. Each failure is classified: signage, proportionality, geometry, enforcement, or vehicle. Sections must be compared within the same period of the year and under similar traffic conditions. If only one section measurement exists, the pilot simultaneously tests enforcement, and this difference must be part of the interpretation. The pilot must conclude with an operational rule: what goal the limit pursues, which data evaluate it, and when the review will take place. Cars, roads, and driving habits change; therefore, the measure must not remain without further scrutiny. 17. A sign is not enough without measurement and review. The first generation of the debate sold the freedom of the steering wheel. The next generation sold zero deaths. Today's slogans sell something greater: the impression that a number on a post governs physics. This is why the competition is not just over 30 or 150. The competition is over which layer is permitted to speak for all the others. The sharper the slogan, the higher the potential cost of oversight. Districts fit poorly into the motorway dispute. Pedestrians fit poorly into the argument about flow. Proportionality fits poorly into a radar that measures the maximum. People cease to distinguish their own section from the slogan in which it has been smoothed over. Limits provide traffic with a common and enforceable rule. However, their proposal requires speed measurements, accident analysis, geometry, procedures for adverse conditions, and regular verification of the original justification. The quality of a limit is determined neither by the lowest number nor the highest penalty. It must correspond to the geometry and users of the specific road, be enforceable, and allow for timely determination of whether the intended effect has actually occurred. The moment we hang a sign, we choose a regulation. The moment we judge overall safety by it, we also choose a new structure of self-delusion. And then the question is no longer: "What number should be on the round sign?" Before making a change, we should therefore ask: What speed are we actually measuring, what risk is the measure intended to reduce, and when will we have enough data for a review? — Jiný Kontext
