items.body: A two-second decision on credit joins several distinct tasks: verifying data, estimating risk, a legal assessment of creditworthiness and telling the applicant the result. An accurate model can work with a faulty input, and a low share of non-performing loans says nothing about the people the system refused in advance. What we know / What we do not know What we know: A lender must assess creditworthiness from information that is necessary, reliable, sufficient and proportionate. Automated decision-making may fall under the GDPR, and some systems for assessing creditworthiness fall into the high-risk regime of the AI Act. What we do not know: Public sources do not show a complete list of variables, thresholds or human-review rules for individual Czech lenders. The use of an address, a device or geolocation therefore cannot be attributed to the market as a whole. 1. A score that is not yet fairness Picture a meeting in a mid-sized Czech bank. The head of retail wants to cut consumer-credit approval to under two minutes, because competitors already do so. The risk manager insists on the model that best predicts twelve-month default on historical data. Compliance recalls Article 22 GDPR, the anti-discrimination act and the European Artificial Intelligence Act. IT wants to connect Open Banking, because movement on an account says more than a payslip. Marketing promises approval on the first click. The customer, who is not in the room, wants to know why they received a no. At first glance this is an argument about speed. In fact each person is describing a different problem. The director compares application conversion. Risk compares loss from non-payment. Compliance compares procedural defensibility. IT compares the availability of data. The customer compares the intelligibility of a verdict that will close the door to housing, a car or a roof repair. A model can predict default well and still fail at justification or at handling a faulty figure. Assessment must therefore separate the prediction of default, the quality of inputs, the risk of discriminatory proxies, the possibility of correction, the legal basis for automation and genuinely available human review. This is not an abstract contest between a human and a machine. What is being compared is a concrete prediction, a decision rule, an explanation to the applicant and a path to remedy; each part has a different test. A model is not fairness. A score is not character. A threshold is not the law. And the speed of a decision is not proof that the decision will stand. — Jiný Kontext 2. What a credit verdict is made of When “approved” or “rejected” appears on the screen, it is easy to form the impression that the model delivered the verdict. The result usually arises in a chain of several layers. Each can raise quality, lower it or change the kind of error. Two lenders with the same foundation therefore need not decide alike, and the same lender may behave differently by channel, product and whether a human still sits beyond the threshold. Five layers of one credit verdict Data: registers, the account and the form; in some systems a device, geolocation or Open Banking may be added. Their actual use must be documented at the particular lender. Model: a statistical or machine prediction of the probability of default. Threshold and policy: from which score lending occurs, at what rate, with what exception. Permissions and channel: what the system may see, trigger, write and to whom it may show it. Governance and accountability: audit, human review, justification, correction of data, complaint. In the scoring chain the model creates only part of the result. An application may insert a business rule before the score, add a channel surcharge after the score, apply currently valid regulatory or internal availability limits and send the file for manual approval. The same number in another product means a different rate. The same rate in another month may mean a different commercial policy. This is precisely where the first error of public debate arises. A headline announces a contest between a human and AI, but in fact it compares two entirely different chains: a manual file with incomplete supporting documents and an automated system with thousands of variables, of which the applicant sees three. Or, conversely, it changes only the marketing word “AI” and presents an old logistic regression as new intelligence. An honest comparison must state not only the name of the model, but also the version, the channel, the available data, the threshold, the time limit and the method of control. This layering is not an academic detail. It determines where to turn when something fails. If the model punished a postcode, the problem is in the data and the proxy. If it punished an evening time of submission, the problem is in telemetry. If it punished correctly, but nobody could say so, the problem is in the justification layer. The sentence “the algorithm rejected it” is the start of a diagnosis, not its end. Illustrative scheme: The same model can, at a different threshold, channel and supervisory regime, create a different human fate. 3. The best system is the one whose error you can afford Alongside predictive performance it is necessary to watch the type of error, its detectability and the possibility of review. An unfavourable rate can sometimes be changed by refinancing. An unexplained rejection may exclude the applicant from the next process and at the same time hide them from the statistics of customers to whom credit was granted. NIST, in its framework for managing artificial-intelligence risk, notes that bias can appear in the data, in the objective, in the threshold and in whom the system measures at all. Risk does not grow only with the frequency of error. It also grows when the professional form of a verdict invites disproportionate trust. [13] Type of failure What it looks like How to test it What limits the harm Proxy discrimination The verdict punishes an address, a device, a contract type or a time instead of the ability to repay Comparison of groups with the same income; proxy ablation A ban on selected features, a disparity audit, human review Data error Outdated income, someone else’s address, an uncorrected register A list of the data used and the date of their validity A right to rectification, short retention, an owner of the datum Opacity “Internal scoring” without the decisive factors Whether the applicant can challenge the premise A meaningful justification, documentation for supervision Threshold error A correct score, an arbitrary boundary, a channel exception The same score in another channel and month A written policy, a ban on silent exceptions This also changes the question we are asking. We do not ask only which system hit default on average. We ask which system will fail in a way that our process will catch. A risk team may tolerate false-positive caution, because it reduces loss. The applicant pays for that caution with a closed market. An accounts department cannot tolerate a hidden change of a decimal sign. A credit model cannot tolerate a hidden penalty on a neighbourhood if the company claims that it must not discriminate. AUC itself does not tell whether the applicant will receive an intelligible justification, whether an input can be corrected and whether limited proxies lead to indirect discrimination. A somewhat weaker prediction may be more acceptable in a particular deployment if it has demonstrably effective control mechanisms. 4. What the share of non-performing loans does not show Market indicators are needed, because they replace part of impressions with a repeatable number. The problem arises at the moment when one percentage begins to stand for the entire fairness of the system. According to the banking statistics of the Czech National Bank, the volume of loans granted to resident households in the Czech Republic in June 2026 reached CZK 2,713 billion. Housing loans accounted for CZK 2,081 billion, that is 77 per cent of this volume. Consumer loans reached CZK 428 billion. The volume of non-performing loans remained at CZK 32.9 billion and their share of the total volume stayed at 1.2 per cent. [2] This is the state of the banking sector for one month, not the sum of all contracts in the CBCB and NRKI registers and not an audit of the fairness of individual models. Segment (CNB, June 2026) Volume Note Loans to resident households CZK 2,713 bn Banking statistics, not registers Housing loans CZK 2,081 bn 77 % of the volume to households Consumer loans CZK 428 bn The highest month-on-month dynamism Non-performing loans CZK 32.9 bn Share 1.2 % Every test contains hidden decisions. Who is in the population? Only banks, or non-bank lenders as well? What is the definition of default and how long is the observation window? How many applications were rejected before a contract arose? An answer to any of these questions can change the meaning of the number. Five figures without which the NPL share is only an advertising number The precise population of contracts, the period and the source of the statistic. The definition of a non-performing loan and the length of the window. The share of rejected applications that never entered the portfolio at all. The difference between groups with the same income and a different data trail. The share of rejections that passed through human review. At a large number of applications, automation can reduce time and costs substantially. Public statistics do not, however, show that full automation is economically inevitable for every product and every application. Portfolio statistics, moreover, see those who received credit, not all who were refused. A public indicator helps in understanding the size of the market; fairness of entry requires a different test. 5. Compare chains, not the “AI” mascot The table separates the form, the registers, the model and human review according to their role in the credit verdict. For each layer it states the context and the failure that a test of the particular lender should look for. The state of models and policies changes; what decides is always the current configuration of the given product. Layer Main working position What to verify in a pilot Typical reason for the choice Registers (CBCB, NRKI, Solus) A shared memory of contracts Correction of an entry, age of the datum, coverage Reducing information asymmetry Form and income What the applicant can document Date of validity, individualisation Statutory creditworthiness Open Banking Movement on the account with consent Scope of items, retention, withdrawal A fresher picture of solvency Telemetry Manner of completion, device, time Whether a person can change the feature without changing repayments Fraud and impulse Threshold and rate Commercial policy The same score in another channel Managing portfolio risk Human review Exception and complaint Whether a human may say yes A high price of error The rows are not a judgment on the quality of banks. The same lender offers several products, thresholds and channels, and each of them may change within a few months. The map is meant to prevent another error: that an institution buys an excellent model into a process that does not see the particular person, cannot explain the verdict or locks it into an environment from which it is later hard to leave. How to read the scheme: Neither the position nor the size of the elements expresses a score. The diagram separates input data, the model, the decision rule and review. 6. Proxies: a ban on a feature is not a ban on information The anti-discrimination act prohibits, in designated areas, different treatment on enumerated grounds; the use of a particular feature or its substitute variable must be assessed in the precise legal and factual context. [14] A model can, moreover, derive from other data information that correlates with a protected characteristic. The risk is called proxy discrimination. [4] Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext A postcode can, in particular data, correlate with social status, income or the composition of a neighbourhood. The kind of purchases, the time of transactions, the sector or the type of contract can function as proxies and create differences between groups. Whether this actually happens and whether the difference is legally permissible must be shown by a test of the particular model; this article does not document the use of these features by Czech banks. A model can, when learning from historical data, reproduce or amplify existing differences if design, testing and supervision do not catch them. That is not an automatic result of every algorithm, nor proof of the programmer’s intent. [4] [12] Barocas and Selbst, in the study Big Data's Disparate Impact , showed that a discriminatory result need not arise from a programmer’s bad intent. It is enough for the model to learn from data that already contain inequality, and for the target variable — here default — itself to be socially biased. [4] Fuster, Goldsmith-Pinkham, Ramadorai and Walther showed on credit markets that a shift to machine learning can increase predictive power and at the same time widen differences between groups. This is empirics of a particular market and particular models, not proof that every Czech bank decides in this way. It does show, however, that accuracy and equality are not the same thing. [5] Three tests of proxy discrimination The first is a test of comparable abilities: do two groups with the same documented income, the same repayment history and the same requested amount have the same chance of approval? The second is an ablation test: does the disparity change when we remove the postcode, the device type and the time of submission from the model? The third is a substitution test: if we remove the proxy, does the model replace it with another variable that carries the same information? A product that “does not use race” need not be fair. It may merely be using an address, a school and a telephone. An illustration, not reportage: applicant A, 32 years old, employment of indefinite duration, net income CZK 42,000, a new-build in the centre, an iPhone, an application in working hours, a loan of CZK 300,000, a rate of 5.9 per cent in 90 seconds. Applicant B, 32 years old, a self-employed person (OSVČ) with a net income of CZK 45,000 and five years without delay, a prefab on the periphery, an older laptop, an evening application, a rejection without a reason. Both have the same ability to repay. What differs is the data trail. If after the removal of the postcode and the device the verdict aligned, it was not character. It was a proxy. 7. Telemetry: typing speed is not character Alongside registers and income, some systems may work with behavioural data about the completion of an application: time on the page, number of corrections, the device or the time of filing. Whether a particular Czech lender collects these data and uses them for the credit verdict must be documented separately. A behavioural feature may in training data correlate with fraud or risk, but correlation itself does not explain the reason. An evening filing may be connected with shift work or care just as much as with financial distress. It is therefore necessary to measure the contribution of the feature, differences between groups and the possibility of correction. Device type is not a direct measure of solvency. It may carry side information about income, age or digital behaviour and become a proxy. Use itself does not yet prove discrimination; what decides are the data, the weight of the feature, the purpose and the impact on comparable applicants. The Basel Committee and related BIS work note that machine learning in financial services changes not only accuracy, but also the way institutions understand their own decisions. The more complex the model, the larger the gap between predictive power and explainability. [1] The gap is not cosmetic. It is the place where accountability is lost. The practical minimum is a map of telemetry. Which behavioural features does the model actually use? Which does it only collect? Which can the applicant change without changing their ability to repay? If a feature can be changed by swapping a telephone, it is not character. It is a costume. 8. Registers: the market’s memory is not a person’s memory CBCB, NRKI and Solus perform a useful function: they reduce information asymmetry between creditor and debtor. [3] Without them part of the market would guess in the dark and the price would rise for everyone. Registers are not, however, a person’s memory. They are a memory of the contracts the market has concluded about the person. Memory has gaps. A person who has never applied for credit has a thin trail. A thin trail is often read in a model as risk, even though it may mean caution. A person who years ago had a dispute with an operator carries a mark longer than their present solvency lasts. A person who repaid on time, but in another regime — abroad, a partner’s account, cash — “does not exist” in the register. An error in a register is especially expensive because it spreads. One bad entry enters several models. Several models produce several rejections. Several rejections thin the future trail. A loop arises: the market’s bad memory becomes the person’s bad future. That is why the right to rectification of historical data is a practical, not a ceremonial, question. An applicant who does not know what the registers claim about them cannot challenge the verdict. An applicant who knows, but has no channel for correction, is challenging a wall. The Consumer Credit Act requires the lender to assess creditworthiness; it does not require it to let the applicant look into every weight of the model. [6] The gap between the duty to assess and the duty to explain is precisely the place where fairness is lost. Registers are therefore usefully understood as infrastructure. Infrastructure needs an audit, retention periods, a right to rectification and an intelligible extract. Without that, “internal scoring” is only a politer name for someone else’s memory that you are not allowed to read. 9. GDPR and SCHUFA: an explanation is not open source Article 22(1) GDPR gives the data subject the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing if it has legal or similarly significant effects. It is not an absolute ban. Paragraph 2 permits necessity for the conclusion or performance of a contract, authorisation by Union or Member State law, and explicit consent. For contractual necessity and explicit consent, paragraph 3 requires at least the possibility of human intervention, the expression of a view and a challenge to the decision; a legal exception must itself lay down suitable safeguards. [8] The Court of Justice of the EU in Case C-634/21 (SCHUFA) held that the calculation of a score can itself constitute such a decision if a third party attributes a determining role to it in its own decision-making. [7] That is sharper than it sounds. The verdict need not be delivered by a robot with a stamp. It is enough for a human employee in practice merely to copy the score. The Court thereby shifted attention from the theatre of “we have a human in the loop” to the question of whether a human actually decides. This is an interpretation of one provision on one type of scoring, not an automatic ban on every banking model in Czechia. It does show, however, where the law looks for a decision: where the score in practice becomes the verdict. The European Data Protection Board, in its guidelines on automated decision-making, emphasises meaningful information about the logic involved, the significance and the envisaged consequences. [16] This need not be a printout of all coefficients, but the sentence “internal scoring” itself usually does not make it possible to challenge an input or a decisive factor — for example outdated income, someone else’s address or a variable with an impermissible discriminatory impact. In practice an open question remains: how to explain the output of a non-linear model so that it is intelligible to a lay applicant and at the same time does not disclose a trade secret? That is not a reason to abandon explanation. It is a reason to separate an explanation for a person from an audit for supervision. The customer needs the decisive factors and the possibility of correction. Supervision needs documentation, disparity tests and evidence that threshold values are not arbitrary. 10. The AI Act: high risk is not finished fairness Annex III of the AI Act ranks among high-risk AI systems those intended to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or to establish their credit score; an express exception covers systems used to detect financial fraud. [9] The regime includes requirements for risk management, data, documentation, logging and human oversight. Article 26 imposes obligations on deploying entities according to their role and conditions of use. Precise applicability to a given system and date must be verified against the regulation’s timetable; transparency under Article 50 is not a substitute for the high-risk-systems regime. [20] [21] Classification is a map of duties. It is not automatically fairness at the branch. A bank can have documentation and still punish a postcode. It can have human oversight and still let a person merely click “I agree”. It can have logs and still not show them to the applicant. The difference between a consumer chat and a credit model is precisely the price of error. A bad slogan can be deleted. A bad mortgage rejection is written into a life course. That is why it is not enough to say “we have the AI Act”. It is necessary to say which layer of the chain is under supervision, who may return the verdict and how it is measured that it is also returned to people who are not the average of the portfolio. Cathy O'Neil described the same logic as a scalable, opaque model that punishes people for the statistics of their surroundings and at the same time presents itself as neutral science. [12] The book is not an audit of a Czech bank. It is a description of a mechanism that the AI Act therefore placed among the high-risk ones. 11. The CNB and the EBA: prudence is not individual fairness The European Banking Authority, in its guidelines on loan origination and monitoring, requires institutions to understand their models, to assess creditworthiness on the basis of proportionate information and to supervise the quality of newly originating contracts. [10] The aim is that new loans be prudent and that practices be aligned with consumer protection. Act No. 257/2016 Coll. requires the lender to assess creditworthiness on the basis of necessary, reliable, sufficient and proportionate information. [6] [11] For housing loans it is also necessary to separate currently effective CNB measures from the creditor’s internal limits; LTV, DTI and DSTI cannot, without a date of effect, be presented as one permanently binding set. [22] Regulation thereby protects the market from systemic collapse and the consumer from a loan that will destroy them. It cannot, however, by itself guarantee individual fairness for every rejected applicant. Prudential supervision sees risk in the portfolio. Anti-discrimination logic sees risk in disparity between people with the same ability to repay. Both axes are legitimate. They are not interchangeable. The EBA, in discussions of machine learning in internal rating models, notes that complexity must not deprive the institution of understanding. [18] The OECD, in work on artificial intelligence in finance, emphasises governance, auditability and human accountability, not a ban on prediction. [17] The CNB Financial Stability Report maps the credit cycle and household vulnerabilities; it does not measure whether a model punishes the self-employed for fluctuating income, or for a genuine inability to repay. [19] The bounds of supervision are therefore necessary and insufficient. Necessary, because without them the market would optimise only profit. Insufficient, because the systemic health of a portfolio can coexist with a quiet unfairness at the entrance. 12. What a justification is for, and where it is not enough Before the duty to explain, the applicant had to check whether the bank would even tell them no. With a justification they check something more complex: whether the stated factors exist, whether they are theirs, whether they are current and whether they actually carry the verdict to which they are attached. A justification is navigation to the evidence. It is not automatic evidence. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext One rejection can combine three true figures into an untrue conclusion. The first describes a postcode, the second self-employment, the third an evening time. Each datum works, but the synthesis punishes the environment, not the ability to repay. Elsewhere the system uses a high-quality register even though a fresh statement is available. Or it cites income that applied two years ago. A four-step check of a justification Existence: the stated datum actually entered the decision. Authority: the datum is primary for the given claim, not a proxy for a prohibited characteristic. Support: the particular passage actually supports the particular no. Scope: the person, the period, the definition of income and the limitations fit. When explaining a rejection, a table of decisive factors, their sources and their limitations is assembled first. The text for the client should arise only from this check. An untraceable datum should not become a reason merely because the model formulated it persuasively. A credit system is safer when it shortens the path to a check, not when it replaces it. For a decision on housing, meaningful human review is a suitable organisational rule especially in disputed or high-impact cases; it is not, however, by itself a universal legal command that a human must always issue the last verdict. 13. Privacy is not a switch. It is the entire data flow The question “is it trained on my data?” is important, but too narrow. The applicant and the institution must also know where forms and statements are stored, for how long, who has access to them, whether audit records are kept, which third parties process scoring and whether a connected tool sends data onward. “We do not use it for training” does not mean “we store nothing” nor “no subcontractor will process anything”. The differences between a consumer click, a bank identity and Open Banking consent are marked in the legal texts. [8] [15] It does not follow that every enterprise regime is suitable for every sensitive datum. It follows that security cannot be judged by a logo without the name of the product, the contract and the configuration. In the European Union the AI Act framework is added. An ordinary chat for drafting a slogan and a system affecting access to credit are not the same. Concrete classification requires a legal assessment. [9] [20] The practical minimum is a map of the data flow. It begins with the applicant, continues through the form, the registers, the model, the threshold, the logs, the exports and ends at the place where a datum can be corrected, deleted or a verdict returned. Without this map a claim about privacy is only a description of one part of the pipe. 14. The price of default is the price of a raw material, not the price of a verdict The market uses several price languages at once. The bank measures loss from non-payment. Marketing measures conversion. The customer measures the rate. Compliance measures the fine. A direct comparison of these price lists without knowledge of the working procedure is therefore misleading. A cheap automated system can be economically excellent for classifying a million short applications for a small limit. The same automated system can be expensive for a task that it repeats three times, consumes an Open Banking trail and in the end requires half an hour of human correction — or, which is worse, no correction, because the rejected person disappears. An expensive manual file can be pointless for a predictable card. It can, however, be cheaper for a one-off decision with a high price of error if it reduces the number of invisible nos. The true price of an accepted verdict Model + data + human assignment + verification + the price of default + the price of a false rejection + the impossibility of a complaint + future dependence on one chain. A verdict is cheap only when it has passed a check and can actually be used. Costs also include fluctuation. If the same application is decided differently in another channel, the average price of a correct result is not the price of one run. If the system exhausts the human-review limit in the middle of the day, the cost is waiting. If thresholds, telemetry and automated systems are firmly bound to one environment, the cost is also a future exit. That is why it is useful to measure the price per accepted verdict , not the price per application. Accepted means that the result met predetermined criteria, passed a check and did not cause subsequent harm that portfolio statistics do not see. This metric can reverse an order that looked unambiguous from NPLs. 15. What to choose for which application A pilot should start with a description of the decision, the data and the control mechanism, not with the brand of a model. The table determines which two regimes to compare on the same data, with the same applicants and with the same budget of time for review. Need First group of candidates Decisive test Unacceptable shortcut A quick small limit Automation with a clear threshold and justification Repeatability for identical applications Swapping speed for fairness Housing and a high amount Automation with documented meaningful human review of disputed cases Individualisation of income, current limits and exceptions Watching only portfolio NPLs The self-employed and a thin trail A manual file with statements and taxes Whether fluctuation is not automatically default Punishing the form of income Fairness of entry A disparity audit, proxy ablation The same income, a different address and device The sentence “we do not use race” Compliance with the GDPR and the AI Act Documentation, a log, a changeable verdict Whether a human may say yes Human-in-the-loop theatre Sensitive movement on an account Narrow Open Banking, short retention A map of the flow and withdrawal of consent Consent as a blank cheque For Czech use a separate test is necessary. A foreign study of machine learning on mortgages will not measure whether the system preserves the significance of a trade, correctly reads a tax return, distinguishes a decimal comma, understands parental leave, or does not translate a Czech postcode into a non-existent analogy. The test set should include the self-employed, a thin trail, a register correction and an application in which the correct answer is “the datum is not enough”. Some institutions ultimately need several regimes. One for a small limit, a second for housing, a third for complaints. That is not a failure of standardisation. It is the same decision as using a different tool for accounting and a different one for graphics. The condition is that the division be intelligible, that data not pass over uncontrolled and that people know where final authority arises. 16. A two-week test that says more than a single AUC A choice can be made without a six-month tender and without an impulsive purchase. A short, disciplined pilot is enough. Its aim is not to prove that a candidate can do something impressive. The aim is to find situations in which it fails, and to establish whether the organisation can catch them. Fourteen days from impression to decision Days 1–2: Write down 20 to 40 anonymised applications, their frequency, the price of error and the present time. Days 3–4: Prepare the same inputs, mandatory points and an evaluation sheet. One version with postcode and device, one without them. Days 5–7: Repeat each important application at least three times and keep a register of verdicts, rates and justifications. Days 8–10: Verify correction of data, human review, export, logs, deletion of the Open Banking trail and a safe return. Days 11–12: Calculate the price of an accepted verdict including the check and the disparity between comparable groups. Day 13: Stress tests: a bad register, old income, evening submission, an older device, a prohibited characteristic. Day 14: Decide according to the matrix, document the limitations and set a date for the next review. What needs to be tested The first examination concerns consistency between channels. The same application from the web, from an app and from a branch is not an identical experiment if telemetry and permissions differ. The second concerns the threshold: the marketing word “instant decision” may mean automation only up to a certain amount. The third concerns data. Open Banking, registers and the form do not measure the same person. They measure three different trails of the same person. The evaluator should if possible not know which regime created the verdict. They watch substantive correctness, completeness of the justification and the possibility of correction. Every failure is classified: proxy, data, opacity, threshold, tool or interruption. A pilot should also have conditions for exclusion. For example: a single unannounced penalty of a prohibited characteristic, a non-existent justification, the impossibility of correcting a register or the impossibility of exporting a record. A high average AUC should not outweigh an error whose impact the organisation cannot accept. The last output is not only the name of a model. It is an operating rule: what scoring is used for, what it is not used for, which data it may see, what a human must approve, how the result is verified and when the decision is opened again. Models, tariffs and conditions change. Without a date of revision even a good pilot gradually turns into a corporate superstition. 17. Open Banking: consent is not a blank cheque The Payment Services Directive allows a provider to see movement on an account with the client’s consent. [15] That can be fairer than a static statement. It can also be a deeper probe into privacy: rent, a pharmacy, maintenance, betting, gifts. Consent to access to an account is not consent for every item to enter a black box without justification. It is consent to a data flow that must be possible to describe. Two similar accounts can have a different data regime. An employee with a regular wage looks clean in Open Banking. A self-employed person with the same net year looks like noise. A partner who pays the rent from their own account “does not exist”. A person who cares and has irregular benefits looks riskier than they are. The system sees items. It does not see the household. Before switching on a fully automated verdict Separate the retrieval of a score from the action that concludes or rejects a contract. Determine the owner of each decisive datum and the date of its validity. Introduce a threshold above which a machine must not decide alone: a high amount, a thin trail, a contradiction in the data. Verify that the applicant sees from which source the verdict drew. Introduce an exclusion condition: an uncorrectable register, a missing justification, a silent proxy. The greatest competitive advantage of enterprise scoring may therefore not be the model. It may be order in the data. And the greatest weakness need not be hallucination. It may be a true answer based on an item that was true two years ago. 18. An invisible rejection outside portfolio statistics The first generation of credit scores sold speed. The next sold accuracy. Today’s products sell something larger: a place in which a person applies, documents, waits and accepts a verdict on a life chance. That is why lenders do not compete only for the best prediction. They compete for the data flow. For Open Banking, for telemetry, for the habit that two seconds are enough. The more comfortable the ecosystem that arises, the higher the price of exit can be. Thresholds are hard to export, automated systems rely on proprietary features and people stop distinguishing their own process from the product in which they built it. That does not mean automation is bad. It is often precisely automation that reduces the arbitrariness of fatigue, mood and the prejudice of a particular officer. It means that it should be bought consciously. An institution needs a transferable justification, an audit of disparities, a right to rectification, an emergency procedure with a human and a regular test of whether the original reasons for the model still hold. Default is visible in indicators of non-performing loans and in impairment allowances. A false rejection does not appear in the portfolio of granted loans. If a model learns predominantly from the results of previously approved customers, a risk of selection bias arises; the particular impact must be shown by an audit of the data and of rejected applications. The best system is therefore not the one that never errs. We do not have such a system today. Nor is it the system with the highest AUC, the fastest click or the longest list of variables. It is the system whose abilities match the actual work and whose errors are visible, reversible and economically and humanly bearable . At the moment when the model only ranks files, we are choosing an assistant. At the moment when it reads an account, selects sources, sets a threshold and itself says no, we are also choosing a new structure of accountability. And then the question is no longer: “Is the algorithm more accurate than a human?” What decides is which error we will see in time, who can review it and who will bear the price of an invisible rejection. — Jiný Kontext

items.title: The law targets housing need. It will not solve high housing costs on its own
items.subtitle: The Housing Support Act targets people without adequate housing, people at risk of losing it, and some households left below the subsistence minimum after the benefit and actual costs. Not every household with expensive rent will qualify; a valid lease alone does not exclude it.

items.body: The Housing Support Act can open a contact point and set an assessment of need, but that does not automatically create a vacant flat. A household with a valid tenancy may fall inside the statutory regime, or outside it, depending on its income, costs and the risk of losing its home. A high rent-to-income ratio is an important signal. It is not, by itself, a universal test of entitlement. What we know / What we do not know What we know: The Act distinguishes inadequate housing, an immediate risk of losing it, and further conditions for support measures. A high rent-to-income ratio alone is not the only statutory test. What we do not know: Without data on the household, benefits, actual costs, legal title and the specific threat, this article cannot determine an individual entitlement. The Act also does not itself create the missing flats. 1. Need and expensive rent are not the same thing Imagine a meeting on the Housing Support Act. The minister for regional development reads that the statute will protect 1.6 million people from falling into need and that it can help up to 53 000 households already in need. The director of the Labour Office recalls that from 1 September 2026 his office decides on support measures. The mayor of a municipality with extended powers says the contact point gives advice but has no vacant flat. A shelter worker reports that without a guarantee the owner will not sign. An analyst shows that 154 000 people in housing need is not the same as 1.6 million at risk. A tenant in a regional city, paying CZK 22 000 for a two-room flat, asks whether the law is aimed at her as well. At first glance this is a dispute about whether the state is “finally dealing with housing”. In fact each person is describing a different object. The minister compares the instrument’s capacity with its preventive ambition. The Labour Office describes the decision agenda. The mayor describes the local stock. The outreach worker describes owners’ willingness. The analyst describes the definition. The tenant describes a market price that does not appear in a law on housing need. The claim that “the era of affordable housing has begun” joins problems that have different instruments. Legal title, the technical fitness of the dwelling, the risk of losing housing, the share of costs in income, the availability of support and the real number of flats in the municipality have to be kept apart. The first important distinction is therefore not whether the Act is pointless. It is what exactly is to be assessed . Otherwise we set a hostel, a market tenancy, a mortgage and a municipal flat side by side and are surprised that each wins a different contest. Need is not expensive rent. A benefit is not a flat. Advice is not a key. And the sieve of the Act is not the market. — Jiný Kontext From housing need to a vacant home An illustrative chain from physical space to stock in the municipality. From housing need to a vacant home Space Title Income Tool Stock JINÝ KONTEXT Illustrative diagram: The chain shows conditions, not the success of the law and not the housing stock of a particular town. 2. From legal title to an affordable flat When the ministry website says “the law will help”, it is easy to hear that it will help everyone who pays a lot for a roof. The outcome is usually produced in a chain of layers. Each layer can raise help, lower it or change the type of error. Two people with the same rent may therefore not fall into the same column, and the same person may look different according to whether they have title, whether the subsistence minimum remains after housing costs, or whether they face a notice to quit within three months. Five layers of one situation Physical space: whether there is a roof, water, heat, safety. Legal title: tenancy, subtenancy, hostel without protection, no title. Income after housing: what remains after rent and energy. Instrument: advice, benefit, guarantee, assistance, municipal flat. Supply: whether the municipality has a unit into which the instruments can be placed. Space decides whether this is a matter of survival, but it is not the only criterion. A person in a shelter may meet the conditions; a household in an ordinary flat may also meet them in some circumstances, for example if after the benefit and actual costs it does not reach the subsistence minimum, or if it is at risk of losing its home. Spending 60% of income on rent does not by itself create an entitlement. A benefit can cut the cost without building a wall; a guarantee can run into missing supply. This is where the first error in public comparisons appears. A headline announces that “the state is finally building affordability”, but in fact it is comparing a safety net with housing policy. Or it counts contact points and treats the result as a count of keys. An honest comparison must state not only the number of the Act, but also the definition of need, the capacity of the measures, the state of the stock, and what remains in the benefit system. Separating need from the market is not decoration on a section. It decides where to turn when something fails. If the applicant did not meet § 17, the title of need may have been missing, not the willingness of the office. If they met the title and found no flat, the stock may have failed. If they found a flat and lost it within a year, assistance may have failed. The sentence “the law does not work” is the start of a diagnosis, not the end of one. Illustrative scheme: The same rent can, in another layer, with another title and another instrument, produce another entitlement. 3. The best law is the one whose error you can see The breadth of a political promise does not show how the system will catch a particular household. Help withheld from a person at immediate risk can have a fast and hard-to-reverse effect. For a high-cost household with a valid tenancy, the statutory conditions have to be checked first; neither the form itself nor a general cost-overburden indicator proves an entitlement. A missing flat, moreover, cannot be repaired by correcting an application. Act No. 175/2025 Coll., on the provision of certain measures in support of housing, as amended by Act No. 129/2026 Coll., is calibrated to obtaining and keeping housing for people in need and people at risk of need. The RIA on the draft sets the aim of reducing the scale of need, preventing it, and shortening the time a household remains in it. That is the purpose of the text. It is not the purpose of regulating market rents. [1] [2] Type of failure What it looks like How to test it What limits the harm Swapping the population 1.6 million is read as the target of direct help Separate need, risk and cost overburden Two figures in every sentence about “help” Swapping the instrument Advice is read as a key Number of decisions vs. number of placements A trail from application to contract Swapping the stock A guarantee is read as a new flat Number of recorded units in the municipality A map of empty flats, not a map of offices Swapping a benefit and a wall An allowance is read as affordability Whether market rent fell, or only the top-up A separate price series and a benefit series That also changes the evaluation question. We do not ask only which law promises the most. We ask which error in our process we will catch. Fieldwork can tolerate a narrow sieve, because a hostel cannot wait for construction. A statistician can tolerate a wide at-risk figure as prevention. A tenant paying CZK 22 000 in rent cannot tolerate both being read as her benefit. The Act has to be judged by who meets the conditions, how long the path from application to help takes, and whether the municipality has real capacity. A clear trail from assessment to a concrete result says more than a wide headline without data on flats. 4. What the ETHOS typology measures The FEANTSA ETHOS typology classifies homelessness and housing exclusion: roofless, houseless, insecure housing, inadequate housing. The Czech Act takes an operational sieve from this map, not the whole European vocabulary. The RIA on the Act states that in 2022 roughly 67 thousand households, with roughly 154 thousand people, lived in housing need in the Czech Republic, with an average household size of 2.28 persons. That is an estimate from sources available for 2022, not a 2026 census. [3] [4] Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext Eurostat measures something else: housing cost overburden, the share of people in households where housing costs, after benefits, exceed 40% of disposable income. In 2024 that share was 9.2% in the Czech Republic and 8.2% in the EU. For tenants at market rent the burden is higher than for owners. This is a SILC survey, not a count of people without a roof. Adding 154 000 and 9.2% into one “housing problem” is a methodological error. [11] [12] Five facts without which a “housing crisis” is only an advertising number Whether this is need under ETHOS / § 17, or a cost-to-income ratio. Period and source: RIA 2022, SILC 2024, a ministry factsheet. Unit: person, household, application, placement. What the instrument can do: advice, guarantee, assistance, building. Whether the municipality has a unit that the instrument can fit into. For policy, therefore, a small internal count of keys matters more than someone else’s headline total of people at risk. Thirty real households from one ORP — with title, income, application date and contract date — can say more than 1.6 million on a leaflet. A public typology helps select candidates. The decision has to be made by work with the definition. Need has several conditions at once Law, benefit, municipality and stock converge on the household’s result. Need has several conditions at once Law Benefit Municipality Stock Need JINÝ KONTEXT Interpretive diagram: Position and size do not rate a municipality; the diagram shows simultaneous conditions. 5. Compare instruments, not headlines The table sorts housing instruments by the problem they are meant to solve: statutory need, high costs, construction or local capacity. For each it states the fact without which the result cannot be judged. Instrument Main position What to check Typical reason for choosing it Housing Support Act Need and the threat of loss § 17, capacity of 53 000 households To integrate the hostel and the shelter Contact point Advice, map, confirmation Whether it ends in advice or a contract A low entry threshold Labour Office Decision on a measure Deadline, ping-pong with the municipality Uniform decision-making Housing benefit Share of costs in income Spending and number of recipients, not the stock To lower the bill of an existing flat Municipal / investment stock Physical units Number of completed flats To change supply Housing First Rapid placement + assistance Retention, not the number of briefings Stability after the key The rows are not a verdict on the quality of the Act. The same state offers several instruments, and each can change during the year by amendment. The map is there to prevent another error: that the reader buys an excellent instrument in a product that does not see their problem, cannot finish it with a key, or locks them onto a waiting list from which it is later hard to leave. How to read the scheme: The size of a political promise does not express the number of available flats. The diagram separates statutory assessment, a service and actual housing capacity. 6. Housing need is not expensive rent In public debate two indicators are mixed. Housing need under the Act works with the absence of adequate housing, the threat of losing it and further conditions. Eurostat, by contrast, tracks cost overburden once housing costs exceed 40% of disposable income. That European indicator is not itself a statutory test of entitlement. Some heavily burdened households may nonetheless meet the statutory conditions on income after the benefit and actual costs, on legal title, or on an immediate risk of losing housing. [1] [11] Imagine two neighbours; this is only an illustration. Ms Marie, a single parent, lives in a market tenancy, pays CZK 19 000 and has a net income of CZK 28 000. Entitlement cannot be read from these three figures: household composition, the state social-assistance benefit, actual costs, the state of legal title and any threat of loss are missing. Mr Karel lives in a hostel without a stable legal title or income. His situation may fit the statutory categories, but even then the office must check every condition and the necessity of a measure. The Act is aimed first at obtaining and keeping adequate housing, not at a blanket cut in market rents. That does not mean Marie can be ruled out in advance, or Karel accepted automatically. Entitlement is decided by statutory conditions, not by a stock story. 7. Anatomy of the Act: who is inside the sieve The Act and Amendment No. 129/2026 Coll. work in § 17 with several paths: the applicant is without adequate housing and cannot obtain it; that situation threatens them in the next three months; or without a support measure they cannot obtain or keep adequate housing. Necessity of the measure and further statutory conditions are also checked. The rules around income, the benefit and actual costs mean that a valid tenancy title does not, by itself, automatically exclude a household. The amendment takes effect in its main parts on 1 September 2026; a decision therefore has to use the consolidated wording in force on that day. [1] [5] Advice at the contact point is more open than the direct measures. Landlord guarantees, contributions to deposits and housing assistance are reserved for the at-risk segment. That is not a hidden clause. It is the design. Anyone who reads a leaflet saying it “will help everyone” is reading a different document from the Collection of Laws. [2] [6] The statutory categories can include people without shelter, people in shelters and hostels, victims of domestic violence, families in inadequate premises and some households with an ordinary tenancy who meet the income and other conditions. A high rent share and the unaffordability of a mortgage do not, by themselves, create an entitlement. A specific classification cannot be decided from a single trait. Who passes the sieve and who does not The first test is title: does the applicant have a contract, or only an oral promise? The second is time: is loss threatened within the horizon the Act knows, or is this chronic expense? The third is what remains of income after rent. Without these three, “I need help” is not the same as an entitlement. An office that confuses them does Karel an injustice, or Marie a false hope. A law does not build a wall An entitlement in the scheme and available housing stock belong to different questions. A law does not build a wall Law Stock Entitlement Advice Home Key Wall JINÝ KONTEXT Interpretive diagram: The sides are not a housing count; they separate the legal sieve from missing supply. 8. The figures: one hundred and fifty-four thousand, 1.6 million, fifty-three thousand Government communication works with several populations at once. 154 000 people, roughly 67 000 households, is the estimate of people in direct housing need according to the RIA from data for 2022. 1.6 million people is, in Ministry for Regional Development (MMR) materials, the number at risk of falling into need; the factsheet promises that the Act will “protect” them. The target capacity of direct measures is, in the same communication, up to 53 000 households in need. The RIA further models a fall in households in need from 67 500 towards 60 000 in 2028 and to 50 000 later; without the Act it expects a slight rise. That is a projection, not a measured result for 2026. [2] [4] [6] The Act therefore does not aim a direct guarantee at 1.6 million people with expensive rent. It aims at a narrow segment and at the same time promises prevention for a wider group, mainly through advice and early capture. Those can be two true sentences. They must not be added into one. The Czech Statistical Office (ČSÚ) records spending on the housing allowance of CZK 20.297 billion in 2024. In the first half of 2024 the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs (MPSV) reports an average of 270.2 thousand housing allowances paid a month, at an average amount of CZK 6 122. That is a benefit system. It is not a count of guaranteed flats. Anyone who reads a falling or rising benefit bill as proof that the need Act “made housing cheaper” is measuring a different column. [13] [14] What has to be tested The first test is the denominator: 53 000 households out of how many? Out of 67 000 in need, or out of 1.6 million at risk? The second is time: capacity “over a few years” is not the state of play in September 2026. The third is the result: the number of decisions on a measure versus the number of signed tenancies. Without the third figure, capacity is a promise, not a key. 9. A contact point is not a key. The Labour Office is not a flat Competences shifted after Amendment No. 129/2026 Coll. From 1 September 2026 there is to be a contact point in every municipality with extended powers; a ČTK report on the Senate debate gave a rise from 115 to 205 points. Advice remains with the municipalities. The Labour Office is to keep a register of flats and decide applications for support measures. The Union of Towns and Municipalities and the Association of Local Governments warned, before implementation, of overload and of people being sent back and forth between the town hall and the office. That is an institutional risk, not proof that officials cannot give advice. [5] [7] [8] Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext Two similar counters can therefore run on different data. The municipality knows the house in the street. The Labour Office knows the file. The applicant knows both as one path. If confirmation that a flat is suitable, the decision on a guarantee and the key to the lock are split across three desks, we are measuring ping-pong even when each desk is doing its job correctly. Before switching on praise for the network Count the contact points and the average time from application to contract. Separate advice from the decision, and the decision from placement. Find out who records the flat and who physically has it. Check that the applicant can see what stage the file is at. Do not treat a map of 205 dots as a map of 205 vacant flats. The Act’s greatest advantage may therefore not be a new power. It may be order in who is allowed to promise what. And the greatest weakness may not be the definition of need. It may be a truthful decision on a guarantee for a flat that is not in the municipality. 10. A rent guarantee does not replace a wall A key limit of the Act is that it does not create new physical flats. Help rests on motivating private owners to let a vacant unit in exchange for a state rent guarantee and assistance. If a region has no empty flats, registers of vetted applicants without units appear. That is not a failure of the guarantee as insurance of the owner’s risk. It is a collision with supply. Housing First and the methods of the Platform for Social Housing rest on rapid placement and support in the flat, not on waiting until the client is “ready”. This approach also needs a flat. A principle is not a stock. Czech experience with housing-first projects shows that assistance reduces a return to the hostel. It does not cut the price of a new building. [18] The State Investment Support Fund and municipal building are another column. If the need Act is not followed by an investment programme on the scale of units the RIA assumes, the system organises a queue in scarcity. That can be said without guessing how many flats are “missing in the whole country” — such a sum would need a single definition, which public statistics do not give in one figure. It can be said that an instrument without a unit ends on a waiting list. The OECD Affordable Housing Database shows that the Czech Republic has a low share of rental housing relative to owner-occupation and that the burden on tenants is higher than the burden on owners. That is an international comparison of structures, not an audit of Act 175/2025. It does, however, recall that a benefit and a guarantee in a country with a thin rental market hit a ceiling that only a brick can raise. [15] 11. A benefit is a raw material. It is not a housing result The market uses several languages of help at once. The need Act speaks of a measure and a guarantee. MPSV speaks of an allowance and a supplement, later of a single state social-assistance benefit. ČSÚ speaks of CZK 20.3 billion spent on the housing allowance in 2024. The municipality speaks of flats it owns. A direct comparison that “help rose because benefit spending rose” misleads. Cheap advice at the contact point can be excellent in a dispute over a notice to quit. The same advice is expensive if it is read as a solution to CZK 19 000 of rent. An expensive guarantee can be pointless where the owner would let the flat anyway. It can be cheaper in Karel’s case if it ends a hostel stay and cuts the cost of crisis services. The RIA estimates the social costs of need in the order of billions of crowns a year and a saving if need falls; that is a model in an impact assessment, not a line in the 2026 budget. [4] [6] The real price of accepted housing Advice + decision + guarantee + assistance + benefit + a missing flat + waiting + a return to the hostel + future building. The result is cheap only once the household lives under an adequate title and that can be checked. Not once a counter opens. The costs also include churn. If the same application comes back three times for completion, the average price of a placement is not the price of one visit. If the office exhausts assistance capacity at a peak, the cost is the loss of the flat after move-in. If promises are tied hard to a headline of 1.6 million, the cost is also Marie’s loss of trust — the Act never promised her a key; she only read it that way. It is therefore useful to measure the price per accepted key , not per number of points. Accepted means a contract, a move-in and retention. That metric can reverse a ranking that looked obvious from the factsheet. 12. How to read statistics of need Before the Act, the reader had to trust the field. With the Act they check something more complicated: whether the figure measures need or risk, whether 53 000 is capacity or a stock, whether 205 points are advice or a flat, and whether the conclusion really follows from § 17. A figure is navigation towards evidence. It is not automatic proof. One report can combine three true figures into a false conclusion. The first is 154 000 people in need as of 2022. The second is 1.6 million at risk in MMR communication. The third is 9.2% cost overburden in SILC 2024. Each figure works. The synthesis “the Act will solve expensive housing” is methodologically wrong. Elsewhere a report uses the number of contact points as proof that “the system is running”, even though only the front door is running. A four-step check of a figure Existence: the figure is in the RIA, in the Collection of Laws, at ČSÚ or at Eurostat. Unit: person, household, point, decision, contract. Support: a specific passage supports a specific sentence. Scope: the year, the definition of need and what the instrument does not build all fit. An impact check starts with a table of claims, statutory conditions and known limits. The headline should come after that. An untraceable count of households actually housed cannot be replaced by the Act’s date of effect. Three tests of a promise The first is definitional: does the sentence speak of need, or of rent? The second is about capacity: 53 000 households when, and with what stock? The third is contradictory: are market rents rising in the same municipality where contact points are multiplying? A product that announces effect a day earlier is not necessarily better if, a year later, no one can find how many keys came from it. 13. Supply is not a switch. It is the whole stock The question “do we have a law?” is important but narrow. A municipality also has to know how many vacant municipal flats it has, how many private owners have entered the register, how long assistance lasts, who pays the social worker after the subsidy ends, and whether the flat returns to the same stock after a move-out. “We have a contact point” does not mean “we have a unit” or “we have retention”. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext Differences between ORPs are larger than the difference between sections. Prague and an Ostrava hostel are not the same. A rural municipality with five flats in its ownership and a city with a developer who does not build rental housing need a different column. SMS ČR repeatedly points to the limits of municipal budgets. That is a local account. It is not a veto of the Act. [8] The practical minimum is a map of the stock. It starts with the applicant, continues through the contact point, the Labour Office, the register of flats, the guarantee and assistance, and ends at the place where the household can be lost again. Without that map, a claim about support is only a description of one counter. The Association of Rental Housing and market rent indexes measure a different series from the RIA. If commercial rents do not fall after the Act starts, that is not a falsification of the need instrument. It is information that the instrument was not aimed at the market. It would be a falsification if we had expected rents to fall because of the Act. We should not expect that in an evaluation that holds the definition. [19] 14. What to choose as an instrument The first step is to name the kind of housing situation and the matching statutory instrument. The table proposes a comparison on the same household, in the same city and over the same time horizon. Need First instrument Decisive test Unacceptable shortcut Leave a hostel Support Act + guarantee + assistance A contract and retention, not a count of advice Reading 205 points as 205 flats Prevent the loss of a flat Advice + a timely benefit Whether the notice fell or did not Waiting for need under § 17 Cut the rent share of income A benefit, or a norm Spending and what remains after housing Waiting for the need Act to cheapen the market Raise supply Municipal and cooperative building, SFPI Completed units A guarantee as a substitute for a wall Stability after move-in Housing First, assistance A return to the hostel within 12 months A key without a worker A mortgage for the young Credit and tax instruments Ability to repay, not ETHOS Mixing this with need Czech use needs a separate municipal test. A nationwide RIA will not measure whether a given ORP has a flat the Act can pay for. The test set should include a hostel, a shelter, Marie’s market tenancy, a notice within three months, and a municipality without empty units, where the right answer is “there is an entitlement, there is no flat”. Some teams will in the end need more than one system. One for need, a second for the benefit, a third for building. That is not a failure of unity. It is the same decision as using one tool for the fire service and another for the land-use plan. The condition is that the split is intelligible, that promises do not migrate between columns, and that people know where the final key is produced. 15. A short test that says more than a press release An evaluation can be done without a decade-long fight over a “right to a flat” and without an impulsive column that “the law failed because rents did not fall”. A short, disciplined audit is enough. Its aim is not to prove that the statute can do something impressive. Its aim is to find situations in which the promise fails, and to see whether the state can catch them. Fourteen days from the factsheet to the waiting list Days 1–2: List 20 to 40 real households: need, risk, expensive rent, no flat. Days 3–4: Assign each a section, an instrument and whether a unit exists in the municipality. Days 5–7: Follow the trail from the contact point through the Labour Office to a contract. Days 8–10: Separate advice, the decision, the guarantee, the key and assistance after move-in. Days 11–12: Count the price of an accepted placement, including waiting. Day 13: Stress tests: a municipality without flats, a notice to quit, a victim of violence, Marie with CZK 19 000 rent. Day 14: Decide which promise may go in the headline, document the reservation and the revision date. The evaluator should preferably not know whether the Act is to be praised. In cases of need they watch placement. In cases of risk, whether the loss of the flat did not happen. On the market, whether the market is being measured at all. Each failure is classified: a confabulated population, an omitted stock, a deadline error, or a conclusion that § 17 did not carry. The conditions have to be comparable. The same ORP, the same month. If one factsheet is allowed to add 1.6 million and 53 000, we are testing finished communication — but we have to name it as such. A pilot should also have exclusion conditions. For example: the single sentence “affordability has begun”, the use of SILC as proof about hostels, or an inability to count placements. A high score for a network of points must not outrank an error whose effect is a waiting list without keys. The last output is not only a grade for the Act. It is an operating rule: what the statute is used for, what it is not used for, which household may enter the promise, what must exist in the stock, and when the evaluation will be opened again. Amendments, benefits and municipalities change. Without a revision date even a good audit slowly turns into a housing superstition. 16. Municipality, market and state: three accounts, one waiting list A municipality has flats, or it does not. The market has listings, or excess demand. The state has a law, a benefit and a guarantee. In a headline the three accounts like to be added together. In the field they do not add. A municipality that sold its stock in the noughties cannot manufacture a wall out of a guarantee. A market that builds owner-occupied housing will not sell Karel a tenancy. A state that promises 53 000 households needs the two earlier accounts to meet, at least in part. That does not mean the Act should wait for construction. Need cannot bear a ten-year cycle. It means the evaluation should hold two times: Karel’s crisis time and the investment time of supply. Anyone who reads the first time as the second harms Karel. Anyone who reads the second time as if the first were already done harms Marie with hope. The government regulation on the amount of contributions under the Housing Support Act and the decree on the scope of assistance are the operating layer. They decide how much money and which activities travel with the flat. They do not change the number of flats. Anyone who does not read them does not know what happens after the signature. Anyone who reads them in place of the land-use plan is again measuring a raw material as a result. [20] [21] 17. Need and unaffordability need different instruments The first generation of housing policy sold municipal flats. The next sold a benefit. The next sold a law on need. Today’s headlines sell something larger: the impression that one statute is the whole housing market. The contest is therefore not only over the best ETHOS definition. It also decides whether Marie stops waiting for a key the Act does not automatically promise her, whether Karel, once he meets the conditions, receives a matching support measure, and whether the municipality has real housing capacity. The more comfortable a single headline is, the higher the price of the swap can be. Waiting lists are hard to explain, and people then stop telling need from high cost. That does not mean the Act is a bad one. A narrow sieve often creates the greatest use where a hostel and a child in a crisis facility are at stake. It means the purchase should be conscious. We need a portable definition, a documented stock, the ability to change the promise when there is no flat, and an emergency procedure without the illusion that a benefit is a wall. The best law is therefore not the one that never leaves anyone outside. Such a text would cease to be a law on need. Nor is it the law with the largest figure on the leaflet, the densest network of points or the longest explanatory report. It is the law whose sieve matches need and whose errors of reading are visible, reversible and tolerable in the headline . The moment the statute only advises, we are choosing a counter. The moment it sorts people, promises a guarantee, waits for a flat and teaches the newspapers what affordability is, we are also choosing a new structure of responsibility for words. And then the question is no longer: “Did the law solve housing?” What decides is to whom the Act offers a concrete measure, where an available flat is, and what remains the task of broader housing policy. — Jiný Kontext

items.title: A voice assistant on a child’s phone: an answer is not the same as a dialogue
items.subtitle: A voice assistant can answer quickly and patiently in a particular interaction, but its behaviour differs by product and settings. Research describes risks of excessive trust, communication failures and data processing; it does not prove that every use crowds out human dialogue.
