items.body: The figures 30.5, 17 and 5.0 per cent are point estimates, not exact vote counts. A methodologically correct calculation can still be read too strongly in a headline, especially for a one-point change or for a party on the five-per-cent edge. A nationwide Chamber of Deputies model, moreover, does not describe the result in a particular municipality or Senate constituency. What we know / What we do not know What we know: The August wave of Trendy Česka used fieldwork on 3–21 August 2026, a CATI/CAWI mix, 1,200 respondents and 991 respondents included in the election model. Czech Television published point estimates and a range of statistical error of ±1.0 to ±3.3 percentage points according to the size of support. [1] What we do not know: From the public article we do not know every parameter needed for a precise interval of the difference between the May and August waves — in particular the covariance, the detailed design effect and the procedure used for a given pair of estimates. The change therefore cannot be tested by a simple comparison with the error of a single wave. [19] 1. A point that lies inside measurement error Imagine a Sunday meeting in a television newsroom. The editor-in-chief wants ANO’s number, because the graphic must have a winner. The statistician wants an interval, because without it the point is only decoration. The political reporter wants a story about a shift towards STAN, because without a story the discussion will not open. The party spokesperson wants “the opponent’s collapse”, because a campaign lives off movement. The sociologist wants to warn that 991 people are not ten million. The viewer wants to know “who is ahead”. At first glance this is a dispute about courage. In fact each person is describing a different problem. The editor-in-chief compares intelligibility. The statistician sampling error. The reporter a narrative. The spokesperson a fight over the frame. The sociologist the population from which inference is drawn. The viewer a desire for a ranking. Each role in the newsroom pursues a different aim, but a point estimate without its uncertainty can create a conclusion that the data do not support. The phrase “mood of the nation” here conceals the selection of respondents, weighting, the wording of the question, the list of parties, declared turnout and the fieldwork period. First it is necessary to determine whether we are comparing point estimates, their uncertainty, the composition of the party list, or actual votes . Each of these quantities answers a different question. A point is not a mood. A mood is not turnout. Turnout is not a mandate. And a headline is not a measurement. — Jiný Kontext 2. From the respondent to the number on television When 30.5% appears on screen, it is easy to form the impression that “this is how the Czech Republic votes”. The figure, however, arises in a chain. Each layer can raise, lower or change the kind of error. Two estimates with the same logo therefore need not measure the same thing, and the same estimate can behave differently according to whether we read the point, the interval, or the headline. Six layers of a single percentage Population: adults in the Czech Republic, not “the nation in its soul”. Sample: who was reached, who refused, who entered the model. Question and list: a stand-alone party, or a coalition. Weighting: certainty of turnout, quotas, corrections. Measurement error: the published range of statistical error and the information the agency gives about how it was constructed. Publication frame: graphic, headline, commentary, sharing. Kantar CZ’s Trendy Česka project for Czech Television is one of the longest-running surveys of this type in the country. That matters, and it is not immunity from the layers. The official description of the August 2026 wave states fieldwork from 3 to 21 August, CATI and CAWI techniques, a representative sample of 1,200 respondents by sex, age, region, education and place of residence, and the entry of 991 respondents into the election model — those who do not rule out voting. In this wave the agency states the model’s statistical error in the range ±1.0 percentage point for parties with a low share to ±3.3 percentage points for parties with a high share . [1] Distinguishing the layers is not a methodological ornament. It determines where to turn in a dispute. If the point moves by one percentage point for a party with a high share, the appetite of the headline may have failed, not the population. If SPD is measured without partners and compared with a coalition result at the ballot box, the list in the question has failed. If a mayor is read from the model, the unit has failed. The sentence “the poll got it wrong” is the start of a diagnosis, not its end. Illustrative scheme: The same point estimate can, in a different interval, with a different question and a different headline, produce a different conclusion. Comparing a point with the ballot box without the layers is the same error as comparing a thermometer with a month-ahead forecast. 3. How costly an error in the headline is The ranking of parties is only part of the information; the meaning of an error depends on its impact. A typo in an infobox can be corrected quickly. A headline about a “fall below five per cent” is far more serious if the published error range crosses both sides of the threshold and a later correction no longer reaches the same audience. ESOMAR and WAPOR, in their guideline on published polls, require that the public be given enough information to judge quality: who measured, when, whom, with what question, how large the sample was and what the uncertainty is. [2] The ICC/ESOMAR code and the Czech SIMAR standards translate the same demand into the operating language of member agencies. [3] [4] It does not follow that every graphic is a fraud. It follows that publication without an interval fails in a different discipline from the calculation. Type of failure What it looks like How to test it What limits the harm A point instead of uncertainty “It fell by a point” Is the uncertainty of the difference between both waves published? The point and the uncertainty in the graphic The threshold as certainty “Six parties in the Chamber” Does the interval cross 5%? Ban a binary reading at the edge Coalition artefact Comparing a party with a coalition at the ballot box The same list in the question? A description of what was merged Non-response The willing speak, the tired stay silent Who refused, whom the weight does not catch Humility towards the unknown remainder A swapped unit A Chamber model as a municipality A different law, a different contest Separate the type of election That also changes the editorial question. We do not ask only which estimate hit the average. We ask which way of publishing will fail so that the reader still sees it. An analytical programme can tolerate ten nuances. A news ticker cannot tolerate a single certainty where the agency itself draws a range of several points. The quality of publication depends not only on the model, but also on the visibility of uncertainty and on the strength of the conclusion in the headline. A clear methodology and cautious wording are more useful for public debate than a sharp number without explanation. 4. What can be read from the published error Polls are needed because they replace part of impression with a systematic estimate. The problem arises at the moment when one number starts to represent a party’s exact support. For the August 2026 wave Kantar published a range of statistical error of ±1.0 to ±3.3 percentage points . [1] This information belongs with the point estimate, not only in a methodological note. For a party with a high share, according to the published description, the upper bound of this range applies. ANO’s point estimate of 30.5% can thus, after simply subtracting and adding the published error of one wave, be written as an indicative band of 27.2 to 33.8% . This is not a formal confidence interval: the public article does not state a confidence level, nor whether the published error fully includes weighting and sample design. Czech Television also reported a month-on-month drop of one percentage point. [1] The statistical significance of this difference cannot be judged by comparing one point with the error of the August estimate. We need the standard error of the difference of both waves and information about their dependence; with independent samples the errors combine, with an overlap of respondents covariance enters the calculation. [19] The published figures therefore do not by themselves suffice for a strong headline about change, nor for the claim that support has not changed. For a party with a low share the agency states ±1.0 percentage point. The Motorists’ point estimate of 5.0% is therefore not the sentence “a sixth party in the Chamber”. Simply subtracting and adding the published error gives only an indicative band of 4.0 to 6.0% , not a documented formal confidence interval; the band reaches both sides of the electoral threshold. [1] [5] Act No. 247/1995 Coll. sets a five-per-cent threshold for a party’s entry into scrutiny; the model does not vote the threshold. [5] Five facts without which a point is only a promotional number The size of the survey sample and the size of the model subsample. The fieldwork period and technique (telephone, online, mix). The wording of the question and whether parties stood separately or in a coalition. The error interval at the given size of share , not “some plus or minus”. What the wave does not measure: the ballot box, a municipality, the Senate, tomorrow’s affair. For the purchase of political calm, therefore, a small honest interval matters more than someone else’s overall ranking. Thirty genuine readings with an interval say more than a thousand shares of a point. 5. Compare constructions, not party mascots The market of models can be described without a false podium of winners. The following map does not say who hit the voter’s soul. It shows around what work the individual constructions build an estimate, and which failure the reader should look for on purpose. Construction Main working position What to check when reading Typical reason for use Kantar / Czech Television, Trendy Česka A hypothetical Chamber, CATI/CAWI mix The wave’s interval, the model’s n, the party list A long series, a public methodology Another agency model A different sample, a different question, a different weight Whether points can be compared across agencies A second estimate, not a clash of logos Aggregation of several waves An average of maps, not an average of souls The weight of n, the age of the fieldwork Damped noise of a single wave The result at the ballot box Actual votes in the given type of election A different law, different turnout The only verdict on seats A municipal / Senate map Thousands of contests, constituencies, a second round A ban on reading from the nationwide model A different unit The table does not rate agencies as a whole. It separates different outputs so that the reader does not mistake a well-calculated model for an unduly certain headline, nor a single wave for a confirmed trend. Interpretive scheme: The columns of the table are not an accounting statement of support. They separate the estimate, the interval, the threshold and the ballot box. 6. Anatomy of a wave: what Kantar actually calculated in August 2026 On the August wave Czech Television reported point estimates and, at the same time, a frame of error. Honest reading holds both in one sentence, not the point in the headline and the interval in a note. [1] Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext Subject Wave point estimate Error Kantar states for the size of share Indicative band from simply subtracting/adding the published error What a headline can bear ANO 30.5% ±3.3 p.p. (high share) 27.2–33.8% A stable first band, not “a fall of a point” STAN 17% in the wave’s range of ±1.0 to ±3.3 p.p. a band of several points around 17 Direction can be watched in a series, not in a single point ODS 15.5% the same range of the wave a band around 15.5 “Stagnation” is often noise Pirates 8.5% the same range of the wave a band around 8.5 A one-point move is weak evidence SPD 6.5% closer to the lower bound of the range a band around 6.5 Comparison with a coalition at the ballot box separately Motorists 5.0% ±1.0 p.p. (low share) 4.0–6.0% The indicative band reaches both sides of the threshold On ANO, Czech Television reported a drop of one point against May and of four points against the election result; on STAN a rise of 1.5 points against May and of six against the election. [1] Comparison with the last ballot box and with the previous research wave are two different things: turnout, the list and the method of measurement all change. Without the uncertainty of the difference, a one-point month-on-month move cannot itself be labelled a statistically demonstrated change. A series of more comparable waves can support a trend, but this article does not determine one from a single pair. [19] Estimated turnout in the same wave was 62.5% of citizens aged over 18; Kantar added that since March the indicator has not changed markedly and that interest usually rises only before an election is held. [1] This is a declaration in a questionnaire, not turnout measured at the ballot box. What needs to be tested The first test is statistical: do we know the uncertainty of the difference between the two waves being compared, or only the error of each point separately? The second is about the list: did the parties stand in the question as they last stood at the ballot box? The third is temporal: which days were used for fieldwork and which event fell into them. The fourth is about the unit: does the text speak of the Chamber, or already of a municipality? For an individual who wants one broad orientation, the Trendy Česka series may be decisive. For a newsroom the sentence “we have Kantar” is not enough. It needs to know n, the interval, the question and the boundary beyond which a person must approve the headline. 7. A coalition is not the sum of parties. A party is not a coalition A second source of crooked reading is the form of the list. If the model tests parties separately — SPD without partners, or ODS, TOP 09 and KDU-ČSL apart — it measures a different thing from the one a pre-election coalition assembled at the ballot box. [1] [6] That is not evidence of an outflow. It is a change of object. Comparing a separately measured party with a past coalition result is a comparison of two accounting axes. Support may genuinely have fallen. It may have fallen only because the adding-up on the ballot paper broke apart. Without the same list in the question this cannot be decided. Kostelecký, on a Czech example, describes a prediction model that combines a nationwide representative survey with the spatial distribution of support from previous elections, and explicitly addresses the conditions that affect the quality of the estimate. [6] Linek and Lyons analyse the long-term stability and change of party support in the years 1990–2010; their work is not evidence that a particular one-point move in the August 2026 wave represents a real change. [7] It does not follow that agencies “cannot count”. It follows that a model answers a particular question by means of particular data and assumptions. A pleasant style of graphic can conceal the same old problem: a smooth curve from two incommensurable points. The quality of the visual lowers the cost of reading. At the same time it can raise the cost of detecting a methodological error, because the line does not look suspicious. 8. Five per cent is a threshold in law. It is not a certainty of the graphic Headlines like to announce that six parties would enter the Chamber. For a party with a point estimate of 5.0% and a published error of ±1.0 percentage point , a simple calculation gives only an indicative band of 4.0–6.0% , which reaches both sides of the clause. It is not a formal confidence interval, because the public source does not describe its full construction. [1] [5] That means something more modest than “a sixth party”. It means that the wave does not know on which side of the legal threshold the party would finish if the election were held on the days of fieldwork. A binary break has a large impact on who would assemble a majority. Presenting the point 5.0 as a completed entry is therefore a crude simplification of the probabilistic nature of the data — and Kantar itself acknowledges that nature in the methodological sentence on error. The law on elections to Parliament sets the clause as a condition of scrutiny, not as a property of a preference on the telephone. [5] A model can estimate who might miss the threshold. It cannot abolish it or confirm it. A newsroom that turns a point into a seat is buying a certainty that a sample of 991 people at the edge does not have. 9. Who picks up the phone is not the same as who comes to vote Even the best model runs into willingness to respond. Groves and colleagues in Survey Methodology describe non-response as a structural feature, not as an isolated defect of a wave: more willing, more educated and more politically engaged people enter a survey differently from the tired and the unreachable. Weights try to correct this shift. They do not remove it without remainder. [8] The AAPOR Transparency Initiative and SIMAR rest on the demand that enough methodology be published for it to be possible to judge who is missing. [4] [9] It does not follow that the 1,200 people reached are a fraud. It follows that inference from 991 model respondents to millions of those entitled to vote is an estimate, not a census. Imagine an illustration, not a report. In July a fictitious Movement X has 22.4% in the model at n around 950. In August 21.1% at n around 980. In the table a minus of 1.3 points lights up. The headline writes of a crisis. The intervals of both waves overlap so widely that support in the population need not have moved. The narrative arose from noise. The names and figures of this illustration are not from Kantar; they are only meant to show the same arithmetic that the August wave itself, for large shares, acknowledges with a range of ±3.3. [1] 10. Declared turnout is a promise. Turnout at the ballot box is something else The August model estimated turnout at 62.5%. [1] The Czech Statistical Office, at actual elections, measures something else: how many of those entitled came to the ballot boxes in the given type of election, in the given round, in the given weather of the campaign. [10] A declaration in August and turnout in October are not two versions of the same column. The difference is not cosmetic. The result is decided by who comes on Saturday afternoon, what mobilisation there is in the last two days, and how many people with a fickle preference stay at home. Linek and Lyons describe this fickleness as part of Czech voting behaviour. [7] Kantar itself, on turnout in August 2026, noted that it has not changed markedly since March and that a rise in interest usually comes only before an election. [1] That is an honest reservation. A headline about “certain turnout” would erase it. Two similar columns can have a different data regime. The same percentage in the model and at the ballot box can arise from different people. A reading pilot must record which regime is being cited. Otherwise the newsroom tests the comfort of the graphic and by mistake issues it as a property of voters. 11. Uncertainty does not vanish after publication Before an interval was published, the reader had to sense that the number was not exact. With an interval the check is something more complicated: whether the headline cites the interval, or overrides it. A headline is navigation towards meaning. It is not automatic proof. A single report can combine three true figures into a false conclusion. First: ANO’s point is 30.5. Second: against May that is one point less. Third: in open questions voters mention promises. Each figure may be in the wave, but the synthesis “the nation has turned away” is wider than the data. At other times a newsroom cites a high-quality secondary comment even though a primary description of n, the fieldwork date and the error is available. [1] A pleasant headline can conceal the same old interval A well-cadenced sentence about “losing one’s breath” sounds like a mark of understanding. It is not one automatically. In news work it is necessary to check in particular whether the system has not mistaken a point for an interval, a stand-alone party for a coalition, the Chamber for a municipality. The quality of wording lowers the cost of reading. At the same time it can raise the cost of detecting a factual error, because the sentence does not look suspicious. A four-step check of the headline Existence: the number is in the wave and has a fieldwork date. Authority: the primary source is the agency and the client, not a copy of a copy. Support: for a claim about change, the uncertainty of the difference between waves is documented; the error of one wave is not enough. Scope: the population, type of election, coalition and unit fit. The most reliable working procedure therefore separates the table from the word. First a row is created: estimate, n, interval, question. Only then the headline. If the interval cannot be opened, a claim is not promoted to a fact merely because it declines well. 12. One model is not a market. Aggregation changes a different error Nate Silver in The Signal and the Noise shows that a single forecast can be noisy, while a set of forecasts with honest uncertainty can damp the noise — and that even then it fails when the model asks the wrong thing. [11] An aggregation of Czech waves is not Silver’s American exchange. It is only a reminder that a clash of agency logos on a single day measures differences of construction more than the voter’s soul. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext The report of an independent inquiry into the failure of British pre-election estimates in 2015 (the Royal Statistical Society and the related inquiry) showed that honest agencies can err in the same direction when sampling, weighting or willingness to respond fails, not when they “calculate the average badly”. [12] This is an audit of one particular election cycle in another country, not evidence that Czech models have no value. It does show, however, that a precise percentage can precisely measure a defective condition. The Czech SIMAR standards and the international ESOMAR/WAPOR guideline therefore insist on transparency of publication, not on a promise of infallibility. [2] [4] Act No. 234/2025 Coll. on election campaigns further addresses, among other things, campaign rules and related transparency of political advertising in Czech law; election laws have long restricted the publication of pre-election polls in the immediate vicinity of voting. That is a legal frame for dissemination, not a correction of the interval. [13] 13. The price of a point is the price of a raw material, not the price of a conclusion The market uses several languages at once. The agency pays for fieldwork. Television pays for intelligibility. A party pays for a campaign according to movement. The reader pays with attention. A direct comparison of “who fell by a tenth” without knowledge of the interval is therefore misleading. A cheap point can be economically excellent for orientation in the rough ranking of large camps whose intervals do not overlap. The same point can be expensive for a task on the five-per-cent edge that a newsroom repeats as a seat. An expensive paragraph on methodology can be pointless for a sporting ranking. It can be cheaper for a decision with a high cost of error if it reduces the number of unsuccessful narratives. The true price of an accepted conclusion Fieldwork + weighting + interval + human reading + verification of the question + correction of the headline + the price of a false movement + interruption of debate. A conclusion is cheap only once it has passed an interval check and can be used without embarrassment the next day. The costs also include fluctuation. If the same shift fits inside the error four times out of five, the average price of a “correct story” is not the price of one graphic. If the model, at the peak of a campaign, measures the affect of a week, the cost is the inertia of the headline. If campaign teams are tightly bound to a single number, the cost is also an inability to see another map. It is therefore useful to measure the price on the accepted reading , not the price on a point. Accepted means that the reading met criteria set in advance: the interval, the question, the unit, and did not cause a later correction that nobody reads any more. 14. What to read for which question Reasonable reading does not start with a party brand, but with the type of question and the control mechanism. The following recommendations are not a ranking of agencies. They are a signpost to a first reading. In each category it makes sense to choose two sources and compare them over the same period and with the same interval. Need First group of candidates Decisive test Unacceptable shortcut A rough ranking of large camps A public wave with n and an interval Do the intervals overlap? Choose by a single tenth The edge of the clause Estimate + lower/upper bound of error Does it cross 5%? “It is in the Chamber” from a point of 5.0 A trend A series of waves, not one month A shift outside the error repeatedly One point against the previous wave A coalition The same list as at the ballot box Party vs. bloc An artefact as an outflow A municipality and the Senate Local data, constituencies, a second round A different law Reading a mayor from Kantar Turnout A declaration vs. the CZSO series at the ballot box A different definition Mistaking a promise for arrival For Czech use a separate language test is necessary. The English “margin of error” translates badly here when all that remains is “plus or minus three” for every party alike. In August 2026 Kantar differentiated the range by the size of share . [1] A test set of headlines should include the five-per-cent edge, a coalition, a municipality and a text in which the correct answer is “the interval is not enough”. Some newsrooms eventually need more layers. One graphic with an interval, a second paragraph on the question, a third ban on reading the Senate. That is not a failure of intelligibility. It is the same decision as using a different tool for sport and a different one for the courts. The condition is that the division is visible and that people know where the final caution arises. 15. A short test that says more than a hundred headlines A reading can be chosen without a month-long seminar and without an impulsive “ANO is falling”. A short, disciplined checklist is enough. Its aim is not to prove that the wave can do something impressive. The aim is to find situations in which the reading fails, and to see whether the newsroom can catch them. Three tests of a single number The first test concerns the difference: is its own uncertainty available for the claimed shift, and are the waves comparable? The second is about origin: is it a primary wave, or a copy of a copy? The third is contradictory: is there an equally honest figure — another wave, another question, turnout at the ballot box — that calls the conclusion into question? A faster headline is not better if it later cannot be traced back to the measurement from which it arose. Before publishing a graphic Write the size of the survey and the size of the model. Write the interval for a high and for a low share. Separate the point that may stand in the table from the sentence that may stand in the headline. Mark whether the parties stood separately. Forbid reading a municipality and the Senate from the model if the model does not measure them. The conditions must be comparable. The same week, the same question, the same type of election. If one text may turn a point into history and another must carry an interval, we are not testing the estimate. We are testing the courage to be imprecise — and we must name it as such. The last output is not only the name of the winning party in the graphic. It is an operating rule: what the wave is used for, what it is not, which shift may enter the headline, what must be approved by an editor who knows the interval, and when the reading is opened again. Models, tariffs and campaigns change. Without a revision date even a good series gradually turns into an editorial superstition. 16. A Chamber model does not measure October in a municipality The last, often cheapest swap is the unit. In August 2026 Kantar measured a hypothetical Chamber of Deputies. [1] October 2026 is about municipal councils and a third of the Senate. These are different laws, different constituencies, different turnout, different names. Chytilek and colleagues in Volební systémy describe that a majority two-round Senate and a proportional Chamber are not two versions of the same ranking. [14] Kostelecký and colleagues, on municipal elections, show the strength of local lists that have no row in the nationwide model. [15] It does not follow that a nationwide mood has no effect on a municipality. It follows that the effect has to be proved by the municipality, not by transferring 30.5% into the town hall. The interval applies here too: even if ANO’s point in the model moved outside ±3.3, it would still not be the result in a municipality where there is a single list. For registration towards October 2026 the Czech Statistical Office recorded 1,842 such municipalities. [16] The Chamber model is silent there. It is not bad. It is about something else. Agresti, in a statistics textbook for the social sciences, recalls that a confidence interval is a statement about a procedure, not a seal on an individual percentage. [17] Šubrt, in a survey of public-opinion research, translates the same point into the Czech tradition of the field: opinion is ascertained, not proclaimed. [18] A reader who wants October needs a different map. A reader who wants the Chamber needs an interval. Both can be right. A shared headline can still be wrong. 17. A graphic can overshadow the method A poll chart today is not only an overview of ranking. Newsrooms build headlines from it, campaign teams adjust communication, and viewers form an idea of a probable result. The contest is therefore not only for the best estimate. It is a contest for political context. For the date of publication, for the graphic, for the habit of reading a point. The more comfortable the ecosystem becomes, the higher the exit price can be. Campaign teams stop distinguishing their own campaign from the product in which it is measured. A regular series can show a longer-term movement better than a single point. Its publication, however, must keep the question, the sample size, the published uncertainty and the comparability of waves, so that short-term noise does not turn into a headline about an earthquake. Responsible interpretation does not pretend to a precision that a sample survey does not have. It formulates a conclusion in the range that the given wave and the published methodology actually support. At the moment when the model only ranks large camps, we are choosing a map. At the moment when we assemble a majority from a point on the five-per-cent edge and a crisis from a single point against May, we are also choosing a new structure of responsibility. And then the question is no longer: “Who is ahead?” Let us ask: what uncertainty belongs with the point and with its change, who may turn an estimate into a headline, and who will correct it when the data cannot bear a strong conclusion? — Jiný Kontext

items.subtitle: The CZSO Compare Regions application uses 34 demographic, social, economic and environmental indicators; daily commuting time is not on their published list. Other frameworks may include it — the OECD has used it in the past as a secondary indicator. It therefore always depends on the specific methodology.

items.body: What we know / What we do not know What we know: In the published methodology of the CZSO Compare Regions application there are 34 indicators, and commuting time is not among them. The CZSO does, however, track the time and mode of commuting in other data products, especially the 2021 Census. The OECD already used commuting as a secondary indicator in How’s Life? 2011. [1] [6] [22] What we do not know: This text has not verified the current complete list and weights of every Czech commercial or local index. It therefore cannot claim that “no index” includes commuting. Nor does a population average say how much time a particular household spends travelling in 2026. Wages, greenery, access to a doctor and time in a traffic jam are not interchangeable indicators. A district may have low unemployment and, at the same time, long commutes. An index may correctly add up its columns and still not measure an individual’s journey time at all. Regional GDP is moreover attributed to the place of economic activity, not automatically to the place of residence. 1. A ranking that does not see an hour in the car Imagine a family meeting about moving. The father wants a district with a high median wage, because the table promises prosperity. The mother wants a nursery and a doctor within walking distance, because the children’s calendar is harder than a ranking. The mayor praises the motorway junction, because the investment is visible. The index analyst praises low crime and greenery, because those can be calculated. The doctor asks about blood pressure and sleep after years behind the wheel. The municipal accountant asks who will pay for the nursery for people whose GDP is counted a district away. At first glance this is a dispute about where life is better. In reality each person is describing a different problem. The father compares income. The mother the accessibility of services in time. The mayor infrastructure. The analyst static territorial quantities. The doctor the burden on the body. The accountant tax revenue. Each family member can therefore correctly describe a different part of everyday life, while the aggregate ranking itself determines none of these priorities. The phrase “quality of life” joins income, services, safety, the environment, journey time and individual preferences; choosing a house by a single score conceals those differences. First it is necessary to determine which household need the comparison is meant to address . Pay, a park, a motorway junction and journey time answer different questions and require different data sources. An index is not a life. A road is not accessibility. GDP is not income. And a district’s rank is not your afternoon. — Jiný Kontext 2. What is hidden behind a single ranking When a gold medal for a district appears in an infographic, it is easy to form the impression that that is where life is best. The result, however, is produced in a chain. Each layer can raise the score, lower it, or change the type of error. Two indexes with the same word “quality” therefore need not measure the same thing, and the same district can behave differently according to whether we read the supply of services or the time a person must travel to reach them. Five layers of one score Supply in the territory: wages, doctors, nurseries, greenery, safety — what indexes can do. Accessibility in time: minutes to work, school, the clinic, not kilometres on a map. Mode of travel: car, public transport, walking; each comes with a different cost. Body and sleep: a burden that does not fit into an ORP. The account and the tax: where GDP is created and where people live. Specific Czech products must be read separately. In the Compare Regions application the CZSO uses 34 published indicators from the demographic, social, economic and environmental domains; commuting duration is not on this list. [1] The Ministry of Regional Development and Obce v datech work with different territorial units and their own sets of indicators. [2] [3] Without the current complete methodology and weights it is not honest to generalise their content. International frameworks also differ: the OECD has eleven well-being dimensions and already in 2011 included commuting as a secondary indicator. [5] [22] The precise conclusion therefore reads only: the specific CZSO Compare Regions set does not measure individual journey time; it is not true that no framework measures it. Without a cut through the layers, praise for a district misses the day. That cut determines where to turn in a dispute. If a district shines and people get up at 5:15, the time layer may have failed, not the wage layer. If a station exists and the service does not run at shift time, accessibility has failed, not the existence of the track. The sentence “life is good here” is the start of a diagnosis, not its end. Illustrative scheme: The same house can, with a different commute, a different mode of travel and a different tax bill, produce a different life. Comparing greenery with a traffic jam is the same error as comparing a menu with the time at which dinner is eaten. 3. What error a ranking can conceal A “good address” also depends on what the table leaves out. A missing park is easy to spot on a visit, but a long peak-hour commute may only become apparent after moving in. Changing nursery is usually easier than changing a mortgage, a workplace and the running of two cars. In How’s Life? the OECD repeats that well-being has multiple dimensions and that an average conceals differences between groups and places. [5] It does not follow that Czech indexes have no value. It follows that an ORP ranking is a map of supply, not a verdict on how much waking time remains after the journey. Type of failure What it looks like How to test it What limits the harm Blind spot of time A top-ranked district, a long commute Door-to-door minutes at peak hours Count time as a negative column Average instead of distribution “27 minutes” as if for everyone Who is above 45–60 min one way A histogram, not a single average GDP instead of income A rich metropolis, a poorer hinterland GDP vs household disposable income Separate workplace and residence Infrastructure instead of a service A station without a clock-face service The timetable against the shift Measure the service, not the track Compensation illusion A larger house for a longer journey Sleep, blood pressure, family time Do not believe that the market will “even it out” That also changes the question we are asking. We do not ask only which district wins the table. We ask which indicator will fail in a way the family will still see before signing. A creative team can tolerate ten bad rankings. A family with children cannot tolerate a single hidden loss of a hundred minutes a day. When choosing housing, therefore, what decides alongside the score is whether journey time can be measured in advance, how hard the choice is to reverse, and how it will hit an ordinary day. A lower overall rank with a documented commute may be more suitable for a particular household than the ranking winner without that figure. 4. A ranking answers only the questions in the methodology Composite indexes are needed because they replace part of impressions with a repeatable table. The problem arises the moment one ranking begins to stand for an entire life. In Compare Regions the CZSO publishes 34 indicators and does not say that the region at the top is the “happiest”. It shows how it stands on the chosen statistics. [1] Every index contains hidden decisions. Who selected the indicators? How are they weighted? Is the unit a region, an ORP, or a municipality? Is the existence of a service measured, or the time to it? Is commuting counted as a cost? The answer to any of these questions can change the ranking. Five facts without which a medal is only a publicity number The territorial unit and the year of the data. The list of indicators and the weights. Whether it is supply, or accessibility in minutes. Whether GDP is counted by workplace. What the index expressly does not measure. For buying a house, therefore, a small personal benchmark matters more than someone else’s overall ranking. Thirty actual journeys — in rain, at peak hours, with school, with delay — can say more than a thousand points for greenery in a district the family will see only at the weekend. 5. Compare columns, not district winners The market in rankings can be described without a false podium of champions. The following map does not say who is the most pleasant to live with. It shows around what work the individual frameworks build their score and which failure the reader should look for on purpose. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext Framework Main working position Individual time spent travelling What to check before you move on that basis CZSO: Compare Regions 34 regional indicators Not in the published set Year, definition, region vs your municipality MMR: Life in the regions ORP dimensions The full current matrix was not checked for this article Open the current indicators and weights Obce v datech / Deloitte Services and environment The full current matrix was not checked for this article Distinguish travel to a service from the journey to work OECD How’s Life? 11 well-being dimensions Historically also a secondary commuting indicator Framework version, year and level of the data Census / Eurostat mobility Commuting, mode, time Yes as a topic, not as an ORP ranking Population, year, one-way time The rows are not a judgment on the quality of the analysts. The same institution offers more than one table and each can change within a few years. The comparison is meant to prevent a different error: that a family takes over an excellent-looking wage column from a product that does not see its morning. Interpretive scheme: The sides of the table are not a ranking of happiness. They separate supply, time, mode of travel and the tax bill. 6. Czech frameworks: what they measure and what time in the car misses When reading methodologies the point is not “that the statisticians overslept”. The point is that a static territorial datum assumes that a person at point A has, without friction, the services and work of point B. Physical distance and the time barrier do not enter the formula, or enter only as the existence of a road and a station. Different methodologies may measure access to a service, commuting duration or only the existence of infrastructure; these quantities cannot be swapped. The OECD framework works with work–life balance and historically used commuting as a secondary indicator, but a national comparison of countries is not a histogram of Czech satellites. [5] [22] The CZSO tracks commuting in the census, separately from its 34-item Compare Regions application. [1] [6] [7] It does not follow that the indexes should be abolished. It follows that their user is buying a map of infrastructure and socio-economics, not a stopwatch. What needs to be tested The first test is definition: does the column measure existence, distance, or peak-hour time? The second is the unit: a region may be green and your slip-road jammed. The third is the population: the average of the employed is not a parent with two children and one car. The fourth is reversibility: can the decision be repaired, or is it already in the land register? For an individual who wants a rough orientation among regions, Compare Regions may be decisive. For a family the sentence “the district won” is not enough. It needs to know the minutes, the mode, the service and the boundary beyond which a person must travel the journey themselves, not read it. 7. The census sees commuting. It does not see your afternoon The 2021 Population and Housing Census is the primary Czech source on commuting. In its publication on commuting to work and school and in the popularising text By car to work and school , the CZSO states that the car was the main means of transport for the journey to work for 60.2% of persons with a recorded means of transport (more than two million persons). Urban public transport accounted for 15.5% (530 thousand), walking 10.4% (356 thousand). [6] [7] This is the main mode of the journey to work among those for whom the means was recorded. It is not the share of all residents of Czechia. It is not time in minutes. On the census page on means of transport the CZSO further states that a car driven by the commuting person was used for the journey to work by almost 1.9 million persons, 54.8% of commuters to work with a recorded means; the difference from 60.2% is that the second figure includes the broader category “car as the main means”, while the first emphasises driving one’s own car. [8] This is not a contradiction between two truths. They are two definitions. A headline that turns them into “seven in ten Czechs drive every day” erases both. The frequency of commuting to work in the census shows that most commuters with a recorded frequency travel at least five times a week; in Prague the share of daily journeys is lower than in the Zlín Region, where the CZSO reports 81.1% against 66.2% in Prague. [9] The census therefore sees regularity. It does not see whether a particular morning stood at 25 or 80 minutes. The article therefore does not use the summary sentence “more than 3.5 million people commute daily”. Without a precise table and denominator it would mix the employed, pupils, work from home, an unrecorded workplace and different frequencies. What is documented are the shares above among persons with a recorded means of transport and the year 2021; this is not all residents of Czechia, nor the situation in 2026. [6] [7] [9] 8. An average of 27 minutes is not your journey In an ad hoc module of the labour-force survey for 2019, Eurostat stated that the average commuting time of employed persons in Czechia was 27 minutes one way ; the EU average was 25 minutes. Latvia had 33 minutes, Cyprus 19. Employed people living in suburbs and rural areas of the EU had on average a longer journey than city residents (31 against 24 minutes). [10] This is a European survey from 2019, one-way time, employed persons. It is not the satellite ring of Prague in 2026. It is not a distribution. More important than the average is the tail. An average of 27 minutes can be produced by people who walk ten minutes and people who travel an hour. In a related report for 2019 Eurostat stated that most employed people in the EU travelled less than 30 minutes and that a smaller share travelled 60 minutes or more. [10] Czech satellites do not have their own row in this statistic. Anyone who wants to know the tail around Prague and Brno must reach for regional census data and transport models, not for a single European average. It does not follow that 27 minutes is a lie. It follows that it is a map of the middle. A family that buys a house according to the middle may buy the tail. 9. Distance is not the same as fitness. Nor sleep Time behind the wheel in a jam is not passive rest. Nor is it automatically a heart attack. Medical studies measure associations, not an individual’s fate. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext Hoehner and colleagues in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine (2012) examined 4 297 adults in 12 Texas metropolitan counties in 2000–2007. Road-network commuting distance was negatively associated with physical activity and cardiorespiratory fitness and positively with BMI, waist circumference and blood pressure; after adjustment for activity and fitness, the relationship with higher blood pressure in particular remained significant among the metabolic indicators. [11] This is a cross-section of a selected American population with a medical examination, not Czech satellites. It does not say that “every 15 km kills”. It says that longer distance commuting by car in this sample went hand in hand with worse fitness and metabolic risk. Hansson and colleagues in BMC Public Health (2011; 11:834) examined 21 088 employed people in Skåne. For public-transport commuting over 60 minutes the odds ratios of worse indicators (sleep, stress, vitality, health, absence) were in the range of roughly 1.2–1.6. For the car the relationship was rather convex: difficulties rose in the 30–60 minute band (OR roughly 1.2–1.4) and in the category over 60 minutes they were lower — the authors read this cautiously, not as evidence that a very long car journey is beneficial. [12] From this study one cannot derive a general claim of “30% more difficulties above 45 minutes”; it describes associations by mode and commuting time band in one Swedish region. Stutzer and Frey in the Scandinavian Journal of Economics (2008) showed on German panels that people with longer commutes report lower life satisfaction, even though the classical model promises compensation in wages or housing. At an average one-way time of 22 minutes in their data this was a reduction in satisfaction on the order of 0.1 points on the scale used. [13] This is Germany and subjective satisfaction, not Czech ORP. It nevertheless changes the ranking question: a larger house need not be the offset that the economic model promised. International comparison holds only where the definitions hold. Texas distance, Skåne time, German satisfaction and the Czech census mode are four maps. Assembling from them a single sentence about the “Czech satellite” without reservation is a synthesis the data do not carry. Assembling from them a warning that journey time belongs in thinking about quality of life is something the data do carry. 10. Time in the car is not leisure. It is a tax on community In Bowling Alone Putnam links long car commuting with less room for clubs, neighbours and informal ties. [14] The book itself is not here a basis for a precise Czech effect “for every ten minutes”, and the article therefore does not take over such a percentage. The safe conclusion is more modest: journey time competes with other parts of the day; the size of the impact on community life in Czechia is not known from the cited source. Walkable access to school is a different, more measurable layer of the same thing. Associations and initiatives that map children’s journeys show that the existence of a school building is not the same as a safe 15 minutes on foot. [15] An index that counts nursery capacity and does not count accompaniment by car measures an institution. It does not measure the morning. Imagine two illustrations, not a report. A family in a regional city with an average index score: work 15 minutes by tram, school 500 metres, home at 16:30. A family in a well-rated district: two commutes of 60–80 minutes by car, return after 19.00. A high territorial score by itself does not say which family has the easier day. There are no names here; the example only shows why journey time should be a separate item in the decision. 11. A district’s GDP is not a household’s income The absence of time in the index meets a second optical illusion. Gross domestic product in regional accounts is attributed to the place of economic activity, not the place of residence. For Prague in 2024 the CZSO reported GDP per inhabitant in purchasing-power parity of 192% of the EU average ; the region thereby clearly leads domestically. [16] The public source therefore supports the value 192%, not a rounded “up to 200%”. The CZSO also publishes net household disposable income per inhabitant, which is closer to the living standard of the place of residence than GDP per head. [16] [17] It does not follow that Prague is not rich. It follows that regional GDP by place of work also includes the output of people who leave in the evening. From regional GDP, however, one cannot without further data infer the budget of a particular municipality or the impact of the budgetary assignment of taxes; that is a different accounting system and this article does not model it. The optical illusion is therefore double. A quality index may praise a hinterland district for incomes and greenery. The GDP account may punish the same hinterland because the work is counted elsewhere. Time in the car joins both errors: a person produces value in the metropolis and spends life in a municipality that does not get a corresponding row in the GDP table. 12. A motorway and a station still do not determine the length of the journey Before the motorway junction, people checked whether a municipality “has a road”. With the junction something more complicated is checked: whether the junction shortens time, or brings a jam to a ramp that used to be quiet. A junction is navigation to capacity. It is not automatic proof of accessibility. One table can combine three true figures into an untrue conclusion. First: there is a station in the municipality. Second: wages in the region are rising. Third: crime is low. Each figure may fit, but the synthesis “living here means a short day” does not follow. Elsewhere an index uses a high-quality secondary environmental score even though a primary timetable is available. A four-step check of accessibility Existence: the road, the track, the stop are there. Authority: the service is at shift time, not only on the map. Support: a concrete door-to-door minute at peak hours. Scope: it fits the school year, the shift, a second car, illness. The most reliable working procedure therefore separates the map from the stopwatch. First a table of journeys, modes and delays is created. Only then is the ranking read. If the journey cannot be travelled in the advertised time, the claim is not promoted to quality of life merely because the district leads. WHO recommendations on physical activity rest on the finding that regular movement reduces the risks of diseases of civilisation; passive sitting in a car does not replace this dose. [18] An IZA discussion of active commuting shows that walking and cycling can have a different health account from the car — again as an association, not as an order to move into the centre. [19] Infrastructure that enables an active mode changes the layer. Infrastructure that only speeds entry into a jam changes the place where one waits. 13. The price of a kilometre is the price of a raw material, not the price of a day The property market uses several languages at once. The developer pays per metre. The bank the instalment. The driver fuel. The family time. The municipality the nursery. A direct comparison of house prices without knowledge of the daily journey therefore misleads. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext A cheap house beyond the city can be economically excellent if the commute is short or the rail service clock-face. The same house can be expensive for a task that both parents repeat twice a day, consume two cars and in the end surrender sleep. An expensive flat by the tram can be pointless for someone who wants a garden and has work in the municipality. It can be cheaper for a decision with a high price of time if it reduces the number of hours that cannot be bought back. The true price of an accepted day Instalment + energy + two cars + fuel + parking + minutes × working days + lost sleep + the price of delay + future unsaleability. A day is cheap only when, after the journey, time remains that could be used. Costs also include fluctuation. If the same journey once in five days stretches to double, the average price of a day is not the price of an ideal morning. If the peak-hour service does not arrive, the cost is a second car. If life is firmly tied to a single ramp, the cost is also leaving. It is therefore useful to measure the price per accepted weekday , not the price per metre. Accepted means that the day met predetermined criteria: work, school, sleep, and did not cause a subsequent correction of the daily regime that the ranking does not see. 14. What to count for which question A reasonable choice does not start with a district medal, but with the type of question and the control mechanism. The following recommendations are not a ranking of municipalities. They are a signpost to the first test. For each category it makes sense to choose two columns and compare them on the same journey, at the same time and with the same budget of minutes. Need First group of evidence Decisive test Unacceptable shortcut Rough orientation among regions CZSO Compare Regions Year and definition of the indicator Buy a house according to the region Services in the municipality Obce v datech, MMR ORP Existence vs the minute Travel to a doctor as the journey to work Daily work Census mode + one’s own stopwatch Door-to-door at peak hours The European average of 27 min Health account Hoehner, Hansson, WHO — with a population caveat Mode and time band, not fate “The study proves your heart attack” Tax account of the hinterland GDP vs disposable income Workplace vs residence Prague 192% of the EU as a wage in the satellite Children to school Walking map, timetable 15 minutes without a car? Nursery capacity without the journey For Czech use a separate peak-hour test is necessary. An English commuting survey will not measure whether a service will catch a shift in an industrial zone, whether a pram fits on the bus in winter, or whether “27 minutes” was ever true on your ramp. The test set should include rain, an accident on the D1, a school trip and a day on which the right answer is “today it cannot be done by car”. Some households in the end need more than one map. One for wages, a second for school, a third for the service, a fourth for tax. That is not a failure of moving. It is the same decision as using a different tool for a mortgage and a different one for a timetable. The condition is that the division is intelligible and people know where the final stopwatch arises. 15. A short test that says more than an ORP ranking A choice can be made without a six-month move and without an impulse to buy the ranking winner. A short, disciplined week is enough. Its aim is not to prove that a district can do something impressive in an infographic. The aim is to find situations in which the day fails, and to see whether the family can bear them. Three tests before moving The first is about time: how many door-to-door minutes on a Wednesday at eight in the morning and at five in the afternoon, not on Saturday at ten? The second is about mode: is there a service that will carry the shift without a second car? The third is about the body: what remains of sleep and dinner when the journey stretches twice a week? A product that answers a point earlier in the table need not be better if, a year later, nobody can find out why the days look different. Before signing Time five working journeys in both directions. Record the mode, delay and the price of fuel or the ticket. Separate travel to a doctor from travel to work. Check school and nursery at the time they actually start. Calculate how many hours a year 90 minutes a day times 220 shifts is. A pilot should also have drop-out conditions. For example: a single journey that regularly eats sleep below six hours, the absence of a service after 19.00, or the need for two cars where the budget counted on one. A high greenery score should not override an error whose impact the household cannot accept. The last output is not only the name of the winning ORP. It is an operating rule: what the index is used for, what it is not used for, which time must be travelled, what must be approved by the person who will drive, and when the decision will be opened again. Rankings, timetables and motorway ramps change. Without a review date even a good moving plan gradually turns into a family superstition. 16. A bedroom can subsidise a metropolis. The index need not see it The last layer joins transport to the account. People live in a municipality that wins on greenery and work in a city that wins on GDP. The CZSO methodologically acknowledges this loop in the regional accounts by the fact that GDP and household disposable income are not the same. [16] [17] On intra-country commuting between regions Eurostat shows that millions of Europeans regularly work elsewhere than they live; Czechia is not an exception to the mechanism, even if the exact counts depend on the definition of the region. [20] An index that adds up wages at the place of residence and doctors at the place of residence may praise the satellite. It does not ask how many of those wages were created sixty minutes away and how many of those doctors suffice in the evening when the family returns at seven. The Ministry of Regional Development and spatial planning can name suburbanisation as pressure on service provision. [2] [21] Without a time column, however, the naming remains without a stopwatch. OECD regional well-being and Czech Compare Regions are useful maps. [1] [22] They are not a verdict on whether it is worth getting up at 5:15. That decision can be borne only by a day that someone has actually travelled. An index can help select candidates. The journey must be done by work — in the literal sense. 17. The price of housing also includes the everyday journey Rankings join figures on services, environment and the economy into a single order. A housing decision, however, also includes the everyday ferrying of children, the journey to work and time that may not have its own column in the table. That is why the contest is not only for the best score. It is a contest for daily context. For the ramp, for the service, for the habit of getting up at 5:15. The more comfortable the house that arises in the table, the higher the price of leaving can be. A mortgage, a school and two cars are hard to export. Space and quiet beyond the city can be a fundamental advantage for a household. Before buying, however, it is advisable to verify actual peak-hour time, the timetable, an alternative to the car and how the week works if one vehicle is out of action. A suitable address for a particular household need not lead the overall index. It must match the actual daily regime, the budget and tolerance of commuting. The moment the ranking only ranks greenery, we are choosing a map. The moment we buy a house by it, build a timetable and surrender sleep, we are also choosing a new structure of the day. And then the question is no longer: “Which district won?” Let us ask: How many minutes will the actual peak-hour journey show, and is this price acceptable even when the ranking has not counted it? — Jiný Kontext

items.title: The retirement age is rising. What does that mean for a body with a different plan?
items.subtitle: Statutory tables are shifting the pension age towards 67. Life expectancy and healthy life years, however, do not measure the same thing — and a body in strenuous work does not follow the average in a mortality table.
