items.body: Section: Technology & AI Author: V Reading time: ~27 min Sources and further reading: 22 items Topics: smartphone, privacy, apps, operator, GDPR, Apple, Google, NÚKIB SEO / working title: What does your mobile phone know about you? What does your mobile phone know about you? The question sounds simple only until we notice that we are not comparing one thing. A device can have an IMEI and the account can still survive a change of handset. Timeline location can be off and a location from another activity can still remain. An operator may, under Czech law, retain traffic and location data for 6 months and still not read the content of an end-to-end chat. [13] A seven-day App Privacy Report can show microphone accesses without being a picture of the whole history since purchase. [7] The following text therefore does not ask what “the phone knows”. It asks which layer knows what — and which controller to ask. 1. Takeout, seven days of a report, and an extract from the operator are not one file Imagine one person and three exports. First they download data from their Google account through Takeout. Then, on an iPhone, they turn on App Privacy Report and for a week watch apps’ accesses to location, camera, microphone and contacts. Finally they ask the operator, under Article 15 GDPR, for data that relate to their contract and traffic. [3] [7] [15] At first glance this is one dispute: what the phone knows about them. In fact each output answers a different question. Takeout describes the account and the services the user chooses to export. App Privacy Report describes app accesses and network activity for the last 7 days after the report is turned on; Apple states that the data are encrypted on the device and that the report is deleted when it is turned off. [7] The operator describes the subscriber relationship, traffic data and location data in the regime of the Electronic Communications Act. [13] They can therefore all be partly right and the shared sentence still wrong. A user who sees search history in Takeout is right that an account can contain a sensitive trail. A user who sees frequent location accesses in the report is right that apps can reach sensors. The operator is right that it does not retain the content of messages under the regime of § 97(3). The error arises only when these layers are made into one all-knowing file. The first distinction is therefore not whether the phone is smart. It is who is the controller of a particular layer. That is not word-play. If we ask the wrong controller, we get a correct answer to someone else’s question. The phone does not know everything. Different layers know — and each has a different controller. — Jiný Kontext 2. A phone has at least six layers When people say “mobile”, they usually picture an object in a pocket. In data terms it is not one object. It is a node between the operating system, apps, an account, the network, advertising measurement, backups and other devices. Each layer has a different technical mechanism and a different law. The first layer is the operating system and the sensors. GPS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, accelerometer, camera, microphone and the address book are not one socket. The system holds permissions over them. An app usually does not ask for “everything”, but for a particular access: location while in use, camera, microphone, contacts. For App Privacy Report, Apple describes that the report shows accesses to sensitive data and sensors and also the domains contacted over the last 7 days. [7] The second layer is apps and their libraries. An app need not be only the programmer’s own code. It can contain an SDK for advertising, analytics, maps or sign-in. NÚKIB therefore recommends downloading apps from authorised stores and watching what they reach, especially in the case of suddenly popular apps. [10] The third layer is a Google or Apple account. An account can survive a change of phone. It can be open in a browser, on a tablet and on a new device. Takeout is therefore not an extract “from the phone”, but an export of account data from selected services. [3] The fourth layer is the operator’s network. Here the SIM, the subscriber contract, identification on the network, traffic and location data, and billing appear. Czech § 97(3) ZoEK works with a period of 6 months for the retention of defined data, but at the same time expressly separates the content of messages. [13] The fifth layer is advertising and measurement. The Android Advertising ID is a resettable and deletable identifier; after deletion, according to Google’s documentation, zeros are returned. [6] Apple IDFA is, after iOS 14.5, available for tracking across third-party apps only after consent in the App Tracking Transparency regime. [8] The sixth layer is backup and other devices. Photographs can be in the cloud, messages in a backup, a sign-in in the browser, devices in a family or company profile. The phone in the hand need not show the whole trail until we look at the account and the backups. 3. The best overview is the one whose gap you see before someone else’s request Users often look for one switch and one extract. That is understandable, but incomplete. One location switch will not cancel every possible source of location information. One report for 7 days will not show history from before it was turned on. One request under the GDPR does not cover all controllers, because the data subject sends it to a particular person or institution, not to “the phone”. [15] [16] Type of failure What it looks like How to test What limits the harm Confusion of layers Takeout, the report and the operator are read as one profile Compare three outputs of the same person Always address the request to a particular controller One location switch Timeline is off, location remains in another activity Check app permissions, Timeline, and Web & App Activity Read Google’s notices about other location settings The report as a complete history A seven-day window is taken as data since purchase Turn the report on and read it as a measurement after it is turned on Do not infer a past that the report did not collect Advertising ID as a permanent identity AAID or IDFA is confused with IMEI or IMSI Reset or delete the advertising ID, check ATT Separate advertising from the network and the device Chat content at the operator It is expected that the operator has the WhatsApp text Separate metadata under ZoEK from the content of the app Do not attribute to the network keys that it does not have Hygiene as a reset of the network Uninstalling an app is taken as erasure at the operator Compare NÚKIB’s recommendations with § 97 ZoEK Reduce the risk of apps and deal with the network separately Interpretive scheme: This is not a ranking of risks. It is a map of places where one controller is often taken for another. That changes the practical question. We do not ask whether we have enough data about ourselves. We ask whether we know which data are missing from the overview. An overview is useful precisely when it does not raise a false sense of completeness. A good overview should therefore not end with the export. It should end with a question about absence. In Takeout I do not see the operator’s traffic data; that is not a failure of Takeout. In App Privacy Report I do not see what an app sent before the report was turned on; that is not proof that it did not happen. In an extract from the operator I do not see the body of an end-to-end chat; that is not a gap in the network, but a property of a separate app. Every output should be read not only for what it contains, but also for what it cannot, in principle, contain. 4. The device is not the account IMEI identifies a mobile device. GSMA, in the standard TS.06, describes IMEI as a unique identifier of mobile equipment; it is the identity of a handset in the technical layer of the network, not a person’s name in civic life. [19] A Google or Apple account is a different kind of identity. It signs the user into services, backups, photos, history and purchases. It can move to a new phone, and the old handset can be wiped. From that it does not follow that IMEI is meaningless. It follows that it does not answer the same question as an account. When an operator sees a device on the network, that does not mean it sees the whole content of a Google account. When Google allows an account to be exported through Takeout, that does not mean it provides an extract of everything that happened on the operator’s radio network. The practical error is simple. A person sells a phone, buys a new one, and believes they are starting from zero. The handset can be new. The account is not. History in the account, synchronised contacts, photos and settings can continue. Conversely a person can wipe the phone and still have data in the account. The same word “mobile” here covers two different things. A cleaner sentence is: the device is a carrier and a party to technical relationships; the account is a longer-lived identity of a service. Sometimes they overlap. They are never the same thing. 5. The OS is not the app The operating system sets the frame. It manages permissions, shows warnings, and allows accesses to be granted, limited or withdrawn. An app in this frame asks for a particular capability. It may need it for a legitimate function. Maps without location work differently from maps with location. A video call without a camera stops being a video call. That does not mean every permission is reasonable. A torch app does not need contacts. A game need not necessarily know a precise location. In its recommendation on suddenly popular apps, NÚKIB points precisely to caution with permissions that are unrelated to the purpose of the app, and to the choice of authorised stores. [10] For App Store privacy labels, Apple distinguishes data used to track, data linked to the user, and data that are not linked to the user. [9] That is not a guarantee of the faultlessness of every app. It is an attempt to describe the data flow beyond the “allow” button itself. And that is where the next layer begins: the developer, an analytics SDK, an advertising network and a server. The OS is therefore not the app. The system can force a question and show a report. It need not itself know the commercial reason why an app collects data, nor how its operator will use them after they are sent to a server. When checking one’s own phone it is therefore necessary to read both columns: what the system allowed, and who the app belongs to. The same permission icon can mean different situations. A navigation app may need location for a route. A weather app may make do with a city. A loyalty-programme app may want location for marketing. The system dialogue usually does not tell the whole business model. It says which technical gate is opening. Whether the opening is proportionate, the user must judge from the purpose of the service, the trustworthiness of the developer, and whether the permission can be narrowed. 6. Location has more switches than one toggle shows Location is among the data for which we most quickly create a false certainty. We turned off location history, so Google no longer stores location. Google’s documentation, however, warns that turning off Timeline or location history by itself need not stop the storing of location data from other settings and sources, for example from Web & App Activity, from Maps, from photos or from an IP address. [4] [5] Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext This is not one secret trick. It is a property of layers. An app’s precise location, an account Timeline, a location inferred from search, and a location from an IP address are not the same switch. Each arises differently and each is managed somewhere else. CZSO, in the VŠIT 2025 survey, reports that 52% of persons aged 16+ in the Czech Republic have at least once changed access to the geographic location of a device. [1] That figure measures a declared change of access among persons 16+ in private households in 2025. It does not measure whether they currently have location on, how many apps use it, or whether it is precise or approximate location. How to test location On one’s own phone it makes sense to go through three places. First, Location permission on individual apps. Second, Timeline or location history in the Google account. Third, Web & App Activity. If some overview claims that “location is off”, it is necessary to ask: which location, in which account, and for which service? One location switch is not enough. Google says so expressly. — Jiný Kontext 7. An advertising ID is not a birth number An advertising identifier is useful precisely because it is not the same thing as a permanent device number. The Android Advertising ID can be reset or deleted; Google Play policy states that after deletion apps are returned zeros. [6] Apple IDFA is, in the App Tracking Transparency regime from iOS 14.5, iPadOS 14.5 and tvOS 14.5, tied to consent to tracking across third-party apps and websites. [8] From that it does not follow that advertising disappears. It follows that a particular path of tracking is limited or must have consent. An app can show contextual advertising, can measure its own service, can work with a signed-in account. ATT is not a ban on advertising. It is a rule for certain tracking across apps and data brokers. Likewise an advertising ID is not IMEI, IMSI or a telephone number. IMEI belongs to the device. [19] IMSI belongs to the SIM and the network. A telephone number belongs to the subscriber relationship. An advertising identifier is a layer of measurement and advertising. When these layers are mixed, an alarm sentence appears that one app knows “the identity of the phone”. Sometimes it knows an account. Sometimes an advertising ID. Sometimes a permission. Each case has to be taken apart separately. Google Play also forbids using other permanent identifiers as a substitute for the advertising ID for advertising purposes if the user has reset or deleted the advertising ID. [6] [21] That is a rule of an ecosystem, not a law of nature. Its meaning stands on enforcement, audit and the behaviour of particular apps. 8. App Privacy Report is not a forensic image App Privacy Report on an iPhone is a strong tool for one’s own inventory. It shows apps’ accesses to location, photos, camera, microphone, contacts, and the domains with which apps communicate. Apple describes it for iOS and iPadOS 15.2 and later; the report concerns the last 7 days, the data are encrypted on the device, and collection starts only after it is turned on. [7] Precisely this precision is its limit. Seven days is not since the phone was bought. The report is not a record of everything an app has ever sent to a server. Turning the report off deletes the data. [7] When a user therefore turns the report on on Monday and on Wednesday sees no suspicious activity, they can say only this much: in this window and with this use, the given activity did not show. That is not a weakness of the tool. It is a correct description of its scope. A forensic image would address other questions, other authorisation and other procedures. This text is not a guide to circumventing a lock, a PIN or encryption. App Privacy Report belongs to the inventory of one’s own device. It helps one see which apps reach sensitive places, but it does not replace a request to the operator of an app, nor an export of an account. What needs to be tested On an iPhone it makes sense to turn the report on and use the phone in the ordinary way for a whole week. On Android it is necessary to go through app permissions and the advertising ID in settings. In both cases the test measures one’s own trail. Not someone else’s device, not the circumvention of someone else’s account, not police work. 9. A backup is not the phone A phone can be empty and an account full. It can be broken and a backup alive. It can be in a pocket while photographs are meanwhile synchronising to the cloud. That is why it is misleading to ask only what is physically in the device. Google Takeout allows data to be exported from selected services of an account. [3] Apple offers overviews and tools within the privacy and security of an account. [9] The user thus sees a different layer from when they open the phone’s settings. They may find data that are no longer on the device, or conversely find that something remains only locally. A backup also changes the security question. When content is protected end-to-end, the service controller need not have readable content available. When it is not protected, or when the user uses an older setting, the scope can be different. This article does not add new figures on the share of backups or on the number of gigabytes, because the dossier does not contain such data. That is more precise than an estimate. The practical sentence is: if I am interested in the phone, I must also ask about the account and the backup. If I am interested in the account, I must not automatically infer from it the state of every device. A backup is also a frequent place of family misunderstanding. One person deletes a photograph from the phone and means “I deleted it”. Another finds it on a tablet or in the web interface of the same account. Both can be right according to the layer they are looking at. It is therefore more precise to speak of deletion on the device, in the account, in the service’s bin and in the backup separately. The GDPR knows a right to erasure under conditions, but even there the request is aimed at a controller and a particular processing, not at the physical feeling that we are holding one handset. [15] [20] 10. The operator does not read WhatsApp The operator sees the network layer. It keeps a subscriber contract, billing, traffic data and defined location data. Czech § 97(3) of the Electronic Communications Act requires providers to retain traffic and location data for 6 months; at the same time, in this regime, it is expressly not a matter of retaining the content of messages. [13] That is a substantial cut. Metadata of a call, an SMS or a data connection are not the body of a message in a chat app. End-to-end encryption separates content from the network that carries packets. An operator can provide connectivity and still not have the key to the content of a conversation in WhatsApp. From that it does not follow that metadata are innocent. Who communicates, when, from where and how often can be sensitive even without the text of a message. It does follow, however, that the sentence “the operator reads WhatsApp” confuses the network and the app. If someone is dealing with the content of a chat, they must ask the app, the account, the device and the encryption settings. If they are dealing with a traffic trail, they look at the network. This distinction also matters for a GDPR request. A request to the operator under Article 15 is aimed at data that the operator processes as controller. [15] [16] It is not a request for an extract from someone else’s app. 11. Blanket retention of metadata is not the same as a duty from the Union The Czech data-retention regime has its own legal dispute. The Supreme Court, in a press release on judgment 30 Cdo 2556/2025 of 8. 1. 2026, stated that the Czech blanket arrangement for retaining data on electronic communication is contrary to Union law. [14] A commentary by Iuridicum Remedium reminds us that such a decision does not itself mechanically rewrite the text of the Act or every practice of operators. [22] That means two things at once. It is not precise to say that “the European Union requires the blanket retention of metadata”. The dispute is aimed precisely against blanketness. It is not precise either to claim that, from the Supreme Court’s press release, no network layer of retention exists. As of September 2026 the dossier works from the premise that the text of § 97(3) ZoEK formally still stands. [13] [14] [22] For this article the main point is the separation of layers. Even if the operator’s legal regime changed, that would not make App Privacy Report into an extract from the operator, or Takeout into access to the network. One layer would change. Not the whole phone. 12. Takeout is access to an account. It is not access to the whole phone The right of access under the GDPR is a strong tool, but not a magic key to all data in a digital life. Article 15 gives the data subject the right to obtain from the controller confirmation and information about processing; Article 12(3) provides for a reply without undue delay and as a rule within 1 month, with a possible extension of up to 2 months for more complex or numerous requests. [15] Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext The controller is particular. Google answers for selected services of an account. Apple for its services and account. The operator for the subscriber relationship and traffic data. The developer of an app for its own processing in the app and on the server. The EDPB, in its guidelines on the right of access, examines precisely the relationship between the data subject and the controller; it does not assume that there is one universal controller of “the phone”. [16] Takeout is a practical example. Google describes it as a way to download data from an account and selected services. [3] It is not an image of the phone’s flash memory. It is not access to the operator’s data. It is not a guarantee that every third-party app will issue everything in the same way. A good request therefore does not start with the sentence “send me what the mobile knows about me”. It starts with a map of controllers. To whom is the request aimed? Which account, contract or app is the subject? Which period and which category of data is sought? Precision in the query raises the chance that the answer will not be correct only formally. 13. Downloading an app does not measure what an SDK sends CZSO in VŠIT 2025 reports that at least one app was downloaded in the last 3 months by 57.3% of smartphone users; in absolute terms that is 4,269.7 thousand persons, which corresponds to 49.1% of all persons aged 16+ in the given survey. [1] The figure is useful. It says that installing apps is an ordinary activity among a substantial part of smartphone users in the Czech Republic in 2025. It does not say how many SDKs are in an average app. It does not say how many permissions users granted. It does not say whether an app sent data to a developer, an advertising network or an analytics service. And it does not say whether it was an app from an official store, or a sideload. That is precisely why it makes sense to read NÚKIB’s recommendation beside the statistic. The statistic describes the extent of use. NÚKIB recommends caution with apps, authorised stores, updates, and restraint with permissions that are unrelated to the purpose of the app. [10] [11] [12] The EDPB, in guidelines 2/2023 on the technical scope of Article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive, reminds us that the rule does not concern only cookies in a browser, but access in general to information in a terminal device and its storage. [17] [18] Mobile apps are therefore not a legal vacuum merely because they are not a web cookie banner. 14. NÚKIB hygiene reduces the app layer. It does not reset the network Security hygiene makes sense. Downloading apps from official stores, updating the system, reading permissions, deleting unused apps and watching suddenly popular services is reasonable. NÚKIB repeats these recommendations in materials for safe movement in cyberspace and for travel. [10] [11] [12] The error arises when hygiene of one layer is read as the erasure of all layers. Uninstalling an app can reduce the risk of its further access. It need not delete data already sent to developers. It does not change the subscriber contract with the operator. It does not change the statutory regime for retaining traffic and location data under § 97(3) ZoEK. [13] Likewise, resetting an advertising ID will reduce the continuity of advertising measurement in the given regime. It will not change the IMEI of the device, the SIM on the network, or a sign-in to an account. Turning off one location history does not mean that all location data in all services have disappeared. [4] [5] That is not a reason to give up. It is a reason to name what we are doing just now. App hygiene is work on the app layer. An account export is work on the account layer. A request to the operator is work on the network layer. Each has its own sense and its own gap. This is precisely where good advice is told from false certainty. Good advice says which layer it reduces and which it leaves alone. False certainty promises that one step will erase a whole digital life. Neither uninstallation, nor a reset of an advertising ID, nor one location toggle can do that. 15. Figures on phone use do not measure the content of data CZSO in VŠIT 2025 reports that a mobile phone was used by 99.1% of persons aged 16+ in private households in the Czech Republic, that is 8,610.0 thousand persons. [1] A smartphone was used by 85.8% of persons 16+, that is 7,456.3 thousand persons. [1] The internet on a mobile phone was used by 82.7% of persons 16+, that is 7,185.0 thousand persons. [1] These figures have a clear strength and a clear limit. They measure the spread of devices and the use of the internet in 2025 in a defined population. They do not measure the content of data in phones. They do not measure the number of apps on an average device. They do not measure the share of iOS and Android in the Czech Republic in the tables the dossier read. They do not measure how much data is in a backup. The age cut shows a further caution. At age 65–74 a smartphone was used by 67.5% of persons in the cohort and a button phone by 33.1% of persons in the same cohort. [1] For persons 75+ the dossier reports a smartphone in 34.8% in 2025, against 14.5% in 2019. [1] That is growth and a minority at the same time. Without this reservation, older persons could easily be described either as digitally excluded or as fully on smartphones. Neither figure by itself is enough. A CZSO press release of 11. 11. 2025 reports that the internet was used daily by 81% of persons 16+ in the 2nd quarter of 2025 and, in the context of the release, recalls that the most frequent device is the phone. [2] Even that, however, is not a measurement of what the phone knows. It is a measurement of internet use. 16. An inventory of one’s own layers will say more than the sentence that the phone knows everything A practical test is not meant to teach the circumvention of someone else’s lock, someone else’s account, or statutory procedures. It is meant to help a person find their way in their own trail. A safe inventory starts where the user has a right and access: at their own account, their own device and their own operator. Three tests of one’s own trail The first test is an account export. At Google that is Takeout and a choice of the services the user has in their account. [3] At Apple it is overviews and privacy settings in the account and on the device. [9] The result must be read as an account layer, not as the whole phone. The second test is the device. On an iPhone, App Privacy Report can be turned on and the phone used in the ordinary way for a week; the output will show the last 7 days after the report is turned on. [7] On Android it makes sense to go through app permissions and the advertising ID, including the possibility of a reset or deletion. [6] The third test is the network. A request under Article 15 GDPR is aimed at one’s own operator and concerns data that it processes as controller; the reply period under Article 12(3) is as a rule 1 month, with a possible extension of up to 2 months. [15] [16] It is not a request about someone else’s subscriber. If one controller really fused the operating system, the store, the account, advertising, the network and the backup into one file available from one request, the main thesis would weaken. The documentation of Google, Apple and ZoEK does not describe such one file. [3] [7] [13] 17. The hidden cost is one handset that we read as one file A smartphone is practical precisely because the layers disappear from view. With one tap we open a bank, maps, messages, photos, a work chat, a shop, a backup and navigation. The user experience joins what is not joined in law and in technology. From that a hidden cost arises. When something goes wrong, we do not know where to ask. A suspicion about an app we take to the operator. A location in an account we look for in a device toggle. An extract from the operator we read as the content of communication. A report for the last 7 days we read as a history since purchase. And a statistic on the spread of smartphones we read as a statistic on the content of data. There is no need to claim that the phone is innocent. There is no need to claim either that it knows everything. The right question is more precise and less comfortable: which layer knows what, under which rule, at which controller, and how do we recognise what is missing from the answer? Such a question is slower than an alarm headline. It has, however, one advantage. It leads to an action that can actually be performed: download one’s own account, go through permissions, turn on a report, reset an advertising ID, ask a controller, and note what each step does not address. At the moment we hold a phone in the hand, we are holding a device. At the moment we ask about data, we enter a network of accounts, apps, advertising identifiers, operators and backups. And then the question is no longer: “What does your mobile phone know about you?” It is: which controller holds which trail — and which layer have you just forgotten to check? Related texts in this series How long does the operator retain data about your phone? — network metadata, not chat content. May the police search your mobile phone? — three regimes of seizure, content and interception. What is a digital footprint… — the phone is one layer, not a biography.

items.title: A missing stamp is not proof of authenticity. A blood-in-the-pixel detector is not a lock.
items.subtitle: For an image or a video you can check a provenance signature and a laboratory artefact, not the truth of the scene. Czech law punishes certain handling of a false likeness, not the file itself.

headings: 1. A journalist, a detector and a prosecutor are not dealing with the same photograph
2. One scene on a display has at least six layers
3. A missing stamp is not proof of authenticity
4. C2PA says who claimed provenance. It does not say that the scene happened
5. SynthID is not a Content Credential
6. The eye on a GAN face hit chance
7. Ninety-six percent on FaceForensics is not a lock on Instagram
8. DFDC left detection open. Nobody on the black box reached seventy
9. A label under the AI Act is not a criminal prosecution
10. A paragraph on non-consensual pornography is not a paragraph on a political video
11. Defamation and fraud punish a lie and a consequence. Not a file
12. A screenshot drops the manifest. It does not drop the event
How to test Content Credentials before and after a screenshot
13. The best check is the one whose false alarm you can bear
14. A signature, a detector and a second channel do not add up to one verdict
What needs to be tested before you trust the eye
15. Personal use is outside the AI Act. It is not outside the Criminal Code
16. A public series of prosecutions under the new paragraphs is still missing
17. The hidden cost is an eye that hit chance

items.body: Section: Technology & AI | Justice & law Author: V Reading time: ~27 min Sources and further reading: 22 items Topics: deepfake, C2PA, Content Credentials, video detection, photography, AI Act, Criminal Code SEO / working title: Deepfake: How can you tell a fake video or photograph? The question is: how can you tell a fake video or photograph? It sounds simple only until we notice that we are not comparing one thing. A missing Content Credentials stamp is not proof of authenticity. C2PA says who claimed provenance, not that the scene happened in the world. A “blood in the pixel” detector is not a forensic conclusion on Instagram. A label under the AI Act is not a criminal prosecution of an offender. Only when these four things are separated can one read what a signature, a laboratory and the amendment of the Criminal Code as of September 2026 actually hold — and what an eye that hit by chance does not hold. This text does not deal with voice. A phone call, a synthetic voice and a payment belong in another article. It also does not deal with the broader question of whether a photograph by itself is enough as evidence before a court; that is a separate text on photography as evidence. Here the question is more practical: what to do with a file that sits on a display and presents itself as an image of the world. 1. A journalist, a detector and a prosecutor are not dealing with the same photograph Imagine an editorial meeting on a day when a short video of a politician is spreading on the network. The editor wants to know whether it carries a clear label under the AI Act. The designer looks for Content Credentials. A forensic enthusiast runs a detector that promises to expose synthetic video from subtle colour changes in the face. The lawyer asks whether this is defamation, fraud, an interference with a likeness, or a new offence in the Criminal Code. A reader in the comments writes that they “see it at first glance”. At first glance this is a dispute about whether the video is genuine. In fact each person is holding a different object. The editor is dealing with a duty to label towards the audience. The designer is dealing with a cryptographic manifest in the file. The enthusiast is dealing with a statistical signal in the image. The lawyer is dealing with the handling of a likeness, intent and consequence. The reader is dealing with an impression. That is why everyone can be partly right and the shared verdict still wrong. A video can be unlabelled and still genuine. It can have a valid manifest and still not capture what a viewer infers from the caption. It can pass a laboratory detector and still be only badly compressed. It can be obviously synthetic and still fail to fulfil a specific criminal offence. The first rule of practical detection is therefore not: find the best detector. It is: name the layer. For a signature we ask whether the file carries a verifiable manifest. For a detector we ask on what population it was tested. For the law we ask what someone did with the image. For the human eye we ask whether it even has a chance of distinguishing what it claims to distinguish. A missing stamp is not proof of authenticity. — Jiný Kontext 2. One scene on a display has at least six layers One picture on a phone looks like one thing. It is not. It is the result of a chain in which a sensor, a container, edits, distribution, captions, algorithmic interventions and legal consequences are mixed. When those layers are mixed, a false certainty appears: metadata are missing, so it is a forgery; the detector showed a high score, so it is settled; there is no label, so the law has been broken; the image looks odd, so it is AI. Six layers of one scene: Sensor and container. Camera, phone, social network, messenger, screenshot and compression. Each step can keep, change or discard metadata. Generator or edit. Face-swap, a GAN face, an image model, a video model, manual retouching, a cut or an ordinary filter. Not every edit is a deepfake and not every deepfake is the same. Detection signal. A visual artefact, a biological rhythm in the face, a watermark, machine metadata, a network trained on a specific set. Distribution. Editorial publication, an advertisement, a private message, campaign material, an anonymous repost. The same file in another channel means another responsibility. Labelling. Machine-readable marking by the provider and a clear deepfake label towards the audience under Article 50 of the AI Act are two things [6] [7] . Law after the act. The Criminal Code, the Civil Code and the protection of personal data assess conduct, consent, harm, intent and context, not only the structure of a pixel [9] [10] [22] . This layering is not wordplay. It changes whom to ask when something fails. If a manifest is missing, a screenshot may have dropped it. If a detector is shouting, it may be seeing bad light. If a work is unlabelled, we still do not know who published it and under what regime. If it is a false likeness, the law will not ask only about the technique of creation, but about the handling of the person shown. Illustrative scheme: Signature, detector and law are three columns. Between them there is no arrow saying “it is fake”. In each column a different question stands: is the manifest valid, on what set was the signal verified, what conduct took place. 3. A missing stamp is not proof of authenticity Content Credentials are sometimes described as a digital birth certificate of an image. That is a useful shorthand if we know where it ends. A C2PA manifest can carry claims about provenance, edits and signed content. But most ordinary files need not have such a manifest at all. The phone did not add it. The social network discarded it. The messenger recomputed the image. Someone took a screenshot. The absence of a stamp is therefore not suspicion in itself. It is often the default state. If a file from an ordinary phone does not carry C2PA, it does not follow that it was generated by artificial intelligence. If an image lost metadata on its way through a chat, it does not follow that the original scene did not happen. It follows only that the specific file we now hold does not carry a verifiable manifest. That is inconvenient for a newsroom, but more precise. A public census of how many news visuals in the Czech Republic as of September 2026 carry valid Content Credentials is not in the dossier. Without such a measurement, the absence of a signature cannot be turned into a rule about Czech media practice. One can only say that a signature helps where it is present and where the chain of trust holds. The practical question is therefore not whether an image “has a stamp of authenticity”. It is whether, for a specific file, a verifiable provenance signature exists and what exactly it signs. Absence is a signal for caution. It is not a verdict. 4. C2PA says who claimed provenance. It does not say that the scene happened C2PA is a technical specification for provenance. At its core it works with a manifest, assertions, a claim and a signature. If a file carries a manifest and the chain of trust holds, verification can say who signed a given claim about the content and whether the signed part has changed since then [1] [2] [3] . That is a lot. It is not everything. Specification 2.2 of May 2025 expressly does not confer a value judgment about “good” provenance [1] . It does not say: this scene happened. It does not say: the caption is true. It does not say: the person shown consented. It does not even say: every later viewer understands the context. C2PA can improve the provenance trail, but it does not turn an image into evidence without further work. Imagine a photograph from a demonstration with a valid camera manifest. The manifest can confirm that the file comes from a given device and was not edited after signing in a way that the signature would survive. It will not, by itself, answer whether the caption named the place correctly, whether the frame is from another day, whether the crop conceals the surroundings, or whether the person in the foreground did what the text attributes to them. The opposite error is equally dangerous. If a manifest is missing, that is not automatically a sign of manipulation. If a manifest exists, that is not automatically a sign of truth. The correct reading is narrower: C2PA is a layer of trust in a given claim about the provenance and integrity of a file. C2PA is not a deepfake detector. 5. SynthID is not a Content Credential Beside manifests there are watermarks. Google DeepMind describes SynthID as a technology that embeds a digital watermark into the outputs of selected models [19] . OpenAI in May 2026 announced the layering of C2PA and SynthID for image content and, in an update of July 2026, added audio as well; this text stays with image and video [20] . The difference is substantial. Content Credentials carry structured claims and a signature in the container. A watermark is a signal embedded in the content. It can survive some transformations better than metadata, but it usually carries less context. It can say that an output probably comes from a given participating system. It cannot, by itself, describe the whole chain of edits, the source of the shot, a person’s consent or the truth of the scene. OpenAI cites the loss of metadata through a screenshot, a re-encode or a crop of the container as a reason to layer a watermark onto C2PA [20] . That does not mean the watermark is a lock. It works for participating generators and according to the properties of the specific implementation. For content from another model, a manual edit, an older file or an ordinary photograph without that technology, there may be nothing to read. This is not a dispute of “metadata versus watermark”. They are two different layers. A manifest gives context and a signature where it has survived. A watermark gives a signal where it was embedded and where a detector can read it. Neither by itself answers the question of what happened in the world. 6. The eye on a GAN face hit chance The human eye is good at many things. It can read expression, mood, intent, social cues. That is precisely why, with synthetic faces, we often trust it more than it deserves. The study by Nightingale and Farid in PNAS from 2022 tested the distinguishing of real and StyleGAN2 faces. In the first experiment 315 participants judged 128 faces from 800 items, of which 400 were real and 400 synthetic. Mean accuracy was 48.2 percent, with a 95% confidence interval of 47.1 to 49.2 percent [13] . That is close to chance. The figure measures a binary task “real vs. synthetic” on static faces in a specific experiment. It does not measure video, a Czech feed, current diffusion models, or the ability to assess the whole context of a shot. That is why it is useful: it does not say that people never recognise anything. It says that the certainty of a glance is a bad detector. The authors also tried training with feedback. In the second experiment 219 new participants reached 59.0 percent, with a 95% interval of 57.7 to 60.4 percent [13] . This too is not a guide to hunting synthetic faces at work. Between the first and the second half of 64 faces, accuracy did not rise: 59.3 against 58.8 percent. The test shows that even short training has a limited effect. It does not follow that a visual check has no value. It follows that the eye belongs at the start of the question, not at its end. When something seems odd, it is reasonable to stop sharing and look for a second channel, a source, an original and context. It is not reasonable to point at a colleague’s face and say: I recognised AI. 7. Ninety-six percent on FaceForensics is not a lock on Instagram Intel in November 2022 presented FakeCatcher as a real-time deepfake detector and, in a product claim, stated 96% accuracy [15] . The academic paper by Ciftci, Demir and Yin describes the detection of synthetic portrait videos using biological signals, especially subtle changes related to blood flow in the face. On the FaceForensics dataset it reports 96 percent accuracy, on FaceForensics++ 94.65 percent, on Celeb-DF 91.50 percent and on the authors’ “in the wild” Deep Fakes Dataset 91.07 percent [14] . These are specific results on specific sets. They are not a door with a lock. Accuracy is not the same as a false-positive rate in operation. FaceForensics is not Instagram 2026. A portrait video in good light is not a dark clip from a concert. A signal in a frontal face is not a profile, make-up, low fps, heavy compression or a newer generator that learns to imitate or blur a similar rhythm. A marketing sentence without a cut of the datasets and without an operational population also slides easily into the wrong use. If someone says “the detector has 96 percent”, the missing question is: on what, when, with what threshold, with what share of false alarms and at what cost of error? For an editorial decision a false alarm is expensive. Labelling a genuine video as a forgery can damage as much as sharing a forgery as genuine. An rPPG detector is therefore not a forensic conclusion. It can be a hypothesis for a portrait video, if we know the conditions and the limits. It should not stand alone in the column “true / false”. Without an independent evaluation on current generators, with a calibrated false-positive rate and real channels of distribution, it is an auxiliary trace, not a verdict. 8. DFDC left detection open. Nobody on the black box reached seventy The Deepfake Detection Challenge was useful precisely because it showed the difference between a known set and a hidden test. According to Meta AI the challenge had 2 114 participants and more than 35 000 models. The dataset described by Dolhansky and colleagues contained more than 100 000 clips with 3 426 paid actors [16] [17] . That is a large, but still specific, construction. On the public set Meta reports the figure 82.56 percent, while in the communication the name of the metric oscillates between accuracy and average precision [16] . On the black-box set the best participant, Selim Seferbekov, reached 65.18 percent; nobody reached 70 percent [16] . The figure measures a specific challenge from 2020, not today’s internet. Its value is in the distinction: performance on known data does not mean generalisation to unseen forgeries. That is the core of the detection problem. Generators change. Compression changes. Publication channels change. A detector can learn a trace of the dataset instead of a general mark of forgery. In the laboratory it then looks precise, and in operation it meets a different world. NIST GenAI Image-D publishes a plan and metrics such as AUC, EER, TPR at a given FPR and Brier score in bins; at the same time it forbids participants from making advertising claims about ranking [18] . That is a reasonable restraint. As of September 2026 the dossier contains no single primary figure of the type “NIST verified 96 percent in the wild”. If such a sentence is circulating somewhere, this text has no support for it. 9. A label under the AI Act is not a criminal prosecution The AI Act introduces transparency duties, not a new universal police detector. Article 3 point 60 defines a deepfake cumulatively: it must be content resembling existing or plausibly existing persons, objects, places, entities or events, and it must falsely appear authentic or true [6] . Article 50 then distinguishes the duties of providers and of deployers [6] [7] . Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext From 2 August 2026 Article 50 applies; for systems placed on the market before that date, machine marking under paragraph 2 is deferred until 2 December 2026 [7] . The Commission in an FAQ of 24 July 2026 also states that content created before 2 August 2026 need not be labelled retroactively [7] . ČTÚ as of 31 July 2026 pointed to the applicability of the transparency rules and referred to the Code of Practice [8] . These dates measure the applicability of duties, not the authenticity of a file. A deepfake label towards the audience under Article 50(4) is not the same as a machine-readable mark by the provider under paragraph 2. The Commission also states that a deployer should not rely only on the provider’s machine mark [7] . When a newsroom publishes a synthetic or edited visual, it is dealing with its own duty towards the reader. When an offender uses an image for fraud, it is hard to expect that they will honestly fulfil the duty. The Commission FAQ states, for breaches of transparency duties, a sanction ceiling of up to 15 million EUR or 3 percent of worldwide turnover, whichever is higher, with proportionality for small and medium-sized enterprises [7] . That is a ceiling, not a tariff for an unlabelled meme. And above all: the sanction regime for transparency is not a criminal qualification of a specific harm. 10. A paragraph on non-consensual pornography is not a paragraph on a political video Czech amendment No. 270/2025 Coll. is in force from 1 January 2026 and adds to the Criminal Code, among other things, § 181(2) and the new § 191a [9] . That is a substantial change, but also a frequent source of shortcuts. The new § 191a concerns the production and dissemination of a pornographic work that exploits a person without their consent. The basic offence states a term of up to 2 years of imprisonment [9] . This figure measures the statutory term of the basic offence from 1 January 2026. It does not measure the number of convictions, it does not speak about every synthetic image, and it does not apply to a non-pornographic political video merely because it was created or edited with artificial intelligence. What matters is the handling of the work, the nature of the content and the consent of the person shown. § 181(2) aims at a false likeness or utterance with the intent to cause serious harm to rights [9] . That is a different construction. Satire and art are not automatically criminal. Likewise, not every bad caption is a criminal offence. The law assesses the specific circumstances. It does not follow that the technology is a legally neutral toy. It follows that “deepfake” is not one paragraph. An image can be a tool of sexual abuse, defamation, fraud, an interference with privacy or a civil dispute over a likeness. One detection app will not distinguish that. 11. Defamation and fraud punish a lie and a consequence. Not a file The Criminal Code knows defamation in § 184, fraud in § 209 and unauthorised handling of personal data in § 180 [10] . The Civil Code protects likeness and privacy in § 84 and following [22] . A deepfake can be a means. It is not automatically an offence. That sounds legalistic, but for practice it is a simple brake. If someone shows a video and asks “is this a crime?”, it is not enough to answer whether the image is synthetic. One needs to know who created it, who spread it, what it claimed, whom it harmed, whether it was a pornographic work, whether there was consent, whether there was intent to cause serious harm, and whether a property or other consequence occurred. A detector from a pixel does not assemble an offence. It can give a reason for caution, it can help a newsroom not to publish quickly, it can be one trace for expert assessment. It cannot replace a legal qualification. Just as a valid C2PA manifest does not replace a person’s consent to publication, a high detector score does not replace proof of intent. The practical recommendation is therefore less spectacular, but firmer: if harm is suspected, stop the spread, keep the available file and context, verify by a second channel, and leave the legal qualification to reporting and to the bodies active in criminal proceedings. The article does not join a specific video to a specific paragraph. It shows why that cannot be done from one score. 12. A screenshot drops the manifest. It does not drop the event The shortest Content Credentials test is deliberately banal. Take a file that you know has signed Content Credentials, and verify it at Content Credentials Verify [5] . Record the state: valid, invalid, missing. Then take a screenshot of it and verify the new file again. You will often see that the manifest is missing. That is not the exposure of a fraud. It is a property of the path. A screenshot does not create cryptographic continuity with the original file. A re-encode, a crop or a change of container can drop the manifest as well; OpenAI cites this as one reason for layering SynthID onto C2PA [20] . The loss of a manifest must therefore not be read as proof that the original event did not happen. Likewise, a valid manifest on the original does not say that a screenshot circulating two hours later carries the same value. The reader holds a different file. It can have a different crop, a different caption and a different context. Verification always concerns a specific file, not a general memory of an image. How to test Content Credentials before and after a screenshot The test has three steps. First verify the original file and save the result of the verification. Then create a screenshot or an ordinary copy through an application that changes the container. Finally verify the new file. If the manifest disappears, you record a difference between files, not a conclusion about the truth of the scene. If the manifest remains, you are still reading only the claims that are in it. 13. The best check is the one whose false alarm you can bear With a deepfake image the talk is often about how to catch a forgery. It is equally important how not to damage genuine content with a false alarm. A newsroom, a firm and an individual need to know what error they can afford. Pausing internal sharing is a cheap mistake. Publicly labelling a person as the author of a forgery is an expensive mistake. Sending money on the basis of a video is a different harm from mistakenly not publishing an illustrative picture. Type of failure What it looks like How to test What limits the harm Absence of C2PA as fake A phone without a stamp is labelled as AI Verify the file, the screenshot and the path of the file Absence is not an edit; a census of Czech visuals is missing Accuracy as operation A laboratory figure decides a dispute on the network Ask about the dataset, the threshold, FPR, the year of the generator The detector only as a hypothesis, not a verdict The eye is enough “I can see that the face is not real” Recall the experiment of 48.2 percent on GAN faces A second channel and restraint A label as an offender We expect a fraudster to label a deepfake Separate Article 50 from the Criminal Code Do not read a label as a punishment One paragraph for everything A political video is automatically § 191a Separate § 191a, § 181(2), § 184, § 209 and the Civil Code Qualification according to the conduct NÚKIB mentions deepfake in cyber-hygiene teaching, not as a certified detector [11] . The National Plan for Research and Development in Cyber and Information Security to 2025 treats deepfake as a risk vector [12] . ÚOOÚ in April 2026 placed deepfake videos in an overview of channels of AI fraud and the digital footprint [21] . The common line of these materials is not “install a magic app”. It is literacy, verification and process. The best check is therefore not the strictest check. It is the check whose error you recognise in time and whose cost you can bear. For low harm, a delay and a second source may suffice. For a public accusation a stricter procedure is needed. For a suspicion of a criminal offence the matter belongs in a different regime from a comment thread. 14. A signature, a detector and a second channel do not add up to one verdict A practical test must not teach how to manufacture a forgery. It should show the reader where a signature ends, where a detector ends, and where verification of the situation outside the file begins. What needs to be tested before you trust the eye The first test is about the signature. Verify a file with Content Credentials, then its screenshot. The second test is about absence. Take an ordinary photograph from your own phone without C2PA and do not attribute an artificial origin to it merely because the manifest is missing. The third test is about the eye. Compare a known synthetic face from a safe demonstration source with an ordinary photograph, and count in advance on the fact that human certainty is a weak tool. Nightingale and Farid give 48.2 percent for the first experiment, not a licence to hunt colleagues [13] . For a news or company visual, look for a clear label where the deployer is to handle it under Article 50(4) [6] [7] . Do not expect it on an anonymous repost as proof of an offender’s honesty. If harm is suspected, verify by a second channel: a known number, a known account, a personal contact or an institution whose communication has its own verification procedure. That is a process, not a detector. A blood-in-the-pixel detector is not a lock. — Jiný Kontext The result of the test does not read “genuine” or “fake” in one word. It reads: signature valid, invalid or missing; the detector is usable only for a given type of file and under given limits; an independent channel confirms or does not confirm the event. Only these sentences together reduce the risk that one impression becomes a public conclusion. 15. Personal use is outside the AI Act. It is not outside the Criminal Code The Commission FAQ states that personal non-professional use is outside the AI Act [7] . That is an important boundary. It does not mean, however, that personal conduct cannot hit other law. If someone creates or spreads a non-consensual pornographic work that exploits a person without consent, § 191a does not ask whether this was an enterprise deployment of an AI system [9] . If someone uses a false likeness or utterance with the intent to cause serious harm to rights, another question arises under § 181(2) [9] . Mixing these layers is convenient, but wrong. The AI Act regulates certain roles on the market and transparency. The Criminal Code assesses certain conduct. The Civil Code protects likeness and privacy. The protection of personal data asks about the processing of data. One file can fall into several layers, or into none of those spoken of in a comment. The practical consequence is simple. When we ask whether the content should have been labelled, we read the AI Act. When we ask whether a likeness was abused, we read Czech law and the specific circumstances. When we ask whether the file is technically signed, we read C2PA. When we ask whether it is safe to act on the content, we call a second channel. 16. A public series of prosecutions under the new paragraphs is still missing As of September 2026 the dossier does not contain public police statistics of the number of prosecutions under § 181(2) and § 191a for 2026. That is not proof that the offences are not happening. It is a gap in the public series. A more precise sentence is therefore not “nobody is being prosecuted for a deepfake”. It is: for the new paragraphs we do not, as of the date of the research, have a public annual overview that could be cited honestly. Likewise we do not have a verified primary figure that FakeCatcher or a similar rPPG detector would hold operational accuracy on the generators of 2025 and 2026 in open social channels. We also do not have an official Czech census of valid C2PA manifests on news visuals. And we do not have one aggregated NIST figure that would allow us to say “detectors are solved in operation” [18] . That does not weaken the main thesis. It rather keeps it on the ground. If C2PA became the default, unstrippable layer of majority sharing, the absence of a stamp would change meaning. If an independent evaluation of rPPG on current generators with a calibrated FPR showed stable operational performance, the detector would have a stronger role. If a challenge like DFDC held well above 70 percent on a hidden set and in operation, the caution would be recalculated. Until that is so, a missing stamp is not authenticity and 96 percent is not a lock. 17. The hidden cost is an eye that hit chance The most comfortable answer would read: learn a few signs, install a detector and look for a stamp. It would be short. And it would be dangerously self-confident. Image and video today do not require one trick, but a change in the order of the check. First we ask what we have in hand. An original, a screenshot, a repost, a compressed video, or only a preview? Then we ask whether a verifiable manifest exists and what it claims. Then we ask whether some detector makes sense for this type of file, this quality and this population. Only then do we ask what follows legally and practically. And if it is about harm, money, reputation or an intimate likeness, we return from the pixel to the person and the institution. That slows the check, but it slows it in the right place. Not on every picture. On every picture on which we are to act. The question is not how to tell a fake video or photograph at a glance. It is: what of the signature, the detector and the law may you trust for this file — and which false alarm, missing stamp or missed strike of the eye can you bear for this scene? Related texts in this series On the site: A photograph is no longer enough by itself. Its provenance becomes evidence too — the value of a genuine image after generative AI. This text is practical detection of video and photo. Is a photograph evidence? When an image can deceive even without edits — deception without pixel edits. What to do when someone misuses your photograph or identity? — the civil, criminal and platform channel.

items.title: History Is Not Written Only by the Victors. It Is Also Shaped by What Survived.
items.subtitle: The past is not the archive. An archive is a fragment that survived literacy, material decay, war, censorship, archival selection, translation and interpretation.
