Context: Our World in Data. How much of the world’s electricity is used for data centers and artificial intelligence? https://ourworldindata.org/how-much-energy-do-data-centers-and-artificial-intelligence-use
items.body: Section: Technology & AI Author: V Reading Length: ~27 min Sources and further reading: 22 items Topics: AI, electricity, data centres, inference, training, PUE, water, ERÚ, IEA SEO / Working Title: How much electricity does artificial intelligence use? How much electricity does artificial intelligence use? The question sounds simple only until we notice that we are not comparing one bill. A data centre is not artificial intelligence. Training is not inference. A watt-hour of a prompt is not a terawatt-hour on the grid. And Czech net 58 TWh is not ChatGPT’s bill in Brno. The article is therefore not looking for one percentage that could carry a headline. It is looking for denominators: which year, which boundary, measurement or scenario, and what still does not belong in it. 1. Four numbers on one table are not one share of “AI” Four numbers lie on one table in the newsroom. A reporter wants to turn the global share of data centres into a sentence about artificial intelligence. An analyst stops them: in 2024 the IEA is measuring data centres, not a pure AI share. An activist cites a median of 0.24 Wh per text prompt in Gemini Apps and multiplies it by an unknown number of queries. An energy specialist shows Czech net 58 TWh for 2024 and a world increase in data-centre use of about 70 TWh between 2024 and 2025. A cloud manager puts Microsoft’s 37,026,353 MWh of electricity for FY2025 on the table and asks how much of that is specifically AI [3] [9] [14] [16] . At first glance this is a dispute about whether artificial intelligence is energetically small or large. In fact each person is holding a different denominator. The reporter holds the global bill of all data centres. The analyst holds the IEA definition. The activist holds a unit of inference at one service and one method. The energy specialist holds a country’s annual balance. The manager holds a corporate bill that includes cloud for customers who need not be using generative AI. That is why everyone can be partly right and the shared headline still wrong. A number without a year, a boundary and a scope is not information. It is raw material for a misunderstanding. A data centre is not the same as “AI” and a watt-hour of a prompt is not the same as a terawatt-hour on the grid. — Jiný Kontext 2. The electricity of artificial intelligence has at least six layers The first layer is the chip and the computation. It depends on the accelerator, utilisation, batching, context length, the number of output tokens and whether the system is running in a simple or a more demanding mode. The IEA states that a top-end GPU can draw up to 1,000 W and that the cluster used for GPT-4 was estimated at about 10 MW for the GPUs alone, or about 22 MW with the rest of IT and cooling [2] . The second layer is training. It is one-off, peaky and concentrated. The third is inference, that is serving: repeated operation after every query, summary, translation, image generation or agent run. The fourth layer is data-centre infrastructure. PUE says how much electricity above the IT load is used by cooling and other operations. The fifth is water, where on-site water differs from water used in the power sector. The sixth is the electricity system, including local grids and the annual balance. The sentence “AI used electricity” is therefore the start of a diagnosis, not its end. Failure may sit in the model, in the computation, in cooling, on the grid, in the emission factor, in the water scope, or in reading a 2030 scenario as a 2024 bill. This layering also changes the political question. Connecting a large campus is planned one way; the carbon of one service is judged another way; and deciding whether a firm should use a demanding agent workflow for a task a smaller model can handle is a third. The grid does not see “AI” as an abstract capability. It sees power, offtake, time, place and reliability requirements. The user, in turn, does not see the grid. They see an answer on a screen. Between these two views sit the data centre, its cooling, electricity contracts and operating rules. That is why it is so easy to talk past one another. One person is dealing with the global climate, another with a local transformer, a third with an API bill and a fourth with water at the cooling site. All of them can use the word consumption. They are not talking about the same boundary. A good sentence about AI electricity must say which layer it stands on. If it does not, it begins to look like a general explanation while describing only one link in the chain. 3. The best number is the one whose denominator you can bear The energy debate does not need the strongest sentence. It needs a number that knows what it measures. The cheap error is to round the share of data centres so that local pressure on the grid disappears. The expensive error is to issue a 2030 projection as 2024 accounts. Still more expensive is to multiply 0.24 Wh by an unknown number of tasks and pretend that the text median of one service explains global infrastructure. Type of failure What it looks like How to test What limits the harm Data centres passed off as AI The bill of all DCs becomes a share of artificial intelligence Check whether the source speaks of DCs, AI-focused DCs, or inference Separate the computation boundary from the infrastructure boundary [1] [3] A scenario as an account The year 2030 appears without the word projection Ask for the year and the method State the 2024/2025 measurement separately from the 2030 scenario Wh times an unknown count A prompt figure is used for a conclusion about the grid Look for the count, the mix of tasks and the percentile Do not add the Gemini median to the global DC bill [9] Mixing water 500 ml for GPT-3 is set against 0.26 ml for Gemini Compare model, year, on-site and total scope Two bills side by side, not one verdict [12] [13] The Czech Republic as payer for AI 58 TWh is read as the bill of one application Separate a country’s annual net from the world increment of DCs Use order-of-magnitude comparisons with a caveat [16] A number is good when we can put it into a sentence without a hidden swap. Year. Population. Unit. Boundary. Measurement or scenario. What is in it and what is not. The same rule holds for comparisons meant to help the reader. Households, states or firms are useful orientation aids if they remain orientation. When the IEA likens a large data centre to households, it is showing a scale of power and offtake. It is not saying that a household has the same daily profile, the same location, the same tariff or the same importance for the grid [2] . When we set the world increment of DCs beside Czech net consumption, we are showing an order of growth. We are not saying that it is the same territory or the same decision. The best number is therefore not necessarily the largest or the smallest. It is the number that can be checked. If a source states 415 TWh, the year 2024 and all data centres, it can be used. If a source states 0.24 Wh, a median text prompt and Google’s method, it can be used as well. The error appears at the moment when one number starts doing the work of the other. 4. A data centre is not artificial intelligence The IEA, in the report Energy and AI , states that data centres used about 415 TWh of electricity in 2024, some 1.5 percent of world electricity use. From 2017, according to the report, their use grew by about 12 percent a year. Of those 415 TWh, according to the IEA, 45 percent fell to the United States, 25 percent to China and 15 percent to Europe [1] [2] . That is a firm orientation point. It is not, however, a bill for pure AI. Data centres serve streaming, enterprise cloud, e-commerce, storage, databases, traditional servers and many other services. AI-focused centres are a subset that is growing faster, because they contain a large number of accelerators for training and running models. If 1.5 percent is turned into the share of artificial intelligence in world electricity, the object of measurement has changed. It does not follow that data centres are negligible. Local pressure on the grid can be high even when the global share looks small. The IEA repeatedly points to the concentration of demand and to connection constraints. What must be said is simply: data centres in 2024, not artificial intelligence as a whole. A local problem can, moreover, be the opposite of a global headline. A world share of around 1.5 percent in 2024 looks small in one sentence. In a particular region a few projects can change grid planning, the need for backup sources and the pace of construction. Energy systems are not decided by a world average. They are decided by a node, a line, a capacity reservation and the time when offtake appears. It is therefore more precise to say that AI is one of the motors of new demand for data centres. It is not precise to say that every data centre is AI. And it is not precise to be reassured by a global percentage if a local connection is hitting capacity. One sentence must carry both sides: the global bill of all DCs and a local electrical constraint are not the same. 5. 485 TWh and +17 percent is a data-centre bill, not a ChatGPT bill In the update Key Questions on Energy and AI the IEA states that data-centre electricity use reached about 485 TWh in 2025, almost 500 TWh, and stood slightly above 1.5 percent of world electricity use. Year on year, according to the IEA, it rose by 17 percent. The difference against 2024 gives an increment of about 70 TWh [3] [4] [5] . That is a large movement in energy. It is still, however, all data centres. When Czech net consumption of 58 TWh in 2024 is set beside it, we get an order-of-magnitude comparison: the world’s annual increment of DCs is larger than the Czech Republic’s full-year net consumption. It is not a claim that the Czech Republic is paying for AI, nor that every new TWh belongs to chatbots [16] . For 2030 the IEA states a projection of about 950 TWh, around 3 percent of world electricity demand. The older report Energy and AI worked, in the Base Case, with about 945 TWh. Both values belong to a future scenario, not to the accounts of 2024 or 2025 [1] [3] . 6. AI-focused centres are growing faster than all data centres In a press release on 2025 the IEA states that the electricity use of AI-focused data centres grew year on year by about 50 percent. That is faster than total data-centre use, for which it states 17 percent, and faster than world electricity use, for which the press release mentions about 3 percent [5] . Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext That is a reason to take AI seriously. Not because every data-centre bill may be rewritten as AI, but because its subset is growing fast. In the Base Case for 2030 the IEA states that AI-focused centres may exceed three times the starting level and reach about 465 TWh. The definition applies to centres with a large number of accelerators for training and running models [4] . A caveat holds here as well. 465 TWh in 2030 is not a measured share of artificial intelligence in all world electricity. It is a scenario for a defined category of data centres. It fits the question of how the grid should prepare. It does not fit a sentence without a year and without a definition. 7. Training is not inference Training is the making of a model. Inference is its use. Training can be energetically concentrated and visible in the media, because it happens as a large campaign on many accelerators. Inference is less conspicuous, because it is spread across billions of individual requests whose cost depends on input length, output, model, batching and mode. Luccioni, Jernite and Strubell, in their work on AI energy, report historical corporate estimates: according to the cited Patterson et al., about 60 percent of Google’s ML energy in 2022 fell to inference and 40 percent to training; according to the cited AWS material from 2019, 80 to 90 percent of ML cloud fell to inference [7] [8] [21] . These numbers must not be frozen as today’s world ratio. The mix changes with reasoning modes, agents, video, longer context and new models. They do, however, show an important principle: a large training run is not the whole bill. Everyday operation of models can, in the sum, be decisive, even if one answer looks small. In inference there is still another hidden difference: the number of steps. A simple query may mean one model call. Agent work may mean a plan, a search, the reading of documents, several drafts, a check, a correction and another pass. The user still sees one task. The data centre sees more computation. That is why the average cost of a prompt cannot, by itself, be transferred to tasks that contain many prompts inside. Here energy meets product design. When an application sets an expensive mode for every query, it can waste. When it turns that mode on only where a simple model is not enough, it can save without a loss of quality. The difference between training and inference is therefore not only a technical definition. It is a rule for where to look for savings: once when the model is built, and again at every use of it. 8. 42.4 GWh of one GPT-4 training run is not a global share The IEA, citing Epoch AI, states an energy estimate of about 42.4 GWh for one GPT-4 training run. The background speaks of training lasting about 14 weeks, 25,000 GPUs and a load factor of 84 percent. Daily use of around 0.43 GWh is likened in the report to about 28,500 households in advanced economies on the given day [2] [20] . It is a good number for a sense of scale. It is not a global share. It measures one training run, not the inference that followed, not the whole data centre, not every repetition of experiments and not every service on the market. The IEA also uses order-of-magnitude analogies: one large data centre can have use comparable to about 100,000 households and the largest under construction up to about 2 million households. Such analogies help with size. They are not an accounting identity of Czech households [2] . Training numbers therefore belong in sentences with a precise boundary. One training run. An estimate. A particular model. Particular assumptions. The moment we turn them into a sentence about all of artificial intelligence, we change a peak into a year and a campaign into operations. 9. 0.24 Wh of a prompt is not 415 TWh on the grid Google, in a study by Elsworth and co-authors, reports for a median text-generation prompt in Gemini Apps a value of 0.24 Wh, 0.03 g CO2e and 0.26 ml of water. The method includes the accelerator, host CPU and DRAM, idle capacity and fleet PUE. Google states a fleet-wide PUE of 1.09 and a 33-fold drop in energy per median prompt over the 12 months to May 2025 [9] [10] [11] . That is an important correction of older impressions that every text answer must necessarily be of a large order. It is equally dangerous, however, to use it the other way as a universal excuse. It is the median of text prompts of one service, one method and one fleet. It does not measure video, agents, long reasoning, other providers, other PUE or the tail of very demanding tasks. How to test a prompt against the grid Does the source have a count of tasks and their mix? Is it a median, a mean, or the tail of the distribution? Is it text, image, video, a coding agent or a long search? Does PUE belong in the number? Is it one fleet with a PUE of 1.09, or another data centre? Without a count and a mix, Wh and TWh do not add. 10. Even if ordinary searches were simple AI text, it would still be less than 4 TWh The IEA, in Key Questions on Energy and AI , states a hypothesis: even if all ordinary searches were a simple AI text query, use would be less than 4 TWh a year, hence less than 1 percent of current data-centre use [3] [4] . This sentence is useful precisely because it is narrow. It speaks of simple text queries. It does not speak of agents that make tens of calls. It does not speak of video generation. It does not speak of long context, of private search in documents or of training a new model. And above all it does not speak of the whole data-centre bill. It does not follow that inference is always small. It follows that an ordinary text prompt and worldwide data infrastructure are different units. If someone has a count of tasks, their mix and a measurement per task, they can estimate. If they have only the median of one service and a feeling for the volume of the internet, they do not have a bill. They have a multiplication missing one factor. The practical implication is simple. A firm that deploys AI in document search, customer support or a coding agent should not count one universal prompt. It should measure its own typical task: how many calls arise, how long the input is, how much output is discarded, how often the work is repeated and when a more expensive mode is switched on. Only then can one speak of use per accepted result. 11. PUE is not the consumption of a model PUE, power usage effectiveness, is the ratio of a data centre’s total electricity to the electricity of the IT load. When Google states a fleet PUE of 1.09, that means that for 1 kWh of IT load there is 0.09 kWh of extra infrastructure. That infrastructure includes cooling, power delivery and other operating overhead [9] [10] . PUE is therefore not a property of a model. It is not “how hungry a transformer is”. It is a property of a data centre and of its operation. Another campus, another climate, another cooling design and another use of capacity can give another result. Strubell, Ganesh and McCallum, in their 2019 paper, used a global average PUE of 1.58 from 2018. That belongs to their estimate and cannot, without adjustment, be transferred to Google in 2025 or to Czech operations [6] . PUE also shows why training, inference and cooling should not be mixed. If we ask about the computation of a model, we care about the IT load. If we ask about the grid, we care about the data centre as a whole. If we ask about carbon or water, the energy mix, the place and the time are added. PUE is also not an excuse. A low PUE says that a data centre has little overhead above the IT load. It does not say that the IT load itself is small. A very efficient centre with a huge number of accelerators can use a great deal of electricity. Conversely, a worse PUE in a smaller operation may be locally less significant. That is why PUE should not be used as a standalone badge of virtue. It belongs beside absolute offtake, capacity utilisation and the source of electricity. A good question is: how much electricity goes into IT, how much does infrastructure add, and how often is the computation actually used? If accelerators wait for a peak, idle capacity may appear in the method as part of serving. If they run at high utilisation, the price of latency and of cooling changes. PUE helps to read operations. It does not close the energy bill. 12. Electricity is not carbon and carbon is not water One TWh of electricity does not have the same carbon everywhere. It depends on the generation mix, the time of offtake and the location. For the Czech Republic in 2024, ERÚ reports net electricity generation of 69 TWh, 3.9 percent less year on year. The export-minus-import balance fell from 9.2 to 6.7 TWh. Installed photovoltaic capacity rose from 3.3 to 4 GWe and generation from PV plants rose by 24.2 percent year on year. Nuclear and steam both fell year on year [16] [17] . Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext These numbers do not state the carbon footprint of one Czech prompt. They give context to the denominator. The same offtake on a grid with a different mix has a different emission impact. The same computation at a different time may have a different marginal source. And the same data operation may have a different water footprint according to cooling and to water used in electricity generation. That is why it is wrong to convert electricity, carbon and water into one sentence without a scope. Electricity is a physical account of offtake. Carbon depends on generation. Water depends on cooling, location and method. When these layers are distinguished, the debate is less striking, but more precise. In the Czech setting this caveat is especially important. ERÚ gives annual figures on the system, generation, consumption and the balance. It does not say what carbon footprint a particular AI service has when a Czech user calls it through a foreign cloud. Such an answer would need to know where the computation ran, at what time, with what electricity source and what contractual instruments the provider uses. The annual Czech mix is context, not the GPS of one prompt. Water, likewise, is not a universal converter of blame. Cooling in a dry region has a different meaning from offtake in a place with a different water balance. Water for electricity generation is not the same as water evaporated on site. Both can be relevant. They must not, however, be added without a label and compared with a number that measures only one of them. 13. On-site water is not a total water footprint and Li is not a rebuttal of Google Li, Yang, Islam and Ren estimate that training GPT-3 in the United States at Microsoft data centres may have used 5.4 million litres of water in total, of which 0.7 million litres were on-site. For GPT-3 inference they report about 500 ml of water per 10 to 50 medium-length answers, depending on place and time. This is on-site plus off-site water, hence also water tied to electricity generation [12] [13] . Google, by contrast, reports 0.26 ml of water for a median text prompt in Gemini Apps according to its method and its operations in 2025 [9] [11] . These two numbers are not a direct dispute about one thing. Li speaks of GPT-3, another year, another scope and the inclusion of water in the power sector. Google speaks of a median prompt in Gemini Apps, another infrastructure and another boundary. It does not follow that one number is the truth and the other a lie. It follows that water without a scope is even more dangerous than electricity without a year. The 500 ml range must not be turned into a constant for every present query. And 0.26 ml must not be turned into a ceiling for all tasks and providers. 14. 626,155 pounds of CO2e from 2019 is not ChatGPT in 2026 Strubell, Ganesh and McCallum estimated in 2019 that training a large Transformer with neural architecture search could reach 626,155 pounds of CO2e. They used, among other things, a US grid factor of 0.954 lb/kWh and a PUE of 1.58. It was one research pipeline tied to an architecture search according to the work of So and co-authors. BERT trained on a GPU without such a search was, in their table, an order of magnitude lower [6] . This number played an important role. It recalled that research search for models has a physical bill. It is not, however, correct to make it the carbon footprint of ChatGPT in 2026. Hardware, data centres, PUE, the energy mix, the models, the method of serving and the scale of use have all changed. Moreover it was training and architecture search, not ordinary inference. The old number therefore belongs to the history of measurement and to the argument that the energy of AI should be visible. It does not belong in a headline about the present global share. When an order-of-magnitude illustration becomes accounting, it stops helping. 15. Microsoft’s 37 TWh is a company bill, not the world’s share of artificial intelligence Microsoft, in its Environmental Data Fact Sheet, reports for FY2025 electricity of 37,026,353 MWh, or about 37.0 TWh. It is the bill of the whole firm. It includes global operations and cloud services for customers who may use AI, but also many services that are not directly tied to generative AI [14] . This number is useful for the question of how large the energy firms among cloud providers have become. It is not useful as a direct share of artificial intelligence in world electricity. If someone adds it to the 415 TWh of data centres, they can easily count part of the same world twice or mix a corporate bill with a category of infrastructure. The right sentence is narrower: Microsoft as a firm reported, in the given financial year, electricity offtake in the tens of TWh. From that we do not know how much falls to AI, how much to other cloud services and how much to the rest of operations. Without an internal allocation and a method, the number remains a company bill, not a bill of models. Company bills are valuable even so. They show that digital infrastructure is no longer a marginal item in energy. If a large provider grows, its decisions on location, electricity purchasing, backup sources and cooling affect public grids and investment. The two sentences must simply be kept apart. First: cloud firms have large and growing energy bills. Second: from one company bill the share of generative AI cannot be read without an allocation. This distinction protects both sides of the dispute. Criticism need not exaggerate in order to be serious. The defence cannot hide behind the fact that the exact AI share is not public. A missing allocation is not proof of zero. It is a reason to formulate the conclusion more carefully. 16. Czech 58 TWh is a country scale. It is not ChatGPT’s bill in Brno ERÚ, in a report dated 18 February 2025, states that net electricity consumption in the Czech Republic in 2024 was 58 TWh, 0.6 percent less year on year. It also mentions a drop in the local consumption of large enterprises. In the same context ERÚ reports net generation of 69 TWh, 3.9 percent less year on year [16] [17] [18] . A comparison with the IEA is strong if it stays precise. The world increment in data-centre use between 2024 and 2025, about 70 TWh, is larger than full-year Czech net consumption. That shows the order of the speed of growth of global infrastructure. It does not say that the Czech Republic used less than AI, nor that a Czech data centre runs at such a volume. The dossier has no ERÚ figures on the use of particular Czech data centres in TWh. Before a comparison with the Czech Republic Are you comparing a country’s annual net consumption with the annual increment of the world’s data centres, or with the inference of one application? Does the sentence contain generation of 69 TWh, or consumption of 58 TWh? Is it a Czech mix, world growth, or a company bill? Without these three answers the Czech number serves more as rhetoric than as a measurement. 17. The question is not how much “AI” uses. It is which bill, which year and which boundary The energy bill of artificial intelligence cannot be cancelled by one prompt coming out small. It cannot be inflated by renaming all data centres as AI. We need fewer labels and more denominators. When someone states a percentage, they must state the year. The year 2024 with 415 TWh of data centres is not the year 2030 with a scenario around 950 TWh. They must state the boundary. All data centres are not AI-focused centres, AI-focused centres are not one prompt, and one prompt is not a video agent. They must state the scope. Is IT load in it, PUE, carbon, on-site water, total water, or a company’s electricity purchase? And they must say whether it is a measurement, an estimate, a company method or a scenario. Three tests of the denominator Year: a 2024 measurement, a 2025 update, or a 2030 scenario? Boundary: all data centres, AI-focused centres, training, inference, or one service? Scope: electricity, cooling, carbon, on-site water, total water, or a company bill? Without a year, a definition and a boundary between training, inference and cooling, a share must not become a headline. — Jiný Kontext The right question is therefore not how much AI uses. It is: which bill are you reading just now — data centres, AI-focused centres, one training run, a median prompt, water or a firm — in which year, and what of that is still not the share of artificial intelligence on the world grid? Related texts in this series ChatGPT vs. Gemini vs. Claude vs. Grok… — a ranking does not measure a watt-hour. IEA Energy and AI : 415 TWh of data centres in 2024 is an infrastructure bill, not the bill of one chat.

items.title: A genuine image can deceive by angle, crop and time. Pixel authenticity is not the truth of the scene.
items.subtitle: In criminal proceedings a photograph is a means of evidence, not a verdict. An unedited image can deceive by the choice of moment, by angle, by crop and by metadata that describe the file, not the event.

2. An unedited photograph has at least six layers
3. The best evidence is the one whose deception you will see in time
4. A means of evidence is not a verdict

7. Angle and focal length are not a measuring tape
8. The camera clock is not the civil time of the act
9. GPS in EXIF is not proof of who stood at the lens
Three tests of metadata
10. Staging is not Photoshop
11. Compression changes the file even without intent to deceive
12. Identification from a photograph is not a search on the internet
Before identification from a photograph
13. An expert clarifies expertise. They do not assess guilt
14. An attachment to an inspection is not viral evidence
15. Generative forgery is a different article. Here a genuine angle is enough
16. A question of one sentence will carry more than a viral JPEG
What needs to be tested
17. The question is not whether the photo is genuine. It is what may follow from it

items.body: Section: Justice & law Author: V Reading Length: ~27 min Sources and further reading: 22 items Topics: photography, evidence, criminal proceedings, EXIF, metadata, rekognice, expert, optics SEO / Working Title: Is a photograph evidence? When an image can deceive even without editing Is a photograph evidence? The question sounds simple only until we notice that we are not comparing one thing. An image can be unedited and still deceive by angle. A hash can confirm a file and say nothing about the scene. EXIF can carry a date that is only the device clock. And identification from a photograph has legal safeguards that a viral “I recognise the perpetrator” does not. The following text is about deception without pixel edits. Generative forgery is a different dispute. 1. Three people over one photograph, three different conclusions Imagine three people over one JPEG in a case file. The prosecutor says: the file is unedited, so it shows what happened. Defence counsel says: the crop is tight, the wide angle enlarges the foreground, and the camera clock is an hour off. The expert says: the copy matches, the metadata are readable, but I do not comment on guilt. A journalist on the network writes: “you can see it.” Each is a little right. No one, however, is comparing the same layer. The prosecutor compares the admissibility of a means of evidence with the weight of a conclusion. Defence counsel compares geometry, frame and time with the caption. The expert compares file integrity and technical questions with a legal assessment that is not theirs to make [3] [6] . The journalist compares the impression of the scene with the process of proof. At first glance this is a dispute over whether a photograph is evidence. In fact it is a dispute over which question the photograph is to carry. Does it prove that the file exists? That it was unchanged after a certain moment? That a person was at the place? That they stood at a certain distance? That they did something intentionally? Each sentence needs a different support. That is why they can all be partly right and a shared verdict still wrong. A photograph can be admissible and weak. It can be unedited and misleading. It can have the right hash and the wrong caption. It can have an EXIF time that does not match the civil time of the event. The first rule is therefore not: believe or do not believe the photo. It is: write one sentence that the image is supposed to prove. 2. An unedited photograph has at least six layers One image looks like one thing. It is not. It is a chain of optics, frame selection, moment, metadata, compression and legal use. If we mix these layers, a false certainty appears: the pixels are unedited, so the caption is true; the metadata contain coordinates, so we know who stood there; the copy has the same hash, so the scene happened. Six layers of an unedited photograph: Optics and geometry. Focal length, wide-angle distortion, space compressed by a telephoto lens, height of the standpoint and direction of view. Distance and size in the image are not a measuring tape. Frame selection. Crop, the boundary of the shot and what remained outside the field. A genuine fragment can support a different event from the one the caption claims. Time. The moment of the shutter, the device clock, the time zone, the GPS date and the file-system time. One date need not be the time of the act [8] . Staging and choice of moment. Posing, rearranging objects and a decisive moment without a frame before and after. SWGDE separates staging from pixel manipulation [10] . File chain. Original, export, JPEG compression, social network, downloaded copy and attachment in the file. Each step can change something else [9] [11] . Procedural use. An object or a document, an attachment to an inspection, identification from a photograph, expert examination or an investigative experiment [1] [2] [4] [5] . This layering is not verbal ornament. It determines where the error arose and who can check it. If the time does not fit, we do not turn first to Photoshop. If the distance does not fit, we do not turn first to EXIF. If someone identifies a person from a photograph, we do not deal only with the sharpness of the face, but also with the procedure, the selection of comparison persons and whether the identifying person saw them in advance [2] [18] . Illustrative scheme: The same JPEG can, in one layer, confirm a bit-for-bit match of a copy, in a second open a question of angle, and in a third serve only as an aid to inspection. None of these sentences, by itself, says what happened in the world. 3. The best evidence is the one whose deception you will see in time With a photograph, authenticity is often what is sought. That is reasonable, but incomplete. Equally important is what deception the image can produce, whether it can be recognised, how much it costs to correct it and whether the conclusion can be taken back. A bad caption on an internal note is a cheaper error than publicly labelling a person as a perpetrator. A badly estimated distance at an inspection can change the whole meaning of a scene. Type of failure What it looks like How to test What limits the harm Angle and perspective A genuine image enlarges the foreground, shrinks the background or distorts distance Inspection sketch, scale, investigative experiment under § 104c More standpoints, measurement on the spot, an expert [4] [5] [12] Crop and moment The event before, after or outside the field is missing Original against crop, a series of images, a description of the source Do not rewrite the caption into proof of the event Metadata as the event DateTimeOriginal or GPS are read as a certain time and place of the act Compare OffsetTime, GPSDateStamp, the device clock and the file chain Treat EXIF as a hypothesis, not as a judgment [8] [10] [13] Staging The scene was physically altered before exposure Comparison with the scene, further shots, witnesses, an expert Separate staging from pixel manipulation [10] [14] Compression and chain An 8×8 artefact or missing EXIF is read as tampering or as purity The original from the camera against a copy from the network Keep the original file and describe the path [9] [11] A photograph’s ability to show something is one axis. The second is the observability of the deception, the third the reversibility of the conclusion and the fourth the impact. Where the harm is low, a careful wording may suffice. Where guilt, identity or an interference with reputation is at stake, the question must be slowed down and split. A hash verifies the file. It does not verify the scene. — Jiný Kontext 4. A means of evidence is not a verdict The Code of Criminal Procedure in § 89 paragraph 2 works with an open list: anything that can contribute to clarifying the matter may serve as evidence [1] . That sentence opens the door to a photograph. It does not say what weight a particular photograph has. It does not say that one JPEG is enough. Nor does it say that the court is to take over the caption with which the image arrived. This is exactly where admissibility is confused with persuasiveness. A photograph can be a means of evidence because it can contribute to clarification. It does not follow that it has itself clarified the matter. It can show the position of an object, the state of a place, a person’s face, damage to an item or the sequence of events. Each of these conclusions, however, must be read together with the other evidence and with the question the photograph is meant to answer. The Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms holds the frame of a fair trial [7] . It is not a slogan that automatically wins for one side. It is a reminder that evidence is assessed in a process where the other side may object, an expert may explain the limits and the court must not mistake an impression for reasons. The right sentence is therefore not: a photograph is, or is not, evidence. It is: a photograph is a possible means of evidence and its weight depends on what we infer from it, how it was made, how it was kept and how it fits the other findings. That sentence matters outside the courtroom as well. Public debate often jumps from admissibility to a verdict in one movement. “It is in the file” is translated as “it is true”. “It is in the photo” is translated as “there is nothing to discuss”. Yet a file can also contain weak evidence that still has to be assessed. And a photograph can be the right beginning of proof, not its end. Free evaluation of evidence is not free storytelling. It means that each means is read according to its content, origin, context and relation to the other evidence. An image without a scale can be strong for the colour of a car and weak for distance. An image with an exact time in the metadata can be strong for the file chain and weak for the time of the act if we do not know the device clock. This unevenness is why a photograph should not carry more sentences than it can actually bear. 5. A hash verifies the file. It does not verify the scene A hash is useful because it holds a very narrow question. If we have the original file and a copy of it, a hash can show whether they are bit-for-bit the same. In forensic work that is an important foundation of integrity. It is not, however, proof that the scene in the world occurred as the caption claims. SWGDE in the document Best Practices for Image Authentication version 2.0 of 20 November 2024, marked as a draft on the title page, distinguishes file integrity, image authentication and content analysis [10] . Integrity of a copy is the question whether particular data have changed. Image authentication examines whether the image shows signs of manipulation or of a virtual origin. Content analysis asks what the image captures. Those are three different jobs. The same distinction is helped by C2PA and Content Credentials. They can carry claims about the origin and edits of a file. They are not proof of the truth of the scene. This technology belongs, in a broader sense, to the origin of the file, not to a verdict about the event [22] . For generative images that is an important contrast, but the core of this text is narrower: even a genuine file can carry a wrong conclusion. So when someone says “the hash matches”, we hear a valuable sentence. We must not translate it as “it happened that way”. The correct translation is: this copy corresponds to this file. Only then do we ask whether the file arose from the given scene, whether the caption fits and whether the image can bear a legal conclusion. The file chain therefore needs to be described in ordinary terms. Who had the original? When was the copy made? Did it pass through an application that changes resolution or metadata? Is the file in the case an original file, an export, a screenshot, or a version downloaded from the network? Each answer changes only a certain part of the certainty. A screenshot can be faithful to what someone saw on a display. It is not, however, the same as a file from the camera. Here the difference between technical cleanliness and evidential meaning appears. Forensic work can say very precisely that a particular copy was not changed after it was secured. That is a firm step. It must not be used as a shortcut to a conclusion about the origin of the whole event. Integrity is the floor, not the ceiling. 6. A crop is a selection. It is not the whole event A crop needs no manipulation of the truth of the pixel. It is enough to move the boundary of the shot. A genuine fragment remains, but it can show a different event from the whole. A hand in mid-movement can look like an attack. A group outside the frame can explain why a person is stepping back. An object on a table can matter precisely because a scale sits next to it, which the crop removed. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext The published Jiný Kontext text on a genuine recording and a false conclusion treats a similar problem in video: a genuine clip can deceive when it is cut out of a wider context [21] . This is not a repeat of that article. This is a still image. With a photograph the crop is even harder, because we often do not see even a second before and after. We see only the boundary someone chose. Pixel non-editing is therefore not completeness. If a photograph is to prove the presence of an object, a crop may suffice. If it is to prove an attack, intent or a sequence of events, one frame may be too narrow. The decisive question is: what remained outside the image and could change the meaning of what remained inside. This is not a call to distrust every image. It is a call to precision. A photograph can be strong evidence of damage to a door. Weaker evidence of a motive. And very weak evidence of what happened two seconds before the exposure. 7. Angle and focal length are not a measuring tape Optics has no morals. A wide angle from close up enlarges the foreground and widens the space. A telephoto lens flattens distance and brings the background closer. A camera at eye height creates a different relation between figures than a camera low to the ground. None of this is fraud. It is the way a lens turns space into a plane. That is why it is dangerous to measure distance, the size of a crowd or the position of a hand from a single image without a scale. Hany Farid, in his work on photo forensics, describes that the geometry of an image can help, but needs support in a camera model, the scene and other data [12] . One photograph can open a question. It need not close it by itself. The Code of Criminal Procedure knows inspection and the investigative experiment. A photograph at an inspection is, together with sketches and aids, to help produce a complete and faithful picture of the object of the inspection [4] . An investigative experiment under § 104c can test whether an event could have happened under certain conditions [5] . That is not editing the photo. It is a way to check angle, distance and the possibility of observation. The practical question is therefore not whether the photograph “looks clear”. It is: do we know the focal length, the camera position, the height, the scale, the distances and the possibility of repeating the shot under comparable conditions? Without that, a metre-long conclusion from a photograph is more impression than evidence. A simple illustration is enough. A person in the foreground of a wide-angle photograph can appear larger and closer than a person a step further away. Two people photographed with a telephoto lens can look as if they stood close together, even if there was open space between them. Both images can be genuine. Both can deceive if metres are inferred from them without more evidence. That is why, in procedural use, a scale, a sketch and the possibility of returning to the place are valuable. Not because the photograph is suspect. Because the plane of the image itself does not contain all the information about the space. Where the point is only to document a damaged lock, a photograph may suffice. Where the point is the distance of a hand from an object or the visibility of a person from a certain place, space has to be brought back into play. 8. The camera clock is not the civil time of the act EXIF can carry data about the file and the taking of the image. That is useful. It is not an independent time seal of the event. The DateTimeOriginal field refers to the time on the device. If the camera clock was wrong, the reading will be wrong too. If the time zone is missing, the figure can look more precise than it is. CIPA gives the history of the Exif standard, including version 2.32 from 2019 and the newer version 3.1 in a 2026 translation [8] . These numbers measure versions of the specification, not the truth of a particular image. Newer metadata can work with fields for a time offset. Older files need not have them. And even with a new file, metadata are a record of a device, not a witness with a memory. The difference between DateTime, DateTimeOriginal, GPSDateStamp, GPSTimeStamp and file-system time can be unpleasant for a layperson. But that is often where the meaning breaks. The civil time of the act is a question of the event. EXIF time is a question of the device. File-system time can arise during copying. GPS time may relate to a different record than the date visible to the user. When these times diverge, that is not automatically proof of fraud. It is a reason to ask a question. The right sentence is: metadata support a hypothesis about the time of capture if we know the device clock, the zone, the origin of the file and the path of the copy. 9. GPS in EXIF is not proof of who stood at the lens GPS in EXIF looks solid because it has numbers and a map. Here too the sentence needs to be narrowed. GPS coordinates in the metadata can say where the device, according to its own record, was located. They do not, by themselves, say who held the device, who is in the image, whether the coordinates were affected by the surroundings and whether the file was original. GPS.gov states for GPS-enabled smartphones a typical accuracy of 4.9 metres in radius under open sky [13] . This number measures the horizontal accuracy of smartphones under good conditions. Accuracy worsens near buildings, bridges, trees, indoors and underground; the figure does not measure the truth of an EXIF record. GPS.gov also expressly distinguishes device accuracy from signal-in-space error, so the number cannot be transferred to an ordinary photograph without knowing the conditions and the receiver [13] . Three tests of metadata The first test is temporal: does DateTimeOriginal fit OffsetTime and any GPS time? The second is of origin: is this an original from the device, or a downloaded copy from the network that may have stripped EXIF? The third is of meaning: even if the coordinate fits, which sentence is it supposed to prove? The presence of a device is not the same as the presence of a particular person in front of the lens. SWGDE expressly notes that metadata can be limited, missing or altered [10] . Absence of EXIF is therefore not proof of purity or of fraud. Presence of EXIF is not the truth of the scene. It is a trace to be read with other traces. The map impression in particular must be handled with care. Coordinates look like a pin stuck into reality. In fact they are a figure written into a file at a certain moment by a certain device. If a photograph circulates as a copy, it may not be clear whether the metadata come from the original, from an export or from later processing. If it was taken in poorer reception, accuracy can worsen. If the question is the identity of a person, even ideal coordinates do not settle it. In practice, then, GPS helps mainly as a direction for verification. It shows a place to which an inspection, a witness or another record should look. It can support a conclusion if it fits the surroundings, the time and the other evidence. It is not itself to take over the role of the person who will explain who held the phone and why the image was taken. 10. Staging is not Photoshop Deception can arise before the shutter. Someone rearranges objects, asks a person to repeat a gesture, moves a sign, removes a scale or chooses a moment that turns the whole situation into a different story. The pixels can then be unedited. The scene, however, is no longer a spontaneous record of the event. SWGDE calls staging a physical alteration of the scene before exposure and distinguishes it from digital manipulation of the image [10] . That is essential. Detection of pixel interventions need not say anything about staging. Error Level Analysis or similar popular shortcuts can look for traces of file edits. They will not say who moved the glass before the image was taken. News ethics has known this boundary for a long time. The NPPA code forbids the staging of news photographs and the alteration of events that are to be documented [14] . It is not a criminal norm for a Czech case file. It is a useful analogy: a journalistic photograph can deceive with a genuine image if the scene was created for the shot. It does not follow that every pose is fraud. A wedding portrait is staged and no one presents it as proof of a brawl. The problem begins where a staged or selected moment is offered as a spontaneous proof of the event. Then it is not enough to examine pixels. The scene has to be examined. 11. Compression changes the file even without intent to deceive JPEG is practical precisely because it makes the file smaller. Lossy compression, however, is not neutral. The ITU-T T.81 / ISO/IEC 10918-1 standard works, for baseline JPEG among other things, with blocks of 8×8 samples [9] . This number measures the technical block of compression, not proof of editing. Artefacts at edges, loss of detail or blocking can arise from an ordinary path of the file. A social network, a messenger or a newsroom system can resample the image. It can discard metadata. It can change the resolution. It can compress again a file that is already compressed. When someone then sees a strange artefact, they cannot automatically make Photoshop of it. And when metadata are missing, they cannot automatically make that proof that someone tried to hide something. ENFSI, in its 2017 manual for forensic enhancement of image and video, treats among other things how adjustments of brightness, contrast or gamma affect what an observer sees [11] . Enhancement can help read a detail. It does not itself mean a conclusion of guilt. A laboratory-improved image is a working output that must describe the method and the limit. The right question is therefore not whether the file “looks compressed”. It is: do we have the original, do we know the path of the file and can we distinguish ordinary compression from a decisive change of content? Without that, a technical artefact becomes too fast a story. The same holds for ordinary enhancement. Brightening a dark image can help read a registration plate or the outline of an object. It can at the same time change the impression of contrast, shadow or colour. If such an output is used procedurally, it must be clear what was done and why. An enhanced image is not a new witness. It is an aid that is to be returned to the original and to the method. 12. Identification from a photograph is not a search on the internet Recognising a person from a photograph is a sensitive matter. The Code of Criminal Procedure in § 104b provides for identification and, for identification from a photograph, sets safeguards. The person to be identified is not to be shown in isolation, but among at least three other photographs of persons who do not differ from them markedly. The person carrying out the identification is to be heard in advance about the circumstances in which they perceived the person. The law also addresses the ban on showing the person to be identified in advance [2] . Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext Three further images are a procedural minimum in Czech criminal proceedings, not a statistical certainty of a correct identification. This number measures the construction of the act, not the probability of error. If the selection of persons is bad, if the witness saw the photograph on the internet in advance, or if a feed becomes an informal “identification”, the procedural value falls. Before identification from a photograph Is the person among at least three other similar images? Was the identifying person heard in advance? Did they not see the person in the media, on a social network or in police material before the act? Is this not a situation in which comments on the internet first created a name and the photograph then only confirmed it? The Supreme Administrative Court, in case law on identification in administrative-offence proceedings, works with an analogy to the safeguards under the Code of Criminal Procedure [18] . That is not a figure about error rates. It is a reminder that recognition from a photograph is not a free vote of an audience. It is a procedural act with rules, because human certainty can look solid even when it arose from a bad selection. 13. An expert clarifies expertise. They do not assess guilt An expert is needed precisely where a lay view is not enough: authenticity of the image, metadata, compression, the possibility of a montage, geometry, light, scale or the file chain. The Code of Criminal Procedure in § 105 to 107 works with an expert and an expert opinion. An expert, however, is not to evaluate evidence or resolve legal questions [3] . The Act on Experts regulates their status and responsibility [6] . This is an important brake on both sides. When an expert says they found no signs of digital manipulation, that does not automatically mean that the act occurred. When an expert says the metadata are not reliable, that does not automatically mean that the photograph is a lie. The expert answers technical questions within the scope of the assignment. The court assesses the evidence as a whole. Viral culture dislikes this boundary. It wants one authority that will say “genuine” or “fake”. Forensic work is often less spectacular. It will say: the copy matches, the EXIF is incomplete, the compression fits a path through a platform, the geometry from one image is not enough, staging cannot be addressed without a comparison with the scene. That is its strength. Expertise is not to replace the judge. It is to narrow uncertainty, name the limits and prevent a lay impression of a straight line, a shadow or an angle from carrying more than it can bear. 14. An attachment to an inspection is not viral evidence A photograph in a record of inspection has a different value from an image in a comment thread. The Code of Criminal Procedure in § 113 provides that photographs, sketches and other aids are attached to the record of inspection if that is needed for a complete and faithful picture of the object of the inspection [4] . Here the photograph is not a lonely image. It is part of an act. Police and criminalistic literature on digital traces stresses documentation, securing and evaluation in a process, not only the visual impression of one copy [19] . At a scene it can matter what the order of the images was, the scale, the orientation, the description, who took the image, when, with what and in what connection. Without that, the same image can lose part of its meaning. The same JPEG therefore proves a different thing in a different context. As an attachment to an inspection it can help towards a picture of the place. As an isolated screenshot on the network it can show only that someone shared a fragment. As a downloaded copy without metadata it can be a useful clue, but a weaker carrier of origin. The point is not that an internet photograph is always worthless. The point is that the procedural frame adds information that the image itself does not carry. When the frame is missing, the viewer must not paint it in with certainty. 15. Generative forgery is a different article. Here a genuine angle is enough After the arrival of image models it is tempting to turn every debate about a photograph into the question whether AI created it. This text stands elsewhere. The published Jiný Kontext article on the fact that a photograph is no longer enough on its own treats synthetic images, C2PA, detectors, watermarks and legal labelling [20] . Here the case is that the image was made by a camera and the pixels were not substantially changed. This boundary matters. A deepfake detector will not verify that an unedited image correctly expresses distance. Content Credentials will not say that a crop left out a decisive person. A hash will not notice that the scene was arranged before exposure. Generative forgery is a hard problem. It is not, however, the only way an image deceives. That also changes the editorial and legal reflex. On a suspicion of a synthetic image we ask about origin, manifest, model and labelling. On a genuine but deceptive image we ask about angle, time, frame, scene and process. Mixing these two questions means using the right tool on the wrong layer. It does not follow that a generative image is not a risk. It follows that sometimes a much older problem is enough: the photographer stood close, the lens was wide, the surroundings stayed out of shot and the viewer completed the story. 16. A question of one sentence will carry more than a viral JPEG The practical test is to be simple and safe. It does not teach how to edit EXIF, how to prepare a staging or how to circumvent identification. It teaches how to split the question. What needs to be tested First write one sentence: what is the photograph supposed to prove? The identity of a person, the presence of an object, a distance, a time, an intent and a sequence of events are different questions. One photograph can carry the first and not carry the second. Then ask for the whole image, not only a crop. If a series of images exists, read it as a series, not as one pulled-out moment. For your own file compare the metadata: DateTimeOriginal, OffsetTime, GPSDateStamp and GPSTimeStamp. Treat them as a hypothesis and write down where the file comes from [8] [10] [15] [16] [17] . Then comes geometry. If distance, size or position is inferred from a photograph, look for a scale, focal length, standpoint and a possibility of verification on the spot. If identity is at stake, do not confuse recognition from a feed with identification under § 104b [2] . If it is a technical question, it belongs to an expert and to other evidence, not to a vote in the comments [3] [6] . The result of the test is not to read “genuine” or “fake”. It is to read: the image supports this narrow sentence, it does not support this other sentence, and for this third one further support is needed. This way of writing a conclusion is less attractive than a viral caption, but it better protects the sense of the evidence. “The photograph shows that the object was on the table” is a different sentence from “the photograph proves who put it there”. “The metadata correspond to the evening hours of the device” is a different sentence from “the act occurred at the given civil time”. “A witness identified the person in an identification procedure” is a different sentence from “the internet recognised the person”. When the sentences are not merged, a photograph can be useful without becoming a switch of truth. 17. The question is not whether the photo is genuine. It is what may follow from it The most comfortable answer would be: an unedited photograph shows the truth. It would be short. And it would be dangerously wide. A photograph is strong precisely because it acts as a direct piece of the world. Yet between the world and the conclusion stand optics, frame, time, metadata, compression, scene and process. The hidden cost is not Photoshop. It is a conclusion that an unedited fragment cannot bear. A person sees a gesture and supplies an intent. They see a GPS coordinate and supply a person. They see three faces in a selection and supply certainty. They see a block artefact and supply tampering. They see a hash and supply the truth of the scene. An unedited image can deceive by angle, crop and time. Pixel cleanliness is not the truth of the event. — Jiný Kontext The question is therefore not whether the photo is genuine. It is: which one sentence is this image supposed to prove — and which layer, optics, crop, time, staging, file or process, that conclusion cannot bear. Related texts in this series On the site: A photograph is no longer enough on its own — generative forgery. A genuine recording, a false conclusion — cropping of context in genuine video. This text is deception without edits . Deepfake: How to recognise a fake video or photograph? What to do when someone misuses your photograph…

items.title: A name in Google is not a case file. It is a mix of registers, namesakes and cache.
items.subtitle: A name search does not assemble a CV or a police file. It ranks a selection of public and semi-public traces, with namesakes, gaps, and a right to deindexing — not a right to delete the page.
