items.body: Section: Technology & AI Author: V Reading Length: ~27 min Sources and further reading: 22 items Topics: AI, benchmarks, ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Grok, Czech, model evaluation SEO / Working Title: ChatGPT vs. Gemini vs. Claude vs. Grok: Which AI is the best? Which AI is best — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, or Grok? The question sounds simple until we notice that we are not comparing one thing. Preference on the Arena is not correctness. SWE-bench Verified is not your GitLab, and five attempts at max effort are not one attempt. MMLU is not general intelligence. An English leaderboard is not Czech use. Only when these four things are pulled apart can we read what the public tables aggregate as of September 2026 — and what they do not imply for Czech work. 1. Each leaderboard defends a different task Imagine four readers of the same word “best”. A product manager opens LMArena and points to the first rows of the public leaderboard. They are right that anonymous pairwise human preferences capture which answer users like more. The Chatbot Arena paper reports more than 240,000 votes from April 2023 to January 2024 and about 90,000 users. It does not measure a factual error, Czech grammar or Czech case law [1] . A head of engineering pulls out SWE-bench. They are right that the share resolved after tests pass is harder than an impression from chat. But SWE-bench Verified is 500 human-verified instances from Python GitHub issues. The original SWE-bench rests on 12 open-source Python repositories. That is not your enterprise monorepo, your GitLab, SAP, internal library or the Czech Cybersecurity Act [6] [7] . A teacher shows MMLU. They are right that 57 subjects and 15,908 questions make a named academic set. It does not measure open work with documents, Czech facts or whether a model admits uncertainty. And after Gema et al., it is no longer possible to pretend that every difference on raw MMLU is pure model ability: the authors of MMLU-Redux estimated 6.49 percent of questions with an error in the key [9] [10] . A Czech user adds BenCzechMark. They are right that Czech is not merely translated English. BenCzechMark has 50 tasks, 14 of them newly collected, in 8 categories, mostly in native Czech and with about 10 percent machine-translated tasks. It uses a duel win score from statistical tests at an alpha of 5 percent, not a simple mean of percentages. Closed models are also often missing, because the authors deliberately do not send samples to paid APIs. “Not measured” is not “lost” [17] [18] . At first glance this is a brand dispute. In fact each person is describing a different task. That is why they can all be partly right and the shared verdict “this AI is the best” still wrong. One table cannot, without reservation, decide chat, programming, school tests, Czech, safety and corporate accountability. A leaderboard is a map of one task. It is not a verdict on whom you may trust in Czech. — Jiný Kontext 2. One “best AI” has at least five layers When people say the best model, they often mean one number. But a public evaluation is built in several layers. The first is the task. Are we asking about chat preference, a GitHub-issue fix, a four-choice test, Czech NLI, a school essay or a search in a legal text? These are not different examples of the same thing. They are different problems. The second layer is the population of prompts or instances. The Arena collects self-selected prompts from real users and is mostly English. SWE-bench works with issues from 12 Python repositories. MMLU is an English exam bank. BenCzechMark adds historical Czech, pupil essays, spoken language and Czech tasks [1] [6] [9] [17] . The third layer is scoring. A Bradley-Terry model from pairwise preferences is not the same as a percentage of tests resolved. Accuracy on four choices is not the same as a duel win score with statistical significance. Each score has its own question and its own blind spot. The fourth layer is the harness and the publication policy. Agent scaffold, thinking budget, number of attempts, Docker, allowed tools and the choice of variant can change the result. The Leaderboard Illusion paper warns about private testing of variants and selective disclosure. That is not a small detail if the ranking is turned into a commercial argument [4] . The fifth layer is cost, latency, language and refusal. Token price, speed, Czech quality, data regime, safeguard and the chance that the system will refuse part of the task usually do not fit into one Elo. For users they often decide more than a one-row difference on a leaderboard. This layering is not a detail. It says whether we are comparing the same work. If one model ran five times at max effort and another ran once in a different month, they do not merely share a benchmark brand. They do not share a protocol. 3. Preference on the Arena is not correctness Chatbot Arena is useful precisely because it measures something static tests often cannot: human preference over real prompts. A user asks a question, receives two anonymous answers and picks the better one. A leaderboard is built from a large number of such duels. The ICML 2024 paper describes data from April 2023 to January 2024, more than 240,000 votes and about 90,000 users [1] . It does not follow that a higher rank means a truer answer. Preference blends tone, length, formatting, willingness to answer, politeness, certainty and sometimes correctness. A user may vote for an answer that is more readable even if it contains a smaller factual error. Or, conversely, for a brief answer, because it better fits their goal. The Arena is not useless. It is a map of behaviour in conversation. It must be read as preference, not as an expert witness of truth. When we ask which system wrote a more pleasant email, the Arena is closer to the task than MMLU. When we ask which system correctly reads a Czech statutory paragraph, Elo alone is not enough. Preference also often arises without knowledge of the correct answer. The user compares two answers at a moment when they themselves may have no primary source, test or legal footing. That is fine if we are measuring user choice. It is a problem if we infer truth from that choice. A model that answers with certainty, fluency and clean structure can win a vote even where a later check would find a faulty citation. A model that answers in a shorter sentence and admits uncertainty can look weaker, even if it is more useful for risky work. As of the research date we did not use a live first place on the text Arena, because without a stable primary snapshot it would be a number without an anchor. That is not a weakness of the argument. It is its condition. A leaderboard changes and must have a date, a URL and a description of what it measured. 4. Length and markdown are not ability. They are a style factor LMSYS does not deal with style by denying it. The blog by Li, Angelopoulos and Chiang of 28 to 29 August 2024 shows that answer length was the dominant style factor in a Bradley-Terry regression. The coefficient on the normalised length difference is given as 0.249. The authors controlled for length and markdown elements, for example lists, headings and bold emphasis [2] . That matters, because many users do not vote only on truth. They vote on the feeling that the answer is complete. A longer answer often looks more industrious. Markdown looks more ordered. Headings and bullets give a sense of structure. That can be a useful product trait, but it is not the same as factual correctness. Style control peels off part of this influence. It does not remove it perfectly. The authors themselves note possible confounders, for example chain-of-thought or other properties of an answer that travel with length. Observational control is not a randomised experiment. It does not say that after subtracting style we have pure truth [2] . That is why it is a mistake to read a style-controlled leaderboard as a universal verdict. It is better than a raw impression. It is still a map of preferences with a correction, not a meter of factual error. If your work depends on whether a citation actually supports a sentence, you must measure citation support. Not merely rank on the Arena. 5. A private variant before publication is not a public record The Leaderboard Illusion paper points to a practice that is uncomfortable precisely because leaderboards look public and simple. The authors report 27 private LLM variants from one provider, Meta, tested before the release of Llama 4. They also estimate an asymmetry of access to Arena data: 20.4 percent for OpenAI, 19.2 percent for Google and 29.7 percent for 83 open-weight models together [4] . LMSYS disputed these shares in its response. They therefore cannot be read as a closed audit of the whole Arena. They can be read as a warning that a public leaderboard is not only mathematics over a neutral world. Who may test privately, who withdraws a score, who publishes only the best variant and who has access to votes all shape what the public sees [4] . This is an audit of one practice, not proof that leaderboards have no value. On the contrary: if they have value, they need a protocol. They need to say which variant ran, when, under what rules and whether the result matches the production model. Without that, a user is not buying a winner. They are buying a name that may have meant something slightly different on the board. 6. SWE-bench Verified is not your GitLab SWE-bench is a strong test because it asks a practical question: can a system resolve a real GitHub issue so that the patch passes the tests? The original benchmark contains 2,294 instances from 12 open-source Python repositories. The score is whether the proposed patch passes both FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS tests in the given harness [6] [8] . Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext SWE-bench Verified exists because the original set had various impurities. In August 2024 OpenAI presented 500 human-verified instances from 1,699 randomly selected test samples. They were judged by 93 Python developers. The verified set has 196 easy instances with a human time estimate under 15 minutes and 45 hard instances with an estimate over 1 hour. These times are a human estimate, not an automatic metric [7] . Verified is cleaner. It is not universal. It still measures Python issues from particular repositories, in a particular harness, with particular tests. It does not measure code review, security, architecture, a TypeScript monorepo, historical SAP or Czech documentation. And SWE-bench Pro is again a different set: harder, more files, less leakage of ground truth. Verified is not Pro and Pro is not your GitLab. That is why it makes sense to take SWE-bench as a filter of programming candidates. It does not make sense to take it as proof that a model will fix your issue at the same speed and with the same risk. Your harness, your tests and your review rules are part of the performance. In a company repository what decides is often exactly what a public benchmark does not see. Code may pass local tests and still break an internal architectural rule. A patch may work and still be unreadable for the team that will maintain it. An agent may fix a symptom and go around the place where the bug is actually born. Or it may fail only because the firm did not give it the same context a person has: runtime variables, historical decisions, an internal library and knowledge of the release process. That is why a programming benchmark has to be complemented by your own pilot. Not because the public set is bad, but because your work has a different boundary of correctness. 7. Five attempts at max effort are not one attempt The largest confusion arises when we place numbers with the same benchmark name and a different protocol side by side. In the Fable 5 and Mythos 5 system card of June 2026, Anthropic reports 95.5 percent resolved on SWE-bench Verified for Mythos 5 and 95 percent for Fable 5. These are self-reported numbers, an average of 5 attempts, adaptive thinking and max effort. Fable has production safeguards including a fallback to Opus 4.8, which the card gives as a reason it may sit slightly below Mythos [11] [12] . On SWE-bench Pro the same card reports 80.3 percent for Mythos 5 and 80 percent for Fable 5. In the Gemini 3.1 Pro model card of 19 February 2026, Google DeepMind reports 80.6 percent on SWE-bench Verified for Gemini 3.1 Pro Thinking High, but as a single attempt. On the public split of SWE-bench Pro it reports 54.2 percent, also a single attempt [11] [14] . In the table for GPT-5.6 of 9 July 2026, OpenAI reports 64.6 percent on SWE-bench Pro. That table does not report SWE-bench Verified. In a comparison table Fable 5 appears as 80 percent Pro, but that is still a number in an OpenAI table and a match of names, not proof of the same run with the same harness. Historically OpenAI reported GPT-4o at 33.2 percent resolved on SWE-bench Verified as of August 2024, in a note on Agentless [7] [13] . What you need to test before you add two percentages Write Verified or Pro. The number of attempts. Thinking. The date of the card. Self-report or independent run. Agent scaffold. Allowed tools. Only then compare. Without that, 95 next to 80.6 cannot be read as a brand contest. It is a contest of two rows with a different protocol. A self-reported score shares a benchmark name. It does not share a protocol. — Jiný Kontext 8. MMLU is not general intelligence MMLU has a good reason to be famous. Hendrycks et al. built a large four-choice academic test in English: 57 subjects and 15,908 questions in total, of which 14,079 are test and 1,540 validation. The original paper uses five few-shot examples per subject [9] . Such a set helped measure breadth of knowledge. But breadth of academic questions is not general intelligence. MMLU does not measure Czech law, Czech facts, open-ended work with a document or the ability to admit that a source is missing. A model can be excellent on a four-choice question and weaker in a long Czech letter to a client. Or the reverse. The human anchor is also often read more strongly than the paper allows. Hendrycks et al. report 34.5 percent for unspecialised MTurk and about 89.8 percent as an estimate of an expert 95th percentile from source exams. That expert figure is an estimate, partly from percentiles and partly an educated guess. It is not a measured expert panel on the whole of MMLU [9] . MMLU-Redux and MMLU-Pro are further objects. A contamination review from GEM 2026 recalls MMLU as an archetype of a set sensitive to leakage into training and to repeated use [20] . That does not mean MMLU has no value. It means it cannot, without reservation, be made into a verdict on work that MMLU never measured. 9. An error in the key is not a difference between models In Are We Done with MMLU?, Gema et al. re-annotated 5,700 questions from all 57 subjects and created MMLU-Redux. They estimated that 6.49 percent of questions have an error in the key. In virology, in the analysed slice, they report 57 percent faulty items [10] . That is methodologically uncomfortable. If two frontier models differ by one percentage point on raw MMLU, part of the difference may be label noise, not ability. A model may answer in substance correctly and be punished by a wrong key. Or it may hit a key that is itself disputed. It is not fair to turn this into a sentence that MMLU is worthless. It is fair to turn it into a rule: the smaller the difference, the greater the need to look at label quality, an interval of uncertainty, contamination and the nature of the task. A precise percentage can precisely measure a defective condition. 10. A cluster at the GPQA ceiling is not a brand verdict GPQA Diamond is a different kind of academic test. Rein et al. built it as a graduate-level science, google-proof set; the diamond subset has 198 questions. Model cards from 2026 show high results: Anthropic reports Mythos 5 at 94.1 percent as an average of 5 attempts, Google reports Gemini 3.1 Pro at 94.3 percent without tools and OpenAI reports GPT-5.6 Sol at 94.6 percent [11] [13] [14] [22] . The difference of 94.1, 94.3 and 94.6 percent looks like a ranking. But it is a cluster at the ceiling, across different cards and protocols. Without the same run in the same week, with the same settings and public logs, it cannot be made into a brand verdict. The practical question is again different. If you are choosing a model for scientific Q&A, GPQA can be a useful map. If you are choosing a model for an internal Czech legal analysis, it maps a different terrain. A ceiling score on English science is not a licence to trust a Czech citation. 11. An English leaderboard is not Czech use Czech is not only a vocabulary. It is syntax, inflection, context, cultural references, schools, offices, legal wording, an error in diacritics and the ability not to translate an English phrase as a Czech sentence. That is why Czech benchmarks matter, even if they are less visible than global arenas. BenCzechMark from TACL 2025 reports 50 tasks, 14 newly collected and 8 categories. Most of it is native Czech; about 10 percent of tasks are machine-translated. The score is not a simple mean of accuracy, but a duel win score from statistical tests with alpha 5 percent. That is a different language of evaluation than MMLU or Arena Elo [17] . A reservation is still necessary. The authors of BenCzechMark deliberately do not send samples to paid APIs, so closed ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini are often missing on BCM. That cannot be read as a defeat. It is a gap in measurement [17] [18] . CzechBench is another Czech trace, but here too it is unwise to pretend precision where the sources diverge. The dossier notes that the BenCzechMark paper mentions 17 tasks and 8 native ones for CzechBench, while the public leaderboard reports 15 tasks. That is why no single official CzechBench number stands here as a fixed figure. A named benchmark Czeval or CzEval was not found in the primary sources as of September 2026 [19] . Whoever reads only LMArena or MMLU does not see Czech duels. Whoever reads only a Czech benchmark without closed models also does not see the whole market. The right sentence is not “this model won Czech”. The right sentence often reads: in this Czech set this was measured, that closed model is missing and your own test is necessary. Czech use also has several shapes. Writing a natural business email is one problem. Summarising meeting minutes with Czech names and institutions is another. Distinguishing whether a cited statutory paragraph is in force, has been amended or belongs to another part of the legal order is another. And correcting a pupil’s text so that the system does not rewrite the author’s style into smooth generic Czech is another. One score can bring some of this work closer. It cannot replace all of it. 12. Price, safeguard and refusal are not Elo A public leaderboard usually does not carry the bill. Yet a user is not buying ability alone, but an accepted result. In June 2026 Anthropic lists Fable 5 at 10 USD per 1 million input tokens and 50 USD per 1 million output tokens. In July 2026 OpenAI lists GPT-5.6 Sol at 5 USD per 1 million input and 30 USD per 1 million output tokens [11] [12] [13] . Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext These numbers are not a verdict by themselves. A cheaper token can be more expensive if the model needs more attempts, more checking and more human correction. A more expensive model can be cheaper if it reduces the number of failed runs. A price list is the price of a raw material, not the price of a result. Safeguard is another layer. For Fable 5 Anthropic reports production safeguards and a fallback to Opus 4.8, which triggers on average in fewer than 5 percent of sessions [11] . That can be a safety advantage. It can also mean that a Czech “this is not working” on a particular task is not model inability, but product policy. Refusal, latency and data regime do not fit easily into Elo. In work they still decide. The best model on a leaderboard need not be the best system for a process in which you need an audit, low latency, a stable answer, cheap review and predictable behaviour. The same logic applies to harm. In a marketing draft, a refusal may be only a delay. In customer support, an unpredictable refusal can be a breach of service. In a legal or medical text, caution can be desirable if the system clearly says what it will not decide and why. A leaderboard that measures resolved issues or chat preference usually will not show this boundary. A pilot in the concrete process must show it. 13. A Grok card is not an SWE table Grok appears in debates as another brand in the same contest. The dossier, however, states a simple limit: the public cards for Grok 4 of 20 August 2025 and Grok 4.20 of 7 April 2026 are safety and dual-use assessments. A comparable SWE-bench Verified number from xAI was not verified in these cards as of the research date [15] [16] . The absence of a number is not proof of inability. It is proof that these cards cannot be assembled into a fair contest on SWE-bench Verified. If one vendor publishes a coding score in a table and another publishes mainly a safety card, we do not have two measurements of the same thing. That is a more general rule. Not every model card is a leaderboard. Not every safety document contains product performance. And not every marketing table has a protocol that would allow comparison with another table. When the basis is missing, the precise answer is “not verified”, not “lost”. 14. The best map is the one whose error you can bear The following recommendations are not a product ranking. They are a signpost to a first run of your own. They follow the text Who you allow to err , which treats the choice of AI by the kind of error you can afford. This is not a second brand verdict. It is about how to read a leaderboard as a map. Type of failure How it looks How to test What limits the harm Preference as correctness Higher Elo = truer Czech Ten tasks in the same language; factual error, not “I like it” Take style control as a reservation, not as a test of truth Hidden harness 95% next to 80.6% as a brand contest Write attempts, thinking, date, Verified vs Pro, self-report vs independent Do not add cards with different protocols English map onto Czech LMArena or MMLU as a verdict for Czech work BenCzechMark, CzechBench or your own set; “not measured” is not “lost” Do not let MMLU or raw Elo be the first column Cherry-pick of variants Private runs, withdrawn scores, only the best number out Ask which variant is in production Leaderboard Illusion as a reservation on the table Cluster at the ceiling 94.1 / 94.3 / 94.6 as a ranking of brands GPQA Diamond: a 1 p.p. difference at the ceiling Do not decide a purchase on one percentage point Illustrative scheme: Three columns — Arena (preference), SWE-bench (tests in a harness), BenCzechMark (Czech duels). An arrow “best” does not run between columns. It runs only inside a column, with a date and a protocol. A good map is not the one with the largest number. A good map is the one whose error you know. If it measures preference, use it for work where preference makes sense. If it measures a patch after tests, use it to pick programming candidates. If it measures Czech, read it in Czech and with a limit of coverage. 15. Ten tasks of your own say more than first place A practical test is not a brand contest. It is a check of whether the map fits your task. Assemble ten tasks in the same language, the same genre and with the same threshold of harm. Ten Czech emails to a customer. Ten issues from your repository. Ten questions from an internal knowledge base. Ten short analyses where you know the right footing. How to test two candidates on the same set Run two candidates on the same day, with the same thinking setting, without switching the prompt between runs and with the same access to tools. Record factual error, a hallucinated quotation, refusal, length, cost and time to a usable result. Do not add Elo. Add which error would pass your review. Three harness tests If the task is Czech, do not let MMLU or raw Arena Elo be the first column. The first column is BenCzechMark, CzechBench or your set. If a closed model is not on BenCzechMark, write “not measured”, not “lost”. If the task is code, state the harness. “95 percent Verified” without the number of attempts, thinking mode and agent stack is a marketing headline, not a laboratory note. If the task is research, check citations sentence by sentence. A citation that exists still need not support a particular conclusion. Your own set need not be large. It must be true. It should measure the work you actually do, in the language in which you do it, and with an error you can imagine. A good set also has the right negative examples. It is not enough to give a model ten tasks that resolve smoothly. Add an assignment in which the basis is missing. Add a document with a contradiction between an older and a newer version. Add a question whose correct answer is “the available data do not allow us to say”. That is when the difference appears between a model that wants to finish the sentence at any cost and a system that helps keep control. Record the result simply. Not only a grade, but the kind of error. An invented source. A correct source, a wrong conclusion. An answer that is too long. A refusal without a reason. A good answer, but too expensive to repeat. Only this record says whether first place on a public map leads to your goal. 16. A self-reported score is not an independent run A vendor’s self-evaluation is not automatically false. It is a different kind of evidence than an independent run. A model card can be honest and still incomparable with a competitor’s card. The difference may be in the number of attempts, the agent scaffold, the date, the allowed tools, the sample or the policy for choosing a variant. A stronger conclusion would require an independent, pre-registered run of the same SWE-bench Verified harness for ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Grok in the same week, with the same scaffold, the same number of attempts, the same commit and public logs. That would still not decide Czech or law, but it would at least remove one source of confusion. For Czech, a public Czech-language preference leaderboard with described sampling and without private cherry-picking, where closed and open models stood side by side, would help. For MMLU, a re-annotated successor without an estimated key-error rate of 6.49 percent, on which the ranking of frontier models stably differed by more than label noise, would help [10] . It would also help to have proof that a style-controlled Arena score predicts your company metric better than your own set: time to merge, number of complaints, number of hallucinated paragraphs or the share of answers returned by an editor. Until that exists, a public leaderboard remains a map of a task. It is not a verdict. 17. The hidden cost is a first place that measures a different task First place is comfortable. It saves a decision, fits a slide and gives procurement a simple sentence. That is exactly where its hidden cost lies. When first place measures a different task, it brings certainty into the firm where there should have been a question. A leaderboard is not an enemy. Without public benchmarks we would have only advertising and personal impression. The Arena helps us see preference. SWE-bench helps us see programming fixes in a given harness. MMLU and GPQA help us follow academic knowledge. BenCzechMark and CzechBench remind us that Czech must have its own measurement. Each map is useful when we know where it leads. That is why it is not precise to say that we should not trust benchmarks. It is more precise to say that we should trust them in the range they themselves describe. If the Arena says that people in an anonymous pairwise comparison preferred one answer, we should not read from it the truth of a statutory paragraph. If SWE-bench says that a patch passed the tests, we should not read from it the safety of a design. If BenCzechMark says that a model held up in a Czech duel, we should not read from it the performance of a closed model that was not in the set. The question is not which AI is the best. It is: which task, which prompt population and which harness does the leaderboard measure — and which error will you see in time on your own set? Related texts in this series Who you allow to err — choosing AI by the kind of error you can bear. This text is a map of leaderboards, not a second brand verdict. Can AI replace programmers? — SWE-bench as a harness of work, not as chat Elo. Which occupations will AI replace… — a model leaderboard does not measure the end of an occupation.

items.title: A perfect copy is not an original. But why?
items.subtitle: Two visually indistinguishable works can have radically different values. An analysis of authenticity, provenance, aura, psychology, artificial intelligence and what we really value when looking at art.

items.body: Two paintings hang in the empty hall. Same dimensions, same canvas, same pigments. Every crack in the paint branches off in the same place. Even under a microscope, one surface corresponds to another. This is not an ordinary reproduction, but a thought experiment: the first picture was painted by a man several centuries ago, the second one was just assembled atom by atom by a machine. As long as the labels are not visible, there is nothing to choose from. Vision receives the same information. Then the labels are revealed. Security, insurance and a crowd of visitors appear in front of one painting. The other can be bought for the cost of the material and operation of the machine. The first explanation suggests itself: rarity . There is only one original, a copy can be made again. The second is less flattering: snobbery . It is said that people do not pay for what they see, but for the opportunity to say that they own "the real thing". Both play a role. But neither is enough. If it was only a matter of rarity, then a randomly created spot that exists in a single specimen would have the same weight. If it was only about social status, the information about the authorship should not change the aesthetic experience of a person who never owns the work. But research shows they are making a difference. And this is where the question begins to fall apart. Perhaps we are not comparing two identical images. Maybe we are comparing two equals appearances — and two completely different things. 01 — The first resolution The price is not an optical test When we say that a copy is "the same", we need to add in what. It can be the same in color, shape, material, chemically and microscopically. But this does not mean that he has the same past, the same legal status, the same function or the same ability to prove something. Digital forensics knows a similar difference. Two files can be bitwise identical and have the same checksum. However, content matching alone does not say where they were obtained, who handled them, whether they were created before or after the event, or whether their chain of custody was intact. The identity of data is not the identity of its history. This is not a peculiarity of the art market. A perfect copy of a wedding ring can have the same weight, purity, and scratches, and still not be the ring that someone received at the ceremony. A replica of a historical seal may leave a matching impression, but it was not the instrument used to authenticate a particular document. Some properties a thing has in itself; others gain by which she participated in . To confuse the two groups is to pre-decide the argument in favor of what can be measured on the surface. In a work of art, these layers often merge into a single word: value. In reality, there are at least several different values. Aesthetic — what we experience when looking. Historical — of which the subject was a part and a witness. Epistemic — what can reliably prove to us. Market value — how much people are willing to pay for it. Institutional — what a museum, connoisseur or catalog recognizes as an original. And personal — how a particular person relates to him. A perfect copy can take over the first of them almost completely. Some others may imitate. He cannot get others because they are not inside the picture as another pigment. They exist in a relationship between image, people and time. Editorial illustration The same image state does not mean the same object Conceptual model Comparison of original and perfectly matched copies in five layers Appearance and material may be the same, while origin, author contact, provenance and status remain different. HISTORICAL ORIGINAL ATOMICLY IDENTICAL COPY Layer by layer comparison Appearance and material MATCHING MATCHING The path of creation historical creative act later reconstruction Contact the author direct no Provenance a centuries-old succession starts today Status and evidentiary role original / historical document facsimile / proof of technology "Same" is always shorthand for the selected property set. The thought experiment assumes a match of appearance and material; the difference remains in causal and social history. 02 — Provenance History as an invisible property Let's imagine that an unsigned painting is found in the depository. Restorers examine it and find nothing out of the ordinary. A year later, convincing documentation appears: the work was created in the studio of a well-known painter, went through a specific collection and captures the decisive phase of his work. Not a single atom has changed on the canvas. Yet almost everything the institution and the market say about him has changed. This may seem like evidence that value is just a deal. But the agreement does not have to be arbitrary. A historical original is not only a bearer of a pleasant image; is also a physical node in the event network . It was present during a certain creative act, it aged in specific conditions, it bore the interventions of restorers, movements, damage and traces of ownership. A perfect copy can reproduce these traces as a shape. He cannot become their originator or witness. The crack in the old painting is the result of his life. The same crack on the new copy is a consequence of the information about this life. Visually they are identical; it causally goes in the opposite direction. Origin is not another layer of pigment. It is a property of the relationship between the subject and the past. That's why provenance — the documented history of a work's ownership and movement — isn't just a fancy pedigree attached for the sake of an auction. It is one of the tools we use to verify whether a given object really continues the life we ​​attribute to it. Of course, it can be incomplete, wrong or fake. But that doesn't mean the past isn't important. It shows why the quality of the evidence is important. In this sense, the price of the original can be understood partly as a price for unbroken causal continuity . We don't just pay for the image. We pay to be able to say reasonably: this is the subject the story is really about. 03 — Psychology of authenticity Contact, Performance and the "Magic" of Origin But people don't just judge the originals as historians. Part of our relationship to them is more intuitive and less easily defended. In a series of five experiments, George Newman and Paul Bloom investigated why people place more value on original works of art than on exact duplicates. Their results showed two recurring components: the perception of unique creative performance and the importance of physical contact with the author. [1] Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext In other words: for many people, the original contains more than just the composition. It also contains an activity trace. A brush stroke is not just a line of color; it is where the author's decision has turned into material. A copy may exactly repeat the result of the move, but it is not itself created by that decision. The second mechanism is often referred to as "contagion" — the belief that contact with a significant person transfers something of their identity to the object. It is not necessary to understand it literally as supernatural energy. It is often a shorthand for psychological closeness: a handwriting, an instrument, a garment or an image allows one to feel a more direct connection with a person who is no longer present. However, even creative effort is not a reliable measure of quality. Hours of work can produce mediocre work, and a single quick stroke can be the result of decades of experience. Effort works more like inferential clue : we try to retroactively estimate attention, skill and intention from the finished object. When the copying process shortens this path, we tend to attribute less human input to the result — even though our aesthetic response to its surface remains the same. This is why an ordinary guitar of a famous musician can command a higher price than a technically superior instrument. Doesn't necessarily sound better. But it functions simultaneously as a relic, a document and a means of imaginary contact. What the study actually shows Newman and Bloom's experiments worked with model scenarios and participants' judgments, not real auction transactions. They support an explanation of why people prefer the originals; they do not prove that every price premium in the market is rational, nor that there is a measurable "essence" of the author in the original. Moreover, two different judgments are mixed here. One can be reasonable: the original is the direct result of a specific creative act. The second may be an exaggeration: any physical contact with a famous person is said to increase the value almost without limit. The market, prestige and the human desire for closeness can turn a real historical connection into a fetish. So the original is not valuable either for good reason or from irrationality. Both layers can be present at the same time. Accurately distinguishing their ratio is more difficult than detecting a fake. 04 — Benjamin's problem An aura without mystique In the 1930s, Walter Benjamin described how technical reproduction weakens the "aura" of the work: its unique presence in time and space, the authority associated with tradition and historical testimony. Reproduction separates the image from the place, allows it to come to the viewer, and replaces a unique existence with a multitude of copies. [2] The word aura sounds mystical, but it can be read soberly. The original is the point around which verifiable events, institutions, and rituals of attention center. The reproduction conveys pictorial information, not this whole relational system. However, Benjamin did not just write an elegy for lost exceptionalism. According to him, reproduction also frees art from traditional rituals, widens its accessibility and changes its social function. So the copy need not be the enemy of the original. It may be the reason why we even know the original, why we can relate to it, and why its image has become part of common culture. The paradox is obvious: the more reproductions there are, the less rare the pictorial motif itself — and the more famous, desirable, and symbolically powerful its only recognized original can be. 05 — First turn When the copy is in a more correct place So far, the original could seem like a clear winner: it has history, contact with the author and authority. But what if the materially genuine object is torn from the environment for which it was created, while an exact copy returns to it? Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext Paolo Veronese painted the monumental between 1562 and 1563 Wedding in Cana for the Benedictine refectory of the monastery of San Giorgio Maggiore in Venice. In 1797, the canvas was removed and transported to the Louvre the following year; the Louvre catalog mentions military booty as a method of acquisition. [4] In 2007, a high-precision facsimile created by Factum Arte was installed on the original wall of the refectory. Bruno Latour and Adam Lowe have shown in this case that the relationship between the original and the copy need not be a simple battle of truth and deception. The material original remains in Paris. However, the Venetian facsimile re-entered the architecture, light, scale and function of the space for which the composition was designed. [5] Which experience is more authentic? A view of the real Veronese canvas in a different institutional and spatial context? Or a look at later facsimiles in a place where painting originally communicated with Palladio's architecture? The question does not have one axis. The Narsk Document on Authenticity, created in 1994 for the field of cultural heritage protection, explicitly extended the assessment of authenticity beyond matter itself. It draws attention to form and design, materials, use and function, traditions and techniques, place and environment, spirit and other contextual properties. [3] It is not a table for deciding which image "won". It's a reminder that authenticity can have multiple dimensions that diverge. Nara frame editorial illustration One original, two different authenticities No numerical score Comparison of the material original in the museum and the facsimile in the original environment The original is strong in material and historical continuity, the facsimile can be strong in place, function and spatial relationship. Authenticity here cannot be reduced to a single YES / NO switch MATERIAL ORIGINAL Louvre — original canvas HIGHLY ACCURATE FACSIMILE San Giorgio — the original refectory THE AUTHENTICITY DIMENSION Material and physical continuity VERY STRONG LIMITED Contact with the original creative act DIRECT MEDIATED Original site and architectural relationship INTERRUPTED RENEWED Original light, scale and spatial effect CHANGED CLOSE TO THE INTENT Institutional and historical status ORIGINAL FACSIMILE Different objects can be authentic in different ways. This is an editorial interpretation, not an official assessment of the image or a claim that the facsimile is "more original". The framework shows why material and situational authenticity need not overlap. Psychological research offers another unexpected detail. In hypothetical scenarios where people could not see the original directly, a proportion of participants preferred direct viewing of a high-quality reproduction over indirect viewing of the original through a monitor or mirror. The authors themselves emphasize the model character of the situation, yet the result weakens the simple rule "any contact with the original is always the best possible experience". [9] Thus, a copy can lose as a historical object and at the same time win as a means of seeing. The original may be materially truer, but experientially more distant. 06 — The Second Turn When can there be more originals The idea of ​​a single original is strongly adapted to painting and sculpture. As soon as we move to other types of art, it starts to fail. Nelson Goodman distinguished art autograph and allographic . For a typically autographed work, such as a painting, the specific history of creation matters: even a perfectly accurate reproduction does not by itself become a genuine specimen. In an allographic work, identity may be maintained through notation or performance rules. Beethoven's symphony is not the only physical sound ever made; can have many valid implementations. [6] The distinction is not the same as the division into "one piece" and "many pieces". A graphic sheet can be an autographed work and yet exist in multiple original prints from an authorized die. The museum definition of an edition therefore speaks of a set of identical prints made from the same printing surface; the number can be limited or unlimited. [7] In the case of a novel, we don't mind that the copy in the library is not the paper the author touched. Text can survive a change in paper, type, and device. With film, technical reproducibility is part of the way the work exists. With a digital image, an exact copy is the norm, not an exceptional technological marvel. This does not mean that a digital creation cannot have an original. It means that originality moves elsewhere: to the authorized version, timed publication, source files, creative process, author signature, contractual rights, or institutionally recognized provenance. Uniqueness no longer has to reside in bits. He may reside in a legitimate relation to them. A simplified decision tree The question "Where is the original?" depends on the type of work The philosophy of the identity of the work A decision tree for different types of art Painting, graphic publishing, music and literature, digital work and AI-powered work have different conditions of identity. What must remain the same so that it is still the same work? PAINTING / SCULPTURE Specific history is a part of the creation identity. GRAPHIC EDITION More original fingerprints from authorized matrix. MUSIC / TEXT More correct ones execution or specimens. A DIGITAL WORK Bits can be copied; provenance depends for authorization and recording. WORK WITH AI Need to separate image, process, author and legal status. Exact copy remains a copy. It is not an exception either molecular conformation. Plurality does not mean unoriginality. It is the binding that decides on the original matrix. Identity can carry notations. There isn't just one "true" sound or print. Uniqueness migrates beyond the data itself. To version, signature, time, process and rights. Aesthetic and legal question are not the same. The measure of human choice can be decisive. First, it is necessary to define what a "work" is. Only then does it make sense to look for its original. The tree deliberately simplifies vast philosophical controversies. Especially in architecture, photography, film, performance and digital creation, the conditions of identity can be more complex. 07 — Generative break AI changes the story behind the image Generative AI adds another layer. Previously, a copy could be suspected of imitating a finished painting. A generative system can create a new image that does not have a single physical prototype — and yet information about its origin changes judgment in us. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext In an experiment published in 2023, participants were given images labeled as either human-made or AI-made. In fact, all the works shown were generated by AI and the labels were randomly assigned. On average, images with a human label received higher ratings in, for example, liking, beauty, depth, and attributed value. A second study replicated the result; part of the difference was related to perceived effort and the story the viewer attributed to the piece. [8] The pixels have not changed. The hypothesis about what caused them has changed. This can easily be dismissed as prejudice against the machine. And sometimes it really can be. The study itself does not support the claim that human art is objectively superior; examines the effect of labeling in a particular experimental setting. The results of other research are not the same in all situations, and attitudes towards AI vary between people. At the same time, it would be too simple to declare every difference a mistake. For many viewers, art is not just a visual stimulus. It is an attempt to interpret the action: why someone chose this particular form, what he risked, what he knew, what he wanted to convey, what he defied. If the supposed originator changes, so does the set of meaningful questions. A simplified psychological model One sentence next to an image can change the entire chain of interpretation This is not an effect size measurement How labeling human or AI origin affects interpretation The same image leads to different expectations, inferences about effort and intention, and subsequently to different evaluations, despite different labels. THE SAME PICTURE without changing pixels "MADE BY MAN" source tag "AI CREATED" source tag INFERENCE intention effort life experience communication gesture INFERENCE automation model selection the role of the contracting authority uncertain intention EVALUATION popularity beauty depth value The label does not change the image. It changes the model of its creation in the viewer's head. The model summarizes one possible mechanism. It doesn't say that every human reacts the same way, or that the label "AI" always lowers the rating. The impact depends on the context, the attitude towards technology, the type of work and the degree of human participation. With the human author, the image can be read as a trace of conscious choice. For a system, it is necessary to first identify where the selection actually took place: in the data, the model architecture, the input, a series of iterations, curated selection, manual intervention, or a combination of these steps. Therefore, the label “created by AI” often obscures more than it explains. There is a wide continuum between one prompt and months of directed creation. One person takes the first exit; another creates hundreds of variations, changes the composition piece by piece, combines his own drawings, retouches and decides on every detail. Both may use the same model, but their causal role is not the same. It would be equally inaccurate to claim that the photograph was "made by the camera" without asking about the scene, the moment, the lens, the exposure, the selection and the adjustments — or, conversely, to pretend that the tool has no influence on the resulting space of possibilities. Law answers this problem in a different language than aesthetics. The US Copyright Office stated in a 2025 report that protection can arise where a person has determined sufficient expressive elements, creatively arranged or modified the output; according to him, entering prompts alone is usually not enough. A December 2025 review by the European Parliament stated that the European Union does not have specific rules for the copyright protection of purely AI-generated output, and the existing European standard emphasizes human creativity. [10] But that's not a verdict on quality. The work may be legally unprotected and aesthetically impressive; legal protected and banal. The law asks to whom and under what conditions to grant exclusive rights. The philosophy of art asks what a work is, how meaning is created, and why origins matter to us. 08 — Composite value So what are we really paying? When someone pays many times more for an original than for a visually identical copy, they are not paying one price for one quality. He buys a bunch of different claims — some well-documented, some speculative. I perceive Color, form, texture and immediate aesthetic experience. A perfect copy can share it. Event Link to a unique creative act and specific decision of the author. Testimony The object's ability to function as a historical document, not just as an image of information. Rarity A limited supply that can be natural, technical, legal or artificially maintained. Authorization Acknowledgment of author, institution, professional catalog or relevant community. Coordination A shared belief by the market and institutions that this very object is where status and memory are concentrated. Personal relationship A memory, identity and meaning that may not be transferable to any other buyer. No equation will determine their correct ratio. The market price can approximate historical value, but it can also be dramatically distorted by fashion, prestige, the tax environment, investment demand or simple competition from wealthy buyers. Therefore, a high price is not a proof of great art. It's proof that at some point, demand, rarity, and story came together strongly enough. However, the opposite simplification is equally wrong: that the difference between the original and the copy is only marketing. If we care about the past, authorship, and human action, then causality is a relevant property. It is not visible in the same way as color, but that does not make it fiction. Practical test When evaluating claims of “authenticity,” it is helpful to ask four separate questions: Is the appearance identical? Is the material the same? Is the same origin history documented? And is the subject similarly authorized? The answer to one of them does not automatically determine the others. This also explains the power of the forgery. A fake is not just trying to create the same image. Attempts to redirect foreign history to a new subject. Its essence is not similarity, but a false causal story. A facsimile that openly admits its nature can be accurate and culturally valuable. A forgery may be technically less accurate but socially more dangerous because it pretends to be an identity it does not have. 09 — Return to the hall The last difference Let's go back to the two canvases in the empty hall. The machine copied the pigment, the base, the cracks, and every trace of wear. In addition, what if all the records disappeared and no one could find out which one was the original one? For the market and institutions, the difference might practically collapse. Without evidence, status cannot be reliably assigned. Both things could become equally uncertain candidates. However, this is not the same as saying that their history was the same. One canvas was still created in an ancient studio, the other in a modern machine. We just lost the ability to know which. This boundary is substantial. The value of authenticity depends on the actual origin and our ability to prove it. Without the first, we have an illusion. Without the other, we may be right, but we cannot legitimately assign it. A perfect copy therefore reveals something unpleasant about the original. Its exceptionality does not lie entirely on the surface. Part is in the material, part in the event, part in the evidence, and part in the collective attention. Therefore, the original can be historically irreplaceable and at the same time aesthetically replaceable. Therefore, the copy may be ontologically different and yet more convincing to the viewer. And that's why the information on a small label can change the experience more than any image change. Generative technology did not create this contradiction. She just deprived him of a comfortable hiding place. It forces us to admit that when we look at art we are not just looking at the form. We also observe human decision, risk, time, authority, memory — and sometimes our own desire to be close to something that cannot be repeated. A perfect copy can inherit every atom of the image. It cannot inherit the moment in which the image first became reality.

items.title: How an Error Happens That No One Made
items.subtitle: A catastrophe, miscarriage of justice, or organizational collapse may have no single author. An analysis of how reasonable individual decisions can create an unreasonable whole.
