items.body: Section: Justice & law Author: V Reading time: ~27 min Sources and further reading: 22 items Topics: police, location data, § 88a, interception, ZEK, data retention, BTS, digital trail SEO / working title: How does police location of a mobile phone work? How does police location of a mobile phone work? The question sounds simple only until we notice that the film and the file are not comparing the same thing. A judge's order opens network metadata, not the content of a call. A cell marks a device inside a transmitter's coverage, not the door of a flat. Six months at the operator is not the same as four months of interception. And a Union finding against blanket retention does not automatically cancel one criminal-procedure order. The text that follows is about the lawful procedure. It is not a forensic reading of a trail as a verdict on a person, and it is not a guide to avoiding the cell. 1. The file holds a cell. At the table sit three other questions The file holds a base-station identifier and a time. The investigator says: the phone was in that cell. The defence lawyer says: a cell is not a door; the device may have been lying in a car. The journalist writes: the police tapped him. An official at the operator says: we have data required by law, including BTS Start and BTS Stop, not a film pin on a screen. At first glance this is a dispute about whether the police can find a phone. In fact each person is describing a different problem. The investigator talks about the registration of a device on the network and about time. The defence lawyer talks about the relation between a device and a person. The journalist talks about the content of communication, even though the file may hold only metadata. The operator talks about what the law requires it to retain and what it may release to an authorised authority. That is why they can all be partly right and the shared headline still wrong. “The police locked onto him” sounds like the end of proof. In the file it is often the start of a chain: number, IMSI, IMEI, cell, time, order, coverage map, other evidence — and only then a person. This article is about procedure. It does not decide whether a particular defendant held the phone in his hand. That is a forensic question, which the Jiný Kontext series treats elsewhere under the sentence “The phone was at the scene of the crime.” Here the question is which legal title opened which metadata. An order opens network metadata. A cell is not proof that the owner stood there. — Jiný Kontext 2. Police location has at least six layers The sentence “police location of a mobile phone” joins things that have to be kept apart. The first layer is the network. A mobile device communicates with base stations, the network works with identifiers, and the statute plus a decree determine which data are retained. Decree No. 357/2012 Coll. lists, among other things, IMSI, a device identifier and the Start and Stop base-station designations [5] . The second layer is time. It is not only about place, but about the start and end of a communication or session and about the period marked out by the order. The third layer is the legal title. In criminal proceedings that may be § 88a of the Code of Criminal Procedure; at other times the consent of the device user, a search under the Police Act, or another power listed in ZEK, the Electronic Communications Act [2] [4] [6] . The fourth layer is the output. The operator does not automatically release a photograph of a person in the street. It releases the data it holds that match the request. The fifth layer is the GNSS contrast. GPS in the phone, or AML on an emergency call, are different methods and often different legal channels from a query to the operator. The sixth layer is the reading about a person. Linking a device to a holder is a further chain of proof. This layering is not an escape from an answer. It is a way not to spoil the answer. If the file holds a cell, we know something about a device on the network. We do not yet know everything about the person. 3. The best reading is the one whose mix-up the file can least bear With location data the most expensive error is often inconspicuous. It is not that every metadata record is worthless. It is that it is read as something else. Metadata as content. A cell as a door. A device as a person. A search for a missing person as a criminal-procedure order. A time in the system as the time of the act. Type of failure What it looks like How to test it What limits the harm Mixing up institutes “Interception” where it was § 88a Compare § 88 and § 88a, content and metadata Read the order and its legal basis Mixing up the output BTS is read as a pin in the door Compare the output with Decree 357/2012 Read a station designation as coverage, not an address Mixing up the person A cell is read as the accused Ask who held the device Supporting evidence beyond the cell itself Mixing up titles § 68 of the Police Act poses as § 88a of the Code of Criminal Procedure Check the purpose: a search, or a criminal case Separate urgency from process Mixing up time The operator’s stamp is read as the civil time of the act Compare the period of the order with the time of the event A timeline, not an isolated figure The table is not a tool for evading the network. It is a tool for reading the file. Good defence, good editing and good investigation need the same brake: first establish what the document actually says. And then what it does not say. It does not follow that a cell is a weak trail. It follows that its strength depends on the chain. The more layers an article or a file skips, the more certainty it borrows without support. 4. § 88 is not § 88a The most common public mix-up is simple: everything is called interception. The Code of Criminal Procedure, however, distinguishes the content of communication from data on completed telecommunications traffic. § 88 governs the interception and recording of telecommunications traffic, that is an interference with content. In general it aims at a crime whose upper prison term is at least eight years, and at listed offences. An order is issued for at most four months and may be extended, each time by at most a further four months [1] . § 88a is a different institute. It concerns data on completed telecommunications traffic, typically metadata. The general branch aims at an intentional offence whose upper prison term is at least three years, or at listed offences. It requires a written and reasoned order of the presiding judge, in pre-trial proceedings a judge on a prosecutor’s motion, and subsidiarity: the purpose pursued cannot be achieved otherwise, or achieving it would be substantially more difficult [2] . The numbers have to be read with their unit. Eight years and four months describe interception of content under § 88. Three years describe the general threshold sentence for metadata under § 88a. They do not measure how often the police apply, and they say nothing about the precision of a cell. When a newspaper text writes “interception” where the subject was location data, it changes the interference for the reader. When the file speaks of § 88a, it is not about the content of a call. It is about another layer. 5. Traffic data are not location data, even when they are often requested together ZEK distinguishes traffic data and location data. Traffic data under § 90 relate to the transmission of a message on the network or to the billing of a service. They are not the content of communication [4] . Location data under § 91 determine the geographic position of the telecommunications terminal equipment of a user of a publicly available service [4] . In practice they may be requested together. That does not erase the difference. Data on who communicated with whom and when are a different layer from data on the position of a terminal on the network. Both can be sensitive. Both can matter in criminal proceedings. But they do not say the same thing. The distinction also helps when reading the words “data on telecommunications traffic”. They do not automatically mean that the police know the content of a message. They do not automatically mean that the police hold a GNSS coordinate from the phone. They may include identifiers, times, directions of communication and network data according to the legal basis and the decree. The right question is therefore not only: did the police obtain data? It is: what kind of data, for what period, under which provision and in what format? Without those answers metadata easily become a story that looked more precise than it was. 6. BTS Start/Stop is not a GNSS coordinate of the phone Decree No. 357/2012 Coll. is more sober than a film scene. For a mobile network it contemplates the Start and Stop base-station designations, IMSI and a device identifier [5] . That is an output about the relation of a device to the network. It is not an automatic GNSS coordinate of the phone. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext GPS.gov states a typical accuracy of a GPS-enabled smartphone of 4.9 metres in radius under open sky [17] . That figure measures the capability of the receiver in the phone under those conditions. It does not measure the accuracy of cell-ID in a file under § 88a. It does not measure the operator’s ability to identify a flat. It is a contrast, not a converter. Forensic literature shows that location from mobile devices is not one quantity. A 2020 DFRWS/Forensic Science International survey cites an example of a GSM antenna with a range of up to 35 kilometres and, beside it, U-TDOA on the order of 30 to 50 metres [16] . These numbers have to be kept on a leash. They are literary examples of methods and orders of magnitude, not an official accuracy table of the Police of the Czech Republic for 2026, and not a measuring manual. Public sources therefore do not allow a single sentence of the type “a police cell has an accuracy of X metres”. Sometimes the figure may be coarse, sometimes supplemented by further data. But BTS Start/Stop from the decree is still not the 4.9 metres from a GNSS chip. The direction of the proof also matters. When the system stores a station designation, an item arises that can be placed into the network. Only a further step says what territory that station practically covered at the given time and whether it could overlap with other stations. That step can be expert and useful. It must not be passed off as the original datum. Otherwise an administrative designation becomes a precise point only because someone drew it over a map base. That is why it makes sense to ask in the file, separately, for the raw output and for its interpretation. The raw output answers what the operator released. The interpretation answers how space is inferred from that. And only further evidence answers who had the phone with them. 7. A judge's order in the Code of Criminal Procedure is not a request under § 68 of the Police Act The police may work with location data in different regimes. Criminal proceedings under § 88a are one of them. A search for a particular wanted or missing person under § 68 of the Police Act of the Czech Republic is another. The purpose here is narrower: to establish the time and place of stay of such a person, and the statute binds the result to that purpose [6] . Before mixing a search with criminal proceedings The first question is which paragraph is in the file or in the request. The second, whether it is criminal activity or a missing person. The third, whether the purpose and the period for which the data are requested are described. § 71 of the Police Act adds a further special branch for a concrete terrorist threat [6] . Even that is not a general “the police at any time”. The Constitutional Court in judgment Pl. ÚS 45/17 of 2019 accepted, for a search, the absence of judicial review in view of urgency and a possible threat to life, but at the same time insisted on a strict application of the retention rules [10] . That is a precise reservation. It does not say that the police may do everything. It says that different titles have different purposes and different safeguards. To mix § 68 for § 88a is to change the nature of the interference. One regime looks for a person. The other serves a criminal case. Both may work with data from the operator. They are not, however, the same door. 8. Six months under ZEK is not four months of interception ZEK requires operators to retain defined traffic and location data for six months. This retention window has applied, in the present wording, since 1 October 2012, when the legislature reacted to the annulment of the previous rules [4] [10] . The statute at the same time forbids retaining the content of messages in this regime [4] . Six months here measure the period of mandatory metadata retention at providers of public networks and services. They do not measure the length of content interception. That, in § 88, the Code of Criminal Procedure sets at most at four months with the possibility of extension, each time by at most a further four months [1] . Different clocks, different object. These numbers also carry a second reservation. From the six-month retention window one cannot simply say that after it expires no data exist anywhere. Other legal grounds may exist for billing, handover or retention inside a particular case. At the same time, however, the window cannot be turned into a live database for anyone. Access is bound to authorised authorities and a title. Four months of interception and six months of metadata easily fuse in headlines. In the file they have to be kept apart. Otherwise the reader does not know whether we are talking about what someone said, or about when and in what network context a device communicated. 9. A Union conflict from 2025 does not automatically cancel one order Czech data retention has a long dispute behind it. The Constitutional Court in Pl. ÚS 24/10 annulled the previous data-retention rules; the judgment was published as 94/2011 Coll. The then § 88a was later annulled as well, published as 43/2012 Coll. [8] [9] . The legislature recast the regime and from 1 October 2012 set six-month retention. In 2019 the Constitutional Court in Pl. ÚS 45/17 dismissed an application to annul the new rules. It stressed, however, a constitutionally conforming application, strict conditions and the importance of judicial control where it is required [10] . Meanwhile the Court of Justice of the EU in Tele2 Sverige of 21 December 2016 and La Quadrature du Net of 6 October 2020 rejected general and indiscriminate retention of traffic and location data, with only narrow exceptions [13] [14] [15] . The Supreme Court on 30 December 2025 in case 30 Cdo 2556/2025, a civil dispute about an apology, stated that § 97(3) ZEK conflicts with EU law; the press release appeared on 8 January 2026 [11] . That is a strong signal of a defect in the blanket regime. It is not, however, an automatic derogation of a criminal-procedure order in every case. The judgment dealt with an apology, not a blanket erasure of § 88a. The correct sentence is narrower and more precise: the Czech retention regime is under pressure from EU law, but as of September 2026 the statute remains in the Collection of Laws and each procedure is assessed according to title, time, purpose and usability in the particular case. For the reader that yields a double caution. It is not precise to say that blanket retention is without a problem because the Constitutional Court dismissed an application in 2019. It is not precise either to say that every datum released under § 88a after the Supreme Court decision automatically vanished from the file. The first sentence ignores the development of EU law. The second turns a civil apology into a procedural magic trick in a criminal case. The better question is concrete. What datum was retained? Under which rules? For what purpose was it released? Could the matter have proceeded with less interference in privacy? And how did the court in the case treat a Union objection, if someone raised one? Only this series of questions keeps the dispute where it actually is. 10. OTT is not a mobile network. A number on the network does not measure WhatsApp A further mix-up concerns applications. The Constitutional Court in Pl. ÚS 45/17 expressly stated that the data-retention duty does not fall on OTT services, that is services that run over the internet on top of an access network, such as some communications applications [10] . In other words: locating a number on the mobile network is not a measurement of an encrypted chat. That does not mean that the content of a phone or an application never enters criminal proceedings. It means that other content requires another title. Examination of device content has its own rules, and § 113a of the Code of Criminal Procedure is a different question from a query to the operator under § 88a [20] . The opinion of NSZ, the Supreme Public Prosecutor’s Office, on securing the content of phones and e-mails shows precisely this boundary between institutes [19] . In practice that means a simple thing. When a file contains data from a mobile operator, it does not thereby automatically speak about the content of WhatsApp, Signal or another application. It may show that a device communicated with the network at a certain time and through a certain cell. It need not say what a person wrote, to whom they wrote in an application, or whether they had the application open. A telephone number used in an application has to be read with the same care. The number may serve as a login or verification datum, but the application itself communicates through the internet layer. It does not follow that an operator extract from the mobile network automatically describes movement inside the application. It may help with a timeline of the device’s connection. It is not a transcript of an encrypted service. A number on the network therefore measures the network layer. The application is a further layer. If the file holds both, each must have its own title and its own reading. 11. Time in a CDR is not necessarily the civil time of the act Location data are read in time. That looks obvious until we ask whose time it is. The operator’s record has its own system stamp, the order marks out a period, and the event in the real world has its civil timeline. These three times are supposed to meet. They must not merely be assumed to be the same. This point is not a guide to evasion. It is a check on interpretation. In the file one needs to know for what period the judge authorised the data, when the operator recorded them and how that relates to the time of the act. A stretch older than the statutory retention window need not be covered by ordinary retention, unless another legal ground for retention or a prior securing exists [4] . A delay in registration, a difference between a session and a communication, or work with a time zone are also questions of data interpretation. They are not proof of error, but they are a reason for a precise reading. One minute may be beside the point in some cases. In another it may be decisive. That is why a good procedure does not begin with a map. It begins with a timeline. When was the act supposed to have happened? What period did the order cover? What time does the operator state? And what happens if these times are not placed in one row, but left as separate layers? A timeline also prevents the opposite error. Sometimes uncertainty is turned into an automatic doubt about everything. That is not necessary. If the order, the operator’s output and the other evidence are aligned in time, the datum may be strong. It only has to be visible what exactly was aligned. Precision does not arise from not talking about time. It arises from describing it. 12. A cell is not a person A cell speaks about a device on the network. It does not itself say who held the device. The phone may have been lent, stolen, forgotten, left in a car or used by someone else. A contract may point to a subscriber, but the subscriber is not always the current holder. IMEI may point to a handset, IMSI to a subscriber identity, a number to a service. The person is a further link in the chain. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext Here this text touches the series “The phone was at the scene of the crime. Was its owner there as well?” only as a reference. There the main question is the forensic reading of a trail. Here we stay with procedure: what a legal title can open, and what does not follow by itself from the released datum. This is not an argument against the police. It is an argument against a shortcut. A cell can be very important when it fits into further evidence: cameras, witnesses, payments, a seized device, phone content or the movement of a vehicle. Without those joins, however, it should not carry more than it can bear. The correct sentence therefore reads: a device was recorded in a certain network context. Not: a person stood at a precise place. Between those two sentences lies the whole of proof. 13. GNSS in the phone is a different title from a query to the operator A GNSS position in the phone and cell-ID from the operator can fuse in public debate. Both are drawn on a map. Both concern a mobile. Legally and technically, however, they are different layers. GPS.gov states for a smartphone a typical accuracy of 4.9 metres under open sky [17] . HZS, the Fire Rescue Service of the Czech Republic, describes for AML that a smartphone can, on an emergency call, send a position obtained among other things from GNSS or Wi-Fi, and that accuracy may be in metres to hundreds of metres according to conditions [18] . Those are data about a device and an emergency channel. Not about a standard operator output under § 88a. If GNSS data appear in the file from the content of the phone, another title enters play. The Code of Criminal Procedure knows procedures for examining device content, including § 113a [20] . That is not the same as requesting metadata from the operator. The mix-up is tempting, because the result may end up on the same map. The path to it is, however, different. That also matters for review. With operator data we ask about the order, the period, identifiers and cells. With phone content we ask about seizure of the device, the scope of examination, the integrity of the data and the title to the content. One map does not cancel the difference between two sources. 14. A three-year threshold sentence is not the police at any time § 88a of the Code of Criminal Procedure has conditions. In general it concerns an intentional offence for which the law sets a prison sentence with an upper term of at least three years, or listed offences. Among those listed are, among others, fraud, unauthorised access to a computer system, dangerous threatening, dangerous stalking or breach of the secrecy of conveyed messages [2] . The figure three years is a threshold sentence in the legal text. It does not measure the gravity of every case and is not a free authorisation for any curiosity. Subsidiarity, a written reasoned order and the identity of the user, if known, join it [2] . In pre-trial proceedings the prosecutor moves and the judge decides. § 88a(3) admits the consent of the user of the telecommunications device. Precision is needed here as well. Consent replaces the order for data relating to the device and the user who gives the consent. It is not the consent of a third person who wants to know where someone else is. The legal frame is completed by the Charter. Article 10 protects private and family life, Article 13 the secrecy of messages submitted by telephone and other devices [7] . That does not bar every interference. It does, however, force the question who authorised the interference and why. 15. The output is a station designation. It is not the address of a flat When a datum is transferred onto a map, it acquires a new authority. A point, a circle or an area look like reality. In fact they are an interpretation of an output. The decree speaks of the Start and Stop base-station designations [5] . Converting BTS onto a coverage map is a further step. That step can be useful, but it is not identical with the original datum. That is why a description of the chain always has to be requested. What exactly arrived from the operator? What station identification? What time? Who created the map reading, and how? What reservations does coverage have at the given place? Public sources do not give one nationwide table of cell-ID accuracy in metres for every Czech situation. Anyone who asserts one without support is adding extra certainty. After a case ends, a person has, under certain conditions, a right to learn of the order and to propose a review of its lawfulness by the Supreme Court; § 88a(2) refers to the rules linked to § 88, including exceptions [3] . That too is not a technical detail. It is a safeguard against metadata remaining entirely out of sight of the person they concerned. In the file, therefore, look for the verbs. The operator “released” data. An expert or a police officer “displayed”, “evaluated”, “compared” or “placed” them on a map. The court “inferred” a certain factual circumstance from them. Each verb marks a further step, and each step may have a different strength. When an article replaces all the verbs with the sentence “the police located”, review is lost. The output is therefore not the address of a flat. It is an item in a chain. The more precise the conclusion that is to follow from it, the more precise the description of every step between the station and the sentence about a person must be. 16. Three tests of what a cell does not prove A practical test is meant to serve legal literacy. Not how to become invisible. It contains no advice on switching off registration, rotating identifiers, jamming base stations or delaying emergency location. What needs to be tested in the file First question: is it content, or metadata? If someone says interception, check whether it is § 88 or § 88a [1] [2] . Second question: is there in the file a written and reasoned order, or alternatively the consent of the device user? Third: what period does the order cover against ZEK’s six-month retention window [4] . Fourth: what exactly arrived from the operator: a number, IMSI, IMEI, BTS Start/Stop, or something else under the decree [5] . The fifth question is often the most practical: where do the data end and the reading begin? If a document contains only base-station designations and a time, it is necessary to describe separately who assigned a coverage map to them and with what reservations. If the file also contains GNSS from the phone, that is not the same metadata from the operator. A separate title for device content, or another source of the datum, has to be found [20] . Three tests of what a cell does not prove First test: a cell is not the door of a flat. If the output holds no GNSS, do not read it as GNSS of 4.9 metres and not as an address [17] . Second test: a cell is not a person. Who held the device must follow from further evidence. Third test: a cell is not interception and is not a search for a missing person. Mixing § 88, § 88a and § 68 of the Police Act is an error of institute, not a small shortcut [6] . The point of the tests is not to weaken every piece of evidence. The point is to stop one kind of datum speaking in the voice of another. A good reading can be strict and at the same time fair. It is strict in that it will not let a cell become a person without further joins. It is fair in that it will not deny the significance of a cell where it fits precisely into a timeline and further evidence. That is the difference between scepticism and review. 17. The question is not how they will find you. It is which title opened which layer The film question is: how do the police find a mobile? The legal question is slower and more precise. Which title opened which metadata? What period did it cover? What did the operator release? Was it content, or traffic and location data? Is the output a station designation, or a coordinate from the phone? And who held the device? The hidden cost of a bad reading is not only an error of a few metres. It is a pin that looks like a person but will only bear the registration of a device on the network. Such a pin can help when it is admitted as a link in a chain. It can harm when it is passed off as the end of proof. It does not follow that police location is unimportant. It follows that its value is procedural and evidentiary, not cinematic. § 88 is not § 88a. Six months are not four months. BTS is not GNSS. A cell is not a person. That is why a file should be readable layer by layer. Not for formality, but so that review sees the same chain as the decision. The right closing question is therefore not: how does police location of a mobile phone work? It is: which title opened which layer, and what still does not follow from a cell designation about a door, about the time of the act and about the person who had the phone in their hand? § 88 is not § 88a. A station designation is not a pin in the door. — Jiný Kontext Related texts in this series Can a person’s location be established from a telephone number? — a number ≠ a coordinate. How long does an operator retain data… — six months of metadata, not content. On the site: The phone was at the scene of the crime. Was its owner there as well? — a forensic reading of a trail. This text is the lawful procedure.

items.body: Prologue — one red pixel Open two front maps a month apart. A few coloured folds have changed. The map may be correct and still explain almost nothing about what happened between the two images. It does not by itself show the resistance overcome, the losses sustained, the logistics strained, or the forces preserved. Territory matters because it contains people, roads, industry, resources and defensive depth. The analytical error begins when a spatial result is treated as a complete measure of military performance. A map measures space. War consumes the ability to keep fighting. 1. A war that changed several times AI-generated illustration — A camouflaged tank in woodland near the front line. The war of March 2022 is not the same operational environment as the war of 2026. The failed Russian attempt at a rapid political-military break around Kyiv, the artillery-heavy fighting in Donbas, Ukraine's autumn 2022 offensives, Bakhmut, the prepared defences confronted in 2023, and the later expansion of drone warfare all emphasised different constraints. The phases overlap. Different sectors can simultaneously show urban attrition, infiltration, positional defence and long-range strike. The essential lesson is that organisations must keep learning while fighting. 2. Kyiv 2022 — superiority that could not add itself up Russia possessed major advantages in equipment and firepower, but the northern operation depended on speed, political assumptions, logistics and coordinated follow-on action. Hostomel showed that capturing a point does not automatically create the air bridge, ground access and sustainment needed to exploit it. A long vehicle column was a visible symptom, not the whole explanation. Combat power is constrained by the weakest links connecting movement, information, fuel, command and resistance. Ukraine's surviving air defence, dispersed forces and functioning command denied Russia the kind of permissive air environment familiar from some Western campaigns. 3. Charkiv and Kherson — the same colour, a different mechanism Around Charkiv in September 2022, Ukraine exploited surprise, uneven Russian dispositions and a tempo that outran the defender's ability to recreate a coherent line. Around Kherson, the crucial process was also sustainability: the Russian grouping west of the Dnipro depended on vulnerable crossings and a supply system under growing pressure. An organised withdrawal can preserve forces while conceding important terrain. A collapse and a deliberate withdrawal may look similar on a simplified map and represent very different conditions inside the force. 4. The 2023 offensive — passing through is not breaking through Prepared defence consists of mines, observation, fire, reserve positions, obstacles and forces capable of reacting. Mines become especially powerful when they slow movement in areas that can be observed and struck. A breaching vehicle by itself cannot solve that system. Successful breaching requires engineers, suppression, protection, communications, command and forces able to exploit a temporary opening. Concentration creates strength but increases detectability. Passing the first obstacle is therefore not synonymous with achieving an operational breakthrough. 5. The battlefield is more transparent, not transparent Reconnaissance drones, thermal sensors, radar, satellites and electronic surveillance increase the probability that activity will leave a detectable signature. They do not give every soldier a live omniscient picture. Visibility depends on terrain, weather, sensor survival, connectivity, attention and deception. Published footage is also a selected sample: we see successful or narratively useful clips more often than failed sorties, ambiguous observations or lost links. 6. From image to effect A useful analytical chain runs from detection through identification, location, tracking and decision to strike and assessment. Each step has its own uncertainty and latency. Correct coordinates can arrive too late. A hit can fail to produce a durable loss of function. The final step, assessment, is especially important. Explosion is an event; loss of capability is an outcome. A repairable interruption and a durable deficit are not the same military result. 7. A drone is not one weapon Reconnaissance multicopters primarily produce information. FPV systems bring guided effects to individual observed targets. Bomber multicopters can return and be reused. Loitering munitions combine waiting, sensing and one-way effect. Long-range one-way attack drones stress rear-area defence and industrial endurance. Fibre-optic systems trade radio vulnerability for physical and weight constraints. Interceptor drones add another layer to air defence. Naval unmanned craft contributed to sea denial in the Black Sea. Ground robots can move supplies, assist evacuation and take on dangerous tasks. Partial autonomy can affect navigation, tracking or image processing without making an entire system autonomous. Cost comparisons must include the whole system: failed launches, operators, reconnaissance, communications, maintenance and the number of attempts required for a verified effect. 8. What FPV can do better than a shell — and what it cannot FPV drones can act against individual observed objects while the operator sees a changing scene. Artillery can deliver suppression, area effects and concentrated fire whose value is not captured by a single destroyed vehicle. Destruction and suppression are different. A force that is temporarily unable to observe, move or fire may be operationally constrained even if much of its equipment survives. Camera-equipped weapons also produce more visible evidence of their own use, creating a publication bias in public debate. 9. Fibre optic — when the countermeasure changes the problem A physical fibre link avoids the particular vulnerability of a radio control channel to ordinary jamming. It does not abolish mechanical limitations, weather, detection, physical interception or the need for correct target identification. The important pattern is adaptation. A countermeasure can force the attacker to redesign a system; the redesign then creates new compromises. Defence can remain useful even when it is not absolute. 10. Electronic warfare — the invisible spectrum contest Jamming interferes with reception. Spoofing attempts to make a receiver accept false information. Electronic surveillance detects and interprets emissions. Protection seeks to preserve one's own functions under hostile interference. Navigation and communications are not identical functions, and friendly jamming can harm friendly systems if not coordinated. Electronic warfare is therefore as much an organisational problem as a technical one. 11. Software as part of the munition Some contemporary systems can change behaviour through software updates: image processing, navigation, stabilisation or data handling. Code does not repeal physics; a small battery remains a small energy store and a poor sensor does not become perfect through software. What matters is the feedback chain from battlefield problem to diagnosis, development, testing, distribution and operator understanding. Rapid iteration can be an advantage, but untested updates and fragmented versions can also create new failures. 12. Ground robots — a machine that is supposed to replace somebody AI-generated illustration — An artillery crew loads a howitzer in winter terrain. Uncrewed ground vehicles can carry supplies, help evacuate casualties, scout or perform dangerous engineering tasks. Their value is measured not by how futuristic they look but by how many risky human journeys or tasks they reliably replace. Terrain, connection, recovery, repair and the possibility of the robot itself becoming a new rescue problem remain practical constraints. 13. Infantry did not disappear New technology did not remove the need for people to hold ground, clear positions, move through buildings, repair systems and make decisions in uncertain conditions. In many places, technology changed how infantry survives and moves rather than eliminating infantry. The density of observation and strike creates pressure for dispersion, concealment and smaller movements, but terrain is still ultimately controlled by people and organisations. 14. What makes a good soldier Individual courage matters, but modern combat also rewards routine, discipline, technical literacy, small-unit leadership and the ability to operate when communications or plans fail. Experienced non-commissioned officers, medics, drone operators, engineers and maintainers can be harder to replace than the equipment they use. Human capital accumulates slowly and can disappear quickly. 15. Mobilisation — population is not a reservoir of soldiers Demographic size is only the first layer. A mobilised person needs screening, equipment, training, leaders, integration and eventually rotation. States also need workers for energy, transport, defence industry, health care and the tax base. Mobilisation is therefore a competition between military manpower needs and the continued functioning of society. The maximum theoretical pool is not the same as sustainable force generation. 16. Losses — the number everybody wants Casualty figures are among the most politically charged and methodologically difficult numbers in war. Killed, wounded, missing and captured must be separated, and “casualties” may combine categories that readers assume to mean deaths. Different sources have different incentives and access. A precise-looking number can still be uncertain if its method, period or category is unclear. 17. How the dead are counted Named lists built from obituaries, graves, official notices and family reports can establish documented cases and useful lower bounds. They inevitably lag and miss cases that are not public. Statistical excess-mortality methods answer different questions and have their own confounders. No responsible estimate should silently mix a documented minimum with a modelled total and call them the same thing. 18. Equipment on video — what is actually confirmed Visual confirmation is powerful because it anchors a claim to observable evidence. It is also incomplete. Some losses are never photographed; the same object can be recorded multiple times; a damaged vehicle can later return to service. Destroyed, damaged, abandoned and captured should remain separate categories unless evidence justifies a change. Visual databases are valuable samples, not omniscient inventories. 19. Artillery — a weapon that is really a chain A gun requires target information, fire control, ammunition, crews, transport, maintenance and barrel life. Shortages at any point can reduce the value of the entire chain. A shell in a warehouse and a shell available to the correct gun at the correct time are not the same military resource. Artillery remains important even in a drone-rich war because suppression, area effects and sustained fire perform jobs individual FPV attacks cannot always reproduce. 20. Barrels, tyres and repair crews High-intensity warfare consumes components that rarely appear in headlines: barrels, tyres, tracks, engines, batteries and tools. Repair capacity determines whether a damaged platform becomes a permanent loss or a temporary absence. A military that can recover and return equipment may preserve combat power even while public imagery shows many damaged vehicles. 21. Logistics — the war that begins far behind the trench Fuel, ammunition, food, medical supplies, spare parts and replacements have to move through a network. Railheads, depots, bridges, trucks and roads create capacity and vulnerability. A route does not have to be completely destroyed to become militarily less useful; reduced throughput and greater uncertainty can be enough. Logistics turns geography into usable combat power. 22. The mine, the engineer and the second trench Mines shape movement even when they do not detonate. They channel forces, slow them and expose engineers and vehicles to observation and fire. Defensive depth matters because clearing the first belt may reveal another obstacle or allow reserves to intervene. Engineering is therefore inseparable from protection, suppression, reconnaissance and tempo. 23. The tank — dead, or simply less forgiving? Tanks became easier to observe and attack from above, but they retained firepower, mobility and protection that infantry still finds useful. The correct conclusion is not that the tank died, but that unprotected and predictable tank employment became more costly. Survivability increasingly depends on combined use with infantry, electronic protection, reconnaissance, camouflage, engineering and recovery. 24. Aviation and glide bombs — why this is not Iraq AI-generated illustration — An operator watches a reconnaissance drone feed on a screen. Neither side enjoyed the permissive air environment seen in some post-Cold War Western campaigns. Surviving air defence constrained manned aircraft and shaped flight profiles. Russia's use of stand-off and glide bombs expanded the ability to deliver heavy effects without routinely flying directly over the most defended front-line areas. Air power here is a contest between aircraft, stand-off weapons, sensors, air defence and the industrial ability to replace munitions. 25. Air defence — with what do you shoot it down? Air defence is layered because different threats demand different interceptors, sensors and engagement ranges. Using a scarce, expensive interceptor against a cheap threat may still be rational if it protects a much more valuable target, but repeated exchanges create an economic problem. Interceptor drones and cheaper layers seek to improve this equation. No single layer can efficiently defeat every missile, drone and aircraft. 26. War far behind the front Long-range attacks aim at headquarters, logistics, airfields, industry, energy and transport. The relevant measure is not only whether something was hit, but how long the function was lost and what resources were required to restore it. Strategic strike is therefore a contest between repeated damage and recovery. 27. Energy — a transformer is not just a budget line Electrical systems depend on generation, transmission, substations, transformers, protection and repair crews. Large specialised components can be difficult to replace quickly. Redundancy and emergency repair can reduce the strategic effect of physical destruction. Energy attacks reach directly into civilian life while also affecting industry, transport and military support. 28. The Black Sea — sea denial is not the same as sea control Ukraine, despite lacking a symmetrical surface fleet, increased risks for Russian naval operations through coastal missiles, intelligence, strikes and unmanned maritime systems. This contributed to changes in deployment and behaviour. Forcing a stronger navy to operate more cautiously is sea denial. It is not identical to owning the sea, and the distinction matters. 29. Satellites and Starlink — when part of war is operated by a company Commercial satellite imagery and private communications services became important parts of wartime infrastructure. That creates advantages in scale and innovation but also dependencies on corporate policy, contracts, terminals, spectrum and external supply. A military capability can therefore depend on a private actor whose decisions are not governed exactly like those of a defence ministry. 30. Command and combined arms Combined arms is not a collection of weapon types standing nearby. It is the coordination of functions so that one compensates for another's vulnerability: engineers open routes, fires suppress, air defence protects, reconnaissance informs and logistics sustains. The harder the battlefield is to move through, the more valuable coordination becomes — and the more costly organisational failure can be. 31. Advance, breakthrough and tempo Advance is movement. Breakthrough means disrupting a defensive system sufficiently to create wider opportunities. Tempo is the rate at which one side can keep presenting problems before the other restores coherence. Kilometres per day do not by themselves tell us which of these is occurring. 32. The city — objective, symbol and trap Cities concentrate people, roads, industry, political meaning and defensible structures. Fighting in them can consume infantry and ammunition at extraordinary rates while turning civilian protection into an immediate operational constraint. A city can matter because of transport, terrain or symbolism; these values should not be silently merged. 33. War is manufactured High-intensity war consumes ammunition, drones, vehicles, air-defence missiles, explosives and spare parts faster than peacetime procurement systems were designed to replace them. Industrial capacity therefore becomes a strategic variable. Production numbers still need context: quality, delivery, repair, component availability and the rate of battlefield consumption determine the usable result. 34. The Ukrainian factory is not one place Ukraine's defence production is dispersed across state firms, private companies, workshops, software teams and foreign partnerships. Dispersion can improve resilience but complicates standardisation, security and logistics. Rapid adaptation is valuable only if successful designs can move from experiment to reliable production and field support. 35. Aid — money that is not yet a weapon Appropriated, allocated, contracted, produced, delivered and operational are different statuses. Headlines often mix them. A large financial commitment can be strategically decisive while still not solving a shortage today. The calendar of foreign legislatures, budgets, manufacturers and training programmes can be as important as the nominal total. 36. Economics — how many resources become power AI-generated illustration — Columns of smoke over the front line at sunset. A larger economy creates more potential resources but must convert them into military output. The Czech master cites SIPRI estimates for 2025 of roughly 190 billion US dollars in Russian military spending and 84.1 billion for Ukraine, alongside very different shares of GDP. Such dollar comparisons do not imply equal domestic purchasing power or equal efficiency. Economic endurance includes labour, taxation, inflation, energy, imports, sanctions, external finance and the opportunity costs imposed on civilian society. 37. The civilian is not a side chapter Civilian deaths and injuries are not merely humanitarian footnotes. Population displacement changes labour markets and local services. Destroyed housing and infrastructure shift public spending. Fear and insecurity alter political behaviour and long-term demographic prospects. A military analysis that removes civilians misunderstands the society sustaining the military. 38. A wounded person is not a closed record Survival does not end the human and strategic cost. Rehabilitation, prosthetics, mental health, chronic disability and family care can last years. The ability to return personnel to civilian life or duty also affects military manpower and public finance. Wounded figures therefore do not translate mechanically into permanent military loss, but neither do they disappear after evacuation. 39. Time is not neutral Time can benefit the side that adapts, replenishes and sustains political support faster. It can harm the side whose experienced personnel, infrastructure or external alliances erode. Both processes can happen simultaneously in different domains. There is no universal rule that a long war automatically favours the larger state or the defender. 40. Five races without a final lap The conflict can be understood as overlapping races: sensors against concealment; strike systems against protection; production against consumption; innovation against countermeasure; and force generation against human attrition. Winning one race temporarily does not finish the others. A technological advantage can be copied, jammed, dispersed against or outproduced. 41. No miracle weapon Every celebrated system enters an ecosystem of countermeasures and constraints. A weapon can be genuinely excellent and still fail to transform the strategic balance because there are too few of them, because the enemy adapts, or because another bottleneck remains. The relevant question is therefore not whether a system is “game-changing” in isolation, but what function it changes, at what scale and for how long. 42. Telegram is not a general staff. A general staff is not an independent source Open-source reporting, social media, official military statements, commercial imagery and specialist analysis each provide different evidence. None should automatically inherit the authority of another. A claim becomes stronger through corroboration, clear methodology and acknowledgement of uncertainty. War rewards propaganda; analysis must reward evidence instead. 43. What would the war look like without drones? Without the mass proliferation of drones, artillery, mines, infantry and aviation would still exist, but observation would often be slower and less granular, movement somewhat easier to conceal, and some precision effects more expensive or less available at unit level. This counterfactual shows why drones matter without pretending they replaced traditional warfare. They changed the connections between old functions. 44. Where is the war now? The Czech master uses a cut-off of 13 September 2026 and distinguishes a dated map from certainty about every metre of front. The essential methodological point survives every update: a map should state its time, source, definition of control and treatment of grey zones or infiltrations. A current front line is an estimate of control, not a legal border and not a forecast of the next month. 45. Who is winning? There is no single metric that closes the question. Territory, force preservation, casualty replacement, industrial output, air defence, the Black Sea, long-range strike, foreign support and political endurance can point in different directions. Any answer should define the time horizon and level. “Winning today” can mean a local tactical advantage and still coexist with a strategic problem. 46. Back to the map The map is most useful when its limits are visible. It is excellent at showing space. It is poor at showing training, repair capacity, ammunition stocks, morale, hospital load, industrial learning or the political reliability of future aid. Instead of discarding the map, we should surround it with the variables it cannot carry. 47. Final evidentiary summary Well supported: the war changed its operational character repeatedly; drones and sensors increased battlefield visibility without creating omniscience; logistics, repair, air defence, engineering, infantry and industrial production remain central; a local territorial gain does not by itself demonstrate an operational breakthrough. Strongly supported interpretation: the conflict is best understood as a system of interacting military, technological, economic and human processes rather than a competition between individual weapons. Still uncertain: exact comparative losses, hidden stockpiles, the durability of some industrial rates and the internal assessments by which both governments evaluate acceptable cost. What public data cannot provide in real time is a perfect balance sheet of remaining combat power. That is precisely why humility about the map is not evasiveness. It is method. Territory is the result. War is the system that produces, pays for and tries to sustain that result.

items.subtitle: Pavements, transport, benches, lighting and missing toilets do not command what we do. They change the cost of our options—and therefore the behaviour that becomes more likely.
