The literature is predominantly observational; it shows average associations, not a simple universal effect. · [1] Ewing, R.; Cervero, R.

Countrywide natural experiment links built environment to physical activity . Nature, 645, 407–413 . ↩ A natural experiment based on relocation and smartphone data. It offers stronger evidence for the mechanism than a cross-sectional comparison, but people were still not randomly assigned to cities. · [2] Althoff, T.; Ivanovic, B.; King, A. C.; Hicks, J. L.; Delp, S. L.; Leskovec, J.

Global Age-friendly Cities: A Guide . WHO . ↩ An international framework based on the experiences of older residents, carers and service providers. It highlights seating, toilets, accessibility, safety and transport as conditions for participating in urban life. · [3] World Health Organization

Would You Be Happier Living in a Greener Urban Area? A Fixed-Effects Analysis of Panel Data . Psychological Science, 24(6), 920–928 . ↩ A panel analysis with statistical controls for stable individual differences. It reduces some bias, but does not turn urban greenery into a randomised treatment. · [4] White, M. P.; Alcock, I.; Wheeler, B. W.; Depledge, M. H.

Environmental Noise Guidelines for the European Region . World Health Organization . ↩ Recommendations and evidence synthesis on transport and other environmental noise. The risks concern long-term exposure and cannot be mechanically attributed to a single noisy street. · [5] WHO Regional Office for Europe

Understanding the Relationship between Urban Public Space and Social Cohesion: A Systematic Review . International Journal of Community Well-Being, 7, 155–212 . ↩ A systematic review highlighting the importance of access, street furniture, informality and perceptions of space. The authors also note the dominance of cross-sectional studies and inconsistent measurement of social cohesion. · [6] Qi, J.; Mazumdar, S.; Vasconcelos, A. C.

Pedestrian fatality risk as a function of car impact speed . Accident Analysis & Prevention, 41(3), 536–542 . ↩ An analysis of pedestrian fatality risk by impact speed. The precise shape of the curve depends on the data and methods used; the sharp increase in risk with speed is robust. · [7] Rosén, E.; Sander, U.

The Fundamental Law of Road Congestion: Evidence from US Cities . American Economic Review, 101(6), 2616–2652 . ↩ An empirical study of metropolitan highways and vehicle miles travelled in the United States. Strong evidence of induced demand in that context, not a claim about every individual local road. · [8] Duranton, G.; Turner, M. A.

Reducing Crime Through Environmental Design: Evidence from a Randomized Experiment of Street Lighting in New York City . Journal of Quantitative Criminology, 38, 127–157 . ↩ A randomised intervention using temporary lighting in public-housing developments. High internal validity for the specific intervention, but limited transferability to other places and forms of lighting. · [9] Chalfin, A.; Hansen, B.; Lerner, J.; Parker, L.

CCTV Surveillance for Crime Prevention: A 40-Year Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis . Criminology & Public Policy, 18(1), 135–159 . ↩ A meta-analysis finding a modest average effect, most consistently in car parks. The result varies by setting, monitoring and whether cameras are combined with other measures. · [10] Piza, E. L.; Welsh, B. C.; Farrington, D. P.; Thomas, A. L.

The London Spikes Controversy: Homelessness, Urban Securitisation and the Question of ‘Hostile Architecture’ . International Journal for Crime, Justice and Social Democracy, 5(1), 67–81 . ↩ An analysis of the London debate over spikes and the broader mechanism of spatial displacement. This is a sociological interpretation of a specific controversy, not a measurement of the universal effect of every feature. · [11] Petty, J.

Distributive justice and equity in transportation . Transport Reviews, 37(2), 170–191 . ↩ A theoretical synthesis of justice in transport. It proposes focusing on access to essential destinations as a genuine human capability, rather than on speed of movement alone. · [12] Pereira, R. H. M.; Schwanen, T.; Banister, D.

The Effects of Exposure to Better Neighborhoods on Children: New Evidence from the Moving to Opportunity Experiment . American Economic Review, 106(4), 855–902 . ↩ Randomisation of voucher offers strengthens the causal interpretation of the wider neighbourhood environment. The study does not, however, separate architecture from schools, institutions, networks and other neighbourhood characteristics. · [13] Chetty, R.; Hendren, N.; Katz, L. F.
items.body: We tend to think that we simply move through a city, carrying our decisions within us. Yet a pavement can offer a route—or break it into a sequence of obstacles. A bench can invite someone to stay—or quietly determine how long they are allowed to remain. Streets, lighting, noise, public transport and even the absence of a toilet do not command us. But they alter the cost of each option. And in doing so, they subtly change what we are likely to do in the city. 01 One kilometre 02 The silent price list 03 Friction 04 Public space 05 Transport 06 Safety and surveillance 07 Hostile architecture 08 Social divides 09 The counterargument 10 Synthesis 01 One kilometre, two different decisions It is Saturday morning. Someone needs to walk to a pharmacy roughly one kilometre away. In the first city, a person leaves home onto an uninterrupted pavement. Along the way, they pass trees, several open shops and a transit stop. Crossings lie in the natural direction of travel, cars move slowly and the street can be crossed without a long wait. Before they have time to calculate whether walking is worth it, they are already on their way. In the second city, the distance is identical. But after a few hundred metres, the pavement ends at a car park. A broad road cuts across the direct route, and the nearest safe crossing requires a detour. Parking outside the pharmacy is easy; walking there demands a series of small decisions: how to get around the slip road, where to cross, whether to squeeze past the crash barriers. The person reaches for the car keys. At first glance, we have watched two personal choices. In one case, walking won; in the other, the car did. It would be easy to read a difference in character into this: the first person is more active, patient or environmentally conscious; the second more comfort-seeking or lazy. Yet it may be the very same person. Neither the person’s will nor the distance changed. What changed was the cost of the two options. One route made walking feel self-evident; the other turned it into a small project. In the second case, taking the car was not a moral failure. It was a response to the offer the built environment had assembled. This is where the city’s second layer begins. A city is not only a place in which people make decisions. It is also a system that adds time, money, effort, risk, discomfort and social meaning to each of those decisions. It does not tell us what we must do. But it creates a silent price list of what will be easy. The same one-kilometre journey in two urban environments On the left, an uninterrupted walking route with trees, a crossing, services and public transport. On the right, a broken pedestrian route, a wide road and easy parking. The diagram illustrates different levels of friction, not measured travel times. VISUALISATION 01 The same kilometre. A different cost of deciding. The distance does not change. The sum of small obstacles does. Low pedestrian friction 1 KM services pharmacy HOME DESTINATION transit stop continuous pavement · direct crossing · shade · services · transit High pedestrian friction 1 KM home pharmacy P broken route · wide road · detour · easy parking The same journey, different friction. This illustrative comparison does not present measured travel times or a universal ranking of cities. It shows how pavement continuity, crossings, services and parking change the relative cost of choosing to walk or drive. 02 The city as a silent price list of choices Urbanism is usually described in the language of buildings, streets, blocks, parks and transport networks. For the person moving through it, however, the same structure appears differently: as a set of possibilities. A door offers passage. Stairs offer ascent to someone who can use them—and an obstacle to someone in a wheelchair or pushing a pram. A well-lit path offers an evening shortcut; a dark underpass can psychologically lengthen the same distance. A bench offers a pause. A public toilet makes a longer stay away from home possible. A stop with frequent service offers the freedom not to plan every journey in advance. Environmental psychology uses the term “affordance” : an environment is not merely seen; it also suggests what can be done within it. This idea must not be allowed to slide into the notion that paving stones control the human mind. The same feature can offer different possibilities to different people, and people often use spaces in ways their designers never intended. It is more accurate to speak in terms of probability. Meta-analyses in transport research find associations between access to destinations, street-network connectivity, density or mixed land use and the way people travel. The effects are neither magical nor equally strong everywhere. But they show that a route to a shop, school or transit stop is not neutral geometry. Its design changes the relative attractiveness of walking, public transport and driving. [1] That distinction matters. “The city causes behaviour” is too crude a claim. “The city changes the conditions under which a behaviour becomes worthwhile” is less dramatic, but more accurate. A city is not a script that people perform without thought. It is a silent price list of possibilities. 03 Friction: small obstacles, a large cumulative effect Each individual obstacle is almost negligible. A kerb. An extra minute of waiting. No shade. A crossing a hundred metres farther away. A timetable that thins out in the evening. A bench without a backrest. Noise that makes a phone call impossible. Rarely does any one of them decide the matter by itself. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext But everyday behaviour does not arise from one great choice. It arises from repetition. Friction is anything that raises the cost of a particular action. It need not be physical effort alone. Friction can be temporal, financial, informational, social or psychological. Confusing signage raises the cost of finding one’s way. An empty street raises the perceived risk for some people. A transfer without a lift increases the burden of travelling with a suitcase. Having to buy something in a café in order to use the toilet turns a public need into a private transaction. The opposite of friction is not automatically convenience. It is a genuine ability to choose. Walkability , or the ease with which an area can be navigated on foot, is therefore not an aesthetic score awarded to a street because it has a few trees. It depends on whether destinations are reachable, routes form a connected network, crossings are safe, pavements are continuous, the surroundings are legible and the journey is comfortable enough for different groups of people. Connections to public transport matter too: even the best service loses value if the final five hundred metres lead across a barrier. A more recent study used people moving between US cities as a natural experiment. Among those who relocated to more walkable environments, the average daily step count increased; moving from roughly the lower to the upper quartile of walkability corresponded to about 1,100 additional steps per day. The effect worked in both directions and proved relatively persistent. [2] This is much stronger evidence than a one-off comparison of two neighbourhoods, but it is still not a random assignment of residents to cities. The authors worked with a particular sample of smartphone users, and walkability overlaps with other characteristics of urban life. That caution is not a footnote. It is part of the point. A neighbourhood is not a laboratory, and a person is not a test animal. People have some choice over where they live, cities attract different groups, and architecture is entangled with income, age, culture, weather and politics. Yet the underlying mechanism remains simple: when an environment repeatedly lowers the cost of one option and raises the cost of another, it need not control anyone in order to alter the aggregate behaviour of thousands. How to read the evidence A neighbourhood is not a randomised trial 01 Correlation Two characteristics occur together. That does not yet tell us whether one caused the other. 02 Natural experiment A change—such as moving home—helps compare behaviour before and after it. Uncontrolled differences nevertheless remain. 03 Randomisation Random allocation of an intervention is the best way to isolate its effect. In cities it is rare and usually local. How the environment changes the probability of behaviour The diagram traces a path from features of the environment, through temporal, financial, physical, risk-related and social costs, to the differing accessibility of particular choices. It is not a deterministic model. VISUALISATION 02 The city does not command. It rewrites the costs of choice. The same person can make a different—yet still rational—decision under different conditions. ENVIRONMENT pavement network service frequency light and shade services and toilets traffic speed changes COST OF THE DECISION time money effort risk social ease Illustrative profiles—not measured values. shifts PROBABILITY option A is easy more readily available option B is costly less readily available AGENCY HAS NOT DISAPPEARED The conditions for using it changed. The mechanism is probabilistic: the environment makes one choice easier and another harder; it does not mechanically control the person. A probabilistic, not deterministic, model. The environment affects time, effort, money, risk and social ease. Those costs then shift which option is feasible in a particular situation. 04 Public space begins with the possibility of staying Public space is often judged by how it looks in a photograph. For everyday life, a different question matters more: who can remain there, and under what conditions? A bench appears to be a minor piece of street furniture. In reality, it extends the reach of the city. A person with limited mobility can travel only as far as the next place to rest. A pregnant woman, a parent with a child, someone recovering from surgery or anyone walking on a hot day does not read distance only in metres. They read it in available pauses. Public toilets work in a similar way. Their absence is more than an inconvenience. For some residents, it imposes an invisible time limit on being away from home. A city may have a beautiful square, but if people cannot sit safely, drink water, find shade or reach a toilet there, it is public only in a limited sense. This is why the World Health Organization’s guidance for age-friendly cities addresses not only transport and health services, but also well-placed seating, toilets and accessibility. [3] Green space is another example in which it is easy to overstate causality. A long-term panel study found an association between living in greener urban areas and better indicators of psychological well-being even after accounting for some stable differences between individuals. [4] That does not mean planting a tree will, by itself, “cure” stress. Greenery is often bound up with lower noise, shade, opportunities for movement, housing quality and socioeconomic status. It is a bundle of mechanisms, not a simple switch. Noise, too, changes behaviour before it appears in health statistics. Loud environments shorten conversations, make concentration harder and can discourage people from staying. Long-term exposure to traffic noise is also associated in WHO guidance with sleep disturbance and other adverse effects, although the scale of risk depends on the intensity, duration and context of exposure. [5] And then there is encounter. A square does not manufacture community, any more than a bench manufactures friendship. But it can make repeated presence possible: familiar faces, brief greetings, the chance to observe others, room for a market, protest, children’s play or a chance conversation. A systematic review of research on public space and social cohesion found numerous associations with accessibility, street furniture, mixed uses and the possibility of informal use. It also warned that much of the research is cross-sectional and that results are strongly conditioned by age, income, perceived safety and local culture. [6] Public space therefore does not command social relationships. It allocates opportunities for them. 05 Transport Is Not Just Movement. It Is an Offer of Possibilities Transport debates are often reduced to an argument over who receives how many metres of street. Yet allocating space also allocates time, risk and access. A wide road may carry many vehicles, but for pedestrians it lengthens the crossing and increases the distance between the two sides of a neighbourhood. Vehicle speed is not determined by a sign alone. It is also shaped by what the street permits and visually suggests to the driver: lane width, sight lines, subdivision, the presence of pedestrians, parking, trees and the frequency of junctions. Research across different contexts repeatedly shows that design speed and the perceived character of a street matter to actual behaviour. Speed is not an abstract parameter. The probability of a pedestrian suffering fatal injuries rises sharply with impact speed, even though precise estimates vary between studies depending on the data, the age of victims and the methodology used. [7] A street that presents itself as a through-route therefore changes not only objective risk, but also whether a parent is willing to let a child cross alone or whether someone chooses to walk there after dark. Public transport works in much the same way. The mere existence of a route is not enough. Frequency, reliability, price, connections, accessibility, the quality of the stop and whether the service still runs when a shift ends all matter. Missing one tram on a five-minute service is an episode. Missing one bus on an hourly service changes the day’s plans. Formally, transport is “available” to both passengers; in practice, they have been offered something very different. Road capacity is not neutral either. A well-known study of US metropolitan areas found that increases in highway capacity were accompanied over time by an almost proportional rise in vehicle miles travelled. Some of the new capacity was absorbed by changed routes, additional journeys, commercial traffic and shifts in settlement patterns. [8] This does not mean that every new lane is pointless, or that the result applies identically to every street. But it reveals a broader principle: infrastructure does not merely serve a fixed level of demand. It changes what becomes worthwhile for people and businesses to do. Transport is therefore less like a pipe carrying a fixed volume of movement and more like a market of possibilities. Change the price of one form of mobility, and you also change the behaviour that depends on it. 06 Safety, light and the camera’s eye Urban safety has at least two forms. One is the probability that something will happen. The other is the feeling that a space can be used without constant vigilance. The two may overlap, but they are not the same. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext Lighting is a good example. It can improve visibility, orientation and the ability to recognise other people. For some, that lowers the psychological cost of an evening journey. But it is not true that every brightly lit space is automatically safe. Placement, glare, shadows, the presence of people, maintenance and surrounding routes all matter. New York provided an unusually strong test: in a randomised experiment, temporary lighting towers were installed at selected public-housing developments. The study found a reduction in some forms of outdoor night-time crime at the treated sites. [9] This is important evidence because the finding was not based on correlation alone. At the same time, it is not a universal prescription for every neighbourhood. It concerned a particular intervention, in particular locations, over a particular period. Cameras require similar caution. A meta-analysis spanning four decades of research into CCTV found a modest average reduction in crime, with the strongest and most consistent effects in car parks. Outcomes depended on the setting, active monitoring, coverage and whether cameras were combined with other measures. [10] A camera, then, is not synonymous with safety. It may deter, assist an investigation or increase the sense of control. But it can also displace behaviour beyond its field of view, create a false expectation of immediate help, or tell some people that they are first and foremost objects of suspicion. Surveillance also changes the social acceptability of behaviour. A space filled with cameras, prohibition signs and physical barriers may be objectively well managed, yet subjectively communicate that people are only meant to pass through. Public gathering, protest, street music or simply lingering then acquire a different cost, even if none is forbidden. Safety is therefore not produced by a single feature. It emerges from the relationship between design, management, people, institutions and trust. A camera can observe a space. On its own, it cannot create a public. A camera can monitor a space. It cannot create a public on its own. 07 When a bench issues a wordless prohibition Some urban features expand possibilities. Others are designed to do precisely the opposite. Dividing armrests in the middle of a bench may help an older person stand up. They may also be positioned so that lying down is impossible. Metal studs on a ledge may protect the surface from skateboards—but also prevent anyone from sitting there. Sloping surfaces, stones in sheltered corners, locked recesses, timed sprinklers or seats too short for rest belong to the broader family of features known as defensive or hostile architecture. The term “ hostile architecture ” gained currency above all in debates about displacing people experiencing homelessness. A study of the London controversy over metal spikes showed that the issue is not merely the design of an individual object, but the way a city translates a social conflict into the physical arrangement of space. [11] The power of such architecture lies in the fact that it needs neither a police officer nor a sign. The rule is embedded in the material. The bench does not say, “Do not sleep here.” It simply creates a shape that a body cannot fit onto. That raises an uncomfortable question: when a city makes a particular behaviour physically impossible, has it solved the problem—or merely moved it elsewhere? For a person without a home, the answer is especially clear. Removing the possibility of lying down does not remove the need for sleep. It moves that need into a less visible passageway, a more distant stop or a more dangerous place. In an administrative report, the problem may disappear from one address; in the person’s life, friction has simply increased. The impact is rarely precisely targeted. An uncomfortable bench does not deter only the person the design was intended to displace. It shortens the rest available to an older person, someone with back pain, a night worker and teenagers who cannot afford commercial space. Architecture can exclude without checking identity—and for that very reason, it excludes crudely. None of this means that public space should have no rules. Cities must manage conflicts involving sleep, movement, noise, hygiene, safety and maintenance. The difference lies between addressing a cause and managing visibility. A defensive feature can work exactly as specified in one location and still leave the overall problem untouched. In this sense, a bench is a small piece of social policy. It simply is not voted on like a law. A typology of public space: open, controlled and hostile Three illustrative urban scenes show a space that invites people to stay, a space where staying is conditional on surveillance and rules, and a space that physically prevents certain forms of presence. VISUALISATION 03 Public does not mean equally accessible. Design can invite people to stay, make staying conditional—or make it impossible for certain bodies. OPEN SPACE OFFERS POSSIBILITIES TOILET / WATER continuous seating · shade · water · unrestricted presence CONTROLLED STAYING IS CONDITIONAL RULES OF USE open until 10 p.m. camera · time limits · gate · rules HOSTILE SOME BEHAVIOURS ARE PHYSICALLY EXCLUDED divided bench · spikes · sloping surface · displacement The typology is illustrative. The same feature can serve several functions; purpose, context, placement and impact on different users determine its meaning. Three regimes of public space. Openness, control and hostility are not absolute categories. The same armrest can help someone stand up or prevent someone from lying down; what matters is its purpose, density, context and ultimate effect. 08 The same map, a different city On a map, distance is measured equally for everyone. In practice, there is no single kilometre, no single transit stop and no single park. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext For someone with a car, a supermarket on the edge of town may be easy to reach. For someone without one, it means two bus routes and a walk along a busy road. A park may be five hundred metres from home, but on the far side of railway tracks with no nearby crossing. A doctor’s surgery may be in the same district, yet upstairs in a building without a lift. A night service may exist—just not in the direction used by people returning to cheaper outer neighbourhoods. Urban access to services is therefore not the same as the number of services present. What matters is how much time, money, physical ability and planning a particular person needs to reach them. Theories of transport justice consequently propose judging a system by access to essential destinations and genuine opportunities, rather than speed or total volume of movement alone. [12] This is where space meets social inequality. A wealthier household can buy back part of a badly designed city: through a car, taxis, a private garden, air conditioning, a paid toilet, a gym membership or housing closer to services. Someone on a lower income depends far more heavily on what public infrastructure actually provides. Spatial segregation then distributes not only addresses unevenly, but also schools, social connections, green space, noise, commuting time and access to work. The Moving to Opportunity experiment, in which some families were given the opportunity to move to lower-poverty neighbourhoods, found long-term benefits for children who moved at a younger age. [13] Even this strong study design does not tell us that the results were caused by a particular street width or the presence of a park. A “neighbourhood” is a package of schools, institutions, peer networks, safety, labour markets, burdens and expectations. This is precisely why it is dangerous to mistake urbanism for an all-powerful cure. It is equally dangerous to treat space as mere scenery. When opportunities are distributed unevenly and the routes to them carry different costs for different people, the city is already participating in social outcomes—even if it does not explain them in full. 09 A person is not a product of the pavement There is a fundamental objection to this entire argument: people are not passive products of their environment. And that objection is correct. People overcome barriers, create desire paths, move chairs, organise neighbourhood festivals in car parks and turn inhospitable corners into meeting places. Cultural practices can change the meaning of the same square. Someone who loves walking will walk even through an unfriendly environment; someone else will drive through a perfectly connected neighbourhood. Work, health, family, weather and personal preference can outweigh any design. Causality also runs in the opposite direction. People do not merely adapt their behaviour to a city; through their behaviour and political decisions, they shape the city itself. Demand for parking produces more parking, improved public transport may attract new residents, and a lively street creates a market for additional businesses. Cause and effect circle back into one another. Urban research therefore faces the problem of self-selection. Are people more active because they live in a walkable neighbourhood, or did they choose that neighbourhood because they were already more active? Is crime lower because of the area’s design, or because it has more resources for maintenance, services and surveillance? Does greenery improve mental well-being, or is greener housing associated with other advantages the data failed to capture? Longitudinal studies, natural experiments and randomised interventions sometimes help. But they can never turn a city into a perfectly controlled laboratory. An honest conclusion will therefore often read: “there is an association,” “the result is consistent with this mechanism,” or “in this context, the intervention changed the outcome.” That is not a weakness of science. It is a precise boundary around what we know. Rejecting determinism does not, however, mean returning to an image of completely free choice. Freedom is not merely the absence of prohibition. It is also the availability of feasible options. METHOD NOTE The article deliberately distinguishes claims based on association, natural experiments and randomised interventions. In relation to crime, mental health, social cohesion, physical activity and other outcomes, urban form is not the sole cause and often cannot be fully isolated from social conditions. 10 The infrastructure of probable behaviour As we move through a city, we can try a different kind of attention. Look not only at façades, but at the moments when space makes something cheaper or more expensive. Where does the pavement continue, and where does it suddenly yield to a driveway? How long does a pedestrian wait compared with a car? Where can someone sit without paying? Who can reach the crossing button? Does a tree shade the route, or merely decorate the rendering? Where is the nearest toilet? Where is the camera pointing? Does the bench invite people to stay, or permit only a brief, obedient pause? This way of looking does not divide cities neatly into good and bad. Every space must reconcile competing needs, and every design has side effects. A wider pavement may reduce space for deliveries. More light can disturb residents and nocturnal wildlife. Trees need room, maintenance and water. Public toilets require operation. Fewer barriers may mean more demanding management. Real urbanism is not a cost-free picture. What changes is the question. Instead of asking, “Why don’t people behave better?”, we can ask, “What price have we set for their choices?” Why does a parent drive a child a few hundred metres? Perhaps it is not merely habit, but a fast road with no safe crossing. Why is the square empty? Perhaps what is missing is not a cultural programme, but shade, a seat and permission to remain. Why do people from the urban fringe attend fewer evening events? Perhaps the last service takes them home before the event is over. The city does not tell us what to do. But every day it quietly tells us which decision will be easy, which uncomfortable, which expensive and which nearly impossible. It does not take away our agency. It becomes part of the conditions under which we exercise it. And that is precisely why architecture is not merely a matter of appearance. It is infrastructure for probable human behaviour.

items.body: First impression One object, three possible rooms The silver Boeing B‑29 bomber bears the name Enola Gay . On 6 August 1945, the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima was released from this aircraft. The metal fuselage, engines, rivets and traces of operation are material facts. This is not a replica of an opinion or a metaphor for history. It is a real machine that formed part of a real event. Now imagine three galleries. In the first, the aircraft hangs among blueprints, engine cutaways and production statistics. Visitors read about long-range bombing, the pressurised fuselage, industrial capacity and the technological leap represented by the B‑29. Here, the exhibit tells a story of engineering. In the second gallery, it stands beside maps of the Pacific War, documents on decision-making by the US leadership, casualty estimates and testimony from crew members. The same machine becomes a node of military strategy and political choice. In the third, it is surrounded by personal belongings from residents of Hiroshima, survivor testimony, data on the effects of the explosion and a timeline of nuclear armament. The technical artefact suddenly becomes a threshold into the history of human consequences. The aircraft has not changed. None of these rooms need be lying. Each, however, asks a different question, gives different weight to the surrounding facts and guides the visitor towards a different conclusion. A dispute of exactly this kind did, in fact, unfold around this aircraft. For the fiftieth anniversary of the bombing, the Smithsonian prepared a script of more than three hundred pages linking the end of the war, the decision to use the bomb, the experience of the crews, conditions in the affected cities and the beginning of the nuclear age. After a fierce public and political conflict, the concept was cancelled in January 1995. A markedly reduced presentation opened several months later: the fuselage, basic facts and information about the restoration were displayed without the broader interpretation and without images of the consequences. 2 That does not prove that one version was true and the other propaganda. It is a particularly clear example of a different mechanism: the dispute was not about whether the aircraft was authentic. It was about what this genuine object should mean . The second layer An object is evidence. It is not a finished sentence. A museum object can establish material, technique, dimensions, wear, style, original function or the fact that something physically existed. Its surface may preserve traces of use and its construction information no later text can replace. In that sense, authenticity is fundamental. But an object has no verbs or conjunctions. It cannot say for itself: “therefore”, “despite this”, “as a result”, “it was inevitable” or “another option existed”. It does not determine whether we should understand it as a masterpiece, an everyday tool, evidence of oppression, a technological breakthrough, a personal memorial or some combination of all these roles. An exhibit can be genuine down to its last scratch. The causal story connecting one exhibit to another, however, is not a discovered object. It is a sentence assembled by curators. Jiný Kontext The word argument does not imply an accusation of manipulation here. In the scholarly sense, an argument is an organised claim supported by reasons and evidence. A good exhibition does exactly that: it selects material, arranges it and proposes which relationships among its parts deserve attention. The International Council of Museums, after all, does not define a museum merely as an institution that collects and conserves. Alongside research, collecting and care, it explicitly includes the interpretation and exhibition of tangible and intangible heritage. 1 Interpretation is therefore not a defect that enters the museum once the “pure” scholarly work is complete. It is one of the museum’s basic functions. The past was larger than everything that survived it. Only a fraction survived—physically, socially and politically. A particular collection was formed from that surviving fraction. A particular exhibition was selected from the collection. The exhibition was arranged into a legible story. The third layer A museum preserves a fragment—and displays a fragment of that fragment. The intuitive image of a museum is simple: the important things from the past were rescued and now stand in display cases. But several consecutive filters lie between the past and the case. First, the object had to survive at all. Paper burns, textiles disintegrate, wood rots, metal is melted down, and everyday objects are discarded precisely because they do not appear exceptional while in use. Someone then had to recognise the object as worth preserving. It had to reach an institution, fit its collecting policy, be legally and ethically acceptable, documented, conservable and sufficiently significant in relation to what the collection already held. Even acceptance into a collection does not automatically begin the journey into a gallery. London’s Natural History Museum says it cares for around eighty million objects, of which only a tiny fraction can be displayed. 3 That imbalance is not a failure. It is intrinsic to large collecting institutions. A store, therefore, is not a rubbish bin for unimportant things. It contains research series, comparative material, objects too fragile for long-term exposure to light, items awaiting processing, things displayed in rotation and objects whose importance will emerge only when a new question is asked. A single butterfly may be an aesthetic exhibit. Thousands of specimens of the same species from different places and decades, however, may form a dataset for studying changes in distribution, habitat or climate. What remains in storage is therefore not simply the opposite of what matters. Often it is material whose value lies precisely in quantity, context and the possibility of repeated examination—not in attracting a visitor’s gaze on its own. From the past to the icon: a series of narrowing selections Each layer can be professionally justified. At the same time, each narrows what the visitor will ultimately see. Visualisation 01 On a smaller screen, swipe the graphic sideways → A diagram of selection from thousands of objects to a handful of iconic exhibits Five narrowing layers represent historical reality, surviving objects, a museum collection, an exhibition and iconic exhibits. ILLUSTRATIVE DIAGRAM · NOT A STATISTICAL RATIO Thousands of traces and objects from historical reality what existed, was used, disappeared or survived Surviving and recognised objects survival · discovery · documentation · accessibility The collection of a particular institution collecting policy · acquisition · care · provenance Selected exhibition theme · space · condition of the object · legibility A handful of icons what an era will remember The diagram shows a logic, not universal quantities. The narrowing begins before the museum exists and continues through acquisition, conservation, research and curatorial selection. The fourth layer Who decides what will be displayed? In the popular imagination, a single curator stands behind an exhibition, selecting favourite objects according to personal taste and writing an authoritative text about them. In reality, the decision is distributed across several professions and constraints. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext The curator formulates the scholarly question and selects material. A conservator assesses whether an object can withstand light, vibration, changing humidity or a particular form of installation. A registrar tracks records, movement and insurance. An exhibition designer translates the concept into physical space. Educators and interpretation specialists consider what visitors without prior knowledge will actually understand. Lawyers and provenance experts may address title, sensitive material, loan conditions or claims by source communities. Budgets, security and the dimensions of doorways can intervene in the story as forcefully as a historiographical dispute. Selection is therefore not a single moment. It occurs at least three times. First, when building the collection: what will the institution accept at all? Second, when designing the exhibition: what will leave storage and enter the public gallery? Third, during installation: what receives the central plinth, its own light, the longest label and a place on the poster? It is the final step that creates iconic objects. Sometimes an object becomes famous because it was historically pivotal. At other times, its public importance grows because the institution repeatedly chooses it to stand for an entire period. From among thousands of surviving objects, one becomes the image through which society remembers an era. This does not mean scholarly criteria are an illusion. It means that even a well-justified selection remains a selection. A transparent museum therefore shows not only the conclusion but, where possible, the rules by which it arrived there. The fifth layer A label is a compressed argument The small card beside an object appears modest. It gives a title, maker, date, material, place of origin and inventory number. This matter-of-fact form creates the impression that the text merely transcribes what is already present in the object. But after the basic data, only a few sentences remain. They must answer why the object is in the room at all. In describing its own practice, the V&A shows that writing gallery text involves both standardised identifying information and the demanding compression of scholarly research without losing its essence. 4 The word limit is not a minor technical detail. It forces a decision about what will be said and what will remain outside the label. Technical frame “Boeing’s B‑29 Superfortress was an exceptionally demanding US aviation project, featuring pressurised crew compartments and long range.” Strategic frame “On 6 August 1945, the atomic bomb on Hiroshima was dropped from this aircraft during the final phase of the Pacific War.” Frame of consequences “The aircraft carried the first atomic bomb used in war over a city whose population suffered both the immediate and long-term effects of the blast and radiation.” All three sentences may be true. Yet each chooses a different grammatical subject, a different degree of human presence and a different scale for the event. Language can also move almost imperceptibly from description to causation. “The event was followed by surrender”, “the event contributed to surrender” and “the event ended the war” are not stylistic variants of one sentence. They are three historical claims of very different strength. A good label is therefore not one that pretends to have no perspective. It is a text that distinguishes established facts from scholarly interpretation, does not burden the evidence with stronger causal claims than it can sustain, and gives visitors a route to a deeper layer—in a catalogue, digital documentation or a later section of the exhibition. One exhibit in three contexts The object remains the same. The neighbouring evidence, the exhibition’s question and the expected mode of reading change. Visualisation 02 On a smaller screen, swipe the graphic sideways → Enola Gay in three hypothetical exhibition contexts Three panels show the same silhouette of the bomber in technological, strategic and humanitarian contexts. CONTEXT A Technology How was this machine possible? Adjacent material blueprints · engines · alloys production · crew · range Central question What could this machine do? CONTEXT B Strategy Why and how was it deployed? Adjacent material maps · orders · casualty estimates alternatives · decision-making process Central question Why was this particular decision made? CONTEXT C Consequences What did the event mean for people? Adjacent material personal belongings · testimony health effects · the nuclear age Central question What happened after the bomb-bay doors opened? All three contexts are hypothetical analytical models and are not mutually exclusive. Combining them may be the most honest approach; space and attention, however, always determine which layer will dominate. The sixth layer Sequence is the grammar of space An exhibition communicates through more than text. It speaks through distance, height, light, sound, direction of movement and the size of rooms. A display case is a sentence, a gallery a paragraph, and the visitor route can function like a plot. If we begin with the invention of the steam engine, move to factory production, then to urban growth and finally to workers’ housing, the physical sequence almost automatically invites a causal reading: technological change led to social transformation. If we instead begin with living conditions, continue with conflict over labour and only then introduce the machines, the same material can tell a history of pressure from below, regulation and institutional response. Neither route need deny the facts. Each, however, determines what the visitor experiences as cause and what as consequence. Architecture also distributes authority. An isolated object in an empty room appears more singular than the same object in a dense row. A monumental staircase prepares the body for a ceremonial entrance. A dark corridor slows the pace and changes the emotional register before a visitor reads the first word. An object placed at eye level enters into a relationship; one suspended high overhead acquires dominance. The art historian Carol Duncan described the public museum as an environment in which visitors pass through a particular ritual script and where the building is not a neutral container for art. 7 We need not accept every strong interpretation of that theory to recognise the basic fact: the visitor’s body reads the space before the conscious mind begins evaluating its argument. The curatorial story therefore emerges not only from what is displayed. It also emerges from what the visitor sees first, cannot avoid, is allowed to pause beside and encounters immediately before leaving. The final room often functions as the conclusion of an essay. The seventh layer When a perspective is missing, the facts need not be missing. The question may be. An exhibition may give the correct date, material and maker yet still miss an important part of the meaning. Most often this is not because a curator consciously concealed evidence, but because both the collection and the scholarly tradition grew from a particular position. A colonial collection may long be organised around European expeditions, collectors and stylistic development. From the perspective of the source community, however, other questions may be equally important: Who was allowed to use the object? Under what circumstances did it leave its place? Was it sold, given, removed under duress or looted? What does its absence mean where it came from? May it be displayed publicly at all? The absence of this perspective does not automatically make every existing sentence false. It changes the scope of the explanation. A history of European collecting may be accurate, but it is not identical to the history of the object. The Benin Bronzes at the Smithsonian offer a concrete example. The museum transferred ownership of twenty-nine objects removed during the British attack on Benin City in 1897 to Nigeria’s National Commission for Museums and Monuments. Nine are now at the US museum on long-term loan with the consent of the Kingdom of Benin; the remaining twenty were returned to Nigeria. 10 This case disrupts the simple model in which restitution and public access must be opposites. An object may remain on display while its owner, the authority behind its label and the relationship between institution and source community all change. The case looks much the same; the argument it presents is different. It no longer says only, “we own this and show it”. It can say, “this has been entrusted to us, and we display it within an agreed relationship”. The eighth layer Provenance: the object’s second life The origin of a collection object is sometimes reduced to a line such as “gift of Mr X” or “purchased in year Y”. Provenance research, however, studies the history of an object’s ownership and movement. The Metropolitan Museum of Art describes it as central to responsible museum practice and as a basis for contextualisation, acquisition, interpretation and possible repatriation or restitution. 8 Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext Every object has at least two biographies. The first is the history of its original use: who made it, what it was for, who touched it and what event it entered. The second begins when the thing becomes a collectable or museum object: who found, bought, inherited, exported, sold, donated, seized, catalogued and displayed it. The second biography can transform the first. Missing decades in a chain of ownership are not an empty field without meaning. They may conceal a forced sale, wartime confiscation or illegal export—or a perfectly legitimate transfer that has not yet been documented. A newly opened archive, scientific material analysis, a dealer’s record or information from a source community can change what a museum knows about an object decades later. The Met therefore stresses that provenance records are continually updated and that curators, archivists, conservators, scientists, legal experts, authorities and source communities collaborate in the research. 8 Provenance is not an automatic verdict on every old collection. It is a method for distinguishing assumption from a documented route and legal possession from responsible title. The ICOM Code of Ethics therefore links acquisition to due diligence on origin, documentation and a willingness to discuss the return of cultural property where substantiated reasons exist. 9 In an exhibition, all this work may appear in a single sentence. But if a label gives only the place of manufacture and skips the route into the collection, the object looks as though it arrived in the case naturally. Provenance restores the human decisions, power, trade, violence, care and cooperation that lie between the object’s creation and the way we see it today. The object’s journey: from use to display case Museum status is not a property with which an object is born. It emerges through a documented chain of events and institutional decisions. Visualisation 03 On a smaller screen, swipe the graphic sideways → The timeline of a museum object Nine stages lead from historical use through transfers, acquisition, registration, conservation, research, curatorial selection and installation to the visitor. Use original function Transfer gift · inheritance · removal Market / collector sale · export · collection Acquisition acceptance into the museum Registration number · description · condition Care conservation · storage Research meaning · provenance Selection theme · argument Display case label · space · viewer HISTORICAL LIFE INSTITUTIONAL LIFE PUBLIC LIFE The arrow is not necessarily smooth. The chain may contain gaps, contested transfers or newly discovered evidence. Those gaps are precisely what provenance research investigates. The strongest counterargument Without selection, a museum would not be a museum. It would be a warehouse. At this point, an easy but mistaken conclusion presents itself: if every exhibition selects and frames, then everything is merely a subjective story and museums cannot be trusted. Such cynicism would confuse the inevitability of interpretation with arbitrariness. A visitor cannot walk past eighty million objects. Nor can they read a complete catalogue, archival file, conservation report and every scholarly dispute for each one. If an institution displayed everything without hierarchy, most objects would become indistinguishable noise. A warehouse maximises storage; an exhibition must create the possibility of understanding. Curating is therefore a form of expert reduction. It requires knowledge of the collection, the ability to compare evidence, identify representative and exceptional objects, verify dates, construct an intelligible structure and respect the material’s physical limits. Twenty well-chosen objects may illuminate a particular question better than two thousand unrelated and unexplained things. Selection need not weaken truth. It can make truth accessible. A model of DNA, a timeline of archaeological layers or a group of objects from one household creates an abstraction that reveals a relationship hidden in the individual pieces. Eilean Hooper‑Greenhill described museums as institutions that have actively helped shape modes of knowledge throughout history; Mieke Bal, in turn, showed that collecting itself can be understood as a narrative activity rather than neutral accumulation. 5 6 The question, then, is not how to eliminate interpretation. It can be eliminated only by hiding its decisions and allowing them to appear as the natural order of things. A more meaningful question is: by what rules was the selection made, how well is it supported by evidence, and how open is it to correction? The ninth layer Can an exhibition be neutral? Not in an absolute sense. The decision to establish a particular kind of museum, divide history into periods, devote a large gallery to one subject and a single case to another, begin with a particular date or use chronology instead of thematic organisation already creates a perspective. That does not mean there is no difference between an honest exhibition and propaganda. Neutrality can be understood not as the absence of choices, but as a discipline that constrains those choices and makes them available for scrutiny. Procedural integrity Six features of a transparent exhibition The selection follows a recognisable criterion. Visitors know which question the gallery investigates and why these particular objects are present. Fact is separated from interpretation. Date, material and a documented event are not conflated with motive or disputed causality. Uncertainty is not disguised. Gaps in provenance, disputed authorship or competing scholarly interpretations are acknowledged in proportion to their importance. Strong counterevidence is not hidden in storage. The exhibition addresses relevant facts that complicate its central story. Source communities are not merely objects of description. Where materially relevant, their knowledge and views also enter the research and interpretation. The story is corrigible. Labels, catalogues and installations change when better evidence appears; the museum’s authority does not rest on pretending to be infallible. Such an exhibition need not be without a point of view. It may even advance a strong thesis. The difference is whether visitors receive only the conclusion or also enough traces to understand how it was assembled. In the case of the Enola Gay , the claim that the limited 1995 display contained no interpretation is itself instructive. Factually, it did omit the broader script and retain basic information about the aircraft and its restoration. 2 Analytically, however, omitting context also creates a frame: the aircraft as a technical and historical artefact takes precedence, while the human, strategic and political layers move outside the room. In practice, “without interpretation” can mean “with an interpretation enacted through the choice of what will not be discussed”. Visitor protocol How to read a museum without cynicism Reading a museum critically does not mean looking for a conspiracy behind every plinth. It means perceiving two layers at once: the past that the exhibition makes accessible, and the present-day decisions that determine its form. What is at the centre of the room? Which object receives the most space, light and text—and what does it stand for? What is the central question? Does the exhibition ask how an object was made, whom it served, what it caused, or how it was later remembered? What does the object itself establish, and what does the label add? A material trace, a documented date and an interpretation of motive carry different evidential weight. How does the sequence work? What is introduced as a cause, what as a response, and which event is given the final word? Who is the agent in the sentences? Active verbs reveal responsibility; the passive voice can unintentionally dissolve it. Is the route into the collection visible? Provenance information often reveals a story as important as the object’s original use. Where is the rest? A digital catalogue, storage, a research database and rotation can show how narrow the slice currently on view really is. None of this robs the museum of its magic. Quite the opposite. An object becomes more interesting when, alongside its age, we see the history of all the decisions that allowed it to survive, receive an inventory number and stand here. The display case ceases to be a transparent window into the past and reveals itself as a precise interface between past and present. A museum visitor is therefore looking not only at the past, but also at the way the present has chosen to arrange it. They see genuine objects, but never all of them. They read documented facts, but in an order someone composed. They move among real traces, but through an architecture that strengthens some relationships and leaves others in shadow. None of this is, in itself, a museum’s failure. It is a condition of the museum’s existence. The most honest museum, then, is not one that claims to have no argument. It is one that lets visitors glimpse the evidence from which the argument was built, what had to be omitted, where uncertainty remains and what might change the story. The past inside the case is no less real. It is simply no longer alone. Beside it stands the selection made by our own era—and that selection, too, is a historical document.

items.title: Six months at the operator is not the content of a call. Billing is not data retention. And Czech law still imposes blanket retention, even though Union and civil case-law say it will not stand.
items.subtitle: The Electronic Communications Act still imposes six-month blanket retention of traffic and location data without content. The Constitutional Court bore that in 2019. The Court of Justice of the EU and, in December 2025, the Supreme Court treat the same blanket measure as incompatible with Union law.
