items.body: Section: Technology & AI Author: V Reading Length: ~27 min Sources and further reading: 22 items Topics: cybersecurity, bank fraud, phishing, smishing, vishing, MFA SEO / Working Title: How do you recognise a fraudulent e-mail, SMS or phone call? The question is: how do you recognise a fraudulent e-mail, SMS or phone call? It sounds simple until we notice that we are not comparing one thing. The number on the display is not an identity. Phishing is not vishing and vishing is not smishing. MFA is not a lock against coercion. An authorised payment that you confirmed yourself is no longer unauthorised. Only when these four things are separated can one read what the Police of the Czech Republic, NÚKIB, ČNB and ČBA actually measure for 2024 and 2025 — and what follows from that before the money leaves. 1. The bank, the police and the office see the same call in three statistics Picture an afternoon at home. A familiar bank name appears on the display. The voice claims that a suspicious operation is running on the account. A message on the phone asks for confirmation. In the e-mail sits a link to “secure verification”. One does not ask for a definition of cyberspace. One wants to know whether one is speaking to the bank, or to someone impersonating the bank. But the institutions that describe the problem do not see the same unit. The Police of the Czech Republic and the Ministry of the Interior track recorded offences in cyberspace. In 2024 there were 18,495 of them, that is 10.67% of 173,322 offences of total crime, 5.5% fewer year on year; the clearance rate was 15.4% [1] [2] . In 2025 there were 21,137 of them, that is 12.4% of 170,051 offences, 2,642 more year on year, that is 14.3%; the clearance rate was 15.1% [3] [4] . That is a broad police category. It is not the number of fraudulent calls. ČSÚ and the criminal statistics for narrowly qualified cybercrime under Sections 230 to 232 of the Criminal Code show a different total: 1,224 offences in 2025, 93 fewer than the previous year, that is 7.1% [5] . NÚKIB, for its part, records cyber incidents under its statutory and working framework. In 2024 there were 268 of them, of which 1 was very significant and 18 significant [6] . For 2025 the Ministry of the Interior reports 203 incidents cited from NÚKIB [4] . The Czech Banking Association speaks of clients of member banks, their losses and attacks [12] [13] . At first glance this is one threat. In fact each is adding a different object. The police see offences. ČSÚ a narrow legal category. NÚKIB incidents at regulated and surveyed organisations. ČBA bank clients. ČNB a legal regime and complaints. That is why they can all be partly right and a shared figure for “how many fraudulent calls there were” still cannot be honestly assembled. A familiar number on the display is not an identity. — Jiný Kontext 2. One request for an action has at least five layers A scam does not begin with the loss. It begins with the channel. An e-mail has a header, a link and an attachment. An SMS or RCS has a short message, a sender name and often pressure for speed. A call has a voice, an intonation and the ability to raise immediate fear. A messenger adds the appearance of a personal relationship. Each channel carries different traces and a different rhythm of decision. The second layer is the sender’s mask. It may be a bank name in an SMS, a similar domain in an e-mail or a spoofed calling number. The mask lowers resistance. It does not prove identity. That is the first practical rule: identity does not begin with what the display shows. It begins with whether verification runs through a channel that you chose and that you know in advance. The third layer is the script. Some legends rest on fear: the account is under attack, the police are investigating, someone has misused an identity card. Others rest on greed: an investment, a quick return, a missed opportunity. Still others rest on trust: a colleague, family, a familiar voice. Time pressure is not evidence of authenticity. It is part of the script. The fourth layer is the requested action. Fill in a datum. Dictate a code. Confirm MFA. Send money. Install remote access. This is precisely where a suspicious message becomes a loss. The fifth layer is the remedy: the bank, the Police of the Czech Republic, the financial arbitrator or a court, according to what happened and which legal regime applies. None of these layers is an instant refund. This construction matters, because the defence must not guess how convincing the mask is. It must stop the action. If a call asks for a code, the problem is not only the voice. If an SMS asks for a click, the problem is not only the text. If an e-mail asks for a login through a link, the problem is not only the logo. We always ask what action the channel wants from us and whether we verify it elsewhere. 3. The number on the display is not an identity People tend to believe what looks familiar. A bank name in a message, a helpline number on the display, the name of an office in an e-mail. But ČNB and NÚKIB both warn about fraudulent calls and spoofing, that is situations in which a fraudster tries to look like a known institution [7] [9] [11] . It does not follow that every familiar number is spoofed. It follows that a familiar number does not, by itself, verify identity. Technical systems for verifying a calling number solve only part of the problem. The American STIR/SHAKEN framework, which the FCC writes about, works with authentication of a telephone number on the network and with operators’ relationship to the number [18] . That is a useful layer. It is not proof of who exactly is speaking, why they are calling and whether they have the right to demand your action. The success of similar verification on Czech networks is not, on the dossier, publicly reported as a map against which every call could be judged. Looking a number up on the internet is not enough. If the mask shows a bank number, the internet will only confirm that the number really belongs to the bank. It will not prove that the bank is calling from it just now. The right step is different: hang up, do not call back the number on the display, and use an official contact from the institution’s website, from the payment card or from the app. Where a bank offers call verification in the app, that is a better check than a voice on the phone. Identity is therefore not what arrives at you. Identity is what you verify. That is a small shift, but it changes the whole decision. 4. Phishing is not vishing. Vishing is not smishing The word phishing is often used for everything. For e-mail, SMS and a phone call. In a headline that helps. In a defence it harms. E-mail phishing leaves different traces than smishing in SMS and vishing in a voice call. ČNB distinguishes the channels in its overview [9] [10] . The point is simple: the same goal, a different channel, a different test. With e-mail one can deal with the address, the domain, the header, the attachment and the link. With SMS there is little space and a greater role falls to the sender name, the urgency and the link. With a call the pressure acts in real time. One does not have time to read in peace. That is why hanging up matters so much on a call. Not because the call is always a scam. Because the same channel that raised the pressure must not be the channel of verification. In the Threat Landscape 2025 report ENISA works with a European dataset of 4,875 incidents for the period from 1 July 2024 to 30 June 2025. It states that 77% of incidents were of the DDoS type and that phishing appears in about 60% as an intrusion vector [17] . These figures cannot be turned into the sentence that 60% of Czech criminal statistics is phishing. They measure a different population and a different unit. They still remind us that a social entry into a system remains important even where the incident is later described in technical language. From a practical point of view it is better to forget the label and look at the request. Does the channel want a datum? A code? A confirmation? A transfer? Remote access? If so, the defence is not to pick the right Latin word. The defence is a second channel. 5. Broad cyberspace is not narrow cybercrime The year 2025 brought, according to the Police of the Czech Republic and the Ministry of the Interior, 21,137 recorded offences in cyberspace [3] [4] . The same year, however, ČSÚ in narrowly qualified cybercrime under Sections 230 to 232 of the Criminal Code reports 1,224 offences [5] . Both figures can be right. They do not measure the same thing. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext Broad cyberspace includes offences in which the digital environment plays a substantial role. They may be advertisement frauds, investment legends, phishing and other forms of social engineering. Narrowly qualified cybercrime aims at offences around unauthorised access to a system, passwords and similar conduct. If someone on the phone persuades a person into a transfer, that can look different in the statistics than an attack on a system. The clearance rate of 15.1% in 2025 for offences in cyberspace is not the share of money returned [3] [4] . It is a police indicator of the clearing of an offence. There can be a case that is cleared while the money is not back. And there can be a payment that the bank helps to stop without a rapid clearing of the whole network of offenders. Here again it is clear why one large number is not enough. The reader does not need to know only how large the problem is in the aggregate. The reader needs to know when to stop acting in the channel that is asking for an action. Statistics show the scale. They do not decide for the reader in the minute of a call. 6. A NÚKIB incident is not a PČR offence NÚKIB is an important institution, but its statistic is not the same as the police statistic of criminal offences. In 2024 it recorded 268 cyber incidents, which the dossier describes as a series record; of them 1 was very significant and 18 significant [6] . In a questionnaire survey of 415 respondents, of whom 324 were regulated and 91 unregulated, more than 90% of respondents encountered phishing and more than 80% fraudulent e-mails [6] . NÚKIB states that it did not verify these questionnaire data. “Encountered” is not the same as “suffered a loss”. For 2025 the Ministry of the Interior reports 203 incidents cited from NÚKIB; the fall against 2024 was linked mainly to DDoS [4] . A direct download of the NÚKIB PDF report for 2025 did not, according to the dossier, load as of 1 September 2026. It is therefore precise to stay with what the Ministry of the Interior states, and not to add one’s own certainty. NÚKIB also draws a boundary to its agenda in fraudulent calls to citizens [7] . That does not mean the call is not dangerous. It means that another institution is watching another piece of the problem. The Velké odhalení campaign can be a useful source of warning and education [21] . It is not a police series of offences. Separating these things is practical. When a firm deals with an incident, it asks about systems, duties and reporting. When a household deals with a call from an alleged bank, it asks about verification of identity and stopping the action. Both belong to cybersecurity. They are not the same door. 7. MFA is not a lock against coercion Strong authentication protects against many attacks. The Payment System Act treats it as a duty of the provider in defined situations [14] . But MFA is not a magic lock against social engineering. If an attacker induces a person to confirm the authentication themselves, the technology has done part of its job and the person has at the same time done an action they should not have done. On 27 September 2024 ČNB warned against frauds with multi-factor authentication. It describes a situation in which the victim confirms the authentication themselves, and notes that after such a confirmation the consumer may bear the loss [8] . That is unpleasant, but for the defence it is fundamental. MFA is meant to stop unauthorised use without cooperation. It stops less well a state in which a person under pressure provides that cooperation. It does not follow that the victim “has themselves to blame” in a moral sense. It follows that the legal and operational regime changes after confirmation. The bank, the police, ČNB, the financial arbitrator and the court will not deal only with the fact that the call sounded convincing. They will deal with what was confirmed, what information the person saw and whether there was gross negligence. The practical sentence is short: do not confirm MFA that you did not start yourself. If someone on a call tells you to confirm an authentication in order to protect you, verify the situation through another channel. Not in the same call. 8. An authorised payment is no longer unauthorised The word “unauthorised” sounds natural in a bank fraud. Someone robbed you, so the payment was surely not yours. But the Payment System Act distinguishes situations in which you do not authorise a payment transaction from situations in which you confirm it, even if the script was fraudulently extracted [14] . In its explanations ČNB notes that a consumer who themselves confirm the amount and the payee or another action may bear the loss as gross negligence [8] [9] . That is not the same as a stolen card without the client’s cooperation. In a remote fraud the key is whether the person disclosed data, confirmed MFA, approved a transfer or otherwise helped the transaction through. That is why so many recommendations focus on the action, not on the look of the message. It does not follow that every case is lost in advance. ČNB itself stresses the circumstances and at the same time says that it does not decide disputes about the return of money; that is for the financial arbitrator or a court according to the nature of the matter [9] . Something more practical follows: the defence must come before confirmation, not after it. When the payment is gone, a rapid reaction remains: contact the bank, block further misuse and file a report with the Police of the Czech Republic. The bank may try to stop an outgoing payment. That is not, however, the same as a claim to an automatic refund. 9. A ČBA loss is not a PČR loss For 2025 the Czech Banking Association, according to a press conference and citations, reports an average loss of CZK 23,462 per client of member banks who suffered a loss. There is further talk of just under 91 thousand attacks, CZK 12.2 billion saved by the banks and an attempt of more than CZK 14 billion [12] [13] . These figures matter, but they have precise boundaries. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext It is not a median. It is not the whole population of the Czech Republic. It is not only vishing. The definition of the unit “attack” is internal, and an official PDF of the association with a complete methodology is, according to the dossier as of the date of the research, missing. One therefore cannot calculate a simple share of victims who got money back after sending it. Nor can one add these figures to police offences and make from them one universal measure. That does not weaken the practical message. Banks catch a large volume of attempts and the loss among those who suffer it is not small. But for the reader the mechanism is the key: a saved amount usually means an intervention before the loss is completed or in its immediate vicinity. If a person themselves confirm a transfer and time is running, the room for remedy narrows. It is therefore more precise to say: ČBA figures show the banking part of the problem. Police figures show the criminal part of the problem. ČNB shows the legal regime. The user’s defence lies between them, in the decision not to perform the requested action in the channel that raised the pressure. 10. A SIM farm explains the mask. It does not explain your transfer In the IOCTA 2026 report Europol describes an operation from 2025 against infrastructure that according to it included 40,000 SIM cards, a network of 7 Latvian nationals, at least 1,200 SIM boxes and numbers from more than 80 countries. On the basis of the service more than 49 million online accounts were said to have been created [16] . That is an example of industrialisation. Not an EU total of all frauds and not a count of Czech victims. Such figures help one understand why a scam need not look amateur. Infrastructure, rented services, automation and AI-assisted impersonation lower the price of the mask. The fraudster need not be technically skilled in everything themselves. They can use services that simplify sending, account management or the imitation of an institution. A boundary is needed here, though: a description of infrastructure is not a guide to its use. For the reader’s defence it is not most important how exactly the mask is assembled. What matters is that the mask itself proves nothing. If an attacker can look more like a bank, then appearance should decide even less. The action and the second channel should decide. A SIM farm therefore explains why many convincing contacts can arrive from various numbers. It does not explain why a person should confirm a transfer. Between the mask and the loss there is still a step. That step must be delayed, interrupted and verified. 11. A deepfake voice is not a condition of the legend A deepfake voice changes the boundary of trust. If someone’s voice can be imitated, hearing ceases to be a sufficient test of identity. Jiný Kontext deals with that in a separate text on a deepfake familiar voice [22] . This article does not want to repeat the same argument. For e-mail, SMS and an ordinary call it is enough to say less: most defences do not rest on recognising a voice. They rest on a second channel. Many documented legends do not need a synthetic voice. A familiar number on the display, an urgent script and a call to action are enough. A person under pressure does not verify because they believe in artificial intelligence. They verify because they want quickly to stop the loss that the caller has just described. That is why it is not good to teach people to listen for “oddities” in a voice as the main defence. The voice can be genuine and the request false. The voice can be unknown and the call genuine. The voice can be synthetic and technically convincing. The test is not hearing. The test is a return to a previously known channel. A deepfake therefore belongs in the picture. But only as a further layer of the mask. Not as a necessary condition of the scam and not as a reason to change the basic rule: do not confirm an action in the channel that requested it. 12. A clearance rate is not a returned amount The police clearance rate for offences in cyberspace was 15.4% in 2024 and 15.1% in 2025 [2] [3] . These figures measure work with a criminal offence in the police statistic. They do not say how many victims got money back. They do not even say that in the remaining cases nothing happened. They say what share of offences was cleared under the rules of the given statistic. A banking interception is another thing. ČBA reports CZK 12.2 billion saved in 2025 [12] [13] . That is banking protection and a reaction to attempts. It is not a police clearance rate. ČNB is a further layer: it supervises, explains the regime, receives submissions, but does not decide a client’s dispute with a bank about the return of money [9] . These three successes must not be added together. A stopped payment, a cleared offence and a won dispute about compensation are different results. Each can occur without the others. For the reader a practical urgency follows from that, not a panic: speed after suspicion matters, but it matters still more not to reach the phase in which one only waits for a remedy. The sentence “the police will investigate it” must not be the last defence before confirmation. The police arrive after the event. The second channel arrives before it. 13. The best defence is the one whose error you can still reverse A defence against a fraudulent e-mail, SMS or call must not be a test of genius. A person need not recognise every mask. They must have a procedure that stops the action even when they do not recognise the mask. The following scheme therefore does not show how to assemble a scam. It shows where it should be interrupted. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext Type of failure What it looks like How to test What will limit the damage The number as identity The display shows a bank or the police Hang up and use a contact from the website, the card or the app Treat spoofing as a possible mask [7] [9] MFA as a lock A person confirms an authentication because “the bank is asking” Do not confirm MFA that one did not start oneself ČNB: after confirmation one may bear the loss [8] Added-up statistics 21,137 = phishing = ČBA loss = NÚKIB incident Separate PČR, ČSÚ, NÚKIB, ČBA and ČNB Do not leave different units in one sentence Authorisation as a stolen card A person waits for an automatic refund Separate authorisation from an unauthorised transaction The bank and the Police of the Czech Republic at once; the dispute belongs to the arbitrator or the court [9] [14] Hearing as proof “I hear the director, so it is him” A second channel A voice is another layer, not a verification [22] Illustrative scheme: In the row stands the channel: e-mail, SMS, call. In the column stands the action: a datum, a code, MFA, a transfer, remote access. The sender’s mask is only a heading. The check sits in the action column and leads through a second channel. The best defence is not the one that never doubts. It is the defence whose error can still be reversed. If you hang up on a genuine banker and call back the official line, you lose time. If you stay on a fraudulent call and confirm a transfer, you lose more. 14. A second channel will say more than a header A second channel is not a call back to the number that has just appeared on the display. It is not a reply to the same SMS. It is not a click on a link in an e-mail and a subsequent “verification”. A second channel is a path you know before the incident: the official website of the institution, the number on the card, the banking app, an internal company contact, a personal verification outside the original message. What needs to be tested before you confirm MFA The first question is: did you start the authentication yourselves? If not, do not confirm it. ČNB expressly warns against frauds in which the victim is steered into confirming MFA [8] . The second question is: do you see an amount and a payee that you yourselves expect? The third question is: why is the authentication arriving just now? If the answer is supplied by the same call that triggered the authentication, that is not a verification. It is part of the pressure. How to test the second channel Hang up or stop answering in the same channel. Take the official contact from the institution’s website, from the payment card or from the app. With a bank that offers call verification in the app, use precisely that option. CISA recommends not clicking links in suspicious messages and verifying through trusted sources [19] . CSIRT.CZ accepts incident reports including phishing and works with URLs and e-mail headers [20] . That is a path for reporting, not for a panicked click. The second channel must be known in advance in a firm as well. It is not enough to write to a colleague in the same thread from which the request came. It is not enough to reply to an e-mail with an urgent invoice. It is not enough to call the number in the message signature, if precisely this signature may be part of the problem. A firm needs a simple rule for payments, changes of a supplier’s account and remote access: verification runs through a contact stored in one’s own system, not through a contact supplied in the request. This procedure is not distrust of colleagues. It is protection of colleagues from having their name become a tool of pressure. An accountant need not decide whether the style of an e-mail really matches the director. An IT technician need not recognise whether a call sounds like a supplier. It is enough that they know that a change of a payment account, a one-time code and remote access do not pass through the same channel in which they are requested. A household needs the same principle on a smaller scale. Parents and grandparents are not helped by a long list of attack types if, at the decisive moment, they are afraid that someone is already emptying the account. What helps is a sentence that can be used without thinking: I will call back the number from the card or from the official app. If the caller presses a person not to hang up, that is itself a reason to hang up. A genuine institution can bear that a client verifies a call through their own channel. A good second channel has one more property: it does not require improvisation. The number for the bank, the procedure for blocking a card, the contact for the accountant and the rule for changing a supplier’s account should be stored before the pressure arrives. In calm one can choose the right path. On a call one often chooses the fastest. A scam relies precisely on this swap. That is why preparing a list of contacts is not an administrative trifle. It is a security tool. Three tests before a transfer First test: hang up and verify through a second channel. Second test: do not confirm MFA that you did not start yourselves. Third test: after suspicion contact the bank at once for a block and the Police of the Czech Republic for a report. Do not deal with a deepfake voice by hearing. Deal with it by the channel. An authorisation you confirmed yourself is no longer an unauthorised payment. — Jiný Kontext 15. A thirteen-month time-limit is not a refund The Payment System Act contains a time-limit for notifying an unauthorised payment transaction. Under Section 188(1) the payer must notify the unauthorised transaction to the provider without undue delay, at the latest within 13 months of the debiting of the amount; if the provider objects to a late notification, the court will not grant the right to a remedy [14] . That is a time-limit. It is not a promise of a return of money. Beside it stand further provisions of the Payment System Act, including the rules of strong authentication and of remedy [14] . And beside them the Criminal Code, for example Section 209 on fraud [15] . This legal map matters for the reader mainly in that it does not lead to one automatic refund. A timely notification is a condition. Not a guarantee. If a person confirmed a transaction under pressure or on the basis of a deception, the dispute may turn on cooperation and gross negligence. ČNB repeats that it does not itself decide a dispute about the return of money [9] . The practical procedure therefore remains twofold: contact the bank at once and file a report with the police. At the same time keep the communication, numbers, messages and time data for further resolution. The best legal time-limit is the one you do not need to use. That is not cynicism. It is a description of the order. Before confirmation the second channel decides. After confirmation the time-limits, banking processes and disputes already decide. 16. Five to ten calls a day on the ČNB line are not an annual map of victims In its FAQ on frauds in payment services ČNB states that on the Green Line it handles 5 to 10 complaints a day about frauds. The same overview says that in 2021 it did not record such complaints and that in 2022 there were already hundreds [9] . That is a useful signal of a change. It is not an annual total of victims and it is not a statistic of successful frauds. The range of 5 to 10 a day is a figure from ČNB’s communication channel. It does not include those who call the bank, the police, the financial arbitrator or no one. It does not say how much loss arose, how much money returned, or how many cases overlap with the police statistic. It is not added to the 21,137 offences in cyberspace or to the average loss of CZK 23,462 among injured clients of member banks [3] [12] . The figure still has a point. It shows that frauds in payment services are not a marginal query. People ask because the boundary of responsibility is not intuitive. A person has the feeling of having been robbed and at the same time hears that they confirmed the payment themselves. That is precisely the place where one needs to speak of a second channel earlier than of a complaint. The statistic of the line is therefore not a map of victims. It is a warning sign at a counter to which people arrive late. 17. The hidden cost is an action in the same channel A fraudulent message or call often does not win by being perfectly genuine. It wins by shortening the path between fear and action. It does not let a person leave the channel. The call continues, the SMS adds a link, the e-mail offers a button, the alleged banker dictates the next step. Everything happens in the same pipe in which the pressure arose. The hidden cost is not only a money loss. It is also the confusion after the event. Whom to call? What is authorised? What is unauthorised? What does MFA mean? Who decides the dispute? Why do the police speak of a clearance rate and the bank of an interception? Why does NÚKIB count incidents and ČBA clients? The later we deal with these differences, the more expensive they are. That does not mean a person must know all the statistics. It means they must have one rule stronger than the mask: I do not verify an action in the channel that asks for it. A number, a logo, a voice, urgency or even correct personal data do not suffice by themselves. A datum, a code, MFA, a transfer and remote access belong only after a second channel. This rule is dull, and that is precisely why it works even under ordinary pressure. The question is therefore not how to recognise a fraudulent e-mail, SMS or phone call by whether it looks like a bank. It is: which action are you willing to confirm in the same channel without a second, previously known verification? If the answer is “none”, that is not distrust of the world. It is a precise placing of the check. Related texts in this series How do you find out whether your password or e-mail has leaked? — a leak in an index is not the same channel as an emergency call. In the folder: A deepfake of a familiar voice — a voice is no longer a seal of identity; this text takes e-mail, SMS and a call as three channels of pressure.

items.title: Seizure of a phone is not interception. Data in memory are not a future call. And a cipher is a factual obstacle, not a prohibition of the law.
items.subtitle: The police may lawfully seize a phone as a thing. Reading what is already in it is, from 1 January 2026, subject to a special regime for examining device content. Watching what has yet to arrive is interception under § 88.
items.perex: The police may lawfully seize a phone as a thing. Reading what is already in it is, from 1 January 2026, subject to a special regime for examining device content. Watching what has yet to arrive is interception under § 88.
headings: 1. A phone on the table after taking of a thing is not interception. Nor free memory content.
2. Access to a mobile has at least six layers
3. The best regime is the one whose key you can name
4. Seizure of a thing is not the reading of data. The reading of data is not interception of future communication.
5. Data already stored are not messages that arrive after seizure
6. § 88 is not § 88a. A seized phone is not an operator.
7. A general examination is not an examination of device content
8. From 1 January 2026 a secured portable phone has its own judicial filter
9. A judicial authorisation is not a technical ability to open the device
10. Four exceptions from an authorisation are not a free licence to the cloud
11. Urgency without subsequent consent makes the evidence unusable
12. Consent to examination of content is not consent to interception of a station
13. Article 13 covers content and numbers called. A smartphone is a denser interference than a keypad phone from 2000.
14. Encryption is a gap in proof. It is not a ban on investigating. Nor a duty of success.
15. An expert may copy without at once becoming acquainted with the content
16. Questions for defence counsel will say more than the sentence “they searched my mobile”
What needs to be tested
Before assessing the lawfulness of a seizure
Three tests of the regime
17. The hidden cost is one device that we read as one key

items.body: Section: Justice & law | Technology & AI Author: V Reading time: ~27 min Sources and further reading: 22 items Topics: mobile phone, criminal proceedings, interception, data, encryption, privacy SEO / working title: May the police search your mobile phone? May the police search your mobile phone? The question sounds simple only until we notice that we are not comparing one thing. Seizure of a device may be lawful and reading the memory may still require another key. A message already in the phone is not a message that will arrive tomorrow. A judicial authorisation to examine content is not a technical ability to open the device. And a cloud visible from the phone without a further lock is not the whole cloud account. The text that follows therefore does not ask how to unlock a phone. It asks which of the three regimes is running, and whether it has its judicial filter. 1. A phone on the table after taking of a thing is not interception. Nor free memory content. A phone lies on the table. A police authority took it after a call to surrender a thing, or took it, or found it during a search. A prosecutor in pre-trial proceedings considers whether it is necessary to go to a judge. Defence counsel does not ask only who holds the phone. Counsel asks what the state then did with it. From 1 January 2026 a judge assesses a written authorisation to examine the content of a secured portable communications device. An expert may be given the task of making a copy. The operator is not sitting at this scene. That belongs to another question. At first glance this is a dispute about the sentence “the police searched my mobile”. In fact each person is describing a different legal key. One key opens disposition of a thing: surrender, taking, a search. The second key opens already stored content of a secured portable device. The third key concerns future communication that is only then passing through the network. The shared word search erases all three keys. That is why they can all be partly right and the shared sentence still mislead. The police may have seized the phone lawfully, but that itself does not say whether they were allowed to read its content. A court may have authorised examination of content, but that itself does not say whether the device can in fact be read. The phone may have received a message after seizure, but that is not the same as a message that was already in it. And the operator may hold traffic data, but a seized device is not the network. This article is therefore not a technical manual for work with a phone lock, biometrics or encryption. It does not say how to hide data. It describes only the regimes in which the state treats a device, content and communication. That is a more useful question. It does not ask whether “a mobile may”. It asks which act took place and which filter belongs to it. Seizure of a phone is not interception. Data in memory are not a future call. — Jiný Kontext 2. Access to a mobile has at least six layers When a phone appears in criminal proceedings, one simple situation does not arise. A chain arises. Each link has a different purpose, a different boundary and a different kind of error. The first layer is a thing in the state’s disposition. A phone may become a means of evidence by surrender of a thing, taking of a thing, seizure during a house or personal search, or a find during an examination. The Code of Criminal Procedure in § 78 and § 79 governs surrender and taking of a thing; after the amendment the possibility of making a copy of data instead of the carrier itself also matters [1] [13] . That is the base. Without it the next step is hard to build. The second layer is already stored content. Until the end of 2025 this problem was in practice read mainly through the difference between a carrier and interception. Opinions of the Supreme Public Prosecutor’s Office proceeded from the view that establishing content already stored in a seized device did not require an order under § 88 [5] [6] . From 1 January 2026 secured portable devices that enable two-way communication have their own regime in § 113a [7] [12] . The third layer is future communication. A call, a message or other traffic that arrives only after seizure is not merely the content of a thing lying on a table. It is traffic on the way. The Supreme Court in a resolution of 15 December 2000, file No. 7 Tz 9/2000, separated delivered SMS messages from SMS messages that arrived only later [3] [4] . The amendment of § 113a does not cancel this cut. For future communication § 88 remains in play. The fourth layer is the constitutional ceiling. Article 13 of the Charter protects the secrecy of messages submitted by telephone [11] . The Constitutional Court has already said of older telephony that the protection does not fall only on the content of a call, but also on numbers called, time, duration and base stations [8] [9] . A smartphone adds photographs, chats, location, notes, health applications, payment trails and work accounts. The intensity of the interference is greater. The fifth layer is encryption as a fact. The law does not forbid an investigation because a device is encrypted. Nor does it order success. The result may be simple: an authorisation exists, but the data are not readable. That is a gap in proof. It is not a technical manual. The sixth layer is the expert. The amendment contemplates that if an expert is appointed to data under § 113a(1), the procedure is analogous under § 113a [7] . Copying without becoming acquainted with the content, and becoming acquainted with the content itself, are not the same. Here too it is important to know in which layer one currently stands. 3. The best regime is the one whose key you can name With a phone in criminal proceedings the greatest risk is usually a procedural shortcut. Not technical complexity. That is real, but legally we ask differently. Who performed which act? At what moment? With what authorisation? And toward what content? Type of failure What it looks like How to test it What limits the harm Mixing the three keys “Search of a mobile” fuses thing, memory and future traffic Name § 78/79, § 113a and § 88 separately Defence counsel asks about the act and the filter Stored as future A later-delivered message is read as the content of a thing Separate the moment of seizure from delivery Later traffic belongs under § 88 Authorisation as opening A judicial stamp is mixed up with factual readability Separate the power from the ability to read the data A cipher is a gap in proof, not a manual An exception as a licence An exception from § 113a is read as a free cloud Read the scope of the exception and the limit of further security An exception is not an infinite account A phone as an operator Network metadata are sought in the device as in the network Separate § 88a from device content A seized phone is not an operator Interpretive scheme: The same phone may be a thing, a carrier of already stored data and an endpoint of future communication. The legal regime is not determined by the brand of the phone, but by the act, the time and the content. It does not follow that every procedural mistake automatically means the unlawfulness of everything else. It follows that without a precise description lawfulness cannot be assessed at all. The sentence “the police had the phone” is a beginning. The sentence “the police read data in a secured portable device after 1 January 2026 without the § 113a regime” is already a legal problem. 4. Seizure of a thing is not the reading of data. The reading of data is not interception of future communication. The Code of Criminal Procedure works with a thing. A person may be called to surrender it. In certain situations a thing may be taken. During a search it may be seized. That is old procedural language. A phone fits into it as a material object that may have evidentiary significance [1] [13] . But a phone is not only an object. It is a data carrier and a gate to further services. That is why it is not enough to say that a thing was seized. Seizure answers why the device is in the state’s hands. It does not itself answer whether the authority was allowed to become acquainted with the content of a secured device. Precisely this second step is, from 1 January 2026, expressly governed by § 113a [7] [12] . The third step is different once more. Interception under § 88 is not the reading of what is already on the carrier. It aims at telecommunications traffic. An order for the interception and recording of telecommunications traffic has its own conditions, its own time frame and its own subsequent treatment of the recording [2] . That is the core of the whole matter. One act may lawfully precede another, but it cannot replace it. Lawful taking of a phone is not a blank cheque for reading secured content. An authorisation to examine content is not an authorisation to watch what will arrive tomorrow. And interception of future communication is not proof that earlier stored data were read under the correct regime. 5. Data already stored are not messages that arrive after seizure The distinction between stored and future is not a new sensitivity of smartphones. In the Czech debate it already appeared with SMS. The Supreme Court in resolution 7 Tz 9/2000, dated 15 December 2000, dealt with the difference between messages delivered into a seized phone and messages that arrived only after seizure [3] [4] . The first were on the carrier. The second were telecommunications traffic that was only then taking place. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext Opinion of the Supreme Public Prosecutor’s Office serial No. 4/2005 followed this cut for a mobile phone [5] . Opinion 1/2015 extended it to further carriers and applications [6] . The essential sentence remains: later delivery is not the same as stored memory. It is a different moment and a different regime. From 1 January 2026 the regime of already stored content changes for a special group of devices. For a secured portable communications device it is no longer enough to lean on the old idea of a carrier. § 113a steps in. But the time cut has not disappeared. The amendment does not rewrite future communication as the content of a thing. What has yet to arrive remains a problem of interception or other regimes, not examination of memory. In practice that means a simple question: were the data in the device at the moment of seizure, or did they arise only afterwards? The answer will not solve everything, but without it the dispute falls apart. Date and time are not a formality. They are the boundary between two legal worlds. 6. § 88 is not § 88a. A seized phone is not an operator. § 88 and § 88a look, side by side, like technical siblings. They are not the same. § 88 concerns the interception and recording of telecommunications traffic. As the Code of Criminal Procedure reads toward 2026 it works, among other things, with the threshold of a crime whose upper prison term is at least eight years, and with further listed offences; one order may last at most four months, though it may be repeatedly extended [2] [20] . This figure measures the ceiling of one authorisation, not an automatic overall period of surveillance in every case. § 88a concerns data on telecommunications traffic. It is access to traffic and location data, typically at the operator. Its threshold is different: an intentional offence with an upper term of at least three years and further listed cases [1] . That matters, but it belongs first of all to the network and the operator, not to the content of a seized phone. A seized phone is not an operator. It has no duty under the Electronic Communications Act to retain data for the state. It is not even a network interface at which the operator ensures the intelligibility of an interception [15] . The device may contain a history of calls or messages. It may show applications. It may have local copies. But legally it does not turn into a telecommunications undertaking merely because it once communicated on the network. This distinction protects precision. If the subject is the future content of communication, we look at § 88. If the subject is traffic data at the operator, we look at § 88a and the Electronic Communications Act. If the subject is the content of a secured portable device, from 2026 we look at § 113a. One paragraph number is not to replace another. 7. A general examination is not an examination of device content Examination under § 113 is a traditional act. It serves to clarify facts by direct observation. A place, a thing, a body, a trail can be examined. This language makes sense for glass on the floor, a broken lock or a phone as an object. But the content of a phone is not only the surface of a thing. § 113a therefore introduces a special regime. It aims at a portable device enabling two-way communication that is secured by the user, and also at a copy of data from such a device [12] . The statute expressly also contemplates data in remote storage if they are accessible from the device without overcoming further security. That last sentence is a boundary, not an invitation. A cloud visible from the phone without a further lock is not the whole cloud account. From the fact that an application shows some data it does not follow that there is a power to bypass further protection of a remote service. It follows that the statute needed to name a realistic situation: device content need not live only on its chip. A modern phone often shows local and remote data at once. Here too there is no space for technical manuals. The legal text says when and in what scope content may be examined. It does not tell the reader how to overcome security. That boundary is both substantive and a matter of safety. The article cites it; it does not shift it. 8. From 1 January 2026 a secured portable phone has its own judicial filter Act No. 270/2025 Coll. was published on 5 August 2025 and the relevant part takes effect on 1 January 2026 [7] . This date is not an ornament. It separates the older reading from a new procedural architecture. For a secured portable communications device, examination of content has an express judicial filter. The default is a written authorisation of a judge. In pre-trial proceedings it is issued on a prosecutor’s motion. The authorisation must be reasoned and the statute works with subsidiarity: the purpose pursued cannot be achieved otherwise, or that would be substantially more difficult [12] . This sentence matters precisely because a phone may contain far more than one piece of evidence. The authority is, under the statute, entitled to obtain access to the data [1] . That is a procedural sentence. It does not mean a claim to success. It does not mean a duty to describe the method. It does not mean that a physical or cryptographic obstacle disappears. It means that the state may, under the conditions of the statute, seek access to data that fall into the regime. § 113a is therefore the legislature’s answer to the density of a smartphone. It is not the cancellation of the possibility to seize a phone. Nor is it a confirmation of the old sentence that a carrier is simply a carrier. It is a separate filter between a device as a thing and a device as a private archive. 9. A judicial authorisation is not a technical ability to open the device This is where most of the confusion arises. A court’s authorisation is sometimes read as a magic key. It is not one. The court deals with the power. The device, the account and the security deal with the factual availability of data. These two planes meet, but they do not fuse. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext Encryption is a good example. If a device is encrypted and the content is not readable, the law is not thereby automatically switched off. The state may have an authorisation and at the same time run into a gap in proof. Such a result is possible. It is not a ban on investigating. It is not a duty of success. And it is not space for a manual on how to bypass the obstacle. In the same way an unavailable cloud account is not the same as a locally available application. The statute speaks of data accessible from the seized device without overcoming further security [12] . Where there is a further lock, there is a further problem. This text names it legally and does not develop it technically. Between authorisation and result there therefore still lies the record. It should be clear what scope the court allowed, which data were only copied, which were read and what remained unavailable. Without that trail it later becomes hard to tell whether failure meant a factual limit, or whether the act exceeded the original authorisation. Precisely here a technical sentence becomes a procedural question. The right question is therefore not whether the court “unlocked the phone”. It did not. The right question is whether the court authorised examination of device content, how it marked out the scope, why it regarded the subsidiarity condition as met and what happened when it turned out that the data were not readable. 10. Four exceptions from an authorisation are not a free licence to the cloud § 113a does not work only with an authorisation in advance. It also contains exceptions. On the wording in the sources there are four situations in paragraph 5: consent of the entitled user, seizure during a search of premises, an unknown user, and a crime scene or a victim unable to cooperate [12] [21] . Four letters are not one large free licence. Consent of the entitled user addresses one situation. Seizure during a search of premises another. An unknown user another. A crime scene and a victim unable to cooperate yet another. Each exception has its reason. If we mix them, a procedural shortcut arises: because an exception exists somewhere, no authorisation is needed anywhere. That is not how the statute works. Remote data have to be read with particular care. An exception does not mean infinite reading of a cloud account. The statute itself limits the cloud overreach to data accessible from the device without overcoming further security [12] . That is precisely the moment when a legal sentence must remain a legal sentence. It is not to become a manual. The exceptions are therefore not meant to cancel the test. They are meant to refine it. We ask which exception was used, why, in what scope and toward which data. If the answer is only “there was an exception”, it is not finished. We are only beginning. 11. Urgency without subsequent consent makes the evidence unusable The statute also contemplates urgency. That is reasonable. Criminal proceedings sometimes do not wait for an ideal order of steps. But urgency is not a magic eraser. § 113a(4) according to the sources requires prompt subsequent consent. If it does not come, evidence obtained by the examination is not used and copies are destroyed [12] . This arrangement shows that a copy of data is not a neutral shadow. It may contain an extensive private life, work communication and data of third persons. If subsequent consent is missing where the statute requires it, a hand should not merely be waved. The statute sets a consequence. The same logic concerns notification of the user. The sources state that the statute governs notification of the authorisation, or a postponement of delivery for the purpose of the proceedings [12] . So again: it is not only whether the state can obtain data. It is whether the act is recorded, marked out and later reviewable. Urgency is therefore a test of discipline. It may explain why one path was taken first. It is not to explain why later no one asked any more. 12. Consent to examination of content is not consent to interception of a station Consent appears in criminal proceedings in more than one place. That is precisely why it is dangerous to speak of it in general. Consent of the entitled user to examination of content under § 113a(5)(a) is not the same as consent under § 88(5) for interception of a station [2] [12] . A different provision. A different subject. A different time. For examination of content we look at data in the device or a copy, or at remotely available data within limits. For interception we look at future telecommunications traffic. That someone consented to one does not automatically mean consent to the other. Still less does it mean consent to operator data under § 88a. There the subject is access to traffic and location data, not the content of a phone and not interception itself [1] . Consent is therefore not a universal password. It is a legal title to a particular act. In practice it therefore pays to read the record slowly. Who consented? To what? When? In what scope? Was it the entitled user? Did the consent concern stored content, future communication, or traffic data? Without these questions the word consent is too smooth. 13. Article 13 covers content and numbers called. A smartphone is a denser interference than a keypad phone from 2000. Article 13 of the Charter protects the secrecy of letters and other writings and of messages submitted by telephone [11] . The Constitutional Court in II. ÚS 502/2000 of 22 January 2001 said that the protection does not concern only the content of a call, but also data on numbers called, date, time, length of a call and base stations [8] . IV. ÚS 1556/07 of 3 August 2010 confirmed this line for records of telecommunications traffic [9] . Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext These decisions are not decisions about unlocking a smartphone. That is an important reservation. They concerned records of traffic and the constitutional protection of telephone communication, not forensic access to today’s device. They nevertheless show a principle: even data that are not the content of a call can be sensitive. A smartphone is still denser. Inside it may be communication with family, work, photographs, location, a health regime, authentication applications, notes, browsing history, documents and access to other people’s data. It is not only a box with a list of numbers. That is why the statutory answer from 2025 is logical: a special filter for examination of content. Not a complete ban on seizure. Not a claim that a phone is always the same as a house. But a recognition that it is not an ordinary thing either. Pl. ÚS 3/09 recalls the court’s role in authorising interferences in pre-trial proceedings [17] . It is not a mechanical stamp. There is to be review before the interference or subsequent review where the statute allows urgency. The denser the interference, the less an indefinite sentence will do. 14. Encryption is a gap in proof. It is not a ban on investigating. Nor a duty of success. Encryption is often spoken of as a legal argument. In fact it is first a fact. Data may be unreadable. An account may be unavailable. A device may be secured. It does not follow that the state may never investigate. It follows that an authorisation and a result are not the same. This distinction protects both sides. It protects the state from the mistaken conclusion that a technical obstacle cancels the legal possibility of an act. And it protects the individual from the mistaken conclusion that a legal authorisation automatically cancels all factual boundaries. The law gives a frame. It does not guarantee yield. The Electronic Communications Act in § 97(1) and (6) governs the operator’s cooperation in an interception and intelligibility at the network interface [15] . That is another matter. It concerns the network and the operator, not the lock of a phone lying on a table. To transfer this duty onto user security of a device would be another shortcut. That is why this paragraph ends at the statute. It does not begin at bypassing a lock. If the result is “there is an authorisation, the content is not readable”, the legal language should say: a gap in proof. Not: here is a procedure. 15. An expert may copy without at once becoming acquainted with the content Digital evidence often needs a specialist. Not because the law has disappeared, but because work with data requires preservation of a trail, a copy, integrity and a description of steps. NSZ opinion 9/2001 dealt with the seizure of computers during a search and questions of confidentiality [14] . Today’s phone is a different object, but the old question remains: how to separate seizure of a carrier from reading of content. The amendment to § 105 according to the sources provides that if an expert is appointed to data under § 113a(1), the procedure is analogous under § 113a [7] . That is a precise procedural sentence. An expert is not a figure outside the law. If the expert works with content, the corresponding regime transfers onto the expert. A copy itself can be ambiguous. A copy can be made without the authority or the expert at once becoming acquainted with the content. And one can become acquainted with the content. These steps should be separated in the record and in the reasoning. Otherwise copying turns into hidden reading. The Supreme Court’s press release on electronic devices in the matter of T. J. shows how sensitive disputes about the surrender and erasure of data are, without itself being a manual for unlocking [16] . That is the right position for this text as well. Electronic devices are not magic. They are evidentiary carriers with a very strong private overreach. 16. Questions for defence counsel will say more than the sentence “they searched my mobile” A practical test does not begin with technique. It begins with paper, time and scope. What needs to be tested First the act of seizure has to be identified. Was it a call to surrender a thing, an order to take, a house search, a personal search, or an examination of a place? If the basic act was defective, subsequent work with content has a weak foundation. If the basic act was in order, the dispute moves on. The second question is whether it is a portable device enabling two-way communication and secured by the user. If so, from 1 January 2026 the default regime is § 113a. A free USB disk without a communications function may fall elsewhere, but even there the general limits of proof do not disappear. Before assessing the lawfulness of a seizure On an authorisation, ask about writing, reasons and subsidiarity. A sentence that the phone may contain evidence is not enough. It is necessary to know why the purpose pursued could not be achieved otherwise or why that would have been substantially more difficult [12] . It is also necessary to know whether an exception under paragraph 5 was used, and if so which one and in what scope. On urgency, ask whether subsequent consent arrived and what happened to the copy if it did not. On notification, ask whether the user was informed, or why delivery was postponed. These are not formalities. They are the points by which the interference can later be reviewed. Three tests of the regime The first test is the thing: was the device lawfully seized? The second test is stored content: was it § 113a, an exception, or an older regime for another carrier? The third test is future delivery: are data as of the moment of seizure separated from messages that arrived later? The third belongs under § 88, not examination of the content of a thing. This test is not “how to lock a phone better”. It is not advice on how to hide data. It is a checklist for the lawfulness of a regime. That is its strength. It turns a general sentence into concrete questions that have a procedural answer. 17. The hidden cost is one device that we read as one key A phone tempts a simple sentence. It lies on the table, it has a screen, it has data, it has a signal. But the law does not see one thing in it. It sees an object, a carrier of stored content, an endpoint of communication and sometimes a gate to remote services. If we call all of that a search of a mobile, we lose precisely what is meant to protect lawfulness. The claim of this article is narrower than it may seem. It does not say that the police may never seize a phone. It does not say that the content of a phone is always inviolable. It does not say that encryption creates a legal ban on investigation. It says something more practical: three different regimes must not be passed off as one. As of September 2026 the research found no Constitutional Court judgment that would expressly decide the dispute whether the police may unlock a smartphone without a PIN. It also found no public statistic of how many phones are seized in Czechia a year, how many of them cannot be read and how often courts authorise § 113a. We therefore know neither the ordinary length of these disputes nor the average yield of an examination in Czech practice. That is not a weakness of the text. It is a limit of the evidence. Inventing a figure would be worse than saying that it is missing. The question is therefore not whether the police may “search a mobile”. It is: which of the three keys it has just used — seizure of a thing, examination of already stored content, or interception of what has yet to arrive — and did that key have its judicial filter? A judicial authorisation is not a technical ability to open the device. — Jiný Kontext Related texts in this series How long does an operator retain data… — a seized phone is not an operator. How does police location of a mobile phone work? — § 88a and a cell, not memory content. Can a person’s location be established from a telephone number? — private “tracing” is not a police title.
