items.body: There are two colours on the screen: petrol blue on the left, rust red on the right. A sharp line runs between them, kinked in places but always precise. Three arrows show the direction of advance. A number glows in the corner: one side controls 61.4 per cent of the area being tracked, the other 38.6 per cent. The map feels calm—like the closing balance sheet of a war. Now let us move to a single place crossed by that line. There is a narrow road between a forest and a handful of houses. A small unit from one side holds the western edge of the village. During the day it can reach the crossroads; at night it withdraws to cover. The other side is not permanently present in the village, but watches the approach road with drones and can strike it with artillery. A supply route runs behind the forest, usable only intermittently. Local residents still live in several cellars. They know when the road is relatively passable, but not who it will belong to six hours later. No one can safely enter the strip of fields between the two positions. On the map, this place must be petrol blue, rust red or grey. On the ground, it is none of those things. It is at once a space of presence, range, risk, movement, observation, administration and uncertainty. One colour is not enough. This is where the problem begins: a war map does not depict control itself. It depicts a decision about how control will be defined for the purposes of the map. ◎ Editorial note This article does not assess the legitimacy, political aims or moral standing of any party to a conflict. All contemporary-looking situations and maps are stylised; the article adopts no unverified claim about any current front line. 01 What does it actually mean to “control territory”? The word control sounds like a switch: either on or off. Either one side holds the territory, or the other does. In reality, it is better understood as a bundle of different capabilities that may overlap, diverge and change over the course of a day. Physical presence means that personnel or equipment belonging to one side are present at the location. It says nothing by itself about whether they can remain there. A brief patrol, a reconnaissance incursion or a house occupied for several hours is not the same as enduring control of an area. Sustained control presupposes the ability to supply a position, rotate personnel, defend it and restore a presence after an attack. Control therefore means more than reaching a place. It means being able to return repeatedly and bear the costs that this entails. Freedom of movement is another distinct layer. One side may have a position in the village yet be unable to use the road leading to it safely. The other side may be physically farther away but still observe, disrupt or constrain movement along that road. Who, then, controls the village: the side standing in it, or the side deciding when it can be reached? Control by fire does not require occupation. Terrain can be kept under observation and within weapons range so that an adversary may enter it but cannot use it routinely. Conversely, weapons range alone does not amount to effective control over every point inside a circle on a map. Visibility, accuracy, available assets, response time, cover and many other variables all matter. Administrative control exists on another plane: who issues documents, runs the local office, organises policing, collects fees, keeps schools operating, records property or settles disputes? In an irregular conflict, an administrative network may function where military presence is discontinuous. Conversely, a unit may occupy the town square without controlling local institutions or information. Control of main routes may matter more than holding the surrounding area. A bridge, railway junction, mountain pass or the only usable road connects supply, evacuation and movement. Military geography therefore distinguishes ordinary ground from key terrain: some places confer a disproportionate advantage because they govern access, observation or transport. [4] Local resistance and the information environment can undermine official control. A local network may pass information, hide people, refuse cooperation or, conversely, enable administration without a large military presence. The colour of a territory therefore does not tell us whether power is accepted, merely tolerated or imposed. Finally, there are contested, buffer and effectively inaccessible zones . They are not “empty”. They may be watched, mined, shelled, visited intermittently or used only at particular times. What they share is that no side can routinely exercise all components of control there at once. Control is not a point on a scale from zero to one hundred. It is a profile of capabilities: to be present, endure, move, prevent the other side from moving, administer, supply and gather information. Political-science research on civil wars therefore often uses more than a simple “government versus rebels” binary. It distinguishes several levels, from complete control by one side through varying degrees of contestation to complete control by the other. Control itself is often treated as a latent state that cannot be measured directly; it is inferred from observable events and behaviour. [7] The map turns that estimate back into a colour. VISUALISATION 02 · LAYERS OF CONTROL One territory, eight different answers A schematic profile of a fictional sector. Bar lengths are illustrative only—they are neither percentages nor data from a real conflict. strength of A overlap / uncertainty strength of B Physical presence Who is physically present now A at the edge of the village; no permanent force in the centre Persistence Who can remain and replenish forces the sustainability of the positions is unclear Movement Who can use the area routinely the main road is passable only intermittently Fire influence Who can restrict movement from a distance ranges overlap Administration Who provides institutions and rules the local authority is linked to A’s structures Lines of communication Who holds hubs and supply routes the crossroads is observed; the route is disrupted Local network Information, cooperation, resistance an unobservable layer with low confidence Safe access Where entry is possible without disproportionate risk most of the zone is effectively contested The diagram shows the principle, not the state of a battlefield. One colour has to compress eight different layers into a single category. The method of a map lies precisely in how it performs that compression. 02 A model is not a lie. A model is a reduction. The International Cartographic Association defines a map as a symbolised representation of geographic reality that depicts selected features and is produced through the decisions of its author. [1] Selection is therefore not a flaw that accidentally found its way into the map. It is a condition of the map’s existence. If a map showed every house, every tree, every movement, every patrol, every instance of signal interference, every unverified report, every moment and every possible interpretation, it would cease to be a map. It would become an unusable warehouse of data. For space to become intelligible, some information must be emphasised, some combined and some removed. The US Geological Survey describes cartographic generalisation in precisely these terms: at a smaller scale covering a larger area, information and detail must be reduced so that the representation remains legible. [2] A road is straightened. Several buildings become a point. A forest receives a single fill. An irregular belt of uncertainty becomes a line. Core argument A model is not a lie. A model is a reduction. The question is not whether a map simplifies reality. The question is whether we know what this particular map has simplified. A good map is not one that contains everything. A good map contains the right things for a particular question. A strategic map may clearly show the overall direction of change. An operational map may emphasise routes, hubs and terrain obstacles. A local map may show individual edges of built-up areas, copses and passages. Each will look different, yet all can be honest. The problem arises when an answer designed for one question is used as an answer to another. A map suited to saying “which side has the advantage in this region” may be unable to tell us “who can safely travel along this road tonight”. Yet our minds readily read it as though it said both. 03 A line that has to run somewhere The front line is often the strongest element on the entire map. It separates colours, closes shapes and creates the impression that a physical boundary like a wall exists at every point along it. In some places that may be reasonably close to reality: continuous defensive positions, obstacles and persistently observed ground can produce a distinct line of contact. Elsewhere, however, the “front” resembles a broad belt of varying risk and incomplete presence. An analyst does not usually observe a line. The analyst observes individual indications: the location of a unit at a particular time, a geolocated recording, movement along a road, an abandoned position, a report of an attack, a change in administrative activity or the prolonged absence of an adversary. A continuous boundary must be inferred from these points. The line is therefore the result of classification and interpolation. It is a conclusion drawn between observations. Its position also depends on the rule chosen. Do we draw it at the furthest confirmed presence? Along the last sustainable positions? Around the area in which manoeuvre is safe? On the centre line between defensive belts? Each option answers a slightly different question. A more candid map may replace the line with an uncertainty band, hatching or several levels of transparency. But that, too, carries a cost. The more uncertainty a map displays, the harder it becomes to read. Research on cartographic uncertainty has long stressed that data quality and uncertainty should be communicated visually, especially where decisions are made from maps under time pressure. [5] [6] At the same time, every additional texture, blur or layer imposes another demand on attention. The clean line is therefore seductive not only politically, but cognitively. It is fast. It instantly declares what lies “on one side” and what lies “on the other”. Yet its legibility can easily be mistaken for precision. 04 Zoom in, and the front dissolves into a system Historical maps of trench warfare reveal what scale does to the idea of a single line. On an overview map of the First World War’s Western Front, a long section can be shown as an almost continuous line. The Library of Congress collection, however, preserves 156 maps at a scale of 1:10,000, made from aerial photographs and observation. They show trenches, wire obstacles, roads, airfields, depots and other positions. [9] Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext On those maps, the “front” is not a single line. It is infrastructure: a forward trench, support lines, communication trenches, firing positions, obstacles, dead ground and routes. From a distance, this system has to be compressed into one symbol. Up close, it becomes clear that between the two colours lies a space in which every separate use of the terrain is contested. The same is true outside trench warfare, though in different forms. In a civil war, state administration may function in a district centre while rural roads are dangerous at night. In mountainous terrain, a valley may be passable while the slopes are observed by the other side. In a city, changing control of a single bridge or passage can reshape the logistics of an entire neighbourhood without producing a visibly large territorial change on an overview map. Scale determines more than the amount of detail. It also determines what we are willing to call the same phenomenon. 05 Colours are not neutral containers Colour on a map does more than explain a category. It creates a sense of ownership. A fully saturated area looks complete, as though every metre inside it were subject to the same power. Its edges appear precise, its interior homogeneous, and empty spaces seem not to exist. Cartography distinguishes among several types of colour scheme. Sequential scales suggest movement from a low to a high value; diverging scales emphasise departure in two directions from a meaningful midpoint; qualitative palettes distinguish categories without claiming that one is “more” than another. [10] Using only two contrasting colours for contested territory is therefore not merely an aesthetic decision. It asserts that reality consists of two mutually exclusive classes. A grey or hatched zone may acknowledge uncertainty, but it too carries meaning. Grey can look like “no man’s land” even though people may live there, local authorities may function and several armed actors may operate. Transparency may indicate weak control, low confidence in the source, or simply a graphic attempt to preserve the basemap. Without a legend, the reader cannot know which of these meanings applies. Military symbols have a standardised grammar. MIL-STD-2525, for example, establishes rules for joint military symbology so that different systems and users interpret the same signs consistently. [3] The standard governs how information is written down, not whether the information itself is complete and correct. A precisely drawn symbol may still rest on an uncertain observation. Arrows work in a similar way. Their heads suggest direction, their length reach and their width strength. But readers must know whether an arrow marks confirmed movement, a reported attack, a possible direction, a planned intention or merely a graphic summary of change between two dates. Without that information, a hypothesis can easily dress itself up as an event. 06 Percentages of territory: precision that may be measuring something else The statement “2.3 per cent of territory gained” looks more objective than a coloured area. In fact, it conceals several decisions. What is the denominator—the whole country, an administrative region, territory originally held, or the area selected for observation? How are contested zones counted? To what time does the figure refer? And what exactly does “gained” mean: first entry, confirmed occupation, or sustainable control? A historical example shows how radically a single choice of unit can change the picture. In 2018, the US oversight body SIGAR tracked control in Afghanistan separately by number of districts, share of population and land area. As of 31 July, it reported that the Afghan government controlled or influenced 55.5 per cent of districts, while roughly 65.2 per cent of the population lived in those districts. A category of contested districts also existed, and the public map used slightly different category names from the accompanying text. [8] The point is not to assess that conflict. It is methodological: numbers of administrative units, numbers of people and land area are not interchangeable quantities. The same situation may look like 55 per cent, 65 per cent or a completely different share depending on what we treat as the object of control. Area is not the same as strategic value. One hundred square kilometres of open, inaccessible terrain may matter less than a few kilometres around a bridge, pass, railway junction or water source. Military geography explicitly works with key terrain, transport chokepoints, routes and supply lines because holding them can confer a major advantage regardless of their small area. [4] Percentages can therefore be calculated correctly and still answer the less important question. They measure how much space changed category. They do not automatically show how the ability to fight, supply, protect civilians or maintain administration has changed. VISUALISATION 03 · AREA VERSUS SIGNIFICANCE LARGE AREA Many kilometres, little change to the network A territorial gain may be extensive without changing access to main routes, hubs or covered terrain. ≠ SMALL HUB Few kilometres, a major change in possibilities A bridge, pass or crossroads can redirect movement and supply across a much wider area. Schematic comparison. Strategic value derives not only from area, but from a place’s function within networks of movement, observation and supply. 07 The same situation at three scales Imagine the same sector on three different maps. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext On a strategic map there are several hundred kilometres of front. The village from the opening is invisible. The entire sector has one colour, and a shift of several kilometres appears as a slight movement of the line. The map answers the question: where are the principal areas of advantage, and what is the overall direction of change? On a operational map cities, rivers, main roads, railways and terrain obstacles appear. The same shift may now reveal that one side has reached a road hub or cut a direct route. This map answers the question: what does the change mean for movement, supply and the spatial system as a whole? On a local map the line expands into a belt. Individual houses, the forest edge, a ridge, culvert, farm track and field of observation become visible. We discover that the main road is not fully passable even though the village has an unambiguous colour on the strategic map. This map answers the question: how is this particular space actually being used? None of these maps need be a correction of the one before it. Each abstracts differently. Error begins only when we digitally zoom into the strategic map and infer the situation at an individual house from its coloured pixels. Enlarging an image does not add resolution to the underlying data. Modern geospatial products therefore work with layers, metadata, sources, accuracy, currency and intended use. A US Army publication on geospatial intelligence notes that products may range from a simple map to a multilayered output tailored to a specific requirement; it also stresses database updates, data provenance and the suitability of resolution for the intended purpose. [4] VISUALISATION 04 · THREE SCALES The same space, three different questions The closer we look, the less the front resembles a line—and the more it resembles a web of relationships. The same military situation at strategic, operational and local scale The first panel shows a simple boundary between two colours. In the second, routes and towns appear. In the third, the boundary becomes a broad contested zone around a village, forest and road. STRATEGIC 1 : 3 000 000 Question: Where is the advantage, and what is the direction of change? OPERATIONAL 1 : 250 000 Question: How does the change affect routes and hubs? LOCAL 1 : 20 000 Question: How can this particular space be used? Zooming in on a map is not the same as obtaining more detailed data. Each scale requires its own selection of features, its own degree of generalisation and its own definition of a useful answer. 08 A map always arrives from the past Every conflict map contains at least two times. The first is the time of the situation it is trying to capture. The second is the time of publication. Between them lie collection, transmission, sorting, verification, comparison and editorial judgement. A fast map may be more current but more vulnerable to false reports. A cautious map may be more accurate but depict a situation that has already changed. Speed, detail and confidence cannot all be maximised at once. Every mapmaker chooses a compromise among them. Sources do not observe the same thing, either. A satellite image captures visible objects at a particular moment. A geolocated recording may confirm presence at one location, not enduring control of the surroundings. An official report has institutional access, but also its own vocabulary and interests. A witness on the ground may be immediate, yet limited by line of sight and conditions. Multiple sources reduce some forms of uncertainty; they do not eliminate them all. That is why a timestamp matters as much as a legend. “Updated today” is not enough if we do not know whether the data describe this morning, last night or the most recent confirmed state from several days ago. A map without time presents itself as the present when it is really a version of the past. Uncertainty should not be attached to an entire map in a single blanket sentence. Different sectors may rest on evidence of different quality. One area may be confirmed by several independent sources, another estimated from indirect signals, and a third left unchanged simply because no new information arrived. The same colour saturation can therefore conceal very different levels of confidence. Reader’s guide A map is a version, not a verdict Serious reading begins with the question: To what time, scale, definition of control and level of confidence does this drawing refer? 09 What a map can do—and what it can never tell us It would be easy to arrive at the striking line that maps lie. But that would be as imprecise as the worst maps the statement is meant to criticise. Maps are indispensable. They reveal spatial relationships that would remain invisible across thousands of reports. They show how routes connect, distances, obstacles, concentrations of events and change over time. Without simplification, we would not understand a conflict better. We would not understand it at all. A good map can reasonably answer questions such as: Under the stated methodology, where does one side exercise predominant control? Where has the situation changed since the previous version? Which areas are contested? How do changes relate to rivers, towns, roads and terrain? What degree of confidence is declared, and how old is the underlying evidence? From a single map, however, we usually cannot tell who is inside a particular house at this moment. We cannot know whether a road is safe for a civilian. We cannot read the morale of units, the quality of command, supplies, local willingness to cooperate or the price paid to take a position. Nor can we infer the legitimacy of political claims, legal responsibility, the causes of the conflict or the lived experience of people beneath the coloured area. Still less does a larger coloured area automatically mean that victory is approaching. A territorial map is only one model of war. Another might track logistics, personnel, industrial capacity, airspace, information networks, political cohesion or time. Each would draw a different geometry of power. Before accepting a clean map as clean reality, then, it is worth asking a few simple questions: How does the author define control? By presence, administration, movement or sustainable possession? To what time do the data actually belong? Not merely when the graphic was published. What do the arrows and shades mean? Observation, estimate, intent or change between versions? What are the scale and resolution of the underlying data? What has been merged, displaced or omitted? How is uncertainty represented? Is there a contested category, interval or confidence information? What exactly do the percentages measure? Area, districts, population or a window selected by the author? Which strategically important points disappear inside the aggregate area figure? These questions do not diminish the map. They restore its proper function. The map ceases to be an image meant to replace reality and becomes a tool for asking a more precise next question. 10 A straight line above an uneven reality Return to the village from the opening: the small unit at its edge, the drone above the road, the artillery range, the forest that cannot be crossed safely, and the people whose lives beneath one colour are far more complicated. The cartographer must ultimately put this place on the map. A single pixel cannot contain every hour, every capability, every source or every doubt. A scale, time, category and confidence threshold must be chosen. A legible answer has to be made from a complicated space. That is not a failure of the map. That is its job. Failure begins on our side, when we forget that a colour is a classification, an arrow a claim, a percentage has a denominator and a line has a thickness that the graphic often conceals. When we begin to mistake the model for the territory itself. A line on a map is not the front. It is our best provisional answer to the question of where, within a complicated reality, the boundary of control currently lies. And the cleaner we draw that line, the easier it becomes to forget how untidy the reality beneath it is. Editorial transparency AI was used as a tool for research synthesis, language processing and the creation of original SVG diagrams. The article deliberately makes no claims about any current front line. All specific scholarly and historical support can be traced to the sources listed; final editorial responsibility for publication rests with the publisher.

items.title: A company computer is not a private vault. Nor is an internal directive permission to read love letters.
items.subtitle: An employer may reasonably check whether company equipment is being misused for private purposes. Reading the content of mail and covert surveillance are an exception bound to a serious reason, information and proportionality — not an automatic right because the computer belongs to the firm.

7. Announced monitoring is not a hidden camera
8. Consent in an employment contract is not free consent
9. Bărbulescu is not a ban on a company IT audit. It is six criteria
What needs to be tested
10. López Ribalda did not legalise changing rooms
11. Hardware can be the employer’s. Personal data in a log are subject to the GDPR
12. The Supreme Administrative Court bore three days after a leak. It would not bear a blanket reading for certainty
13. A camera in an office with a kitchenette is not a camera at a checkout
14. A ceiling of a fine is not an average of imposed fines
15. A result may serve only the purpose of the check
16. A checklist before an interference will say more than the sentence it is our computer
Three tests of the depth of an interference
Before introducing monitoring
How to test whether a milder means suffices
17. The hidden cost is privacy that a directive only enumerated
Related texts in this series

items.body: Section: Justice & law | Technology & AI Author: V Reading Length: ~27 min Sources and further reading: 22 items Topics: employer, e-mail, monitoring, § 316, GDPR, Bărbulescu, metadata, privacy SEO / Working Title: May an employer read your e-mails and monitor a computer? May an employer read your e-mails and monitor a computer? The question sounds simple until we notice that we are not comparing one thing. A check of time on the web can be reasonable and the reading of the body of a message still an excess. A directive can exist and the scope can still be missing. A hidden camera at a checkout can stand in one judgment and in a changing room it must not stand. Consent in an employment contract can be signed without being free consent under the GDPR. [9] The following text therefore does not ask to whom the computer belongs. It asks how deep the interference reaches — and whether it can bear a reason, information and a milder path. 1. One hundred and two hours on the web in one September is not an opened body of work mail in January Picture a meeting after an incident. The employer says: the laptop and the mailbox jmeno@firma.cz are ours. The employee answers with Article 13 of the Charter and the secrecy of messages. [3] IT shows a listing of visited pages and of time. HR prepares a disciplinary proceeding. The labour inspectorate reads Section 316 of the Labour Code. ÚOOÚ asks about the controller of personal data and the legal title. Everyone speaks of a check. Everyone, however, means a different depth of interference. The Supreme Court in the matter 21 Cdo 1771/2011 dealt with a listing of internet activities of one employee for the period 1.–30. 9. 2009. In the facts there appeared 102.97 hours of surfing unrelated to work. The court stressed that it was not a reading of the content of e-mails, SMS or MMS, but a check of the use of work resources. [6] An expert analysis of the same decision on epravo.cz works with the same cut: for the assessment of private use of the internet the record of activity was decisive, not the opening of private communication. [17] That matters, because the dispute is often told as a general permission for monitoring. A more precise reading says something narrower. The Supreme Administrative Court in judgment 6 Ads 21/2026-27 of 18. 3. 2026 dealt with a different situation. After a particular leak of personal data at ČÚZK the content of the work mail of one civil servant was checked in a narrow window 2.–4. 1. 2024. The disciplinary measure was 15% of salary for 3 months; it is a sanction in one service matter, not a tariff for reading mails. [7] At first glance this is a dispute “may or may not read e-mails”. In fact we are comparing a listing of activities with the opening of the content of mail. That is why they can all be partly right and the shared sentence still wrong. Company equipment is not a private vault. Nor does ownership of a computer give a free right to read every message. A company computer is not a private vault. Nor is a directive permission to read love letters. — Jiný Kontext 2. A check at the workplace has at least six layers The first layer is ownership of the resource. A laptop, a telephone, a work e-mail and a company network can belong to the employer. Section 316(1) of the Labour Code forbids an employee, without consent, from using the employer’s production and work resources including computing technology and telecommunications equipment for personal need; the employer may check compliance with this prohibition in a reasonable manner. [1] The second layer is an expectation of privacy at the workplace. In the decisions Halford, Copland and Bărbulescu the ECtHR works with the fact that even communication from a work environment can fall under private life and correspondence. [16] [12] [4] The Supreme Administrative Court 2026 cites this line beside Article 13 of the Charter. [7] [3] The third layer is the depth of the interference. A block of websites is not the same as a log of time and URL. A log of time and URL is not the same as an e-mail header. A header is not the body of a message. The body of a message is not the tapping of a call. A camera at a publicly accessible checkout is not a camera in employees’ back rooms. The fourth layer is legal regimes side by side. The Labour Code deals with the labour-law boundary. The Charter protects privacy and messages. The GDPR deals with personal data, purpose, minimisation, information and legal title. The Labour Inspection Act sets administrative offences. With cameras the methodology of ÚOOÚ enters as a guide. [1] [8] [13] [14] The fifth layer is transparency and the exception. The general rule is to inform in advance of the scope and manner of the check if the employer introduces an interference under Section 316(2). [1] The exception for a covert interference is, in European case-law, bound to a strong and concrete reason, not to the convenience of surveillance. [5] The sixth layer is the use of the result. A log or an e-mail that was obtained for the protection of property or data must not end as entertainment in a collective. The Supreme Administrative Court in 2026 expressly assessed that the results of the check were not used for another purpose. [7] 3. The best check is the one whose interference you can bear to explain Technology can log many things. That is not an answer. The right question is which interference can be explained to an employee, a court, a labour inspectorate and ÚOOÚ. If the explanation stands only on the sentence “it is our computer”, it is weak even before the first log. Type of failure What it looks like How to test What will limit the damage A swap of paragraph 1 and paragraph 2 A listing of URLs is taken as permission to read the body of a mail Compare NS 21 Cdo 1771/2011 with the wording of Section 316(2) Metadata earlier than content, and a narrow reason A directive without a scope The sentence “we may monitor” does not say how Use the Bărbulescu criteria and Section 316(3) Direct information about scope and manner Blanket coverage for certainty A reading of all mailboxes without a particular incident Compare NSS: one employee, 2.–4. 1. 2024, a leak of data A time window, a subject and subsidiarity A hidden camera outside an extreme A hidden recording in back rooms, a changing room or a kitchenette Compare López Ribalda and the Regional Court in Ostrava Visibility, a public space and a serious reason Consent as a stamp Consent in a contract is to replace a GDPR title Read WP29 2/2017 on the inequality of the parties A legitimate interest or a duty plus information A foreign purpose of the result A log from a check is used for slander or other pressure Check purpose, access and the period of retention Access rights and an audit Interpretive scheme: The table does not say that every check is forbidden. It shows the places where a reasonable check becomes a deeper interference without support. A good process therefore does not begin with what IT can switch on. It begins with which harm the check is to avert. Otherwise the tool begins to expand according to convenience, not according to a reason. First more websites are logged, then more headers, then several messages are opened and finally no one knows exactly when a check of a work resource became surveillance of privacy. Precisely this transition must be visible before a dispute arrives. 4. A check of the use of resources is not a check of the content of mail Section 316 of the Labour Code is short, but it matters precisely by the distinction of layers. Paragraph 1 aims at the use of the employer’s resources. An employee must not, without consent, use work resources for personal need and the employer may reasonably check this rule. [1] That is the basis for a check of whether company equipment is being misused. Paragraph 2 is another level. It forbids the employer, without a serious reason consisting in the special nature of his activity, from interfering with an employee’s privacy at the workplace and in common spaces by open or covert surveillance, by tapping of calls, by a check of electronic mail or of letter consignments. [1] Paragraph 3 then says that if a serious reason under paragraph 2 is given at the employer, the employee must be directly informed of the scope of the check and the manners of its carrying out. [1] A directive is therefore not a magic word. It must say what is checked, how and why. It does not follow that an employer may never check an electronic trail. It follows that a reasonable check of the use of resources and a check of the content of messages are not the same interference. The first asks whether and for how long. The second asks what exactly was written. 5. Metadata are not content Metadata are not insignificant. They show who communicated, when, through which service, with what length or volume. With the web they can show a visited domain and a time. With e-mail they can show a sender, an addressee, a subject, a time or a size. All of that can be sensitive. Content is something else. The body of an e-mail, an attachment, the text of a private message or a recording of a call interfere more deeply. The Supreme Court in judgment 21 Cdo 1771/2011 built precisely on the fact that the employer did not check the content of e-mails, SMS or MMS, but a listing of activities on the internet and time spent outside a work purpose. [6] That is the practical strength of the word metadata. It does not excuse blanket surveillance. It helps to find a milder means. If an employer is dealing with whether an employee spends working time outside work, a listing of time and of categories can be less invasive than the opening of personal communication. If the employer is dealing with a leak of particular data, the question can move to content. But precisely then the demand for a reason, a scope and safeguards grows. Metadata also show better when it is necessary to stop. If a listing is enough to confirm a breach of a rule, there is no reason to open the body of a message out of curiosity. If a listing is not enough, the next step must receive its own reasoning. This sequence is not a bureaucratic ornament. It is a way not to turn every problem into the deepest possible interference. The example is plain. If the suspicion is of excessive private surfing, the body of an e-mail will usually not answer better than a work listing of web activity. If the suspicion is that a particular file has left an office or a firm, the mere number of visited pages may not suffice. The precision of the means should follow the precision of the reason. Not the other way around. Metadata are not content. A listing of pages is not an opened mailbox. — Jiný Kontext 6. A company address with a name is not a free vault. A private account is another thing E-mail is not one type of space. A private Gmail or Seznam opened on a company computer is a different case from a work address jmeno@firma.cz . A functional address of the type info@firma.cz is still another. The expectation of privacy differs according to the purpose of the account, the designation, internal rules and information. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext Expert literature citing the historical opinion of ÚOOÚ 2/2009 describes the difference between a private free-mail, a work address with a name and a functional mailbox. A private account has the strongest expectation of privacy. With a work address with a name a check of headers rather than of content is typically admitted. A functional address has a lower personal element. [10] [11] A reservation is needed here. The opinion of ÚOOÚ 2/2009 was not, as of September 2026, found on the website of ÚOOÚ as a current document in the dossier. It therefore cannot be treated as a binding living rule. It is a historical interpretation cited by literature. The valid framework needs to be built mainly on Section 316, the Charter, the GDPR, the ECtHR and Czech case-law. [1] [3] [8] [4] [7] It is therefore not a free vault. Nor is it a company notice-board without privacy. It is a work tool in which a personal trail can lie. And the depth of the interference must match the reason. 7. Announced monitoring is not a hidden camera Visible monitoring with a clear announcement and a hidden recording are not two versions of the same thing. They differ in the interference with an expectation of privacy. An employee who knows what is measured, when and why can adapt their behaviour and can defend themselves. A covert interference takes this possibility away. The ECtHR in the matter López Ribalda and Others v. Spain assessed hidden cameras at supermarket checkouts. The Grand Chamber on 17. 10. 2019 by a ratio of 14 : 3 found no violation of Article 8 of the Convention. What mattered, however, was that it was a space open to the public, a reasoned suspicion of thefts, losses and a recording limited to 10 days in 2009. [5] It does not follow that a hidden camera is generally in order at work. It follows that an extreme and narrow set of facts can stand before the ECtHR. Czech Section 316(2) expressly ranks covert surveillance among interferences that must not occur without a serious reason consisting in the special nature of the activity, and paragraph 3 requires information about the scope and manner of the check. [1] The practical distinction is simple. A checkout open to the public is not a changing room. A visible camera with a pictogram is not a hidden camera. A short check after losses is not blanket surveillance for certainty. 8. Consent in an employment contract is not free consent In labour law consent easily changes into a stamp. An employee signs a contract, an annex or a directive because they want work or want to keep it. That is precisely why WP29 in opinion 2/2017 on the processing of data at the workplace stresses the inequality of the parties and caution in using consent as a legal title. [9] The GDPR requires for the processing of personal data a legal title, a purpose, transparency and minimisation. [8] With an employer it is usually more appropriate to think of a legal duty or a legitimate interest, if the conditions are met. A mere “I agree to all monitoring” is weak, because the employee may not have a real choice. That does not mean that an employee should not receive information. On the contrary. Information is distinct from consent. The employer should describe what is processed, why, for how long, who has access to it and how the employee can defend themselves. With interferences under Section 316(2) the Labour Code moreover works with direct information about the scope and manner of the check. [1] The short sentence is therefore: consent is not a covering sheet. If a check would not stand without consent, an employee’s signature will usually not save it. 9. Bărbulescu is not a ban on a company IT audit. It is six criteria Bărbulescu v. Romania is often used as a hammer. One side says: the ECtHR forbade employers to read messages. The other says: the employee used a company account, so they lost. Neither shortcut matches the judgment of the Grand Chamber of 5. 9. 2017, which by a ratio of 11 : 6 found a violation of Article 8 of the Convention because the domestic courts did not sufficiently verify the protection of the employee against arbitrariness. [4] What matters is the test. The ECtHR formulated questions around prior information, the scope of monitoring, a legitimate reason, the possibility of using less invasive means, the consequences for the employee and safeguards against abuse. The Supreme Administrative Court in 2026 summarised this test in point [27] and applied it to the Czech facts. [7] What needs to be tested The test is not done over a sentence in a directive. It is done over a particular interference. Was the employee informed in advance of the nature and scope of the monitoring? Was the interference limited in subject and time? Was there a legitimate reason? Would a milder means have sufficed? To what was the result used? Were there safeguards against arbitrariness? It does not follow that an IT audit is forbidden. It follows that its depth must be borne. An audit of accesses after a leak of data is different from a blanket reading of the mailboxes of all employees. A listing of metadata is different from the opening of the body of a message. 10. López Ribalda did not legalise changing rooms The judgment López Ribalda is well cited badly. Yes, the ECtHR in it admitted a hidden camera recording without prior information. But it was supermarket checkouts, a suspicion of thefts, losses, a space open to the public and a recording lasting 10 days in 2009. [5] Precisely the details hold the result together. If we remove them, there remains no rule “hidden cameras are permitted”. There remains only a convenient phrase. A changing room, a toilet, a rest room or an office kitchenette have a different intensity of privacy than a checkout where an employee works in front of customers. The Czech regime is moreover not only a copy of Article 8 of the Convention. The Labour Code in Section 316(2) expressly speaks of open and covert surveillance and binds them to a serious reason in the special nature of the employer’s activity. [1] Labour inspection can assess a work regime even when someone argues with a European judgment. It is not a ban on cameras. It is a demand for place, purpose, visibility, scope, information and a period of retention. 11. Hardware can be the employer’s. Personal data in a log are subject to the GDPR Ownership of a computer deals with property. The GDPR deals with personal data. These regimes meet, but they do not merge. An employer can own a laptop and at the same time be the controller of data in a log, an e-mail header, a camera recording or an export from a security tool. [8] A controller under the GDPR determines the purposes and means of processing. They must have a legal title under Article 6, observe the principles under Article 5 and inform under Article 13. [8] Act No. 110/2019 Sb. supplements the Czech framework of the processing of personal data. [15] With deeper or systematic interferences an impact assessment can also come into consideration if the conditions of Article 35 GDPR are met. [8] The practical error is the sentence: “It is our computer, so we can do as we like with the data.” No. It is our computer, so we can protect property and organise work. If personal data about an employee arise in that, purpose, minimisation, transparency and access rights enter the game. The Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU protects private and family life and the protection of personal data in Articles 7 and 8. [21] The Czech Charter in Article 13 protects the secrecy of messages submitted by telephone, telegraph or another similar device. [3] Company ownership does not switch these layers off. The GDPR at the same time forces an employer to describe even apparently technical details in human language. A log is not only a line in a system. It is a datum about a particular person, their working day, sometimes about their contacts and habits. A camera recording is not only a security image. It is a record of movement and behaviour. An e-mail header is not only an operational mark. It can show a relation, a time and a direction of communication. That is why it is not enough for the IT department to know the rule. It must be intelligible also to the person whom it concerns. That has an operational consequence. An employer should be able to show which data are collected automatically, which only upon an incident and which must not be opened without a special approval. Otherwise the access of a controller becomes the informal power of an administrator. The law does not assess only a technical possibility, but also a purpose and the safeguards that have been set. 12. The Supreme Administrative Court bore three days after a leak. It would not bear a blanket reading for certainty The judgment of the Supreme Administrative Court 6 Ads 21/2026-27 matters precisely because it admitted a check of the content of work mail within particular limits. It was a service relationship, a particular leak of personal data, one civil servant of ČÚZK, a time window 2.–4. 1. 2024 and information by an internal regulation and by a message at login. [7] Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext Commentaries on the judgment stress that the Supreme Administrative Court assessed a narrow interference after an incident and that employers should not infer from it a free licence for a preventive reading of mail. [19] [22] That is the right reading. The judgment is more a map of conditions than a permit. The Supreme Administrative Court applied the Bărbulescu test and assessed among other things the reason, the scope, the information and the use of the results. [7] If an employer read all mailboxes every month for certainty, precisely what the judgment holds would be missing: a particular incident, a limited time, a limited circle of persons and a connection with the protection of data. It does not follow that the content of mail is always inviolable. It follows that the opening of content is a late and narrow tool. First come prevention, permissions, training, a technical restriction, headers, an audit of accesses and other milder paths. The judgment is useful for an employee as well. It does not tell them that a work mailbox is a private diary. It tells them that even a service mailbox is not a space without rules. If an employee is informed in advance, works in a service account and a particular suspicion of a leak of data arises, their expectation of privacy can be narrower. If, however, an employer lets blanket surveillance run without a clear reason, without a scope and without a check of use, the resemblance to the Supreme Administrative Court disappears. 13. A camera in an office with a kitchenette is not a camera at a checkout The Regional Court in Ostrava in judgment 22 Ad 11/2023-29 dealt with a fine of CZK 28,000 for cameras in an office with a kitchenette without a serious reason. [18] The figure is a fine in one court matter, not an average price for a badly set camera system. More important than the amount is the distinction of space. A supermarket checkout is a place where an employee works in front of a customer and where property losses are dealt with. An office kitchenette is a back room. A changing room and a toilet are still more sensitive. To transfer a conclusion from one space into another without this layer is a methodological error. The ÚOOÚ methodology on camera systems works with information and the requirements of the GDPR as a guide for a controller. [14] It is not a substitute for the Labour Code. It does, however, help to put practical questions: why a camera exists, what it covers, how long a recording is kept, who can see it, whether there is a pictogram and where an employee finds a second level of information. A camera is therefore always also a spatial question. The same device can have a different legal meaning according to where it points. 14. A ceiling of a fine is not an average of imposed fines The law works with ceilings. The media often make from them an expected fine. That is an error. The Labour Inspection Act in Section 24a sets for an interference with an employee’s privacy under defined facts an upper rate of up to CZK 1,000,000 and for a failure to inform about a check under Section 316(3) an upper rate of up to CZK 100,000. [13] The GDPR has its own sanction regime. For selected breaches under Article 83(5) the upper limit can be up to EUR 20,000,000 or 4% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever value is higher. [8] That is a ceiling of an administrative fine in the European regime, not an automatic fine for one work e-mail. These figures need to be read with a unit, a period and a regime. They are upper rates in legal provisions valid according to the dossier as of 2026. They do not measure an average of imposed sanctions. They do not measure the probability of a check. They do not measure reputational harm or the costs of a dispute. The sense of the ceilings is different. They show that monitoring is not only an internal IT setting. It can change into a labour-law and data matter with responsibility before two types of authority: labour inspection and ÚOOÚ. 15. A result may serve only the purpose of the check The lawfulness of obtaining is one question. The use of the result is a second. An employer can have a reason to check access to data after an incident. That does not yet mean that the content of communication may circulate in the firm, end in an unlimited folder or be used for a purpose that is not connected with the original reason. The GDPR stands on the principle of purpose limitation and of minimisation. [8] If a log is collected for a security incident, it should be used to resolve the incident. If a camera protects property, it should not become a tool of permanent evaluation of every movement, unless there is a separate reason and information for that. The Supreme Administrative Court in judgment 6 Ads 21/2026-27 also assessed that the results of the check were not used for another purpose. [7] That is not a formality. Precisely the purpose holds the interference within limits. Once the result is used outside the original frame, the assessment of proportionality changes as well. The practical rule is: before collection it must be clear where the result will go. Who will see it, how long it will be retained, whether it will end in a disciplinary file, whether it will be handed to a lawyer and when it will be deleted. Without that a check is only an open drawer. 16. A checklist before an interference will say more than the sentence it is our computer A good check does not begin with the installation of a tool. It begins with a description of the interference. What exactly do we want to find out? Which incident or risk are we dealing with? Which data suffice for that? Which legal regime switches on? Who will read the result? Three tests of the depth of an interference The first test is the object. Is company hardware being checked, a company account, a private account opened on a company computer, or a private telephone? Each object carries a different expectation of privacy. The second test is content. Are time and URL being captured, a mail header, the body of an e-mail, an image, sound or a GPS location? If it is the content of a message, tapping or covert surveillance, we enter the stricter regime of Section 316(2). [1] The third test is the reason. Is it a particular leak, a property loss or a security incident, or only prevention without a boundary? Bărbulescu and the Supreme Administrative Court require more than a general possibility that something might happen. [4] [7] Before introducing monitoring An employer should have a written and intelligible notice of the scope and manner of the check if they introduce a check under Section 316(2). [1] Beside that they must, under the GDPR, inform about the processing of personal data, the purpose, the legal title, the recipients and the rights of the data subject. [8] How to test whether a milder means suffices First there offer themselves a block of categories of websites, a restriction of permissions, a log of headers, training, two-person approval, an audit of accesses or a check of only a few days. Only when a milder path does not suffice for the protection of a particular interest does it make sense to think of content. And even then only in a narrow window. Whoever has a doubt deals with two addresses. A regional labour inspectorate assesses the labour-law side. ÚOOÚ assesses personal data. Fulfilment of one layer does not automatically excuse a breach of the other. [2] [8] A checklist has one more advantage. It forces the end of the interference to be written. When will the monitoring end? When will the recording be deleted? Who will confirm that the purpose has been fulfilled or has fallen away? Without an end even a reasonable check easily changes into a permanent infrastructure. And a permanent infrastructure then looks for new reasons for itself. The practice of ÚOOÚ shows that these questions are not only training for lawyers. The authority’s inspection materials work with attendance, GPS, cameras and Section 316(2) as with an ordinary boundary between the management of work and an interference with privacy. [20] The earlier a firm draws this boundary, the less it later has to explain why it crossed it. 17. The hidden cost is privacy that a directive only enumerated An internal directive often creates a feeling of a finished thing. The employee has confirmed that they can be monitored. The IT tool is running. HR knows where to find a listing. A lawyer has a paragraph on the protection of property. But the real interference does not take place in the sentence of the directive. It takes place in what is collected, for how long, with whom, in which space, after which reason and who reads it. A directive should therefore be more a map than a shield. It should tell an employee what they can expect, and set brakes for the employer. If it only enumerates all possible interferences, but does not separate an ordinary operational log from the opening of content, it helps neither side. The employee does not know what privacy really remains. The employer does not know when they are crossing their own rule. The hidden cost is therefore not only a loss of trust. It is also imprecision. A firm that does not distinguish metadata from content will use too strong a tool on a weak problem. A firm that swaps a checkout for a kitchenette will transfer a foreign judgment into another space. A firm that builds on consent in a contract will overlook the inequality of the parties. A firm that makes from NSS 2026 a blanket rule will overlook three days, one employee and a particular leak. It does not follow that an employer is defenceless. It follows that the protection of work, property and data needs a precise depth. Sometimes a ban on private use and a reasonable listing suffice. Sometimes an audit is necessary. Sometimes in a narrow matter even the content of work mail can come. But every time we ask whether the interference can bear a reason, information, proportionality and a milder path. At the moment when an employer buys a laptop, they buy a work resource. At the moment when they watch what a person does on it, they enter privacy and personal data. And then the question is no longer: “Is it our computer?” It is: how deep does the interference reach — and why precisely so deep? Related texts in this series May the police search your mobile phone? — another title, another filter. A company IT audit is not a criminal inspection. What does your mobile phone know about you? — layers of a device versus a work account.

items.title: Crime and Fear Do Not Have to Move Together
items.subtitle: Police statistics, hidden crime, victimisation surveys and the sense of safety measure different layers of reality. Apparently opposing statements can therefore be true at the same time.
