items.body: Article contents People or numbers? · The path into the statistics · Czech data · The country versus the street · What fear measures · Media availability · The limits of statistics · Fear as a signal · Conclusion At a press conference, a downward-sloping line appears on the screen. The police announce that they recorded fewer offences nationwide than the year before. A few hours later, at a district council meeting, a woman says she no longer uses the underpass by the station after dark. A convenience-store owner describes aggressive customers, parents circulate footage of a fight in a local group, and someone comments beneath the post: “And then they’ll tell us it’s safe.” At first glance, there seem to be only two possibilities. Either people are exaggerating because the media and social networks have frightened them, or institutions are hiding reality behind tables. One side must be naïve and the other dishonest. Yet the police chart, the woman’s experience in the underpass and the parents’ anxiety can all be true at the same time. They are not three answers to the same question. The first describes the number of recorded offences across a large territory. The second describes how a particular person makes decisions in a particular place and time. The third captures how information about danger spreads through a community. The dispute arises only when we call all these phenomena by a single word: crime. Crime statistics are a map of what has passed through an institution. A sense of safety is a map of how people move through the world. Both maps can be accurate—and still use different legends. 1. The False Referendum: People or Numbers? The question “Is crime rising?” sounds as though it calls for a single figure. In reality, it contains at least five further questions. Has conduct meeting the legal definition of an offence become more common? Are there more victims? More reports? More police records? Or has people’s sense that they can use a street, park or public transport without disproportionate fear changed? These variables are related, but they are not interchangeable. The true incidence of crime cannot be observed directly. Some incidents are never recognised as crimes, some are not reported by victims, some reach the police by other routes, and some reported events do not appear in the final statistics in the same form in which the reporter described them. At the other end lies the sense of safety: it may respond not only to the probability of an attack, but also to the severity of the possible consequences, personal vulnerability, control over the situation, the condition of the environment and confidence that someone will intervene in an emergency. Six Different Meanings of the Word “Crime” The infographic distinguishes actual incidence, experienced victimisation, reported incidents, police-recorded offences, convicted crime and the sense of safety. When two people say “crime”, they may not be talking about the same thing Each measure is legitimate. The error begins when we switch from one to another without saying so. 01 Actual incidence Measures All acts that meet the chosen definition. Does not itself measure It cannot be observed directly; it is the target variable, burdened by hidden crime. 02 Experienced victimisation Measures What people or households report in a survey. Does not itself measure It misses victimless offences, businesses, deceased victims, and anything respondents do not remember or disclose. 03 Reported incidents Measures What reaches the police or another institution. Does not itself measure Depends on trust, effort, loss, insurance, shame and fear. 04 Recorded offences Measures What the police enter under the rules and classifications in force. Does not itself measure It is neither a list of every event nor of every final conviction. 05 Convicted crime Measures Offences confirmed at the end of the criminal process. Does not itself measure An even narrower slice, shaped by evidence, legal classification and the court’s decision. 06 Sense of safety Measures How people assess risk, vulnerability, control and their environment. Does not itself measure It is not a count of offences; it captures a different social cost. Infographic 1: Six legitimate meanings of “crime”. The contradiction often lies not in the data, but in an unannounced shift from one measure to another. Police-recorded crime is therefore not a false version of “real crime”. It is a distinct and important administrative indicator: it tells us which offences came to the police’s attention and which they recorded under the applicable rules. Nor is a victimisation survey simply a better police statistic. By asking a representative sample about their experiences, it can illuminate part of the dark figure; at the same time, it is affected by memory errors, reluctance to disclose sensitive events, differing interpretations of questions and the fact that some offences have no living individual victim who can be asked. 2. How an Event Becomes a Row in a Table Between an offence and the annual total there is no single neutral sensor. There is a chain of human and institutional decisions. Someone must notice the event, judge it serious enough, decide to report it, describe it, substantiate it and classify it. The Police of the Czech Republic state that their statistics use recorded offences under tactical-statistical classifications for which criminal proceedings were initiated. The figures are therefore neither a list of final convictions nor a mechanical transcript of every call to emergency number 158. [1] The size of the “loss” between experience and reporting varies dramatically by offence. A Czech victimisation study by the Institute of Criminology and Social Prevention, published in 2019, found that among the most recent incidents examined, 92 per cent of car thefts were reported to the police, compared with only 31 per cent of physical assaults, 21 per cent of sexual assaults, 17 per cent of domestic violence and 12 per cent of stalking. For online-shopping fraud involving financial loss, the figure was eight per cent. [5] These figures are not a current estimate of today’s prevalence and cannot simply be transferred to every case. Their value lies elsewhere: they show that there is no single universal “under-reporting rate”. Car theft is often tied to insurance and an unmistakable loss. When violence occurs between people who are close, fear of the perpetrator, shame, financial dependence and doubt that institutions will help may all shape the decision. Two categories with the same actual incidence can therefore generate entirely different numbers of records. The Path from an Actual Incident to Police Statistics Five stages show that an event must occur, be recognised, reported or otherwise discovered, recorded and only then aggregated. Below the chart are examples of differing reporting rates for various offences from a Czech victimisation study published in 2019. The number emerges only at the end of the process Every gap changes what reaches the table. Not all gaps are the same size for every offence. 1 Event in the real world Conduct that may meet the definition of a criminal offence 2 Recognition The victim or witness understands it as harm and a possible offence 3 Report / detection The police learn of it from a person or through their own activity 4 Recording The act is classified and enters the police system 5 Statistics The record is aggregated by time, place and classification Invisible harm victimless offence, unrecognised assault, normalised behaviour Non-reporting shame, fear, low loss, distrust, relationship to the perpetrator Procedural filter legal threshold, available information, counting and classification rules Aggregation changes in recording, temporal assignment, merged categories Share of victims who reported the incident to the police IKSP, study published in 2019 · most recent incident in the period examined Car theft 92 % Robbery 54 % Physical assault 31 % Sexual assault 21 % Domestic violence 17 % Stalking 12 % Online-shopping fraud 8 % What follows from this? A fall in the police figure may mean fewer offences, but it may also mean fewer reports. A rise may mean more offences, but also greater trust, better detection or a change in recording. Diagram 2: “Actual offence → report → recording → statistics”. The lower section uses selected reporting rates from the Czech victimisation study; it illustrates differing dark figures, not a current time series. This is where the first paradox arises. If victims begin to trust an institution more, the police improve the intake of reports, or a specialised unit actively uncovers more cases, recorded crime can rise without the actual incidence rising at the same pace. Conversely, declining trust, victims’ resignation or a shift into less visible settings can push the statistics down even though people’s everyday experience has not improved. 3. What the Czech Data Actually Say In 2025, police in the Czech Republic recorded 170,051 offences, 1.9 per cent fewer than the year before. That statement is true. It is equally true that violent crime rose slightly to 13,752 offences and sexual and morality offences rose by 8.8 per cent to 3,695. The fall in the total was driven by other parts of the sum. [1] [2] Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext The total number of offences is not an index of social harm either. One record of a less serious property offence and one record of a violent offence each count as one unit in the total, even though their impact on the victim and on public space may be incomparable. A declining total can therefore contain growth in a category to which people are more sensitive. Yet growth in a category does not automatically mean an equal rise in real-world conduct: for example, police linked part of the increase in recorded child pornography in 2025 to a greater volume of intelligence from international databases and targeted operations. The capacity to see the phenomenon had changed as well. [1] The long Czech time series provides an even more important correction. Between 2002 and 2023, the number of recorded offences fell from roughly 372,000 to 181,000—about half. Over comparable CVVM surveys, the share of people who felt safe in the Czech Republic rose at the same time from 45 to 82 per cent. [2] [3] The Czech data therefore do not support the cheap thesis that the public simply succumbs to ever-greater fear regardless of reality. Even this long series is not laboratory-clean. The police note that raising the loss threshold in October 2020 reduced the number of recorded offences, especially in property and economic crime, and that the structure of tactical-statistical classifications underwent extensive revision from 2021. Part of the break therefore describes a change in reality and part a change in the measuring instrument; the share of each cannot be separated from a single total. [1] The two curves do not move as mechanical mirror images. Between 2019 and 2021, recorded offences fell by more than 23 per cent, while the share of people who felt safe nationwide fell by two percentage points. Pandemic restrictions reduced opportunities for some offences and changed the number of recorded events, but they certainly did not create a general sense of calm and predictability. From 2021 to 2022, recorded crime then rose by almost 19 per cent and the sense of safety fell by five points. In the following year, the offence count barely changed while the sense of safety rose slightly again. Recorded Crime and the Sense of Safety in the Czech Republic, 2002–2023 Two aligned charts show the long-term decline in police-recorded offences and the rise in the share of people who feel safe in the Czech Republic. Over shorter periods, however, the curves do not always move in opposite directions. 2002 2006 2010 2014 2018 2021 2023 150k 200k 250k 300k 350k 400k 40 % 50 % 60 % 70 % 80 % 90 % A · Police-recorded offences Absolute annual count · Czech Statistical Office / Police Presidium 2002: 372,341 recorded offences 2004: 351,629 recorded offences 2006: 336,446 recorded offences 2008: 343,799 recorded offences 2010: 313,387 recorded offences 2012: 304,528 recorded offences 2013: 325,366 recorded offences 2014: 288,660 recorded offences 2015: 247,628 recorded offences 2017: 203,303 recorded offences 2018: 192,405 recorded offences 2019: 199,221 recorded offences 2021: 153,233 recorded offences 2022: 181,991 recorded offences 2023: 181,417 recorded offences B · Share of people who feel safe in the Czech Republic Sum of “definitely yes” and “rather yes” responses · CVVM 2002: 45% felt safe in the Czech Republic 2004: 55% felt safe in the Czech Republic 2006: 65% felt safe in the Czech Republic 2008: 68% felt safe in the Czech Republic 2010: 68% felt safe in the Czech Republic 2012: 74% felt safe in the Czech Republic 2013: 73% felt safe in the Czech Republic 2014: 71% felt safe in the Czech Republic 2015: 76% felt safe in the Czech Republic 2017: 85% felt safe in the Czech Republic 2018: 85% felt safe in the Czech Republic 2019: 87% felt safe in the Czech Republic 2021: 85% felt safe in the Czech Republic 2022: 80% felt safe in the Czech Republic 2023: 82% felt safe in the Czech Republic 2019 → 2021: fewer offences, less confidence Recorded offences: −23% Sense of safety: −2 percentage points Note: The points correspond to years in which CVVM published a comparable figure. The year 2025 is not appended because the methodology changed. Chart 3: Two separate time series on a shared timeline. The CVVM question measures a general sense of safety in the Czech Republic, not a precise fear of a specific offence. The charts are therefore deliberately separated and do not share a Y-axis. The police series also contains known methodological breaks around 2020–2021. Sources: Czech Statistical Office / Police Presidium and CVVM. [1] [2] [3] Data integrity It would not be honest to describe the current nationwide Czech sense of safety simply as “rising fear”. In the 2023 survey, 82 per cent felt safe in the country as a whole and 91 per cent in their neighbourhood. In 2025, 88 per cent reported feeling safe nationwide and 93 per cent where they lived, but CVVM fundamentally changed its methodology from January 2025, so the new data point cannot be connected directly to the older series. [3] [4] The purpose of this article is therefore not to manufacture a national panic that does not exist, but to explain why periods, places, groups and different forms of measurement can diverge. 4. The National Average Is Not the Street You Walk Home On A national average is essential for governing a country, but no one lives in a national average. People move along a handful of routes, at particular hours and among particular people. Their personal risk depends not only on the number of inhabitants, but on exposure: how often they enter a given environment, what kinds of situations occur there and whether they can escape them. A resident can therefore be entirely justified in saying that conditions in their neighbourhood have worsened even as the nationwide figure falls. The particular offence they fear may have increased nearby. A few repeat offenders may have concentrated their conduct in a small area. Evening transport, lighting or the presence of people who once provided natural surveillance may have deteriorated. Some changes need not themselves meet the legal definition of a crime: loud conflicts, visible intoxication, harassment, disorder or abandoned premises can alter how legible and controllable a space feels before police statistics move significantly. Research on fear of crime has long shown that people read the condition of their surroundings as information about informal control and community cohesion. In a large British analysis, fear of violence was associated not only with personal experience, but also with perceived disorder and weaker collective capacity to uphold ordinary rules. [8] Transferring the finding to the Czech context has limits, but the mechanism is readily understandable: a broken light is not an assault, yet it can signal that an assault would be harder to see and help might not be close at hand. The difference between the whole country and one’s place of residence is visible in Czech surveys as well. In 2023, 91 per cent of respondents rated safety where they lived positively, compared with 82 per cent for the Czech Republic as a whole. [3] That does not prove that the nine-point gap was created by the media. It does show, however, that people assess nearby and distant environments under different information regimes: they know their street from everyday life, while they assemble their picture of the country indirectly. 5. Fear Is Neither a Single Emotion nor a Single Question The phrase “fear of crime” is often used in debate as though it were a thermometer with a single scale. Academic work, however, distinguishes specific episodes of worry, broader anxiety, estimates of the probability of victimisation, and behaviour altered because of perceived risk. Gray, Jackson and Farrall also distinguish functional worry—which leads to proportionate caution—from dysfunctional worry that repeatedly restricts movement, relationships and quality of life. [7] Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext The wording of the question matters too. “How likely is it that you will be mugged?” measures an estimate of risk. “How many times in the past month did you actually feel worried?” looks for specific emotional episodes. “Do you feel safe walking alone after dark?” includes vulnerability, possibilities of escape, lighting, the presence of other people and expected assistance. A respondent may consider an attack unlikely and still change route because the possible consequence is unacceptable. A subjective feeling is therefore not an inaccurate copy of objective risk. It measures another layer of safety: the degree of control and freedom. Two people facing the same statistical probability can bear different expected costs. A person with limited mobility, a woman returning from a night shift or someone who has previously been assaulted may not be “bad at percentages”. They may be realistically accounting for a reduced ability to escape, a higher cost if something happens, or vivid knowledge of how quickly an ordinary situation can change. Objective risk probability × exposure × severity of consequences Requires the correct type of offence, place, time, population and denominator. Subjective safety risk × vulnerability × control × trust Captures how easily ordinary life can be lived without restrictive fear. 6. How One Event Can Fill the Entire Mental Field The best-known explanation draws on the availability heuristic. When estimating frequency, we do not always consult a statistical set; often we rely on how easily an example comes to mind. A vivid, recent and emotionally powerful case is recalled faster than hundreds of days on which nothing happened. Tversky and Kahneman described this mechanism as early as 1973. [9] That does not make human judgement worthless. Availability is a useful shortcut in environments where personal experience often does reflect frequency. The problem begins when the selection of remembered events is not representative. The modern information environment radically changes that selection. One case does not appear once. There is the first report, a video, a police statement, a politician’s reaction, a profile of the offender, an interview with a witness, the trial, commentary and an anniversary. It is still one event, but a person experiences it as many separate encounters with danger. A study of US television news found an association between viewing crime-saturated local news and greater fear even after local crime levels were taken into account. [10] That is not proof that every Czech programme has the same effect; it is evidence of a mechanism that must be tested, not assumed. Social networks add personalisation, repeated sharing and competition for attention. Research on tweets from eighteen Latin American countries found a strong overrepresentation of violent and sexual offences and only a weak correlation between the volume of posts and crime itself; the posts reflected levels of concern more closely. [10] Another study, based mainly on young adults in the United States, found a relationship between total social-media consumption and fear of crime, while explicitly noting the limitations of its sample and the preliminary nature of its conclusions. [10] None of this warrants the cheap conclusion that “the media frighten us”. Media can expose a problem that long remained hidden, give victims a voice and increase willingness to report. A social network can exaggerate frequency yet accurately show that a particular group has lost trust in an institution or that harassment below the threshold of criminal law is recurring in a specific place. Visibility is a filter, not automatically a lie. 7. When Distrust of Statistics Is Justified Official statistics are not automatically propaganda. Without them, we would be left with the loudest stories, political campaigns and our own limited surroundings. Police data make long time series, geographical breakdowns and analysis by offence type possible. But it is a mistake to attribute a quality they do not possess: a complete and consistently measured picture of every offence. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext Eurostat explicitly warns that police-recorded counts are shaped by legal definitions, people’s willingness to report and police recording practices, and that methodological changes can create breaks in a time series. [6] A new offence, a broader definition, electronic reporting, a specialised campaign or better training can increase the number of records. A stricter threshold, administrative overload or a loss of trust can reduce it. For offences discovered mainly through proactive state activity, the statistics also partly measure the intensity of enforcement. Public scepticism is therefore legitimate when an institution presents only an overall total and conceals changes in categories, methodology, reporting or local distribution. Scepticism is equally legitimate toward a campaign that turns a single increase in one category into the collapse of safety across an entire country. In neither case need the number be falsified; what is falsified is the scope of the claim the number is made to carry. Editorial lens Fact The total number of recorded offences fell year on year in 2025. Interpretation “The Czech Republic is safer.” That is already a broader conclusion, not a transcription of the table. Missing context Which categories, regions, victims, reporting rates, severity levels and recording rules? 8. When Rising Fear Is a Relevant Signal A sense of threat is not suitable for estimating the number of crimes. It can, however, be an important indicator of the quality of public space—especially when the same change repeatedly appears in the same place, among the same group and under the same question; when it is accompanied by route changes, fewer evening passengers, business closures, school absences, more requests for accompaniment or consistent experiences captured in victimisation research. The most revealing case is the exposure paradox. A park may record fewer assaults because it has become safer. But it may also record fewer because people avoid it out of fear. The number of potential victims falls, opportunities for offences diminish and the police statistics improve—at the cost of the public space no longer serving its purpose. Statistically, the place is quieter; socially, it has been lost. The opposite paradox is just as important. Recorded cases of domestic or sexual violence can rise at a time when victims are less afraid to report, institutions recognise the conduct more effectively and society stops tolerating certain behaviour. The statistics worsen, while the institution’s capacity to see the problem may improve. The direction of the number and the direction of reality are therefore not synonyms. Public feeling is also a relevant signal when it responds not to frequency but to predictability. People may tolerate a stable level of risk better than an environment in which they do not know whether rules apply, whether help will answer and whether an institution will even acknowledge the event. In such a case, fear speaks not only about crime. It speaks about trust, control and the social contract. 9. Is It Safer Today? Without further specification, the question is not precise enough. Safer where —in the country as a whole, in one municipality, at the station, at home or online? Safer for whom —for the average resident, a child, an older person, a woman working nights, a shopkeeper or a repeatedly victimised household? Safer from what —from theft, physical assault, fraud, domestic violence or public harassment? And by what measure—police records, victimisation surveys, final convictions, harm, sense of safety, or freedom to use public space? An honest answer therefore does not emerge from one curve defeating another. It emerges from triangulation. Police statistics show offences captured by institutions. Victimisation surveys illuminate experiences that never entered the records. Local data reveal concentration. Surveys of safety measure human costs and trust. Changes in law and recording show whether the measuring instrument itself has changed. And this is where the simple dispute turns inside out. Crime can fall even as fear rises. Fear can fall even while a particular form of crime rises. Recorded crime can rise because an institution has begun to see reality more clearly. And it can fall because people no longer believe reporting it is worthwhile. The most precise question, then, is not merely: “Is it safer today?” It is: Safer where, for whom, from what, by which measure—and what changed on the path from the actual event to the number used to describe it?

items.body: Section: Justice & law Author: V Reading time: ~27 min Sources and further reading: 22 items Topics: personality rights, likeness, identity, DSA, GDPR, criminal law, platforms SEO / working title: What to do when someone misuses your photograph or identity? What to do when someone misuses your photograph or identity? The question sounds simple only until we notice that we are not comparing one form. A notice to a platform is not a court order. A criminal complaint is not an interim injunction. A complaint to ÚOOÚ is not an action for the protection of personality. And ČTÚ, as the digital-services coordinator, is not a takedown service. This article therefore does not look for a delete button. It asks which regime can carry which harm, when it makes sense to run them in parallel, and which promise of a takedown by morning is only a dangerous shortcut. 1. A fake profile with your photo is not one form A woman finds a fake profile with her photograph. It is not a caricature, nor an old shared party picture. The profile speaks in her name, adds someone else’s sentences and sends messages to people who know her. A friend says: report it to the platform. A lawyer says: secure the evidence, send a demand for removal and, if needed, a claim under the Civil Code. A police officer says: come and file a report if there are signs of a criminal offence. Someone from compliance asks whether this is processing of personal data by a controller. On the ČTÚ page it says that the digital-services coordinator has no power to order content removed [12] . At first glance this is one deletion. In fact each person is describing a different problem. The friend is talking about a notice of illegal content under the platform’s rules and the DSA. The lawyer is talking about likeness, privacy, an order to cease the interference, removal of the consequence and satisfaction. The police are talking about the elements of an offence. ÚOOÚ is talking about a controller, processing and rights under the GDPR. ČTÚ is talking about the procedural duties of digital-service providers. They can therefore all be partly right and a shared plan can still fail. The bad plan sounds like this: fill in one form, delete the evidence, wait for an authority and promise the family that it will be over by morning. A better plan starts more dully. URL, date, screenshot, account identification, the exact electronic location. Without that, a notice can be weak at the very moment when it needs to be specific [14] . A platform notice, a criminal complaint and a lawsuit are three different regimes. None of them is an instant-delete button. — Jiný Kontext 2. A likeness has at least six layers When we say “they misused my photo”, it sounds like one act. Law and platforms, however, see several layers. Each of them changes the question, the evidence and the result one can expect. Object: likeness, voice, name, a fake profile, intimate material or manipulated material. Channel: social network, advertising, a website, a messenger, e-mail or storage. Civil regime: consent, withdrawal of consent, an order to cease the interference, removal of the consequence, satisfaction and compensation. Criminal regime: depending on the features of the case it may be § 191a, § 181, § 184, § 175, § 209 or another offence. Platform regime: notice, statement of reasons, internal appeal and out-of-court dispute settlement under the DSA. Supervisory regime: ÚOOÚ for the processing of personal data, ČTÚ for the procedural duties of providers in the Czech Republic, the European Commission for very large online platforms. This layering is not official pedantry. It decides what you can ask for and from whom. A court can hear a personality-rights claim under the Civil Code. The police can investigate a criminal offence. A platform must have a mechanism for notices of illegal content, but its decision is not a judgment. ČTÚ can address a provider’s duties; it does not replace a court in assessing every photograph. “Identity abuse” therefore hides the difference between three situations. Someone published another person’s photo without consent. Someone set up an account that impersonates a particular person. Someone created intimate manipulated material. In ordinary speech that is one blow. In law it is several paths that sometimes meet and sometimes miss one another. 3. The best channel is the one whose failure does not promise a takedown by morning With a misused photograph a person naturally wants speed. The fastest sentence, however, is usually the worst legal advice: “You report it somewhere and they delete it.” Sometimes a platform acts quickly. Sometimes it does not. Sometimes it removes one account and a copy lives on. Sometimes an interim injunction is needed. Sometimes a criminal file. And sometimes it turns out that the supposed takedown authority has no such power at all. Type of failure What it looks like How to test it What limits the harm Wrong channel A complaint to ÚOOÚ about casual sharing among people Is there a controller, or a personal and occasional operation? A civil claim and a court; ÚOOÚ only where there is processing A 24-hour promise Waiting for ČTÚ or the platform to delete everything by morning ČTÚ does not order takedown; DSA Art. 20 is not a deletion deadline Traces, parallel tracks, an interim injunction Swap of offences Every deepfake as § 191a, or every profile as mere defamation The elements of the particular offence, not a headline in an e-mail A report to the Police of the Czech Republic with a description, not a confident qualification A notice without a URL The platform cannot find the content Does the notice give the exact electronic location? URL, screenshot, date before sending Takedown of one copy One page disappears, the material remains in messages Is mirroring and re-upload being looked for? Expect repeated steps, not one form A well-chosen channel is not the one that promises the most. It is the channel whose failure is understood in advance. When the platform does not reply, you have a trace for the next step. When criminal law does not cover the particular situation, a civil interference with likeness or privacy may still exist. When ÚOOÚ says there is no controller, that does not mean the interference did not happen. It means you were in a different regime. 4. Personality rights are not the GDPR The Civil Code protects a person’s personality, likeness, privacy and manifestations of a personal nature. For likeness and an image recording it starts from the rule of consent. Capturing a person’s likeness so that their identity can be determined from the depiction is, as a rule, possible only with consent. Consent is likewise required for disseminating the likeness [1] . It does not follow that every photograph on the internet is unlawful. The Civil Code knows statutory licences. A likeness may, under certain conditions, be used to exercise or protect other rights, for an official purpose, reasonably for a scientific or artistic purpose, and for reporting. These exceptions are not a blank cheque. § 90 recalls proportionality: a statutory ground must not be used disproportionately in conflict with the person’s legitimate interests [1] . The GDPR addresses something else. It addresses the processing of personal data by a controller or a processor. A photograph can be personal data. That does not mean that every conflict about a photograph is automatically a complaint to ÚOOÚ. Casual sharing among people, a purely personal operation or a one-off dispute about a likeness need not fit the same procedural frame as a customer database, a company profile, a camera system or systematic publication. The practical difference is simple. Civil law asks whether personality has been interfered with and what the other party is to do or make good. The GDPR asks who the controller is, what legal basis they have, how they fulfil the data subject’s rights and who supervises. That is not the same thing. It is the neighbouring floor. 5. A complaint to ÚOOÚ is not an action for the protection of personality ÚOOÚ is the supervisory authority for the protection of personal data. It can be approached with a complaint against a controller or a processor if a person believes that the processing of their data has breached the GDPR [8] . That is an important path. It is not, however, a court action for the protection of personality, and the authority does not order an apology or damages for pain and suffering. ÚOOÚ’s annual report for 2025 records 3,854 submissions, of which 2,514 were complaints and 1,340 were suggestions. The report states a year-on-year rise of 68%. The same document records 392 notifications of personal-data breaches [10] . These figures do not say how many people in the Czech Republic found a fake profile with their photograph. They measure the broad agenda of a supervisory authority, which includes among other things consents, camera systems, healthcare, breaches at controllers and further areas. The GDPR gives the data subject a right to lodge a complaint, and Article 78 speaks of a right to a judicial remedy if the supervisory authority does not handle the complaint or does not inform the data subject within three months of progress or of the outcome [7] . Three months here is not a deadline within which a platform must delete someone else’s profile. It is a procedural rule for communication by the supervisory authority. Before a complaint to ÚOOÚ The first test is: who is the controller? Is this a company page, a database, an advertising system or systematic publication? Or is it a casual personal interference that belongs rather in civil law and on the platform? The second test is: can you describe the processing, the controller and the right that was breached? The third: are you asking ÚOOÚ for something that only a court can order? 6. A criminal complaint is not a private-law ban on dissemination A criminal complaint has a different purpose from a lawsuit. The police and the public prosecutor’s office deal with whether the elements of a criminal offence are present. A civil court may deal with whether someone is to cease an interference, remove the consequence, apologise or make good the harm. These paths can complement each other. They do not replace each other. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext That matters in practice for things that are on fire. A criminal complaint by itself need not stop dissemination quickly. A civil application for an interim injunction can aim at a ban or a removal, but it needs a different argument and a different process. A platform notice can remove the availability of content on a particular service, but it is not a judgment on the offender’s liability. It is not the injured person’s task to write a perfect legal qualification in the heading of a filing. Their task is to describe what happened, when, where, who is affected, what content was published, what was said and what harm is threatened or has arisen. Legal qualification then belongs to the authorities conducting the criminal proceedings. An over-confident heading can do harm if it covers other features of the case. In the misuse of a photograph, provisions on defamation, extortion, fraud or the newer offences linked to an inauthentic work and pornographic material may appear in different situations [3] [4] [5] . It does not follow that every copied photograph is a criminal offence. It follows that criminal law is a path for certain serious cases, not a universal button. 7. § 191a is not § 181(2) From 1 January 2026 the Czech Criminal Code expressly provides for new situations around identity, likeness and inauthentic works. Act No. 270/2025 Coll. inserted, among other things, § 191a and an amendment of § 181(2) [6] . It is tempting to say: a deepfake is the new crime. That is too coarse. § 191a is aimed at the misuse of identity to produce pornography and to disseminate it without the consent of the person depicted. The basic range is up to two years’ imprisonment, besides alternatives, and qualified cases have a higher range of one to five years [5] . What matters is that it is a pornographic work and the consent of the person depicted. In the basic offence, proof of serious harm is not required as a separate element. § 181(2) is different. It works with an inauthentic work that uses a person’s likeness or another manifestation of a personal nature, but it requires intent to cause serious harm. The basic range under § 181 is up to two years [3] . Precisely the intent to cause serious harm can be the difference between a criminal and a non-criminal case, even if a civil interference with personality may remain. As of September 2026 no annual statistic of prosecutions under these new provisions can be drawn from that. No such public annual series exists in the dossier. The precise sentence is therefore not that “X cases are rising”. It is that the legal framework has distinguished several types of inauthentic material and each has its own elements. 8. § 180 is not every copied selfie The Criminal Code also knows unauthorised handling of personal data under § 180 [2] . People often ask about it in a misused-photograph case because a photograph can be personal data. § 180 is not, however, a general crime for every copying of a selfie. The provision is aimed at specific situations, for example data collected in connection with the exercise of public authority or a breach of a duty of confidentiality. That does not mean a copied photograph is without protection. It means the protection may lie elsewhere. In interference with likeness and privacy in the Civil Code. In defamation, if someone spreads a false statement capable of seriously endangering a person’s standing. In extortion, if image material is used for pressure. In fraud, if the misuse of identity serves to obtain money or access [4] . This is precisely where it is dangerous to write oneself a legal diagnosis from the internet. One case can have several layers. A fake profile can be an interference with personality, a breach of platform rules, sometimes part of a fraudulent course of conduct and sometimes a criminal matter of another kind. But without the concrete content, communication, intent, harm and context, the mere sentence “they took my photo” cannot be turned into a finished offence. A good filing therefore does not play legal bingo. It describes the facts, attaches the traces that are available and separates what is certain from what is supposed. That is not weakness. It is precision. 9. A DSA notice is not a court order. ČTÚ will not order a takedown The DSA, the Digital Services Act, requires hosting services to have a mechanism that makes it possible to notify illegal content. Article 16 describes notices and action, Article 17 statements of reasons, Article 20 the internal complaint-handling system and Article 21 out-of-court dispute settlement [11] . That is important infrastructure. It does not mean that the user has been given a European “delete” button. A notice must be specific. In its materials ČTÚ stresses the requirements of a notice, including the exact electronic location of the content [14] . If the platform decides, a statement of reasons is to follow for some services. If the user disagrees, they may use the internal complaint. The DSA also provides for out-of-court bodies. The most common swap concerns ČTÚ. On its page about the digital-services coordinator, the Czech Telecommunication Office states that it has no power to order content removed or to assess the unlawfulness of particular content [12] . A complaint to ČTÚ is therefore not a request that the office delete a photograph. It may aim at a procedural failure of the provider, for example that the mechanism does not work or that a required statement of reasons is missing. Article 20 moreover sets a period of at least six months for lodging an internal complaint against a platform decision [11] [13] . That is not a deadline within which the notified content is to be removed. Anyone who turns it into a promise of takedown is swapping a procedural right for a result. ČTÚ as digital-services coordinator does not order content taken down. A complaint about process is not a request to delete a photo. — Jiný Kontext 10. A host has no general duty to monitor Act No. 480/2004 Coll. on certain information-society services works with the liability of information-society service providers. For the storage of information at a user’s request, the host’s liability is linked among other things to knowledge of the unlawful nature of the content or to circumstances from which the unlawfulness is obvious. § 6 also says that providers have no general duty to monitor the content they transmit or store [15] . That does not mean a hosting service is to do nothing. It means that the law has long refused a general watch over all content in advance. The DSA continues that with procedural rules for notices, statements of reasons, complaints and transparency. It is neither a simple “the platform is always liable for everything” nor “the platform is never liable for anything”. In its information on the DSA, the Ministry of Industry and Trade gives the sharing of private photographs without consent as an example of illegal content [20] . That helps to understand why a notice makes sense. It does not add a public guarantee that particular content will disappear in a given number of hours, nor does it deal with copies outside that service. The practical question for the injured person is therefore twofold. Can I notify the platform of the content so that it can find it and assess it? And do I have, beside that, a path toward the person or entity that caused the interference? The platform regime may be the fastest way to limit availability. It need not be the most complete path to liability. 11. Directive 2024/1385 is not an already finished Czech crime Directive (EU) 2024/1385 of the European Parliament and of the Council deals with combating violence against women and domestic violence. Article 5 requires the criminalisation of certain forms of non-consensual sharing of intimate or manipulated material, including material created or altered by means of technologies. Recital 19 also speaks of deepfake material [16] [17] . It is an important European framework. It is not, however, a sentence that can be copied into a Czech criminal complaint as a finished offence. The directive has a transposition deadline of 14 June 2027 [16] . The Czech Criminal Code has already adjusted some parts by an amendment effective from 1 January 2026. But the Union minimum and the Czech sections must not be equated without the text. The difference is practical. The European text says what Member States are to ensure. The Czech Criminal Code says by what the authorities conducting criminal proceedings assess a particular act in the Czech Republic. If these sentences are mixed, an appearance of certainty arises that does not help a filing. The directive is therefore a support for a broader trend and for reading a political commitment. It is not a substitute for an analysis of § 191a, § 181(2) or other provisions in a particular case. 12. A takedown on one platform is not a takedown everywhere Even if a platform removes the content, the problem need not end. A photograph may be downloaded, forwarded, uploaded again, stored in archives, spread in messages or placed on another website. A re-upload is not proof that the first step had no point. It is the expected scenario for material that has once left control. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext That is why it is dangerous to speak of “erasing the internet”. In practice we often deal with limiting availability, removing particular copies, an order to cease further dissemination, identifying the originator and compensation. Each aim needs a different tool. A platform notice can resolve one link. Civil proceedings can aim at a person or an entity. Criminal proceedings can address serious conduct. ÚOOÚ can address a controller and processing. The same is true of evidence. If a person deletes everything they see so that they do not have to look at it, they may weaken their own ability to prove what was published. A copy for evidence is not a guide to dissemination. It is caution toward a future dispute. What is needed is what serves to substantiate the claim: the address, the time, a screen capture, identification of the account, communication with the platform and confirmation of the filing. No public series in the dossier says by what median time Meta, Google or another platform in the Czech Republic deletes a misused likeness. Precise advice therefore cannot promise a number of hours. It can say how not to lose traces and how not to confuse channels. One more difference matters. Removal of content and a ban on further conduct are not the same aims. The first looks at a particular copy: this link, this profile, this file. The second looks at the behaviour of a person or an entity: do not continue, do not upload again, do not approach those around the person, do not impersonate the injured party. A platform can solve the first aim inside its service without itself solving the second. A court path can aim at the second goal, but it need not immediately remove every existing copy beyond the defendant’s reach. That is why a good record does not merely note “deleted”. It notes where the content was, when it was reported, how the platform replied, whether a new copy appeared and whether the same conduct is repeating. Repetition is then not only a further unpleasantness. It can be evidence that this is not a chance mistake, but a continuing interference that needs a stronger procedural response. It is likewise useful to separate the result visible to those around from the legal result. Those around see that the profile has disappeared. The file, however, needs to know whether it disappeared after a notice, after a demand, after an intervention by a controller, or simply because the author moved it elsewhere. For the person, the first difference is psychologically smaller. For the next step it is decisive. 13. An intimate deepfake is a legal heading, not a detection contest With intimate manipulated material the debate often turns to whether one can tell that the material is synthetic. That can be relevant to proof. It is not, however, the core of this legal question. This is not a contest of image detectors, nor voice forensics. It is likeness, consent, dissemination, harm and a legal heading. The new § 191a is expressly aimed at the misuse of identity to produce pornography and to disseminate it without the consent of the person depicted [5] . § 181(2) works with an inauthentic work that uses a likeness or a manifestation of a personal nature, if there is intent to cause serious harm [3] . Directive 2024/1385 in turn shows the European frame for non-consensual intimate and manipulated material [16] . It does not follow that every manipulated image is the same act. It follows that the word deepfake is not enough by itself. What decides is what the material depicts, whether it is pornographic or intimate, whether it was disseminated, to whom, with what consent, with what intent and what interference arose. The AI Act and the labelling of synthetic content do not settle this question as the deletion of someone else’s photograph. A label can matter for transparency. It does not by itself answer whether particular material is to be removed, whether harm has arisen or whether someone has committed a criminal offence. Those are other regimes. 14. 21,137 acts in cyberspace are not the number of misused photographs The Police of the Czech Republic reported for 2025 a total of 21,137 registered acts in cyberspace [18] . The Ministry of the Interior, in the report on public order and internal security for 2025, records morals crime of 3,695 acts and a rise of 8.8%. It also notes a change of offences from 1 January 2025 [19] . These figures are useful as context. They are not counts of misused photographs of adults, nor counts of deepfake pornography in the Czech Republic. Cyberspace covers many types of conduct. Morals crime covers various acts, including rape, child pornography or sexual abuse. The unit is not “a fake profile with a photo”. Precisely on sensitive topics the temptation arises to fill a missing figure with an estimate. That would be a mistake. The dossier expressly contains no verified statistic of victims of deepfake pornography in the Czech Republic. It also contains no public annual series of cases under the new § 191a and § 181(2) for 2026. That is why no such figure is used in the article. Three tests of the regime The civil test: is this likeness, privacy and dissemination without consent, or is there a statutory licence within proportionate bounds? The criminal test: are there elements of § 191a, § 181(2), defamation, extortion, fraud or another offence? The platform test: can you mark illegal content with an exact location, or are you only writing that you dislike the account? 15. Parallel channels are not an order of magic In a sound procedure there is no single royal step. There is a parallel. First the traces: URL, date, screenshot, account identification, the text of messages, confirmation of the notice. Then the platform: a notice of illegal content with a concrete location and a reason why the content is illegal. Then the civil plane: a demand to cease the interference and remove the consequence, and if needed an application for an interim injunction or a claim under § 81 to 90 of the Civil Code [1] . A criminal complaint makes sense if the situation carries the elements of a criminal offence. With intimate pornographic material without consent that may be § 191a. With an inauthentic work using a likeness and intent to cause serious harm, § 181(2). With pressure, false statements or pecuniary harm, other provisions may come into play [3] [4] [5] . ÚOOÚ belongs in the plan when this is processing of personal data by a controller or a processor. ČTÚ belongs in the plan when we are addressing a provider’s procedural duties under the DSA, especially for services established in the Czech Republic. The European Commission has a role for very large online platforms. None of these sentences, however, means that the authority itself deletes someone else’s profile. What needs to be tested Do you have the exact location of the content? Do you know whether the other side is a controller, a platform, a private person or an unknown account? Do you want removal of particular content, a ban on further dissemination, compensation for harm, a criminal response, or a procedural check of the platform? The answer decides the channel. Not the other way around. 16. A documentable parallel says more than one form One form can help. One form, however, rarely carries the whole harm. A documentable parallel means that each step leaves a trace and each aim has a matching path. A platform confirmation shows what was notified. A demand shows what the injured person asked for. A criminal complaint shows how the facts were described. An application to a court shows what ban or removal is sought. This is not a guide to waging war on an account. The aim is not to silence criticism or to misuse a notice against inconvenient content. The aim is to protect likeness, identity and privacy where a person’s rights are in fact being interfered with. Equally, the aim is not to explain how to produce manipulated material or how to circumvent a platform’s rules. The article describes defensive channels and their limits. A documentable procedure has one more advantage: it blocks exaggerated promises. If the platform does not reply, we know what is missing. If an authority is not competent, we know why. If a court path needs more evidence, we know which evidence had to exist before the content vanished from the screen. The best practical advice is therefore not “click here”. It is the sentence: do not lose the traces, do not confuse the regime, and do not expect from one actor a power they do not have. Such a procedure also protects the other side from an overshot claim. Not every unpleasant comment is identity abuse. Not every use of a photograph is without a licence. Not every breach of platform rules is a criminal offence. A precise distinction is therefore not a concession to an offender. It is a condition for the interference to be handled where it has a chance of standing. If this is a news photograph in a proportionate context, the dispute will be different from a fake profile. If this is a company profile that uses an employee’s portrait after consent has been withdrawn, the dispute will be different from an unknown account that spreads intimate manipulated material. This is where the value of a short internal map shows. Column one: what the content is. Column two: where it is placed. Column three: which regime is triggered. Column four: what result we expect from it. When a row stays empty, that is not a detail. It is the place where time will later be lost. 17. The question is not how to delete it. It is which regime can carry which harm A misused photograph creates a legitimate need for a quick end. Internet content, however, has no single switch, and the law has no single form. Personality rights address an interference with a person. Criminal law addresses an act that society treats as so serious that it answers with punishment. The platform regime addresses the availability of content at a provider and the procedures under the DSA. Supervisory authorities address their own stretches, not everything at once. It does not follow that the injured person is to give up. It follows that they are to refuse a false simplicity. Anyone who promises an instant takedown often skips the evidence, the court claim and the procedural limits. Anyone who sends everything to one office can lose time. Anyone who names everything a crime can miss the civil path, which is more important for removing the consequence. The right question is therefore not: how do we force the internet to delete the photo? It is: which of the three regimes are you triggering now, what can a court order, what can the police investigate, what is a platform to assess, and why the DSA coordinator in the Czech Republic is not a delete button. Identity is not defended by the single word “report”. It is defended by not letting three different regimes melt into one promise. Related texts in this series Deepfake: How to recognise a fake video… — detection of a file vs. a legal takedown channel. Is a photograph evidence? How to find out whether your password has leaked… — another kind of identity abuse.

items.title: An Authentic Recording, a Wrong Conclusion
items.subtitle: How authentic footage can support a false story, and why verifying a file does not by itself verify the interpretation attached to it.
items.perex: A ten-second video can be genuine and still create a false picture. The crucial distinction is between technical authenticity and evidential completeness.

items.body: Model scenario The following situation is fictional. It is not a report about real people and does not show how often this kind of manipulation occurs. Its purpose is to separate the technical authenticity of a recording from certainty about its meaning. Ten seconds. That is the length of the video that has just appeared in your feed. The vertical footage was recorded through a tram window. Two men are standing on the pavement. One suddenly shoves an older man carrying a shopping bag, knocks him to the ground and points at him. The video ends. Its caption reads: “Another brutal attack in broad daylight in the city centre!” Brain networks that rapidly process possible threats can trigger an emotional response before we have consciously analysed the scene. The amygdala is one important part of this network, not the brain’s single “alarm”. In the comments under this model post, people are already demanding punishment, and someone writes: “There is nothing to discuss. It is perfectly obvious what happened.” Because this is a model, the following paragraphs do not add newly verified facts. Each adds a different hypothetical detail to show how broader context can alter the interpretation of the same fragment. 1. The same fragment, different possible stories First imagine adding thirty seconds. The older man had pulled out a pocket knife and threatened a woman with a pram; the second man intervened. The original fragment has not changed, but the act may now look like a defensive intervention. Add a different hypothetical fact: the object was not a knife but a set of keys, and the older man was severely disoriented by hypoglycaemia. The moral and legal assessment reopens. Add a call to emergency medical dispatch and a possible systemic cause appears. The epistemic point New information changes the meaning of the scene, not the image data in the original ten seconds. Technical authenticity alone therefore cannot establish motive, cause or responsibility. 2. Authenticity is not completeness Debates about disinformation often focus on synthetic voices, photomontages and fabricated reports. But there is another problem alongside technical falsification: a genuine recording may be paired with an interpretation that the recording itself does not establish. Question A: “Is this recording authentic?” (technical authenticity) Question B: “Does it support the interpretation attached to it?” (evidential meaning) A positive answer to the first question is not automatically an answer to the second. A real person and real words may be recorded accurately while the account of motive, cause or sequence remains wrong. A truthful fragment removed from context may be more persuasive than a complete fabrication because part of the message survives an authenticity check. That does not mean every short recording misleads or that nothing can be learned without complete context. 3. Why a quick story can feel persuasive Psychological research describes several tendencies that can influence judgement under incomplete information. These are not three buttons in the brain and they are not a diagnosis of every act of sharing. Their strength depends on the person, task and situation. AI-generated illustrative image · Jiný Kontext. An illustrative scene of comparing details in two visual records. Experimental tradition Availability heuristic A scenario that is easy to recall may receive disproportionate weight when people estimate likelihood. Classic experiments support this tendency, but they did not measure the prevalence of context manipulation on today’s platforms. Research concept Emotional contagion Other people’s emotions can influence our own experience. It does not follow that every angry caption automatically disables critical thinking. Experimental studies Motivated reasoning In studies of political arguments, people more readily challenged information that conflicted with their existing position. Applying that result to every other setting is a plausible hypothesis, not a universal law. 4. Manipulation by subtraction Propaganda has long worked by adding, distorting and omitting information. Digital distribution has made it exceptionally cheap to circulate a short extract detached from its original time, place and source. Temporal crop: show the reaction while hiding the event immediately before it. Spatial crop: exclude what is outside the camera’s field of view. Semantic isolation: detach a sentence from the condition, negation or question to which it belonged. Conversation crop: display one message without the preceding exchange, timing and relationship between participants. Manipulation does not always need to add anything. Sometimes removing two seconds before and two seconds after is enough. — Jiný Kontext editorial principle 5. When context excuses nothing Context is not a universal solvent of truth or responsibility. It may change the meaning of an act, or merely explain its circumstances without excusing it. We therefore separate four steps: Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext Level Meaning Example 1. FINDING What was directly recorded or observed. At 14:02 the footage shows a hand movement and a person falling. 2. EVIDENTIAL TRACE The finding assessed with its origin, integrity and other traces. Longer footage, metadata, a medical report and independent testimony. 3. INTERPRETATION A hypothesis about cause, motive and meaning. Was it an attack, defence, accident or medical crisis? 4. CONCLUSION A moral, expert or legal assessment under the relevant rules. A legal conclusion after admissible evidence has been assessed. The problem begins when we jump from a single finding to a certain conclusion and treat the invisible intermediate steps as facts. 6. Five questions before sharing A mental safety protocol What exactly can I see or hear directly? Separate observation from the caption. Who published the recording, and where did it come from? Look for the original file and timeline. What happened before and after? Check a longer version if one is available. What remained outside the frame? Absence from the shot is not proof of absence from the scene. Which other explanation fits the same fragment? What evidence would distinguish between them? 7. What this article claims — and what it does not We can say Technical authentication confirms properties of a file or recording within the scope of the analysis. It does not by itself establish that the event is complete or that an attached interpretation is correct. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext We cannot say This model scenario does not determine how often genuine recordings online are misleading. The cited psychological work does not measure the prevalence of such cases. 8. What would weaken the empirical part of the claim? It would be materially weakened by a series of preregistered experiments across different event types in which adding verified events before and after an extract almost never changed participants’ judgements compared with the fragment alone. The logical distinction between authenticity and completeness would remain, but the claim about the practical power of contextual cropping would be weaker. 9. Conclusion The sentence “It is obvious what happened” can end an inquiry at the moment it should begin. Immediate certainty does not always come from stronger evidence. Sometimes it comes only from fewer visible questions. Before asking whether something is true, ask one quieter question: how much relevant information can I not see yet? — Jiný Kontext

items.title: The truth doesn't start with a headline
items.subtitle: The same facts can create opposite stories. Not because the truth has changed, but because the selection, order and framing of information has changed.
items.perex: The same facts can create opposite stories. Not because the truth has changed, but because the selection, order and framing of information has changed.
headings: Fact is not the same as story
Six places where context is lost
The brain does not want to wait for the whole file
When the true image is deceiving
The headline is not the enemy. But it must know its limits
Three tests of an honest headline
Seven Questions That Will Slow Down Misjudgment
Reader's log
What the Other Context will mean
Editorial commitment
sources: : The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice , Science 211(4481), 453–458. DOI and publication record . · Tversky, A.; Kahneman, D.
: Confirmation Bias: A Ubiquitous Phenomenon in Many Guises , Review of General Psychology 2(2), 175–220. DOI and publication record . · Nickerson, R.S.
Society of Professional Journalists: SPJ Code of Ethics . Official wording .
Reuters: Journalistic Standards and Values . Official standards .
items.body: An eleven second video will appear on the phone screen. A man on the platform violently punches another man in the face. Attacked falls. Recording ends. The picture is sharp, the sound is clear and the punch is real. Within minutes, the first headlines will start rolling. Model situation — not a real case Brutal attack on the platform: the aggressor knocked down a passenger with a single blow. The first framework assumes a gratuitous attack. A passenger stopped a man who was threatening the neighborhood. The second framework assumes a defensive intervention. Police investigate conflict between two men; the circumstances of the strike are not yet clear. The third framework admits what we do not yet know. All three captions can describe the same visible moment. But each of them adds a different role: aggressor, defender or participant in an unclear conflict. The image has not changed. Its framework has changed — and with it the moral judgment that the reader will likely begin to form. A few hours later, a longer recording appears. It shows the argument, the shoving and the moment the man, who was later hit, reaches into his pocket. Even that may not explain everything. The pocket could contain a knife, a telephone, and an ordinary handkerchief. Another witness claims a threat was made before the video began. Another witness denies this. Police say they did not find a weapon at the scene. Each new piece of information changes the likelihood of each version — but none of them automatically completes the story by itself. The headline is not the beginning of the truth. It is the beginning of interpretation. Jiný Kontext Fact is not the same as story A fact can be narrow and precise: a man hit another man. The story is a larger construction that answers the questions of why, what preceded it, who had what intention, and what the blow meant. Without these layers, we have an event, but not necessarily an explanation of it. This does not mean that we should fear any conclusion or that all interpretations are equally good. Some versions are supported by evidence, others are speculation, and others may be disproven. The context is not meant to dilute responsibility. The point is to determine it according to the most complete picture possible, not according to the first emotionally convincing shortcut. A true sentence can be deceiving without containing a single falsehood. It is enough if he selects a fact from the whole, which, although correct, is insufficient for understanding the situation. The sentence "the company laid off a hundred people" can act as evidence of collapse. It acquires a different meaning if the company simultaneously hired two thousand employees. And yet another if the layoffs hit the entire department after management had reassured employees about its future for months. Verifiable fact The footage shows one man punching another. Interpretation It was an attack, self-defense, retaliation or an attempt to prevent an imminent attack. The problem arises when the interpretation is given in the language of fact. Words like "aggressor," "victim," "savior," "provocateur," or "failure" are not always descriptive. They often contain a conclusion that should emerge from the evidence. The same event can act as attack, defense, chaos or heroism in different viewports. Illustration graphics created for Jiný Kontext; it is not a documentary photo. Six places where context is lost Context is not lost just by rough handling. It often disappears during normal shortening, selection and sorting of information. Each medium has limited space. Each author decides what to start with. Each reader pays attention to only part of the message. It is in these decisions that the framework is created. Selection Which facts got into the text and which remained outside it. Order What will the reader see first and what only when he has already formed an opinion. Time Where the record or narrative begins, where it ends, and what happened before. Scale Whether the figure is set to population size, usual development or a longer period. Language Whether the text describes the observation or subtly inserts cause and blame into it. Source Who provided the information, what he could see and what interest he may have in its form. For example, one figure shows that the number of a certain type of incident increased by one hundred percent year-on-year. It sounds dramatic without a base. In fact, it may have been an increase from two cases to four. A percentage is correct, but without an absolute number, it doesn't give the reader a yardstick. Conversely, an absolute number without information on population size can create the impression that two cities of different sizes face the same risk. The order is just as important. The first piece of information acts as a frame into which we begin to insert more. When the reader first hears that a man "assaulted a policeman," he may subconsciously judge later footage as seeking an explanation for his guilt. When they first hear that a police officer "assaulted an unarmed person," they may read the same material in reverse. The evidence is the same, but the opening description has determined what questions we ask. The brain does not want to wait for the whole file Humans are not machines that first unbiasedly read all the data and only then form a conclusion. The way the same problem is framed can change our decisions and preferences. This principle is known in psychology as framing effect — framing effect. The classic work of Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman showed that a different formulation of the same decision problem can lead to different choices, even though the essence of the options has not changed. 1 Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext Once we commit to one version, another risk arises: we tend to more easily seek, receive, or interpret information to be compatible with what we already believe. Psychologist Raymond Nickerson summarized this broad set of phenomena under the term confirmation bias. 2 It does not mean that every opinion is irrational. It means that the first version can affect how strongly we evaluate the evidence for and against it. If we believe that the person in the video is the aggressor, we will see his fast movement as an attack. If we believe they are defending themselves, the same movement can act as a response to a threat. The difference is not necessarily in the eyes. It's in the hypothesis we already have in our heads. The easiest manipulation does not have to invent a lie. Just cut her the truth right. Jiný Kontext What is seen can be accurate — and yet form only a small part of the event. Illustration graphics created for Jiný Kontext; it is not a documentary photo. When the true image is deceiving The photo may be authentic. Video may be unedited. The quote can be spoken exactly as it is written. Neither of these characteristics alone guarantees that the resulting story corresponds to reality. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext Every image has boundaries. The camera shows what is in front of the lens, not what is happening behind it. A record has a beginning and an end. The cutout can hide a person standing half a meter next to it. Slow motion can create the impression of balance where in reality the reaction took place in a fraction of a moment. On the other hand, a fast or too short clip can hide hesitation, warning or the possibility to retreat. This is not an argument against video as evidence. It is an argument against the notion that a single angle automatically contains the entire meaning of an event. The image is a trace. His interpretation must be checked against the timeline, other records, physical evidence, statements, and what can be reliably verified. A short recording can be especially persuasive when it seems self-evident. The reader feels that they don't need anything else. In fact, it can only know what fit in the screen rectangle. The headline is not the enemy. But it must know its limits The headline has a legitimate job: to quickly communicate what the text is about and help the reader decide whether to pay attention to it. It cannot contain the entire file, all caveats, or a complete timeline. Brevity in itself is not manipulation. The problem arises when the headline feigns greater certainty than the evidence allows, or when it turns one possible interpretation into a seemingly settled fact. Professional journalism standards therefore emphasize not only accuracy, but also context, fairness and caution against simplification. The Code of the Society of Professional Journalists explicitly calls attention to the need to provide context and not to mislead when promoting or summarizing a story. 3 Reuters values ​​accuracy and balance over speed in its standards. 4 An honest headline doesn't have to be boring. They only have to distinguish between what is confirmed, what is the claim of one side, and what remains open. The difference between the sentences "the driver deliberately drove into the crowd" and "the police are investigating why the car drove into the crowd" is not a stylistic subtlety. The first sentence attributes intent. The other admits that the cause is yet to emerge from the evidence. Three tests of an honest headline A test of certainty Is the strength of the claim used commensurate with what is actually verified? Omission test Would one crucial missing piece of information change the meaning of the headline? Confusion test Doesn't the headline present an interpretation, accusation, or guess as fait accompli? Test the body of the article Does the headline match the actual content or is it significantly more dramatic than the text? Seven Questions That Will Slow Down Misjudgment The reader cannot always do his own investigation. But he can change the way he handles the first impression. The goal is not to believe anything. The goal is to correctly distinguish what we already know, what we only imagine, and what could change our opinion. Redakční ilustrace · Jiný Kontext Reader's log What is actually verified? Separate an observable fact from an inference of cause, intent, or blame. Who is the original source? Is the information from a document, direct recording, testimony, press release, or anonymous account? What happened before and after? A short clip can accurately capture a moment while distorting the plot. Is the headline stronger than the article itself? Look for words that later weaken the text inside with "allegedly," "according to one version," or "not yet clear." What information is missing from the text? Ignorance may not be evidence of manipulation, but it should limit the certainty of the conclusion. Is there a reasonable alternative interpretation? Not to forcefully excuse the obvious, but to test the strength of your version. What would change my mind? If the answer is “nothing,” you are no longer evaluating the evidence; you are protecting your identity or camp affiliation. This procedure does not lead to an eternal "maybe". On the contrary, it makes it possible to draw stronger conclusions. The difference is that their strength corresponds to the strength of the evidence and that they remain correctable as new information emerges. What the Other Context will mean Jiný Kontext does not want to be a project that automatically claims the opposite of what others say. The opposite opinion is not deeper in itself. Contrarianism can be as superficial as mob certainty. Our goal is a different discipline: not to pass judgment before we separate the proven facts, the disputed claims, the unknown parts, and the possible interpretations. Sometimes, after adding context, the original caption holds up. Other times, it turns out to be too hard, too soft, or asked the wrong question. Editorial commitment We will clearly distinguish fact, source claim, analysis and opinion. In disputed cases, we will show what is confirmed, what is missing and which version has which support. We'll be looking for the strongest counterargument, not its weakest caricature. We will not mask uncertainty with confident language. We will fix the error visibly and explain what has changed. We will not use context as an excuse to relativize clearly documented actions. The truth doesn't start with a headline. It starts early — for events, clues, witnesses, documents, measurements, and questions that don't yet have an answer. The caption is a later layer. It can be a good introduction to a story, but it shouldn't become its judgment. That's why, with every big story, it's worth stopping at a simple question: have the facts changed, or only their context?

items.title: When postpartum psychosis disrupts the perception of reality
items.subtitle: What we know about a rare acute condition after childbirth, what remains uncertain, and why a medical description alone does not determine moral or legal responsibility.
items.perex: What we know about a rare acute condition after childbirth, what remains uncertain, and why a medical description alone does not determine moral or legal responsibility.
headings: 1. There is no single presentation or established single mechanism
2. What reviews of the evidence show
3. What was measured — and what was not
4. Medical explanation, moral judgement and law
5. What this article claims — and what it does not
6. What would weaken the main explanation?
sources: Phenomenology, epidemiology and aetiology of postpartum psychosis: A review. Brain Sciences, 11(1), 47. https://doi.org/10.3390/brainsci11010047 · Perry, A., Gordon-Smith, K., Jones, L., & Jones, I.

Postpartum psychosis: Madness, mania, and melancholia in motherhood. American Journal of Psychiatry, 173(12), 1179–1188. https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.ajp.2016.16040454 · Bergink, V., Rasgon, N., & Wisner, K. L.
